distinctions.note: Behind describes a position at the back of something, while after is used for sequence or time, as in 'after lunch'.
Behind is the standard American preposition, while in back of is a more informal, regional variation of the same meaning.

examples.everyday: The keys are behind the couch cushion, so check there before you leave.
examples.professional: The backup server sits behind the firewall, so only internal traffic can reach it.
examples.analytical: Behind every policy choice lies an assumption about human nature that is seldom stated openly.

nuance.analogy: Like the stage crew standing behind the curtain, out of the audience's view but essential to the show.
nuance.etymology: From Old English behindan, from be- plus hindan (from behind, at the back).
common_mistakes: Saying the first syllable as bee-, rather than the weak bih-.
Adding of after behind, as in 'behind of the house', which is incorrect.

behind.etymology: From Middle English *behinde*, *behinden*, from Old English *behindan* (“on the back side of, behind”), from **bihindan*, **bihindini* (“on the back side of, in the rear of, behind”), from **bi-* + **hindō* (“the hind side, back part”), equivalent to *be*…

senses.definition: A performance measurement according to a benchmark.

core.definition: The practice of measuring performance against a standard or against competitors to find areas for improvement.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, BENCH. Keep the 'ar' in 'mark' as a clear rhotic sound and do not add an extra syllable before '-ing'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it suggests disciplined improvement and objective measurement.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use benchmarking in business, engineering, and data science when talking about comparing performance. You can say 'We're doing benchmarking this quarter' in a meeting, which sounds natural. As a verb form, you would say 'We're benchmarking our servers against the competition.'

distinctions.note: A comparison is any side-by-side look at two things; benchmarking is a more systematic, often repeated measurement against a defined standard.
Evaluation is the broader process of judging quality; benchmarking is a specific kind of evaluation using a reference point.

examples.everyday: My brother works in logistics, and they're always doing benchmarking to see how fast their trucks unload.
examples.professional: Our benchmarking showed that the new database is about thirty percent faster than the old one.
examples.analytical: Benchmarking reveals what we measure, but it cannot tell us whether the measure captures what matters.

nuance.analogy: Like comparing your race time to the course record to see how much faster you need to run.
nuance.etymology: From 'benchmark' (the surveyor's reference mark) plus the suffix '-ing' used to form a noun.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable instead of the first.
Confusing 'benchmarking' with 'benchmark', which is the standard itself rather than the process.
Using 'benchmarking' for a single measurement; it implies a systematic comparison.

senses.definition: (obsolete) Betrothed or engaged to be married.
senses.example: Sir, my daughter is already bespoken to the miller's son, so please step aside.
senses.label: obsolete

senses.definition: Past participle of bespeak.

core.definition: Past participle of bespeak: already reserved, ordered, or requested in advance, or shown by signs.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, SPOH, and the ending '-en' is a weak, unstressed 'un'. Do not pronounce the final syllable as a full 'ken'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use 'bespoken' outside of passive forms or literary writing, such as 'The room is already bespoken.' In everyday talk they say 'reserved' or 'booked'. The adjective 'bespoke' for tailored suits is more common in British English; Americans say 'custom-made' or 'tailor-made'.

distinctions.note: Bespoke is an adjective meaning custom-made; bespoken is a verb form, the past participle of bespeak.
Spoken is the ordinary past participle of speak; bespoken is a rarer form with the sense of reserved or shown.

examples.everyday: Sorry, that table is already bespoken for seven o'clock, but we can seat you at eight.
examples.professional: Those conference rooms are already bespoken through Friday, so we will need to use the Zoom link.
examples.analytical: The poem's symbolism is bespoken by its opening image, which anticipates the ending without naming it.

nuance.analogy: A bespoken seat is like a name tag on a chair: it has already been claimed.
nuance.etymology: Past participle of bespeak, from Old English besprecan.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'bespoken' with 'bespoke', which is an adjective meaning custom-made.
Using 'bespoken' in everyday speech where 'reserved' or 'booked' is more natural.
Pronouncing the final syllable as a full 'ken' rather than a reduced 'kun'.

senses.definition: Very absorbent.
Given to or marked by the consumption of alcoholic drink.
senses.example: The bibulous old colonel spent every evening at the club, waving his glass at anyone nearby.

core.definition: Fond of drinking alcohol, or heavily associated with drinking; in technical use, very absorbent.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, BIB, and reduce the middle to a quick 'yuh'. The final -ous is an unstressed 'us', not 'OHS'.

nuance.connotation: Negative or humorous, suggesting heavy or habitual drinking in a mildly disapproving way.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use 'bibulous' in speech; it appears in writing, humor, and literary description, sometimes to describe a jovial old man or a wedding reception. In everyday talk, 'boozy' or 'a little tipsy' is more natural and less formal. The absorbent sense is technical and mainly found in chemistry or paper science.

distinctions.note: Boozy is casual American English for involving or affected by alcohol; bibulous is more formal and literary.
Alcoholic is a clinical or serious term for dependence; bibulous describes a lighter, habitual fondness for drink with a humorous or formal tone.

examples.everyday: Uncle Ray got a little bibulous at the wedding and told the same joke five times.
examples.professional: Our team lunch turned bibulous, so Monday's meeting started late and nobody was sharp.
examples.analytical: The bibulous culture of the old club was celebrated in memoirs but rarely examined for its costs.

nuance.analogy: Like a sponge that soaks up everything, a bibulous person keeps drinking until the evening is over.
nuance.etymology: From Latin bibulus, 'fond of drinking', from bibere, 'to drink'.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'bibulous' with 'bibliophile', which means a lover of books.
Pronouncing it 'bib-you-lus' with a full 'oo' vowel in the middle.
Using 'bibulous' as a casual synonym for 'drunk' in ordinary conversation, which sounds stiff or humorous.

bibulous.etymology: From Latin *bibulus* from *bibō* + *-ulus* from Proto-Italic **pibō*, from Proto-Indo-European **píph₃eti*, from root **peh₃-* (“drink”); whence also *imbibe* and *beverage* via.

senses.definition: Taking place every two years.

core.definition: Every two years; once in each two-year period.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on EN, the second syllable. The ending is a single 'lee' sound, not the double-L of the dictionary spelling, and the middle syllables are quick and reduced.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is precise and businesslike, with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use biennially mainly in formal or official writing, such as bylaws, schedules, conference announcements and government reports, where it means exactly every two years. In everyday speech they usually say 'every two years' or 'every other year' instead. Avoid 'biannually', which many Americans use to mean twice a year, so 'biennially' is the clearer choice when you mean every two years.
word_family: biennial (noun, a plant that lives two years or an event held every two years)

distinctions.note: Careful usage makes biannually mean twice a year, while biennially unambiguously means once every two years, so biennially avoids confusion.
Annually means once a year; biennially means once every two years.

examples.everyday: Our family reunion happens biennially, so the next one is two years from now.
examples.professional: The board reviews the vendor contracts biennially, so the next review is in March 2027.
examples.analytical: The constitution provides that the legislature convenes biennially, a rhythm that shapes the entire political calendar.

nuance.analogy: Like a comet that returns on a fixed two-year schedule rather than every year.
nuance.etymology: From Latin biennis, 'lasting two years', from bi- 'two' and annus 'year'.
common_mistakes: Using biannually to mean every two years, which causes confusion with twice a year.
Pronouncing the ending with a double L sound instead of one clear 'lee'.

senses.definition: A short period of excessive consumption, especially of food, alcohol, narcotics, etc.
A compressed period of an activity done in excess, such as watching a television show.
senses.example: We spent the whole weekend on a binge of old sitcoms.

senses.definition: To engage in a short period of excessive consumption, especially of excessive alcohol or media consumption.
senses.example: I binged on ice cream.

core.definition: A short period of doing something to excess, especially eating, drinking, or watching a lot of TV or videos in one sitting.

pronunciation.tip: The vowel is short, like the i in bit. The ending -nge is pronounced as a single 'j' sound with no hard g, so say 'binj', not 'bing-gay'.

nuance.connotation: Usually negative for food, alcohol or spending, but neutral or positive for watching shows.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'binge' casually for overindulgence, as in 'a snack binge' or 'binge-watching a series.' Saying 'binge' about food or drink can suggest loss of control, so it may sound like a joke or a warning. In clinical or health contexts, Americans use more precise terms such as 'binge eating' or 'binge drinking.'

distinctions.note: A splurge is a deliberate, enjoyable indulgence, often spending money, while a binge suggests excess and loss of control.
Bender is informal and mainly means a drinking spree, while binge can refer to food, shopping or watching TV.
Overindulge is a general and more formal word for having too much, while binge emphasizes a short, intense period.

examples.everyday: I went on a snack binge last night and ate the whole bag of chips.
examples.professional: We had a coding binge last week to hit the deadline, but it burned everyone out.
examples.analytical: A binge is defined less by the total amount than by the loss of control within a short period, which is why clinicians look at patterns.

nuance.analogy: A binge is like a sudden downpour: a lot falls in a short time, unlike steady rain over days.
common_mistakes: Using 'binge' as an adjective; say 'binge-worthy' or 'binge-watching' instead.
Pronouncing it 'bing-gay' with a hard g.
Using 'binge' for a single meal with no sense of excess.

binge.etymology: From Leicestershire and Northamptonshire dialect, of unknown origin.

senses.definition: The application of statistics to the study and analysis of biological and medical data.

core.definition: The branch of statistics applied to biological and medical research, such as clinical trials, genetics, and public health studies.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on TIS, the third syllable, and the middle syllables are quick and reduced. Don't stress the 'stat' syllable, and remember the ending is 'tiks', not 'teeks'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It is a respected discipline in medical research and public health.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'biostatistics' for graduate programs in schools of public health and for statistical work in clinical trials. People in the field are biostatisticians, and informally they say 'biostats'. The term is rarely used in casual conversation, so when speaking with non-specialists, many Americans say 'stats for medical research'.

distinctions.note: Epidemiology studies patterns and causes of disease in populations and relies heavily on biostatistics for its methods.
Bioinformatics focuses on computational analysis of biological data such as DNA sequences, while biostatistics focuses on statistical inference from study data.

examples.everyday: My sister works in biostatistics, so she always checks whether the headline numbers in medical news are trustworthy.
examples.professional: Please loop in biostatistics before we finalize the endpoints for the trial.
examples.analytical: Biostatistics gives us formal tools to infer causal effects from observational data when randomization is impossible.

nuance.analogy: Biostatistics is the referee who keeps a clinical study honest about what the numbers can and cannot prove.
nuance.etymology: From bio- (Greek bios 'life') plus statistics, from Modern Latin statisticus 'of the state'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the bio- syllable, as in 'BYE-oh-stat-istics'; the main stress falls on TIS.
Confusing 'biostatistics' with 'biometrics', which is about identifying people rather than analyzing research data.

senses.definition: A practice such as witchcraft, sorcery, necromancy, or black magic.
senses.example: dabbling in the black arts

senses.definition: A process that is esoteric or difficult to master.
senses.example: Operating a hand card punch was something of a black art.

core.definition: Magic or sorcery believed to use dark powers; also a complicated skill that few people fully understand or master.

pronunciation.tip: Give 'art' the primary stress, with a clear r after the vowel. In a fast phrase the first word is lighter, so say 'blak AHRT' rather than two equal beats.

nuance.connotation: Mixed. It can suggest evil magic or, playfully, a skill that seems mysterious and difficult.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use black art mostly in literature, history, or humorous talk about a difficult skill, such as 'Excel macros are a black art.' For actual witchcraft, say witchcraft or black magic. In serious conversation, the phrase sounds slightly old-fashioned.

distinctions.note: Black magic refers to evil uses of magic; black art is broader and often figurative, meaning a mysterious skill.
Dark arts is closer to fantasy or literary usage; black art is a more old-fashioned phrase.
Craft is a respected, learnable skill; black art emphasizes mystery and the difficulty of mastering it.

collocations: a dark and mysterious black art

examples.everyday: Making sourdough bread feels like a black art to me.
examples.professional: Tuning the cluster's memory settings is still a black art unless you have the runbook.
examples.analytical: Modern historians treat medieval alchemy as a black art, though its practitioners saw themselves as rational investigators.

nuance.analogy: A black art is like a recipe written in code: the results can be impressive, but only the initiated understand the steps.
nuance.etymology: From black and art, meaning skill; the magical sense developed from older black arts meaning sorcery.
common_mistakes: Using black art for simple magic tricks, when it implies arcane or dark knowledge
Thinking it refers to a visual art, such as painting or drawing

senses.definition: In a blandiloquent manner.

core.definition: In a smooth, mild and flattering way, often in order to persuade or to avoid saying something hard.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on '-DIL-', the second syllable, and the ending '-ly' is a clear long E sound. The middle syllables are reduced to a quick 'uh'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. It suggests flattery that is smooth but perhaps not fully honest.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use 'blandiloquently' in speech, and it is mainly found in literary and academic writing. In everyday talk, people say 'in a flattering way' or 'smoothly.'

distinctions.note: 'Flatteringly' is a common, neutral everyday word, while 'blandiloquently' is rare and suggests smooth, insincere speech.
'Smoothly' can describe any easy or skillful action, while 'blandiloquently' is specifically about speech.

examples.professional: The vendor replied blandiloquently to our concerns, but the contract still did not address the delays.
examples.analytical: The critic argues that the novel's narrator speaks blandiloquently, hiding his real motives behind polite phrases.

nuance.analogy: It is like a warm, soft blanket that covers and comforts, but also keeps you from seeing what is underneath.
nuance.etymology: From blandiloquent plus the adverb ending -ly.
common_mistakes: Using it in casual speech where 'smoothly' or 'flatteringly' would be clearer.
Misplacing the stress on the first syllable.

senses.definition: Something that is clear and empty, or free from preconceptions and biases.
senses.example: She told herself she would start the new job with a blank slate.

senses.definition: Synonym of blank canvas.
senses.example: Her new office was a blank slate, ready for whatever projects the team would dream up.

senses.definition: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see blank,‎ slate.

core.definition: A person, mind, or situation with no prior ideas, history, or commitments, so that everything can start fresh.

pronunciation.tip: As a noun, this compound usually puts the main stress on blank, unlike the phrase 'a blank slate' where stress shifts to slate. Pronounce slate with a long a, as in 'slate' rhyming with 'late'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It can sound hopeful, as a fresh start, or slightly negative if it suggests someone is naive or lacks experience.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say blank slate when describing a new employee, a newborn child in theories of learning, or a company starting over. People often say 'we're starting with a blank slate' in meetings. A natural reply is 'Right, so let's not assume anything from last year.'

distinctions.note: Clean slate often implies a fresh start after past mistakes are forgiven, while blank slate focuses on having no prior ideas or information.
Blank canvas emphasizes creative possibility and what could be made, while blank slate emphasizes the absence of prior conditions or assumptions.
Tabula rasa is a Latin philosophical term for the mind before experience, so it sounds academic, while blank slate is the everyday American phrase.

collocations: treat it as a blank slate

examples.everyday: Let's just start with a blank slate and forget about what happened last summer.
examples.professional: The new team has a blank slate, so we can design the process without inheriting the old tools.
examples.analytical: The theory of the mind as a blank slate assumes that experience alone writes the self, an assumption many psychologists now challenge.

nuance.analogy: Like a new notebook with every page still empty.
nuance.etymology: Blank comes from Old French blanc, white; slate comes from Old French esclate, a thin stone sheet, from Latin roots.
common_mistakes: Stressing slate too heavily or pronouncing it like 'slat'.
Saying 'blank slat' or dropping the final t.
Using it for a single object in a literal sense; it is mainly figurative.

core.definition: The fourth book of the Pentateuch, named for the censuses of Israel's tribes and recounting their wandering in the wilderness after leaving Sinai.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, NUHM. The -ers ending is a single r-colored syllable, like 'burz,' and the b must be clearly pronounced before z.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a standard reference in Bible study, and the title does not carry emotional weight.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'the book of Numbers' or just 'Numbers' in church settings. Do not confuse the title with the everyday word numbers, which means digits or quantities. Pastors often refer to its wilderness narrative, and it is rarely read in full on Sunday.

distinctions.note: In everyday speech numbers means digits or quantities, while the Book of Numbers is a biblical text, so use the phrase 'the book of Numbers' for clarity.
Leviticus is mostly priestly law and ritual instruction, while Numbers combines census lists, travel narrative and laws.

examples.everyday: My husband keeps reading Numbers at night, mostly for the wilderness stories.
examples.professional: When we teach the book of Numbers to the youth group, we focus on the spies and what the story says about trust.
examples.analytical: The book of Numbers alternates between legal material and narrative, so its structure invites reading the wilderness generation as a theological warning about unbelief.

nuance.analogy: Like a travel log that also keeps the roll call of the travelers, Numbers records both the counting of the people and the long road they walk.
nuance.etymology: The English title comes from the Greek Arithmoi and the Latin Numeri, both referring to the counts in the book; the Hebrew title is Bemidbar.
common_mistakes: Confusing the book title with the everyday word numbers
Pronouncing the word as NOO-mbers
Assuming the book is only a list of counts
nuance.biblical_note: Hebrew Bemidbar, meaning 'in the wilderness', taken from the book's first verse. Numbers 1 records a census of the fighting men of Israel. Numbers 6:24-26 gives the priestly blessing for the people. Numbers 13 and 14 tell of the twelve spies and the people's refusal to enter Canaan. Numbers 21:4-9 describes the bronze serpent lifted up for healing.

senses.definition: The lowest part of anything.
senses.example: Footers appear at the bottoms of pages.

senses.definition: The lowest or last position in a rank.
senses.example: The Red Sox are at the bottom again.

senses.definition: A garment worn to cover the body below the torso.
senses.example: There’s a hole in her pyjama bottoms.

senses.definition: The lowest part of a container.
Spirits poured into a glass before adding soda water.
senses.example: Start with a bottom of bourbon in the glass, then top it off with soda water.

senses.definition: The working portion of a moldboard-style plow.
senses.example: single-bottom plow

senses.definition: The remotest or innermost part of something.
senses.example: There’s a fairy at the bottom of my garden.

senses.definition: The fundamental part; a basic aspect.
senses.example: get to the bottom of it

senses.definition: Low-lying land; a valley or hollow.
senses.example: Where shall we go for a walk? How about Ashcombe Bottom?

senses.definition: Low-lying land near a river with alluvial soil.
senses.example: The farmers planted corn on the bottom along the river, where the soil stays rich.

senses.definition: The buttocks or anus.
senses.example: She slipped on the ice and landed hard on her bottom in the parking lot.

senses.definition: The bed of a body of water.
senses.example: Divers found an old anchor resting on the bottom of the lake.

senses.definition: An abyss.
senses.example: The climbers peered over the cliff edge into a dark bottom that seemed to have no end.

senses.definition: A person who has a receptive role or has a preference for that role during intercourse.
senses.example: James and Lukas would make a great couple if they weren't both bottoms.

senses.definition: A sexual submissive.
senses.example: In the BDSM community, he identifies as a bottom rather than a top.

senses.definition: A ball or skein of thread; a cocoon.
senses.example: She wound the yarn into a tight bottom before knitting the sweater.

senses.definition: Ellipsis of bottom quark.
The second half of an inning, the home team's turn at bat.
senses.example: bottom of the ninth, bases loaded, two outs

senses.definition: The bass or baritone instruments of a band.
senses.example: a soda and a bottom of brandy

senses.definition: A cargo vessel, a ship.
senses.example: The old bottom sailed up the coast carrying grain to the port city.

senses.definition: Certain parts of a vessel, particularly the cargo hold or the portion of the ship that is always underwater.
senses.example: Water had seeped into the ship's bottom, so the crew pumped the cargo hold dry.

senses.definition: (dated) Power of endurance.
senses.example: Though exhausted, the runners showed real bottom in the final mile.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: (rare) A trundle or spindle of thread.
senses.example: The weaver counted each bottom of linen thread before loading the loom.
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: To furnish (something) with a bottom.
senses.example: to bottom a chair

senses.definition: To pour spirits into (a glass to be topped up with soda water).
senses.example: The bartender bottomed the glass with whiskey before adding a splash of soda.

senses.definition: To establish or found (something) on or upon.
senses.example: They bottomed the new theory on decades of careful measurements.

senses.definition: To lie on the bottom of; to underlie, to lie beneath.
senses.example: A thick layer of silt bottoms the riverbed beneath the old dock.

senses.definition: To reach or strike against the bottom of something, so as to impede free action.
senses.example: The heavy barge bottomed out on a sandbar and could not move until the tide rose.

senses.definition: To reach the bottom of something.
senses.example: After the bad quarter, sales bottomed in March and began to recover.

senses.definition: To fall to the lowest point.
To take on the receptive role during intercourse.
senses.example: I've never bottomed in my life.

senses.definition: (dated) To be the submissive partner in a BDSM relationship.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: The lowest or last place or position.
senses.example: Those files should go on the bottom shelf.

senses.definition: Relating to the genitals.
senses.example: bottom dysphoria

core.definition: The lowest part or underside of something, or the lowest position in a ranking or list.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The final syllable is a weak schwa plus m, not 'tom'. In casual speech the t is often a soft flap, sounding like 'BAH-dum'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral when describing position. Negative in 'rock bottom' or 'hit bottom', meaning a very low point.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'bottom' for the lowest part of almost anything: the bottom of a glass, the bottom of the stairs or the bottom of the list. In a body sense, 'bottom' is informal and mildly playful; people more often say 'butt' or 'rear'. 'Bottoms' in the plural means pants or trousers in fashion talk, and 'bottom line' means the most important point or the final result.

distinctions.note: 'Base' is the support under something; 'bottom' is the lowest surface or position, even if it is not a support.
'Floor' is the interior surface of a room or building; 'bottom' can refer to any lowest part, including outside or in a container.

examples.everyday: Put the heavy cans on the bottom shelf so they don't fall on anyone.
examples.professional: We're at the bottom of the priority list, so the security patch will have to wait until next sprint.
examples.analytical: The argument rests on a bottom layer of assumptions that the author never examines.

nuance.analogy: The bottom is like the foundation of a house: you rarely look at it, but everything above depends on it.
nuance.etymology: From Old English botm, meaning base, foundation or lowest part, from a Germanic root.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'bottom' with 'butt' or 'buttom'; the correct spelling has no extra t.
Using 'bottom' as a verb in everyday speech; the verb 'bottom out' is more common in American English.

senses.definition: To abstain, either as an individual or a group, from using, buying, or dealing with someone or some organization as an expression of protest.
senses.example: Students decided to boycott the cafeteria until the company restored the cheaper meal plan.

senses.definition: The act of boycotting.
senses.example: The boycott of the grocery chain lasted six weeks and cut its sales sharply.

core.definition: To refuse to buy from, use, or deal with a person, company, or country as a way of protesting against it.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on BOY, and the second syllable is a clear AH vowel, as in cot, not a long O. Don't say the final t as a hard, separate sound in fast speech; it is often softened.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative: the word describes a deliberate protest, and the target usually experiences it as hostile, so it carries political weight.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use boycott for consumer protests, labor protests, and political or sports protests, such as boycotting a company over its policies or a country over its actions. Saying you are boycotting a store is natural in casual talk, but it implies a deliberate and public stance. A natural reply to news of a boycott is 'Are you going to join it?' or 'Do you think it will work?'

distinctions.note: A strike is a refusal by workers to work, while a boycott is a refusal by customers or others to buy from or deal with someone.
An embargo is an official government ban on trade, while a boycott is usually voluntary and organized by individuals or groups.
Protest is the broad word for any public objection, and it can include marches or speeches, whereas boycott specifically means refusing to buy or deal.

examples.everyday: My sister is boycotting that grocery chain until they change their policy on farm workers.
examples.professional: Our marketing team warned that a social media boycott could hurt sales if we don't respond quickly.
examples.analytical: Historians often argue that a boycott succeeds only when it imposes real economic costs and when participants sustain it over time.

nuance.analogy: A boycott is like a silent vote made with your wallet: you don't speak, you simply stop paying.
nuance.etymology: Named after Captain Charles Boycott, an English land agent in Ireland in 1880 whose tenants refused to deal with him.
common_mistakes: Using 'to' after boycott, as in 'boycott to a product'; say 'boycott a product' directly.
Pronouncing the stress on the second syllable, as in 'boy-KOTT'.

boycott.etymology: From Charles Boycott, an English evicting land agent in Ireland who was subject to a boycott organized by the Irish Land League in 1880.

core.definition: The ancient fortified city and capital of Edom in the Hebrew Bible, also the name of an Edomite king.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and pronounce the final -ah as a light schwa, like 'uh'. American English is rhotic, so the r is clearly heard, and the vowel is not a long 'ah'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a place name, though in prophetic passages it stands for judgment against Edom.
nuance.usage_note: Bozrah is used mainly in Bible study, sermons and commentaries. Americans may also see it on maps of modern Jordan, where Buseirah is the site often identified with it. Do not confuse it with Bosra, a Roman city in Syria.

distinctions.note: Bosra is a Roman-era city in southern Syria, not the biblical Edomite Bozrah, though the spellings are often confused.
Edom is the whole region and people south of the Dead Sea; Bozrah was one of its principal cities.

examples.everyday: Our Bible study is reading Isaiah this week, and we got stuck on the verse about the man coming from Bozrah.
examples.professional: The commentary identifies Bozrah as the chief stronghold of Edom, which helps explain the oracles against it.
examples.analytical: Isaiah 63 portrays a warrior returning from Bozrah, the Edomite fortress, as an image of divine judgment on the nations.

nuance.analogy: Like a capital city that becomes the symbol of a whole nation, Bozrah stands for all of Edom in the prophets' speeches.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew Botsrah, probably from a root meaning 'fortress' or 'enclosure'; the exact meaning is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Confusing Bozrah with Bosra, the Syrian Roman city.
Pronouncing the final syllable as a long 'ah' or 'ay' instead of a reduced 'uh'.
nuance.biblical_note: Hebrew Botsrah, probably from a root meaning fortress or enclosure. Genesis 36:33 names Jobab, son of Zerah, as a king of Edom who reigned from Bozrah. Amos 1:12 announces fire against the strongholds of Bozrah as judgment on Edom. Isaiah 63:1 describes a victorious figure arriving from Edom in crimsoned garments from Bozrah.

senses.definition: To neither gain nor lose a quantity of something, money.
senses.example: After an entire night playing poker, he nearly broke even.

senses.definition: To stay the same; to neither advance nor regress.
senses.example: It's a lot of work just to break even and keep the weeds down.

core.definition: To end a business transaction or period with neither a profit nor a loss, or to earn just enough to cover costs.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second word, EE, and say the vowel as a long 'ee' like 'see'. The final syllable is a short, unstressed 'in' with a reduced vowel, so do not stress it.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a financial result without judgment, though it can imply a disappointing outcome if the goal was profit.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use break even in business, personal finance, and everyday talk about money, as in 'We'll break even if we sell fifty tickets.' It is common in meetings and planning discussions, and the term 'break-even point' is standard in accounting. In casual conversation, it can refer to any situation where you lose nothing but gain nothing either.

distinctions.note: Come out even is casual and everyday, while break even is more common in business and finance.
Profit means gaining money above costs, while break even means gaining nothing and losing nothing.

examples.everyday: I sold my old bike for about what I paid, so I basically broke even.
examples.professional: The pilot program should break even within six months if adoption meets our forecast.
examples.analytical: Whether the policy is justified depends on whether the program can break even without distorting the market it aims to serve.

nuance.analogy: Like a seesaw balanced perfectly level, neither side goes up or down, and nothing is gained or lost.
nuance.etymology: Break from Old English brecan, and even from Old English efen, meaning level or equal; the financial sense developed in business usage.
common_mistakes: Using 'break even money' as if it were a transitive verb; say 'break even on the deal' or 'break even on the project.'
Confusing break even with a net gain: break even means no profit and no loss.

senses.definition: To exhale.
senses.example: Please breathe out slowly as you lower the weight, and hold the position for two seconds.

core.definition: To let air out of your lungs, especially after holding your breath or after exertion.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on the particle OUT, not on breathe, so say 'breeth OWT' with a clear ow sound. The t in out is flapped in fast speech and may sound like a soft d.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a practical, everyday instruction, often used to calm or guide someone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say breathe out in everyday instructions, such as 'Breathe out slowly' in yoga class, at the dentist, or in childbirth classes. The noun form is exhale, which is more technical and common in medical settings. A natural reply to the instruction is simply to do it and say 'Okay.'

distinctions.note: Breathe out is the everyday phrase for letting air leave the lungs, while exhale is more formal or medical.
Blow out means to force air out through the mouth, often in a strong puff, as with candles, while breathe out is gentle and normal.

examples.everyday: When the doctor says breathe out, just let the air go slowly and relax your shoulders.
examples.professional: During the video call the presenter asked us to breathe out and reset before the next question.
examples.analytical: The phrase breathe out suggests a release of tension, which is why many spiritual traditions use it as an image of letting go.

nuance.analogy: Breathing out is like opening a window after a stuffy room has been closed for hours: the old air leaves so that the fresh air can come in.
nuance.etymology: Phrasal verb formed from breathe and the adverb out.
common_mistakes: Stressing breathe rather than out, which makes the phrase sound flat.
Using breathe out for blowing out a candle, which uses more force and a different sense.

senses.definition: Stunningly beautiful; amazing.
senses.example: He went to the Grand Canyon and spent a week taking in the breathtaking scenery all around him.

senses.definition: Very surprising or shocking; to such a degree as to cause astonishment.
senses.example: breathtaking stupidity or rudeness

core.definition: So beautiful, impressive, or surprising that it seems to take your breath away.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on 'BREATH,' with a lighter secondary stress on 'TAY-king'; do not reduce 'taking' to 'tuh-king.' Keep the 'th' voiceless, as in 'thin,' and do not use the short vowel of 'breath' in the verb 'breathe'.

nuance.connotation: Strongly positive when praising beauty, skill, or performance; it can be sarcastic when used for something outrageous, such as 'breathtaking prices'.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'breathtaking' for scenery, performances, athletic plays, and impressive work, and it works well in both conversation and writing. The word can also be used sarcastically for shocking or outrageous things, like 'breathtaking audacity' or 'breathtaking prices,' so context matters. A natural reply to someone who shows you a view is 'It really is.'

distinctions.note: 'Stunning' is slightly more casual and focuses on appearance; 'breathtaking' suggests a more emotional, awe-filled reaction.
'Impressive' is a measured, respectful word; 'breathtaking' is stronger and implies the thing is almost overwhelming.

examples.everyday: We drove up to the lookout at sunset, and the view over the valley was absolutely breathtaking.
examples.professional: Her team delivered a breathtaking turnaround, cutting the reporting time from three days to under an hour.
examples.analytical: The argument is breathtaking in its ambition, yet it quietly assumes the very conclusion it sets out to prove.

nuance.analogy: Like the first step onto a cold lake, the experience knocks the air out of you for a moment.
nuance.etymology: From 'breath' and 'taking,' the present participle of 'take,' meaning something that takes away one's breath.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing 'breathtaking' with the vowel of the verb 'breathe' (/briːð/) in the first syllable.
Using it for mildly pleasant things; Americans usually reserve it for something truly impressive.

senses.definition: Construction using whatever materials were available at the time.
senses.example: Her garden shed was built through bricolage, from scrap lumber and whatever she had on hand.

senses.definition: Something constructed with whatever materials were available at the time.
senses.example: The cabin was a bricolage of salvaged doors, scrap lumber, and leftover tin.

senses.definition: A rhetorical style that brings together excerpts or samples of others' rhetoric in some constructive way (to produce, for example, synthesis, extension, or beauty).
senses.example: In her essay, the author relies on bricolage, stitching quotations from poets and preachers into a new argument.

senses.definition: An instance of this rhetorical style's use, or a work produced with its use.
senses.example: Her latest album is a bricolage of found sounds and samples from decades-old radio broadcasts.

core.definition: The making of something from whatever materials or ideas are on hand, or the thing created that way, often with creative improvisation.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the last syllable, which ends in a soft zh sound like the s in 'measure'. The first syllable has a short i as in 'brick', not a long ee sound. Avoid a hard j at the end.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive in art, design, and theory, where it suggests creative resourcefulness. In casual speech it can sound pretentious.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use bricolage mainly in art criticism, architecture, cultural theory, and academic writing. In a kitchen or garage, people would say 'we made do' or 'DIY' instead. Expect listeners to recognize the word from design or literary contexts, and use it sparingly in everyday talk.
word_family: bricoleur (noun, one who makes by bricolage)

distinctions.note: DIY is everyday home-improvement language, while bricolage is a learned term for creative improvisation with found materials.
Pastiche imitates a style, while bricolage assembles existing pieces into something new, often with ironic effect.

examples.everyday: That backyard fence is pure bricolage, with old doors and pallets nailed together.
examples.professional: The team built the prototype as bricolage, reusing existing APIs rather than writing new modules from scratch.
examples.analytical: Lévi-Strauss describes the mythic thinker as a bricoleur whose method is bricolage, working with the materials at hand.

nuance.analogy: Bricolage is like a patchwork quilt made from whatever fabric was in the closet, each piece giving the final design its character.
nuance.etymology: From French bricolage, from bricoler, meaning 'to tinker'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as 'BRIK-oh-lahzh' instead of putting the main stress on the last syllable.
Using bricolage for any cheap or messy work, when the word implies deliberate creative resourcefulness.
Pronouncing the ending with a hard j sound instead of the soft zh sound.

related: bricoleur (noun, one who makes by bricolage)

senses.definition: A consoling aspect of a difficult situation.

core.definition: The positive or encouraging aspect of a difficult situation.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on 'side', while 'bright' gets only secondary stress. Non-native speakers often stress both words equally, which makes the phrase sound stiff.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It is used to comfort or encourage, though it can sound dismissive right after serious loss.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'look on the bright side' or 'the bright side is' in casual conversation, often after something goes wrong. A natural reply is 'Yeah, at least...' or 'You're right, I hadn't thought of that.' Used too soon after someone's serious loss, it can sound like you are minimizing their pain.

distinctions.note: 'Silver lining' is a near-synonym with a more poetic tone; 'bright side' is more everyday and conversational.
'Upside' is neutral and often used in business for potential gains, while 'bright side' carries emotional comfort.

collocations: always look on the bright side

examples.everyday: The car broke down, but the bright side is that we're near a diner with great pie.
examples.professional: The budget cut hurts, but the bright side is that the team now has time to clean up the data pipeline.
examples.analytical: Job's friends offer consolation, yet the bright side they point to misses the depth of his lament.

nuance.analogy: Like finding a patch of sun on a cloudy day and stepping into it.
nuance.etymology: From bright (Old English beorht) and side (Old English side).
common_mistakes: Using 'good side' instead; 'good side' usually refers to the better-looking side of a person or object, not an encouraging aspect of a situation.
Stressing 'bright' as strongly as 'side', which makes the phrase sound unnatural.

senses.definition: The sulfur of hell; hell, damnation.
Used attributively as an intensifier in exclamations.
senses.example: What the brimstone is that smell coming from the oven?

senses.definition: The butterfly Gonepteryx rhamni of the Pieridae family.
senses.example: A brimstone butterfly landed on the purple coneflowers in our backyard garden.

senses.definition: Online content of exceptionally poor quality, lower than coal.
senses.example: That forum thread was pure brimstone, the worst content I've seen all week.

core.definition: Sulfur, especially as a religious image of hell and divine punishment, as in 'fire and brimstone'.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The final -stone is a reduced syllable sounding like 'stun', not a long 'stohn'.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it evokes punishment, judgment, and terror.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mostly hear brimstone in the phrase 'fire and brimstone', used by preachers or in jokes about strict churches. In ordinary talk, people say 'sulfur' for the chemical element. Exclaiming 'Brimstone!' is old-fashioned and mainly found in literature.

distinctions.note: Sulfur is the scientific and everyday name for the element; brimstone is an old, religious or poetic word for it, especially in contexts of punishment.
Hellfire is the general term for the fire of hell; brimstone is the sulfur that accompanies it in religious imagery.

examples.everyday: My grandmother said the old preacher's sermons were all fire and brimstone.
examples.professional: Let's keep the postmortem blameless; we don't need fire-and-brimstone language about the incident.
examples.analytical: Jonathan Edwards uses brimstone imagery to make divine judgment feel immediate, drawing on the Bible's own language of punishment.

nuance.analogy: Like a stage special effect, the fire and the sulfur smell make judgment feel visible and frightening.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English brimstan, roughly 'burning stone', from Old English brynstān.
common_mistakes: Spelling it 'brimston' without the final e; the standard spelling is brimstone.
Using 'brimstone' for chemistry; in everyday or scientific talk say 'sulfur'.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew word is gophrit (גָּפְרִית), sulfur, and the Greek word in Revelation is theion (θεῖον), also sulfur. Genesis 19:24 (RSV) describes the LORD raining brimstone and fire on Sodom and Gomorrah from heaven. Psalm 11:6 (RSV) pictures God raining fire, brimstone, and a scorching wind on the wicked as their portion. Revelation 14:10 (RSV) describes those who worship the beast being tormented with fire and brimstone in the presence of the holy angels and the Lamb.

brimstone.etymology: From Middle English *brymston*, *brimston*, *bremston*, forms of *brinston*, *brenston*, *bernston*, from Old English *brynstān* (“brimstone”), equivalent to *burn* + *stone*.

senses.definition: Beginning to develop.
senses.example: He's a budding deejay.

senses.definition: The development of buds on a plant.
senses.example: Early budding in the orchard warned us that frost could follow soon.

senses.definition: The practice of uniting a single scion bud with rootstock or bark.
senses.example: Budding is faster than whip grafting for stone fruit trees in summer.

senses.definition: The result of this practice.
senses.example: The budding on the peach tree took well, and new shoots appeared in June.

core.definition: Just starting to develop; showing early signs of becoming a particular kind of person or thing.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The middle vowel is short, like 'bit', and the -ing ending is soft; avoid 'BOO-ding'.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it praises early promise and potential.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use budding for someone starting out in a field, like a budding actor or a budding entrepreneur, usually with praise. It describes early potential, so do not use it for someone long established. As a noun, budding also names the spring growth of buds, and as grafting it is a technical term.

distinctions.note: Aspiring describes someone who wants to become something; budding means they already show real signs of it.
Emerging suggests a trend or field becoming visible; budding often describes a person or project.
Up-and-coming usually describes a successful person just getting noticed; budding focuses on early promise.

examples.everyday: My daughter is a budding artist, and she already wants to sell her paintings at the school fair.
examples.professional: She is a budding data scientist who already leads our churn analysis.
examples.analytical: The budding field of machine ethics was still defining its questions when the first serious papers appeared.

nuance.analogy: Like a seedling in spring, a budding career shows promise before it is fully grown.
nuance.etymology: Formed from bud with the suffix -ing.
common_mistakes: Spelling it buding with one d; the final consonant doubles before -ing.
Calling an established expert budding, which sounds like a mistake or an insult.

senses.definition: To incompetently perform (a task); to ruin (something) through incompetent action; to botch up, to bumble.
senses.example: The technician bungled the software update, and the entire server crashed overnight.

senses.definition: To act or work incompetently; to fumble.
senses.example: Rather than admit he didn't know the answer, he bungled through the explanation.

senses.definition: A botched or incompetently handled action or situation; a blunder.
senses.example: The rollout was a bungle from start to finish, with missing files and angry customers.

core.definition: To do something badly or incompetently, so that the result is ruined or the task fails.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, BUNG. The ng is followed by a hard g, and the final -le is a weak syllable, so it sounds like 'guhl', not 'gel'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes careless or incompetent work, and it often sounds mildly critical or humorous.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use bungle in everyday conversation and at work, for example 'They bungled the launch.' A natural reply is 'Ouch, what happened?' or 'Who was in charge?' It is casual enough for talking about a colleague or a government program, but avoid it when you want to be very polite about someone's mistake.

distinctions.note: Botch means to spoil work through clumsy execution and is slightly stronger. Bungle is a little more general and can refer to mistakes in planning or handling.
Mess up is very casual and common in speech. Bungle sounds more deliberate and is usually used for a larger failure.
Fumble suggests clumsy handling, like dropping a ball. Bungle covers the whole task being done poorly.

examples.everyday: I bungled the cake, so we're ordering pizza instead.
examples.professional: We bungled the database migration, so the reports were wrong for two days.
examples.analytical: The committee bungled the procedural steps, and the decision was overturned on appeal.

nuance.analogy: Like a juggler who keeps dropping the balls: the act is attempted, but it falls apart.
nuance.etymology: Origin uncertain; possibly related to Scandinavian dialect words, and recorded in English from the 1500s.
common_mistakes: Using 'bungle' for deliberate sabotage, which is not the intended meaning
Pronouncing the final syllable as 'gel' instead of a weak 'guhl'

bungle.etymology: The origin of the verb is; it is either:

senses.definition: A tobacco grown mainly in Kentucky, used in making cigarettes.
Burlesque.
senses.example: The vaudeville troupe performed a burley revue of tired jokes and cheap costumes.

core.definition: A light-colored tobacco grown mainly in Kentucky and Tennessee, used in making cigarettes and blended tobacco.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the first syllable, and the r is strongly colored, so say 'BUR-lee' rather than 'boor-LAY'. Do not confuse it with 'burly', which sounds the same but means big and strong.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in agricultural and commercial contexts; in public health discussions tobacco is often viewed negatively.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'burley' mainly in farming, tobacco industry and Kentucky contexts, for the tobacco that is blended into many American cigarettes. The fishing sense, bait made of blood and offal, is rare and mostly historical. Most Americans will not know the adjective sense, which is archaic.

distinctions.note: Burly means big and strong; burley is a type of tobacco. They sound identical but are unrelated in meaning.
Virginia tobacco is flue-cured and sweeter, while burley is air-cured and used for a stronger, nuttier blend.

examples.everyday: My uncle's farm in Kentucky grew burley for years before he switched to soybeans.
examples.professional: The supplier's contract covers two thousand acres of burley, with delivery scheduled for the fall harvest.
examples.analytical: Historians of the tobacco economy often trace the rise of burley production to changes in cigarette blends after the 1920s.

nuance.analogy: Like a regional wine grape: named for where it is grown and the style it produces.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'burly', which means big and strong, and using it in a sentence about a man's size.
Pronouncing the second syllable as a long 'ay' sound, as in 'BUR-lay'.

core.definition: A title of Roman emperors, and in the Bible, the emperor who ruled Rome and its provinces, including Judea, during the time of Jesus.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and pronounce the second syllable with an American r-colored vowel, not a full "ar." Do not say "KY-sar"; the English form uses a soft s.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; in religious contexts it refers to imperial authority, and it can carry a political tone.
nuance.usage_note: In American speech Caesar is mostly a historical reference, a Roman title, or a salad name (Caesar salad). In Bible study or church, people use it for the emperor, as in the question of paying tribute to Caesar. Do not use it casually for a powerful boss; that sounds odd unless you are joking.

distinctions.note: Emperor is the general English term for a supreme ruler; Caesar was originally a family name that became the title of Roman emperors.
Caesarean is the medical term for a surgical birth; Caesar is the name or title of the ruler.
A king is a ruler of a kingdom; Caesar refers specifically to Roman imperial authority.

examples.everyday: Have you tried the Caesar salad here, or is the dressing too garlicky?
examples.professional: The history class assignment asks students to compare the Caesar's administrative reforms with those of later provincial governors.
examples.analytical: When Jesus says to render to Caesar what is Caesar's, the question turns on the proper limits of civil authority under God.

nuance.analogy: Caesar is like the word Pharaoh in Egypt: a name that became a title for the highest political power.
nuance.etymology: From the Roman family name Caesar, which became the title of Roman emperors; its origin is uncertain, possibly from a Latin word for a head of hair.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it like the name of the Latin Caesar with a hard k or "KY-sar"; in English it is SEE-zer.
Confusing the emperor with the salad or the surgical term Caesarean in formal writing.
nuance.biblical_note: Caesar is a title of Roman emperors in the New Testament. Luke 2:1 places the decree of Caesar Augustus at the time of Jesus' birth, and Luke 3:1 names Tiberius Caesar as the emperor during John the Baptist's ministry. In Mark 12:13-17 and parallel passages, Jesus answers a question about paying the tax to Caesar, and in Acts 25:11-12 Paul appeals his case to Caesar.

senses.definition: The recreational or educational activity of temporarily living in a tent or similar accommodation.
senses.example: Camping is a favorite summer activity.

senses.definition: The act of setting up a camp.
senses.example: Camping on the ridge took longer than we expected because of the wind.

core.definition: The recreational activity of living temporarily in a tent or similar shelter outdoors, often in a park or forest, for fun or as a vacation.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, KAMP, and the final -ing is a short, unstressed /ɪŋ/, not /iŋ/. Americans flap the t in related forms like camp-er, so the sound is closer to a soft d.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests fresh air, relaxation and adventure, though it can sound rustic or inconvenient to people who prefer hotels.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say we're going camping to mean spending nights in a tent or an RV, and the word is used constantly in everyday talk about weekends and vacations. You can go camping at a state park, or go on a camping trip. A natural reply to 'Do you like camping?' is 'I love it, as long as there are showers.' For a fancy, comfortable version, Americans use the informal word glamping.

distinctions.note: Camp as a noun can mean a campsite or a summer program for children, while camping is the activity itself.
Backpacking usually means hiking with everything on your back and moving from place to place, while camping often means staying at one spot with a car nearby.
Glamping means glamorous camping with beds, electricity or luxury tents, and it is informal and often a little playful.

examples.everyday: We're going camping at Yosemite this weekend, so I need to find my sleeping bag.
examples.professional: Our team offsite is a camping retreat in the mountains, so bring a headlamp and wear layers.
examples.analytical: Camping can be understood as a deliberate return to simpler living, where comfort is traded for closeness to the natural world.

nuance.analogy: Camping is like wearing a loose sweater instead of a suit: it is simpler, less polished, and closer to the body's natural state.
nuance.etymology: From camp (verb), from Latin campus meaning open field.
common_mistakes: Saying 'I go to camping' instead of 'I go camping', since camping is used without to here.
Pronouncing the word as KAM-peeng with a long ee sound at the end.

conversation.text: We're going camping this weekend if it doesn't rain.
Have you ever been camping in the mountains?
Camping with little kids is fun, but it's a lot of work.

senses.definition: Relating to or affected with cancer.
Growing or spreading rapidly to the point of harm.
senses.example: Corruption had become cancerous, spreading quietly through every department of the city government.

senses.definition: Extremely unpleasant; detestable.
senses.example: I love this show, but the fanbase is so toxic and cancerous.

core.definition: Relating to, caused by, or affected by cancer; or, figuratively, spreading harm in a way that is hard to stop.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, then reduce the middle vowel to a schwa and pronounce the final -ous as a short 'us'. The r is rhotic and light, so it sounds like 'KAN-suh-russ' rather than 'kan-SER-us'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. In medical use it is neutral description, but in figurative use it describes something harmful that spreads.
nuance.usage_note: In American medical talk, 'cancerous' describes tissue, cells, or tumors, as in 'a cancerous lesion'. Americans also use it figuratively for a problem that spreads, such as corruption or resentment on a team. In medicine, 'malignant' is often the more precise term, but 'cancerous' is common in everyday talk.

distinctions.note: Malignant is the precise medical term for a growth that invades nearby tissue, while cancerous is the everyday term for the same meaning.
Benign means harmless and not spreading, which is the opposite of cancerous.

examples.everyday: The doctor said the mole was not cancerous, so you can stop worrying about it.
examples.professional: The engagement survey showed a cancerous attitude on the team, where gossip spread faster than any fix.
examples.analytical: Some historians describe propaganda as cancerous to public trust, because it spreads quietly through every institution it touches.

nuance.analogy: A cancerous problem is like a weed that spreads underground, hidden until it has taken over the garden.
nuance.etymology: From cancer plus the English suffix -ous, from Latin cancer, 'crab'.
common_mistakes: Using 'cancerous' for a person who has cancer; say 'a person with cancer' or 'a cancer patient'.
Stressing the second syllable, as in 'kan-SER-us'; the stress falls on the first syllable.

cancerous.etymology: From Middle English *cancerous*, from Latin *cancerōsus*, from *cancer* (“crab; tumor, cancer”) + *-ōsus*.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to Cappadocia.
A native or inhabitant of Cappadocia.
senses.example: The museum guide explained that the traveler was a Cappadocian merchant from central Anatolia.

core.definition: Relating to Cappadocia, an ancient region of central Anatolia, especially the fourth-century church fathers Basil, Gregory of Nazianzus, and Gregory of Nyssa.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on DOH, and the final -ian is reduced to 'ee-un', with no strong vowel at the end. Many learners put the stress on the first syllable or pronounce the ending as a separate 'an' syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise historical and theological term, so it sounds scholarly and is not used in everyday talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use Cappadocian mostly in church history, theology courses, and Orthodox discussions, usually in the phrase Cappadocian Fathers. In everyday talk, Americans simply say Cappadocia for the place, and the adjective is rare outside scholarly contexts. If you talk about the region in a travel conversation, say 'the Cappadocian valleys' or 'Cappadocia in Turkey'.

distinctions.note: Cappadocia is the name of the region, while Cappadocian is the adjective for things relating to it or the word for a native of it.
The Church Fathers are the early Christian writers in general, while the Cappadocian Fathers are a specific group of three fourth-century theologians from that region.

collocations: the writings of the Cappadocian Fathers

examples.everyday: Have you been to Turkey? My friend took a hot-air balloon ride over the Cappadocian valleys and said the view was unforgettable.
examples.professional: Our Orthodox study group is reading the Cappadocian Fathers on the Trinity this semester, so please come prepared to discuss their arguments.
examples.analytical: The Cappadocian Fathers distinguished between ousia and hypostasis, a move that clarified how one divine essence can exist in three persons and shaped later Trinitarian doctrine.

nuance.analogy: The Cappadocian Fathers are like three architects who drew the blueprint for the doctrine of the Trinity, and later builders relied on that plan.
nuance.etymology: From Latin Cappadocia, from Greek Kappadokia, the name of an Anatolian region; the origin of the name is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as in KAP-uh-DOH-shun, instead of the third syllable DOH.
Saying the ending as a full 'an' syllable, instead of the reduced 'ee-un'.
nuance.biblical_note: Cappadocia appears in Scripture only as a place name, in Greek Kappadokia. In Acts 2:9 it is listed among the regions whose people heard the apostles speaking at Pentecost, and in 1 Peter 1:1 Peter addresses the exiles scattered in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia. The Cappadocian Fathers are not a biblical term, but their theology grew from the scriptural teaching about God as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

senses.definition: The amount that a cart can carry.
Any large amount.
(historical) A load: various English units of weight or volume based upon standardized cartloads of certain commodities.
senses.example: The old statute set the price of coal by the cartload, a unit fixed by custom.
senses.label: historical

core.definition: The amount a cart can carry, or in informal speech, a very large quantity of something.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, KAHRT. Say the r clearly and blend the t and l without adding a vowel between them.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in the literal sense; in the phrase cartloads of it is informal and hyperbolic, suggesting a lot of something.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use cartload literally today, since most carts are shopping or hand carts. The common expression is cartloads of or by the cartload, meaning a huge amount, as in cartloads of mail after the holidays. Use it in casual speech, not in formal writing.

distinctions.note: Cartful is a literal fill of a cart and is less common; cartload is more natural in idioms and figurative phrases.
Truckload uses the same idea for trucks and sounds more common in American business talk, while cartload sounds old-fashioned.
A heap is a loose pile, while cartload suggests a large quantity you could imagine loading onto a vehicle.

examples.everyday: After the holidays we had cartloads of leftovers in the fridge.
examples.professional: After the outage we got cartloads of support tickets, so we added two people to triage the queue.
examples.analytical: Some historical English units of weight were defined as a standard cartload of a commodity, tying measurement to what a horse-drawn cart could carry.

nuance.analogy: It is like a pile you could load onto a cart: vast, visible, and hard to move all at once.
nuance.etymology: From cart, from Old English cræt meaning a small vehicle, plus load.
common_mistakes: Writing cart load as two words; the standard form is one word, cartload.
Using a cartload for one item or a small amount, which sounds exaggerated and odd.

senses.definition: The act of seizing or capturing.
senses.example: The catch of the perpetrator was the product of a year of police work.

senses.definition: The act of catching an object in motion, especially a ball.
senses.example: The player made an impressive catch.

senses.definition: The act of noticing, understanding or hearing.
senses.example: Good catch. I never would have remembered that.

senses.definition: The game of catching a ball.
senses.example: The kids love to play catch.

senses.definition: Something which is captured or caught.
senses.example: The fishermen took pictures of their catch.

senses.definition: A find, in particular a boyfriend or girlfriend or prospective spouse.
senses.example: Did you see his latest catch?

senses.definition: A stopping mechanism, especially a clasp which stops something from opening.
senses.example: She installed a sturdy catch to keep her cabinets closed tight.

senses.definition: A hesitation in voice, caused by strong emotion.
senses.example: There was a catch in his voice when he spoke his father's name.

senses.definition: A concealed difficulty, especially in a deal or negotiation.
senses.example: It sounds like a great idea, but what's the catch?

senses.definition: A crick; a sudden muscle pain during unaccustomed positioning when the muscle is in use.
senses.example: I bent over to see under the table and got a catch in my side.

senses.definition: A fragment of music or poetry.
senses.example: The singer repeated a haunting catch of an old folk melody between verses.

senses.definition: A crop which has germinated and begun to grow.
senses.example: By early April, the first catch of barley had pushed through the frosty soil.

senses.definition: A type of humorous round in which the voices gradually catch up with one another; usually sung by men and often having bawdy lyrics.
senses.example: After dinner, the men sang a bawdy catch that made the whole table roar.

senses.definition: The first contact of an oar with the water.
senses.example: A good rower keeps the catch sharp so the blade bites cleanly into the water.

senses.definition: A stoppage of breath, resembling a slight cough.
senses.example: He felt a catch in his breath when the cold air hit his lungs.

senses.definition: Passing opportunities seized; snatches.
senses.example: He managed only brief catches of sleep between feedings and late-night phone calls.

senses.definition: A slight remembrance; a trace.
senses.example: There was a catch of her father's accent in the way she said goodbye.

senses.definition: The refrain; a line or lines of a song which are repeated from verse to verse.
senses.example: Everyone in the bar joined in on the catch, bellowing the chorus at the top of their lungs.

senses.definition: The act of catching a hit ball before it reaches the ground, resulting in an out.
senses.example: The shortstop made a diving catch to end the inning with the bases loaded.

senses.definition: A player in respect of his catching ability; particularly one who catches well.
senses.example: Our new center fielder is a superb catch, and he rarely drops anything.

senses.definition: To capture, overtake.
senses.example: I hope I catch a fish.

senses.definition: To capture or snare (someone or something which would rather escape).
senses.example: I hope I catch a fish.

senses.definition: To entrap or trip up a person; to deceive.
senses.example: The lawyer tried to catch the witness in a contradiction during cross-examination.

senses.definition: To reach (someone) with a strike, blow, weapon etc.
senses.example: If he catches you on the chin, you'll be on the mat.

senses.definition: To overtake or catch up to; to be in time for.
senses.example: If you leave now you might catch him.

senses.definition: To discover and observe (someone or something while it takes some action or exists).
senses.example: He was caught in the act of stealing a biscuit.

senses.definition: To record, for example on film or tape.
senses.example: It's the very first time such an elusive bird has been caught on film.

senses.definition: To travel by means of.
senses.example: catch the bus

senses.definition: To seize hold of.
senses.example: I caught her by the arm and turned her to face me.

senses.definition: To take or replenish something necessary, such as breath or sleep.
senses.example: I have to stop for a moment and catch my breath

senses.definition: To grip or entangle.
senses.example: My leg was caught in a tree-root.

senses.definition: To be held back or impeded.
senses.example: Be careful your dress doesn't catch on that knob.

senses.definition: To engage with some mechanism; to stick, to succeed in interacting with something or initiating some process.
senses.example: Push it in until it catches.

senses.definition: To have something be held back or impeded.
senses.example: I caught my heel on the threshold.

senses.definition: To make a grasping or snatching motion (at).
senses.example: He caught at the railing as he fell.

senses.definition: To spread or be conveyed to.
senses.example: The fire spread slowly until it caught the eaves of the barn.

senses.definition: To grip (the water) with one's oars at the beginning of the stroke.
senses.example: Coach reminded the crew to catch the water cleanly at the start of every stroke.

senses.definition: To germinate and set down roots.
senses.example: The seeds caught and grew.

senses.definition: To contact a wave in such a way that one can ride it back to shore.
senses.example: Right after paddling out, he managed to catch a wave and ride it all the way in.

senses.definition: To handle an exception.
senses.example: When the program catches an exception, this is recorded in the log file.

senses.definition: To intercept.
senses.example: I will throw you the ball, and you catch it.

senses.definition: To seize or intercept an object moving through the air (or, sometimes, some other medium).
senses.example: I will throw you the ball, and you catch it.

senses.definition: To receive (by being in the way).
senses.example: You're going to catch a beating if they find out.

senses.definition: To be the victim of (something unpleasant, painful etc.).
senses.example: You're going to catch a beating if they find out.

senses.definition: To be touched or affected by (something) through exposure.
senses.example: The sunlight caught the leaves and the trees turned to gold.

senses.definition: To become infected by (an illness).
senses.example: Everyone seems to be catching the flu this week.

senses.definition: To spread by infection or similar means.
senses.example: The virus began to catch among the younger players during the long road trip.

senses.definition: To receive or be affected by (wind, water, fire etc.).
senses.example: The bucket catches water from the downspout.

senses.definition: To acquire, as though by infection; to take on through sympathy or influence.
senses.example: She finally caught the mood of the occasion.

senses.definition: To be hit by something.
senses.example: He caught a bullet in the back of the head last year.

senses.definition: To serve well or poorly for catching, especially for catching fish.
senses.example: This lure doesn't catch well in murky water, so we switched to bright spoons.

senses.definition: To get pregnant.
senses.example: Well, if you didn't catch this time, we'll have more fun trying again until you do.

senses.definition: To take in with one's senses or intellect.
senses.example: Did you catch his name?

senses.definition: To grasp mentally: perceive and understand.
senses.example: Did you catch his name?

senses.definition: To notice, to detect.
senses.example: -You made a typo. -Ah, thanks for catching that.

senses.definition: To take in; to watch or listen to (an entertainment).
senses.example: I have some free time tonight so I think I'll catch a movie.

senses.definition: To reproduce or echo a spirit or idea faithfully.
senses.example: You've really caught his determination in this sketch.

senses.definition: To seize attention, interest.
senses.example: He managed to catch her attention.

senses.definition: To charm or entrance.
senses.example: The old jazz singer completely caught the audience with her smoky voice and easy grace.

senses.definition: To attract and hold (a faculty or organ of sense).
senses.example: He managed to catch her attention.

senses.definition: To end a player's innings by catching a hit ball before the first bounce.
senses.example: Townsend hit 29 before he was caught by Wilson.

senses.definition: To play (a specific period of time) as the catcher.
senses.example: He caught the last three innings.

senses.definition: (dated) To marry or enter into a similar relationship with.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: (rare) To become pregnant. (Only in past tense or as participle.)
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: (dated) To grab, seize, take hold of.
senses.example: I caught her by the arm and turned her to face me.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: (rare) To seize (an opportunity) when it occurs.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: To grab or capture something moving, such as a ball, or to arrive in time to board a bus, train or plane.

pronunciation.tip: Use the short a from 'cat' and finish with a clear ch sound. Do not let the vowel drift toward 'keh' or add a vowel after the ch.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. The verb is positive or neutral depending on context, as in catching a ball or catching a cold.
nuance.usage_note: 'Catch' is one of the most common verbs in American English and appears in everyday talk about transportation, sports, health and understanding. 'I'll catch the bus' means you will board it in time, and 'I didn't catch that' is a polite way to ask someone to repeat. 'Catch you later' is a casual goodbye, and a natural reply is 'Sure, see you.'

distinctions.note: 'Grab' means to seize quickly with the hand, while 'catch' implies intercepting something in motion or arriving in time.
With transportation, 'take the bus' means ride it, while 'catch the bus' emphasizes timing and getting on before it leaves.
'Capture' is more formal and often means taking control of a person or place, while 'catch' is everyday and flexible.

examples.everyday: I'll catch the 7:15 bus, so I can't stay for dinner tonight.
examples.professional: Our QA team usually catches these regressions before they reach production.
examples.analytical: A good model catches patterns that a simple rule would miss, but it also raises new questions about what counts as a pattern.

nuance.analogy: Like a goalie's hands closing around a fast ball, 'catch' is about stopping something that is already moving.
nuance.etymology: From Anglo-Norman cachier, from Latin captiare, 'to seize,' from capere, 'to take.'
common_mistakes: Confusing 'catch' (to arrive in time) with 'take' when talking about transportation; both work, but 'catch' stresses timing.
Using 'catched' as the past tense; the correct past is 'caught.'

catch.etymology: From Middle English *cacchen*, from Anglo-Norman *cachier*, variant of Old French *chacier*, from Late Latin *captio*, from Latin *captō*, frequentative of *capiō*.

senses.definition: The point in the interior of a circle that is equidistant from all points on the circumference.
The point in the interior of a sphere that is equidistant from all points on the circumference.
The middle portion of something; the part well away from the edges.
The point on a line that is midway between the ends.

The point in the interior of any figure of any number of dimensions that has as its coordinates the arithmetic mean of the coordinates of all points on the perimeter of the figure (or of all points in the interior for a center of volume).
senses.example: The centroid is one of the centers of a triangle

senses.definition: A point on a triangle's plane that is in some sense in its middle.
senses.example: There are several centers of a triangle such as its circumcenter, incenter, orthocenter and centroid.

senses.definition: A place, especially a building or complex, set aside for some specified function or activity.
senses.example: shopping center, convention center, civic center, garment center, Lincoln Center for the Performing Arts, Rockefeller Center

senses.definition: The ensemble of moderate or centrist political parties.
The venue in which the head of government in a centralized state is situated.
A topic that is particularly important in a given context, the element in a subject of cognition, volition or discussion that is perceived as decisive.
senses.example: the center of the controversy

senses.definition: The player, generally the tallest, who plays closest to the basket.
The forward that generally plays between the left wing and right wing and usually takes the faceoffs.
The person who holds the ball at the beginning of each play.
A player who can go all over the court, except the shooting circles.
A pass played into the center of the pitch.
One of the backs operating in a central area of the pitch, either the inside center or outside center.
A certain mechanical implement functioning in the middle of a whole apparatus.
One of the two conical steel pins in a lathe, etc. upon which the work is held, and about which it revolves.
A conical recess or indentation in the end of a shaft or other work, to receive the point of a center, on which the work can turn, as in a lathe.
The ring in the gambling game two-up in which the spinner operates.

The set of those elements (of a given algebraic structure) that commute with every other element, usually denoted Z(G). In the case of (semi-)groups, it is required that they commute under the (semi-)group operation; in the case of rings and (Lie) algebras, under multiplication (i.e. the bracket for Lie algebras)
A player in the middle of a playing area.
A temporary structure upon which the materials of a vault or arch are supported in position until the work becomes self-supporting.
Of, at, or related to a center.
To cause (an object) to occupy the center of an area.
senses.example: He centered the heading of the document.

senses.definition: To cause (some attribute, such as a mood or voltage) to be adjusted to a value which is midway between the extremes.
To give (something) a central basis.
To concentrate on (something), to pay close attention to (something).
senses.example: The plot centers on the life of a working-class family.

senses.definition: To form a recess or indentation for the reception of a center.
