senses.definition: For a given directed graph G, a directed acyclic graph with one vertex for each strongly connected component of G, and an edge connecting pairs of components that contain the two endpoints of at least one edge in G.
senses.example: The condensation of the directed graph collapses each cycle into a single vertex, yielding an acyclic structure.

senses.definition: The conversion of a gas to a liquid.
senses.example: Condensation is a challenge that has to be carefully planned for in home-building, to avoid problems such as mold and structural damage.

senses.definition: The reaction of two substances with the simultaneous loss of water or other small molecule.
senses.example: The aldol condensation joins two carbonyl compounds and releases a molecule of water.

core.definition: Tiny water droplets that form when water vapor cools and collects on a cold surface, such as a window or a glass of iced tea.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on SAY, and the -tion ending is pronounced as shun, not tee-un. Many learners pronounce the middle syllable too fully, but it is a reduced uh.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a plain descriptive term in everyday life and in science.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American English, condensation almost always means the water droplets on a cold surface, as in 'There's condensation on the windows.' Scientists and engineers also use it for the change from vapor to liquid. People rarely say 'condensation' in casual talk about a summary, where they would say summary or shortened version.

distinctions.note: Moisture is a general word for wetness, while condensation specifically refers to water forming from vapor on a cool surface.
Dew forms on grass and plants overnight, while condensation forms on any cold surface, including indoor windows and glasses.

examples.everyday: There's so much condensation on the bathroom mirror after my shower.
examples.professional: We need to add a vent to the server room to prevent condensation from damaging the circuit boards.
examples.analytical: Her argument treats condensation as the moment when a diffuse cloud of ideas becomes a definite claim, which is a useful but contestable metaphor.

nuance.analogy: Condensation is like a cold glass of water on a summer day, where invisible vapor in the air becomes visible droplets.
nuance.etymology: From condense, from Latin condensare, to make dense or thick.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it kon-den-SAY-shun with a clear first syllable; the first syllable is kahn.
Using condensation as a verb; the verb is condense.
Confusing the noun in the physical sense with the abstract sense of 'shortening'.

senses.definition: A state of being subject to conditions.
A condition applied to the access of a government to credit facilities and other international financial assistance, especially from the IMF and the World Bank.
senses.example: The IMF attached strict conditionality to the loan, requiring tax reforms before any money was released.

core.definition: The state of being subject to conditions; in finance, the requirements attached to a loan or aid from an international lender.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress shifts to the 'nal' syllable, away from the stress on 'condition'. Keep the middle syllables short and reduced, and end with a clear 'tee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in economics and policy writing, but it can carry a critical tone when used to describe lenders imposing rules on borrowers.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mainly in economics, policy and news coverage, for example about IMF or World Bank loans. In everyday talk people more often say 'strings attached' or just 'conditions'. Using it at a casual dinner may sound stiff.

distinctions.note: A condition is a single requirement, while conditionality refers to the whole system or principle of attaching requirements.
'Strings attached' is informal and everyday, while conditionality is formal and used in policy and economic analysis.

examples.everyday: Honestly, the loan came with so much conditionality that they ended up not taking it.
examples.professional: Our donor's conditionality requires quarterly audits before each tranche of funding is released.
examples.analytical: Critics argue that the conditionality attached to IMF programs shifts key policy choices from elected governments to international lenders.

nuance.analogy: Like a grant with fine print: the money arrives, but only with rules attached.
nuance.etymology: From conditional, from condition, plus the English suffix -ity from Latin -itas, 'state or quality'.
common_mistakes: Using 'conditionality' for any requirement in everyday speech; Americans usually say 'conditions' or 'strings attached'.
Putting the main stress on 'con-DI-tion' instead of on 'NAL', the syllable that carries the stress in the full word.

senses.definition: Comfort, support or sympathy.
senses.example: There was not much to do after the accident but offer what condolence I could.

senses.definition: An expression of comfort, support, or sympathy offered to the family and friends of somebody who has died.
senses.example: I sent her a card expressing my condolences after her mother passed away.

core.definition: An expression of sympathy offered to someone whose family member or close friend has died.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on DOH, the second syllable, and the final -ence is a reduced, unstressed sound. Learners often say KON-do-lens, with the stress on the first syllable and a sharp e.

nuance.connotation: Positive and caring. It is always a respectful gesture, though the subject is sad.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'my condolences' or 'please accept my condolences' at funerals, in cards, and in emails. Singular 'condolence' is less common in speech, where the plural is the usual form. For a warmer and more casual tone with a friend, say 'I'm so sorry for your loss.'

distinctions.note: Sympathy is a general feeling of compassion in any hard situation; condolence is specifically expressed after a death.
Congratulations is for good news, so using it after a death would be a serious social mistake.
Sorrow is the feeling of grief itself; a condolence is the outward gesture of offering comfort to the bereaved.

examples.everyday: Oh, I'm so sorry about your dad, Maria. Please accept my condolences.
examples.professional: Please send our condolences to the family, and let me know if they need help with the paperwork.
examples.analytical: Condolence rituals reveal what a community believes about grief, presence, and the limits of language.

nuance.analogy: Like a casserole left at the door: small, expected, and meaningful because it says you are not alone.
nuance.etymology: From Medieval Latin condolentia, from Latin condolere 'to suffer together', from com- 'with' and dolere 'to grieve'.
common_mistakes: Misspelling it as 'condolance' or 'condolense'.
Using it as a verb in conversation; say 'offer condolences' or 'express sympathy' instead.
Saying 'condolence of your loss'; the usual phrases are 'condolences on your loss' or 'for your loss'.

condolence.etymology: From *condole* + *-ence*, or from Middle French *condoléance*, or formed from the root of Latin *condoleō* (“to sympathize”), from *con-* (“together, with”) and *doleō* (“to hurt, suffer, have pain”).

senses.definition: The act of congregating or collecting together.

A gathering of faithful in a temple, church, synagogue, mosque or other place of worship, especially those present at a devotional service or who regularly attend such services, particularly in contrast to the leadership, choir or others.
A Roman Congregation, a main department of the Vatican administration of the Catholic Church.
A corporate body whose members gather for worship, or the members of such a body.
Any large gathering of people.
A flock of birds.
A group of alligators or crocodiles.

core.definition: The group of people who gather together for worship at a church, synagogue, or other place of worship.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress is on GAY, the fourth syllable, with a secondary stress on KAHNG. The r is pronounced, and the middle syllables are reduced to a quick schwa. The final -tion is pronounced 'shun.'

nuance.connotation: Positive to neutral; it describes a community of worshippers and carries a sense of belonging.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use congregation mainly for religious groups, as in 'the congregation sang the hymn' or 'our congregation is growing.' In casual speech people often say 'church members' or 'the people at church.' The word can also mean any gathering, but in everyday American talk it usually refers to worship.

distinctions.note: Church can mean a building, a denomination, or the community of believers; congregation refers specifically to the people gathered for worship at a particular place.
A crowd is any large group of people in one place; a congregation is a group gathered for worship.

examples.everyday: Our congregation is putting on a potluck dinner after the service on Sunday, so please bring a dish.
examples.professional: Before the new software rollout, we need to explain the changes to the congregation at the Tuesday meeting.
examples.analytical: The Psalmist praises God in the congregation of the upright, emphasizing that worship is a communal act.

nuance.analogy: A congregation is like a choir in a concert hall: each voice is separate, but together they form one sound.
nuance.etymology: From Latin congregare, to gather into a flock, from com- 'together' and grex 'flock'.
common_mistakes: Using congregation for any group of people, not only those gathered for worship.
Pronouncing the g in congregation as a 'j' sound.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew word qahal and the Greek word ekklēsia are both translated as congregation or assembly in the RSV. Exodus 12:6 says the whole assembly of the congregation of Israel shall kill the Passover lamb. Psalm 111:1 says the psalmist will give thanks to the LORD in the company of the upright and in the congregation. Acts 7:38 refers to the congregation in the wilderness.

congregation.etymology: From Middle English *congregacioun*, from Old French *congregacion*, from Latin *congregātiō*, itself from *congregō* (“to herd into a flock”).

senses.definition: Training a model to follow a written set of principles, using AI feedback guided by those principles.
senses.example: Our team used constitutional AI to train the chatbot on a written set of ethical principles.

core.definition: Training an AI model to critique and revise its own outputs against a written set of principles, with AI feedback instead of human labels.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on TU in constitutional and on EYE in AI. Say the letters A and I separately, as ay-EYE, not as the single word eye.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a technical term; some people hear it as reassuring because it suggests built-in values.
nuance.usage_note: Mainly AI researchers and engineers use this term, especially in company papers and technical articles. Outside technical circles, Americans usually explain it as teaching the AI with a rulebook it applies to itself. A natural reply is: 'Yeah, it's a method where the model checks its own answers against written rules.'

distinctions.note: Reinforcement learning from human feedback uses human preference labels; constitutional AI relies mainly on AI feedback guided by written principles.
Fine-tuning is any further training on task data; constitutional AI is a specific method that uses principles to guide that training.
Guardrails are external filters on outputs; constitutional AI tries to build the principles into the model's own training.

examples.everyday: My friend works at an AI lab, and she says their chatbot is trained with something called constitutional AI.
examples.professional: We're testing whether constitutional AI reduces harmful responses in our customer support model before the launch.
examples.analytical: Constitutional AI makes the normative content of training explicit, so the model's values can be inspected, debated and revised.

nuance.analogy: Like a student who grades their own essay against the rubric before turning it in.
nuance.etymology: From constitution (Latin constitutio, 'arrangement, establishment') plus AI; the term was introduced by Anthropic researchers in 2022.
common_mistakes: Assuming the phrase means the AI follows a national legal constitution.
Pronouncing AI as one word like eye, instead of the letters ay-EYE.
Confusing constitutional AI with RLHF, since constitutional AI relies mainly on AI feedback.

conversation.text: Constitutional AI uses a written set of principles to guide a model in critiquing and revising its own outputs.
In constitutional AI, much of the harmlessness feedback comes from a model judging responses against those principles.
Constitutional AI is like giving the model a short rulebook and having it check its own answers against it.

senses.definition: The head or ruler of a constitutional monarchy.
senses.example: The constitutional monarch opened Parliament with a speech written by elected ministers.

core.definition: A king or queen whose powers are limited by a constitution, with an elected government doing the real ruling.

pronunciation.tip: Constitutional has its main stress on TOO, and monarch is MON-urk, with the r pronounced in the second syllable. The given dictionary form had an extra syllable, which General American speakers do not use.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a political system without judgment, though some people admire it for stability and others see the monarch as only a symbol.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use constitutional monarch when discussing countries like the United Kingdom, Spain, Japan or Sweden, since the United States has no monarch. The phrase appears in news and history class. Americans would not normally call a president a monarch, since presidents are elected and limited by a constitution.

distinctions.note: An absolute monarch holds unlimited power; a constitutional monarch's power is limited by a constitution and laws.
A president is elected and holds executive power; a constitutional monarch is usually hereditary and mostly ceremonial.

collocations: ceremonial role as a constitutional monarch

examples.everyday: Most Americans don't realize the British king is a constitutional monarch with no real power to make laws.
examples.professional: In our history seminar we compared the constitutional monarch of Spain with a presidential system in Latin America.
examples.analytical: The constitutional monarch reigns but does not rule, a distinction that makes the crown a symbol of continuity rather than a source of policy.

nuance.analogy: A constitutional monarch is like a figurehead captain on a ship: the ship has a respected leader, but the course is set by the crew under agreed rules.
nuance.etymology: Monarch from Greek monarkhēs, 'sole ruler', from monos 'alone' and archein 'to rule'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable in monarch; say MON-urk, not mon-ARK.
Confusing constitutional monarch with constitutional monarchy, which names the system rather than the person.
Assuming the monarch has real political power; in these systems the monarch usually does not make laws.

senses.definition: To transport (cargo) in large, standard containers.
senses.example: The shipping company chose to containerize most of its cargo to speed up loading at the port.

senses.definition: To modify (a ship or industry) to use such containers.
senses.example: The port authority paid to containerize the old ferry so it could carry standard shipping boxes.

senses.definition: To run an application in a software container.

core.definition: To package an application and its dependencies into a software container so it can run in a consistent environment.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on TAY, and the final -ize is pronounced like 'eyes'. Do not stress the -ize ending, and keep the middle syllable short and weak.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical; used mostly among developers and IT staff.
nuance.usage_note: Developers say this casually in meetings, as in 'We still need to containerize the billing service.' In shipping and port contexts, it means moving cargo into standard containers. Outside work, it is rarely used.

distinctions.note: Dockerize is informal and refers specifically to using Docker, while containerize is the general term.
Package is a general word for bundling something, while containerize specifically means putting it into a container.

examples.everyday: My brother works in logistics, and he says they plan to containerize more of the cargo at the port next year.
examples.professional: Let's containerize the reporting service this sprint so we can deploy it independently.
examples.analytical: To containerize an application is to make its runtime assumptions explicit, which is why the exercise often exposes hidden dependencies.

nuance.analogy: To containerize an app is like putting each dish in a labeled food container before it goes into the fridge, so nothing gets mixed up.
nuance.etymology: From container plus the verb suffix -ize, meaning to make into or treat as.
common_mistakes: Stressing the final syllable, as in 'kun-tay-nur-IZE'.
Using it for any packing task; in software it refers specifically to containers.

senses.definition: The state of being contrite; sincere penitence or remorse.

core.definition: Deep, sincere sorrow for having done wrong, together with the desire to change.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable. The first vowel is a weak schwa, and '-tion' is 'shun'.

nuance.connotation: Positive in moral and religious contexts, since it signals genuine repentance; can sound heavy or stiff in casual talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it in religious, legal and literary settings, such as a judge noting a defendant's lack of contrition. In casual speech people say 'remorse', 'regret' or 'being sorry'. It suggests real inner sorrow, not just an apology.

distinctions.note: Remorse is painful guilt and may lack any turn toward change; contrition implies repentance and a resolve to amend.
In Catholic theology, attrition is imperfect sorrow, motivated by fear of punishment, while contrition arises from love of God.
Regret is milder and need not involve guilt or wrongdoing.

examples.everyday: He showed real contrition when he apologized to his sister.
examples.professional: The judge noted the defendant's contrition before handing down a lighter sentence.
examples.analytical: In classical moral theology, contrition is not mere feeling but a turning of the will away from sin.

nuance.analogy: Contrition is the heart breaking over the wrong, not merely the mind admitting it.
nuance.etymology: From Latin contritio, 'a crushing', from conterere, 'to grind down'.
common_mistakes: Placing stress on the first syllable (KON-tri-shun).
Confusing it with 'contribution'.
Using it for mild regret, such as being sorry for being late.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew idea is a 'contrite' (dakka, crushed) heart or spirit. Psalm 51:17 says God will not despise a broken and contrite heart. Isaiah 57:15 says God dwells with the contrite and lowly in spirit. Psalm 34:18 says the Lord is near to the brokenhearted and saves the crushed in spirit.

traditions.view: Contrition is sorrow of soul and detestation of sin with the resolve not to sin again, and it is the first act of the penitent in the sacrament of Penance. Perfect contrition springs from love of God; imperfect contrition (attrition) springs from fear or the ugliness of sin.

The corresponding idea is compunction (katanyxis), a piercing sorrow that opens the heart to God. It is part of ongoing repentance (metanoia) and is expressed in prayer and confession to a priest, without the Western scholastic scheme of contrition and attrition.

Contrition is generally understood as sorrow for sin that accompanies repentance and faith. Lutherans treat contrition and faith as the two parts of repentance; Reformed and Baptist traditions emphasize it as a fruit of regeneration. Protestants do not treat it as a sacramental act.

senses.definition: With a reversed relationship.
From another point of view; on the other hand.
senses.example: Some employees prefer remote work; conversely, others miss the daily energy of the office.

core.definition: In the opposite way; used to introduce a statement that reverses or contrasts with what was just said.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, and the vowel is the stressed American 'ur' sound made with an r-colored vowel. Don't pronounce the 'ver' as 'vair'; the final -sly cluster is often shortened to 'slee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it signals logical or structural contrast without judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use conversely mostly in writing, argument, and careful speech to introduce a reversed relationship, as in 'Sales rose; conversely, returns fell.' In casual talk people more often say 'the other way around' or 'on the flip side.' A natural reply is simply to continue the argument, since the word itself needs no response.

distinctions.note: On the other hand presents a second side of the same item, while conversely reverses the relationship between two items.
Similarly signals that two things share a feature; conversely signals that they are opposite in that feature.

collocations: conversely, the effect works the other way

examples.everyday: My sister loves going to the beach, and conversely, I would rather stay home with a book.
examples.professional: Engagement went up for mobile users; conversely, desktop users dropped off after the redesign.
examples.analytical: Freedom presupposes order; conversely, order without the possibility of freedom becomes tyranny.

nuance.analogy: Like a mirror image: the same shape, but flipped in the opposite direction.
nuance.etymology: From converse, from Latin conversus, past participle of convertere 'to turn around'.
common_mistakes: Using conversely to mean 'similarly' or to add an unrelated point.
Stressing the first syllable as 'KAHN-verse-lee'.

senses.definition: (dated) Convincing.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: Dated word meaning convincing or persuasive; able to make someone believe something is true.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable and keep the first vowel short and relaxed. The final -tive is reduced to a short 'tiv' sound, not 'teev'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. The word has no emotional charge, but it sounds old-fashioned, so it can make your speech or writing seem stiff or antique.
nuance.usage_note: You will mostly meet convictive in older books, legal or theological writing, or in deliberately old-style prose. Americans today say convincing for the same meaning. Using convictive in everyday conversation would sound odd and dated.

distinctions.note: Convincing is the normal modern word for the same meaning; convictive is dated and rare, so use convincing in almost all modern speech and writing.
Conviction is a noun meaning a firm belief or a formal finding of guilt, while convictive is an adjective describing something that makes others believe.

examples.everyday: Grandpa's old sermons had a convictive force that still makes me think about my choices.
examples.professional: Our reviewer called the data convictive, but the wording in the report sounds more formal than we use today.
examples.analytical: Early modern theologians often wrote in a convictive style, aiming to persuade readers through clear logic and scriptural citation.

nuance.analogy: A convictive argument is like an old-fashioned key that still opens the door, though most people now carry a newer key called convincing.
nuance.etymology: From convict, from Latin convincere, to overcome or prove wrong.
common_mistakes: Using convictive in casual or modern professional speech, where convincing is the natural word.
Confusing convictive with conviction, which is a noun meaning a firm belief or a guilty verdict.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to coordination.

core.definition: Relating to coordination, or to the linking of parts so that they work together or hold equal rank.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the AWR syllable, not the -ay- syllable. The final -tive is short: 'tiv'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a technical adjective used to describe a function or relationship.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use coordinative mainly in linguistics, psychology, management, and formal writing. In everyday speech, they use 'coordinating' or simply 'organizing.' It sounds stiff in casual talk.

distinctions.note: Coordinating is more common and can describe a person or an action. Coordinative is more technical and describes a relationship or function.
Cooperative describes willingness to help others. Coordinative describes structural or organizational linking.

examples.everyday: Her coordinative skills kept our whole family trip on schedule.
examples.professional: The program office has a coordinative role, syncing deadlines across the four product teams.
examples.analytical: Coordinative structures in grammar link elements of equal rank, such as two parallel clauses joined by a conjunction.

nuance.analogy: A coordinative role is like the traffic light at a busy intersection: it does not drive the cars, but it keeps them moving without collisions.
nuance.etymology: From coordinate plus the suffix -ive, from Latin co- 'together' and ordinare 'to arrange.'
common_mistakes: Using coordinative for a person; use coordinator for the person and coordinative for the function or relationship.
Stressing the wrong syllable as koh-or-duh-NAY-tiv.

senses.definition: To compare things and bring them into a relation having corresponding characteristics.
senses.example: We will correlate survey responses with purchase records to see which messages worked.

senses.definition: To be related by a correlation; to be correlated.
Either of a pair of things related by a correlation; a correlative.
senses.example: Each term in the proof has a correlate on the other side of the equation.

core.definition: To have a statistical or systematic relationship with something, so that changes in one tend to occur along with changes in the other.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on KOR, and the final syllable is 'layt' as in 'late'. The noun is pronounced the same, so don't shift the stress to the last syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; precise and analytical, used to describe measured relationships without claiming cause.
nuance.usage_note: In American business, science, and data work, correlate is common in reports, such as sales correlate with ad spending. It is less common in casual talk, where people say go together or are linked. The most natural form is correlate with. Remember that correlation does not prove causation.

distinctions.note: Cause means one thing produces another; correlate only means two things tend to change together, which does not prove causation.
Relate is general; correlate implies a measurable or systematic connection, often statistical.

examples.everyday: Honestly, my energy seems to correlate with how much sleep I get.
examples.professional: Our churn rate correlates with the number of unresolved support tickets, so we should look at the onboarding flow first.
examples.analytical: Hume argued that our sense of causation rests on repeated observation of events that correlate, not on any direct perception of necessity.

nuance.analogy: Correlate is like two dancers moving in step: when one turns, the other tends to turn too, though neither is leading.
nuance.etymology: From Medieval Latin correlatus, from com- 'together' and relatus 'related'.
common_mistakes: Saying correlate to instead of correlate with.
Assuming that correlation means cause, which is a serious logical error.

senses.definition: The universe regarded as a system with harmony and order.
A harmonious, ordered whole.
Harmony, order.
Any of various mostly Mexican herbs of the genus Cosmos having radiate heads of variously colored flowers and pinnate leaves.
senses.example: Along the fence line, the bright pink cosmos attracted monarch butterflies all summer.

core.definition: The universe regarded as an orderly, harmonious whole, rather than as a random collection of things.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and end with a clear 'ohs' sound, not 'oyz'. The word has two syllables, so do not add an extra vowel between the z and m.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests order, beauty, and harmony, and it is often used in a reflective or poetic way.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use cosmos in literary, philosophical, and scientific-popular contexts, such as talking about the vastness of the cosmos or the order of nature. In casual conversation people usually say 'the universe' or 'space.' The word can sound a bit lofty if used about everyday matters.

distinctions.note: Universe is the neutral, standard term for all of space and everything in it; cosmos suggests a more orderly, harmonious, or philosophical view of the same thing.
World usually refers to Earth or human society; cosmos refers to the whole ordered universe and is much broader in scope.

examples.everyday: Lying on the grass and watching the stars made me feel small in the cosmos, but in a good way.
examples.professional: Our analytics pipeline sits inside a much larger data cosmos, so every schema change affects several downstream teams.
examples.analytical: For Thomas Aquinas, the ordered cosmos reveals a design that points beyond itself to its Creator.

nuance.analogy: The cosmos is like a well-tuned orchestra, where every instrument has its place and the whole piece makes sense together.
nuance.etymology: From Greek kosmos, meaning 'order, world, or adornment'.
common_mistakes: Using cosmos in casual speech for outer space, where Americans would say 'space' or 'the universe.'
Pronouncing the final -os as 'oys' instead of 'ohs'.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek word kosmos is used often in the New Testament, usually meaning the world, the created order, or humanity in its relation to God. John 1:10 says that the Word was in the world that was made through him, yet the world did not know him. Romans 1:20 speaks of God's invisible qualities being seen in the things he has made since the creation of the world.

senses.definition: A noise or sound like a cough (etymology 2, noun sense 1).
senses.example: A sharp cough from the back row interrupted the silence during the funeral.

senses.definition: A bout of repeated coughing (verb etymology 1 sense 2.1); also, a medical condition that causes one to cough.
A sudden, often involuntary expulsion of air from the lungs through the glottis (causing a short, explosive sound), and out through the mouth.
senses.example: Behind me, I heard a distinct, dry cough.

senses.definition: A vocalisation from a bird or other animal resembling a human cough.
senses.example: Every evening, the male pheasant gave a low cough from the edge of the field.

senses.definition: Used to represent the sound of a cough (noun sense 1), especially when focusing attention on a following utterance, often an attribution of blame or a euphemism: ahem.
senses.example: He was—cough—indisposed.

senses.definition: Sometimes followed by up: to force (something) out of the lungs or throat by pushing air from the lungs through the glottis (causing a short, explosive sound), and out through the mouth.
senses.example: Sometimes she coughed up blood.

senses.definition: To cause (oneself or something) to be in a certain condition in the manner described in etymology 1 sense 1.1.
senses.example: He almost coughed himself into a fit.

senses.definition: To express (words, etc.) in the manner described in etymology 1 sense 1.1.
senses.example: She coughed out a short apology before turning back to the stove.

senses.definition: To surrender (information); to confess.
senses.example: After two hours of questioning, the suspect finally coughed and told detectives everything.

senses.definition: Chiefly followed by up: to give up or hand over (something); especially, to pay up (money).
senses.example: The company was ordered to cough up the back taxes within thirty days.

senses.definition: To push air from the lungs through the glottis (causing a short, explosive sound) and out through the mouth, usually to expel something blocking or irritating the airway.
senses.example: I breathed in a lungful of smoke by mistake, and started to cough.

senses.definition: To make a noise like a cough.
senses.example: The engine coughed and sputtered.

senses.definition: To surrender information; to confess, to spill the beans.
senses.example: The accountant coughed after the auditor pressed him, admitting that the figures were falsified.

core.definition: To force air suddenly and sharply out of your lungs, making a harsh noise, often to clear your throat or because of irritation.

pronunciation.tip: The 'gh' is silent, so the word ends with an f sound. Many Americans with the cot-caught merger say /kɑf/, which is also acceptable, but /kɔf/ is the standard dictionary form.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'cough' in everyday talk, in doctor's offices, and in pharmacies. Coughing in public without covering your mouth can seem rude, so people usually say 'Excuse me' afterward or cough into their elbow. The noun 'cough' is often used when describing a symptom, as in 'I have a cough.'

distinctions.note: A cough is a forceful expulsion of air from the lungs through the throat, while a sneeze expels air through the nose and mouth.
Clearing your throat is a gentler, quieter action to remove mucus, while coughing is more forceful and often repeated.

examples.everyday: Sorry, I've had this annoying cough since last week, so I'm going to step outside.
examples.professional: If you feel unwell, please don't come to the office; I'll cough into my elbow and keep my distance during the call.
examples.analytical: To cough is to force the body's protective reflex into speech, as though the lungs themselves were objecting to something unsaid.

nuance.analogy: A cough is the body's built-in vacuum cleaner, pushing irritants out of the airways with a sudden burst of air.
nuance.etymology: From Old English cohhian, of imitative origin.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the 'gh' as a sound, which makes the word sound like 'coff' with an extra syllable.
Saying 'I have a cough' when you mean you are coughing right now; both are correct, but 'I have a cough' describes a lasting symptom.

cough.etymology: From Middle English *coughen*, *coghen* (“to cough; to vomit”), from Old English **cohhian*, from **kuh-* (“to cough”), ultimately of onomatopoeic origin.

conversation.text: My cough is worse at night.
That cough sounds bad. Have you seen a doctor?
I coughed all night and didn't get any sleep.

senses.definition: (linguistics) A "what if" statement.
senses.example: A counterfactual conditional like 'If I had left earlier, I would have caught the train' describes an unrealized past.

core.definition: A 'what if' sentence with a false if-clause, such as 'If I had studied harder, I would have passed'.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on FAK in the first word and on DISH in the second. In the second word, the 'di' sounds like 'dish' and the 'tion' is a reduced 'shun'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical, used in linguistics, logic, and philosophy courses.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this term mainly in linguistics, logic, and philosophy classes, to name a sentence like 'If the bridge had been built, traffic would be lighter'. In everyday conversation, people simply say 'a what-if sentence' or describe 'an if-then about something that did not happen'. The term is common in academic writing about grammar and reasoning.

distinctions.note: An indicative conditional talks about possible situations, such as 'If it rains, we will stay home', while a counterfactual conditional talks about what did not happen.
Hypothetical is a general word for imagined situations, while counterfactual conditional is a specific grammatical or logical form.
Subjunctive is a verb mood used in many contexts, and counterfactual conditionals are one common use of it in English.

examples.everyday: My friend said, If I had known about the sale, I would have bought two, which is a what-if sentence.
examples.professional: In our analytics writeup, we used a counterfactual conditional to describe how revenue would have changed without the price increase.
examples.analytical: Lewis's semantics for the counterfactual conditional evaluates such sentences by considering the closest possible worlds where the antecedent is true.

nuance.analogy: Like rewinding a film to a different scene and asking how the story would have changed.
nuance.etymology: Counterfactual (from counter- plus factual) combined with conditional (from Latin condicionalis).
common_mistakes: Saying 'counter factual' as two words in formal writing; the standard form is counterfactual.
Stressing 'conditional' on the wrong syllable, saying 'kun-DI-shun-ul' instead of 'kun-DISH-uh-nuhl'.

senses.definition: To revoke (a former command); to cancel or rescind by giving an order contrary to one previously given.
senses.example: to countermand an order for goods

senses.definition: To recall a person or unit with such an order.
senses.example: The general countermanded the order and recalled the battalion before it reached the river crossing.

senses.definition: To cancel an order for (some specified goods).
senses.example: We countermanded our order for two hundred folding chairs after the wedding was postponed.

senses.definition: To counteract, to act against, to frustrate.
senses.example: Rising interest rates countermanded the stimulus, frustrating the bank's plan to boost lending.

senses.definition: An order to the contrary of a previous one.
senses.example: The mayor's countermand arrived minutes after the first directive, leaving the police confused.

core.definition: To officially cancel or reverse an order or instruction by giving a new order that contradicts the first.

pronunciation.tip: The first syllable KOWN is strong, and the second syllable 'mand' has a short 'a' as in 'hand'. Many learners wrongly stress the end, saying 'kown-ter-MAND', which sounds unnatural.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative, since it suggests overriding an authority.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word in military, legal, business, and government contexts, such as when a manager or official reverses a previous decision. In everyday speech, people more often say 'cancel' or 'override'. It is a formal word, and using it in a casual conversation may sound stiff or dramatic.

distinctions.note: Cancel is common and general, while countermand specifically means reversing an order by issuing a contrary order.
Override means to take precedence over a decision or system, while countermand means to issue a direct order against an earlier one.
Revoke usually refers to rights, licenses, or permissions, while countermand refers specifically to orders or instructions.

examples.everyday: My mom countermanded my dad's decision and said we would eat out tonight instead.
examples.professional: The director countermanded the earlier instruction and asked the team to keep the old database running.
examples.analytical: The court's ruling countermanded the executive order, arguing that the president lacked the authority to issue it.

nuance.analogy: Countermanding an order is like a referee reversing a call after seeing the replay.
nuance.etymology: From Middle French contremander, from contre (against) plus mander (to command).
common_mistakes: Using 'countermand' as a noun in place of the verb; the noun is used as 'a countermand' for a contrary order.
Putting the stress on the last syllable, saying 'kown-ter-MAND', which is less natural for American speakers.

countermand.etymology: From Old French *contremander*, from Medieval Latin *contramandō*, from *contra* + *mandō* (“to order; to command”).

senses.definition: Of unsound mind; insane; demented.
senses.example: His ideas were both frightening and crazy.

senses.definition: Out of control.
senses.example: When she gets on the motorcycle she goes crazy.

senses.definition: Very excited or enthusiastic.
senses.example: He went crazy when he won.

senses.definition: In love; experiencing romantic feelings.
senses.example: Why is she so crazy about him?

senses.definition: Very unexpected; wildly surprising.
senses.example: crazy work

senses.definition: Very, extremely.
senses.example: That trick was crazy good.

senses.definition: An insane or eccentric person; a crackpot.
senses.example: Everyone on the block called him the neighborhood crazy, though he was harmless.

senses.definition: Eccentric behavior; lunacy; craziness.
senses.example: Her sudden crazy at the budget meeting shocked everyone, especially her own manager.

core.definition: Mentally unsound; or wildly unreasonable, out of control, or very enthusiastic about something.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The final y is pronounced like ee, and the r is rhotic, so do not drop it. Avoid making the last syllable sound like 'zy' with a long i.

nuance.connotation: Varies. It can be neutral or humorous in casual talk, but it can insult people with mental illness and sounds dismissive in serious contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use crazy very casually, as in 'That's crazy!' to show surprise, 'crazy good' to mean excellent, or 'I'm crazy about her' to mean deeply fond of someone. For serious mental health topics, people choose words such as mental illness or unwell. Calling someone crazy in a dispute can sound rude.

distinctions.note: Insane is stronger and more formal, often used in legal or medical contexts; crazy is informal and used in everyday speech.
Wild suggests energy or unruliness, while crazy adds a sense of unreasonableness or strangeness.

examples.everyday: That new taco place is crazy good, so let's go there tonight.
examples.professional: Shipping the update by Friday is crazy ambitious, but we can try if QA is ready.
examples.analytical: Many people call a theory crazy simply because it challenges a comfortable assumption, but the label alone does not settle the question.

nuance.analogy: Like a radio stuck between stations, sending out signals that no longer make sense to the listener.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English crased, cracked or broken, from crasen, to crack; the sense of madness developed later.
common_mistakes: Using crazy about with of or for; the correct phrase is crazy about.
Using crazy as a neutral medical term; in serious contexts, say mental illness or psychiatric condition.

senses.definition: Tending to create things, or having the ability to create; often, excellently, in a novel fashion, or any or all of these.
senses.example: a creative dramatist who avoids cliche

senses.definition: Original, expressive and imaginative.
senses.example: a creative new solution to an old problem

senses.definition: A type of set of natural numbers, related to mathematical logic.
senses.example: a creative set

senses.definition: Designed or executed to deceive or mislead.
senses.example: creative accounting and bookkeeping

senses.definition: Bad, unartistic, busy.
A person directly involved in a creative process; a creator of creative content.
senses.example: He is a visionary creative.

senses.definition: Artistic material used in advertising, e.g. photographs, drawings, or videos.
senses.example: The design team has completed the creative for next month's multi-part ad campaign.

core.definition: Having the imagination and ability to produce original ideas, works, or solutions.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on AY, and the ending -ive is a short 'iv', not 'eev'. Do not stress the final syllable.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it praises imagination and originality, though 'creative accounting' or 'creative spelling' can imply bending rules.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use creative to praise ideas, designs, cooking, problem solving and people in fields like design, writing, marketing or teaching. In the workplace, 'You're so creative' is a compliment, and a natural reply is 'Thanks, I had fun with it.' The word can also be a polite way to describe unconventional work, but 'creative' with money or facts suggests bending the truth.

distinctions.note: Imaginative focuses on the mind forming images or ideas, while creative stresses making something new and useful or expressive.
Innovative usually means new in a practical way, often in business or technology, while creative can be artistic or expressive.
Original means not copied, while creative adds the sense of inventive making.

examples.everyday: My sister is really creative; she made her own birthday cards this year.
examples.professional: We need a creative approach to the dashboard, so let's sketch three layouts before we build anything.
examples.analytical: Kant treats the mind as creative in its synthesis of experience, which means it actively structures what we perceive.

nuance.analogy: A creative mind is like a jazz musician who starts from a familiar tune and plays something no one has heard before.
nuance.etymology: From Latin creativus, from creare, to create.
common_mistakes: Saying great creative when you mean great creativity; creative is an adjective and creativity is the noun.
Stressing the ending as kree-ay-TEEV; the stress belongs on AY.

senses.definition: To crackle, to make a crackling sound. to flatulate.
To crackle, as crepitant lungs do, as some arthritic joints may do, or as some fractured bones may do.
senses.example: The old knee would crepitate loudly whenever he climbed the stairs, a sound that embarrassed him.

senses.definition: To flatulate.
senses.example: After the beans, the dog began to crepitate under the dinner table, and everyone pretended not to notice.

core.definition: To make a crackling or popping sound, especially as a joint, lung or fractured bone does during a medical examination.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, KREP, and the final syllable is a long A as in 'rate.' Do not reduce the middle syllable to nothing; it is a short i followed by t.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and clinical. It is a precise medical term without emotional force.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'crepitate' almost only in medicine or medical writing, for example when a doctor describes a joint that makes a grinding or popping sound. In everyday talk people say 'pop,' 'crack' or 'grind' instead. It is correct American usage but rare outside clinics and textbooks.

distinctions.note: Crackle is an everyday word for a sharp, repeated snapping sound, while crepitate is a precise medical term for a sound made by joints, lungs or bones.
Pop is informal and general, while crepitate is clinical and specific to body sounds.

examples.everyday: My doctor asked if my knee crepitates when I bend it, and I said it makes a crackling sound on stairs.
examples.professional: The clinical report notes that the patient's shoulder crepitates on movement, which the physician recorded during the exam.
examples.analytical: Auscultation of crepitant lungs reveals the abnormal sound produced when air moves through fluid-filled or collapsed alveoli.

nuance.analogy: Crepitate is like a dry leaf crushed underfoot, but used only for sounds inside the body.
nuance.etymology: From Latin crepitare, to rattle or crackle, a frequentative of crepare.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'crepitus' (the noun) and using it as a verb in place of 'crepitate.'
Using it in everyday talk where 'pop' or 'crack' would sound more natural.

crepitate.etymology: Latin *crepitātus*, perfect passive participle of *crepitō* (“to creak, rattle, clatter, crackle”) (see *-ate*), itself a *frequentative* of *crepō* (“to creak, rattle, etc. burst or break with a noise, crash”).

senses.definition: A point-counting card game for two players, with variants for three or four players; the cribbage board used for scoring to 61 or 121 points in numerous small increments is characteristic.
senses.example: Grandma beat us all at cribbage again, pegging her way to 121 with a perfect hand.

senses.definition: A variety of pocket billiards that, like the card game, awards points for pairs that total 15. A player who pockets a ball of a particular number must then immediately pocket the companion ball that brings the number to 15.
senses.example: We tried cribbage on the felt table, sinking the 4 and then its partner, the 11.

senses.definition: A point scored in this variety of pocket billiards.
senses.example: Her final shot earned her a cribbage, putting her ahead of the table by two points.

core.definition: A card game for two or more players in which points are scored for card combinations and tracked on a pegged board.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, KRIB, with a short i. The ending is -ij, like the j in judge, and the middle vowel is a quick reduced ih.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, describing a traditional game often played at home or in family settings.
nuance.usage_note: Cribbage is a traditional American card game, especially popular in New England, the Midwest and older family settings. People often keep a wooden board and pegs for scoring. You might say let's play a game of cribbage, and a natural reply is sure, deal the cards.

distinctions.note: Gin rummy scores by forming melds and going out, while cribbage scores points during play and in the count.
Poker usually involves betting, while cribbage is a point-scoring game without betting.

examples.everyday: My grandpa always wanted to play cribbage after dinner, and he never lost gracefully.
examples.professional: Our office holds a monthly cribbage tournament in the break room.
examples.analytical: Cribbage rewards combinatorial reasoning, because players must spot every pair, run and fifteen in their hand and in the crib.

nuance.analogy: Like a race on a looping track, the pegs crawl around the board until one player reaches the end.
nuance.etymology: Named after the crib, the extra hand built from discards; the exact origin of the game is debated.
common_mistakes: Confusing cribbage with crib, the discard hand, as if they were the same thing
Pronouncing the ending as ahj, rather than the ij sound of judge

senses.definition: The state of being critical.
senses.example: They weren't aware of the criticality of the situation.

senses.definition: A disposition for purposeful thinking and acting guided by criteria that are considered to be contextually appropriate and that are expected to result in positive outcomes related to the purpose.
senses.example: Her criticality shone through in the seminar, where she questioned every assumption the author made.

senses.definition: The point at which a nuclear chain reaction becomes self-sustaining.
senses.example: Engineers reached criticality at dawn, when the reactor's chain reaction became self-sustaining.

core.definition: The quality of being extremely important or urgent, or the state of being crucial to a system or outcome.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress shifts to the CAL syllable, unlike critical, which stresses the first syllable. Many learners keep the stress at the front, but Americans say krit-ih-KAL-ih-tee.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it signals urgency or importance without implying blame.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use criticality in business, engineering and IT to describe how important something is, as in 'the criticality of the deadline' or 'rate each incident by criticality.' It is more formal than importance and often sounds technical. In everyday speech, saying 'how important it is' is more natural.

distinctions.note: Importance is the general word, while criticality stresses that something is crucial to success or safety.
Urgency is about time pressure, while criticality is about how essential something is, whether or not it is urgent.
Significance is the meaning or weight of something, while criticality is the degree to which a system depends on it.

examples.everyday: I can't stress the criticality of getting that prescription filled today, so please call the pharmacy.
examples.professional: We rank each incident by criticality so the on-call team handles the worst outages first.
examples.analytical: The criticality of the question lies in whether justice can be achieved without some form of forgiveness.

nuance.analogy: Like the keystone in an arch: remove it, and the whole structure falls.
nuance.etymology: Formed from critical, from Greek kritikos, 'able to discern or judge', plus the suffix -ity.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, as in CRIT-ih-kal-ih-tee.
Confusing criticality with criticism, which means disapproval or judgment.
Using it in casual speech where importance would sound more natural.

senses.definition: The art of criticism.
senses.example: Her professor said that a good critique requires patience, precision, and genuine respect for the author's intentions.

senses.definition: An essay in which another piece of work is criticized, reviewed, etc.
senses.example: His critique of the new housing report ran twelve pages and was published in the local journal.

senses.definition: A point made to criticize something.
senses.example: Bob liked most of my presentation, but offered three minor critiques.

senses.definition: To review or evaluate something.
senses.example: I want you to critique this new idea of mine.

core.definition: A detailed analysis that evaluates the strengths and weaknesses of a work, idea, or plan.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the second and only stressed syllable, TEEK, which rhymes with 'week'. Do not say 'KRIT-ik'; the final 'que' is silent.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. A critique can be positive or negative; it is a careful evaluation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use critique in academic writing, design reviews, and professional feedback, such as 'a critique of the draft'. In everyday talk, people usually say 'feedback' or 'review'. As a verb, 'critique' is common in education and design, where students critique each other's work.

distinctions.note: Criticism is the general act or the negative judgment; a critique is a structured, detailed evaluation.
A review is a general assessment, often for publication; a critique is more analytical and often focused on method or argument.

examples.everyday: My roommate gave me a critique of my cooking, which was honest but kind.
examples.professional: Please send me your critique of the dashboard design by Thursday so we can revise it.
examples.analytical: Her critique of the argument shows that its central premise assumes what it sets out to prove.

nuance.analogy: A critique is like a home inspection: it finds what works, what is broken, and what needs repair.
nuance.etymology: From French critique, from Greek kritikē, 'the art of judging'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final 'que' as 'kyoo'.
Using 'critique' as a synonym for complaint, when it is more analytical.

critique.etymology: from New Latin *critica* (“critique”), feminine of *criticus* (“critical”); see critic.

senses.definition: A royal, imperial or princely headdress; a diadem.
senses.example: The jeweler polished the gold crown that had sat on the queen's head for decades.

senses.definition: A wreath or band for the head, especially one given as reward of victory or a mark of honor.
senses.example: The runner received a laurel crown after winning the marathon in a close finish.

senses.definition: Any reward of victory or mark of honor.
senses.example: the martyr’s crown

senses.definition: Imperial or regal power, or those who wield it.
senses.example: Under the old treaty, the colonies remained subject to the crown in London.

senses.definition: The sovereign (in a monarchy), as head of state.
senses.example: Parliament reports to the crown, which formally signs every bill into law.

senses.definition: The police (referring to Crown Victoria police cars).
senses.example: Dispatch radioed that a crown was parked outside the diner with its lights off.

senses.definition: The top part of something:
senses.example: The crown of the old oak tree was damaged by last winter's ice storm.

senses.definition: The topmost part of the head.
senses.example: The barber trimmed the hair at my crown, where it had grown thin.

senses.definition: During childbirth, the appearance of the baby's head from the mother's vagina.
senses.example: The midwife said the baby's crown was visible, so the next push should be soon.

senses.definition: A round spot shaved clean on the top of the head, as a mark of the clerical state; the tonsure.
senses.example: The monk's crown was shaved each month as a sign of his devotion.

senses.definition: The highest part of a hill.
senses.example: We hiked to the crown of the hill to watch the sunset over the valley.

senses.definition: The top section of a hat, above the brim.
senses.example: The felt hat had a tall crown and a narrow brim.

senses.definition: The raised center of a road.
senses.example: The road has a steep crown so rainwater drains off toward the shoulders.

senses.definition: The highest part of an arch.
senses.example: The keystone sits at the crown of the arch and holds the stones together.

senses.definition: The upper range of facets in a rose diamond.
senses.example: The cutter angled the crown of the rose diamond to maximize its sparkle.

senses.definition: The dome of a furnace.
senses.example: The crown of the furnace cracked after years of extreme heat and repeated firing.

senses.definition: The upper part of certain fruits, as the pineapple or strawberry, that is removed before eating.
senses.example: Cut off the crown of the pineapple before slicing it into rings.

senses.definition: The top of a tree.
Splendor; culmination; acme.

Any currency (originally) issued by the crown (regal power) and often bearing a crown (headdress); various currencies known by similar names in their native languages, such as the korona, koruna, krona, króna, krone.
A knot formed in the end of a rope by tucking in the strands to prevent them from unraveling.
The part of an anchor where the arms and the shank meet.
The rounding, or rounded part, of the deck from a level line.
A standard size of writing paper measuring 19 × 15 inches.
A rounding or smoothing of the barrel opening.
The area enclosed between two concentric perimeters.
A whole bird with the legs and wings removed to produce a joint of white meat.
A formal hat worn by women to Sunday church services; a church crown.
The knurled knob or dial, on the outside of a watch case, used to wind it or adjust the hands.
The state, the government (headed by a monarch).
senses.example: Treasure recovered from shipwrecks automatically becomes property of the Crown.

senses.definition: A kind of spire or lantern formed by converging flying buttresses.
The part of a plant where the root and stem meet.
The part of a tooth above the gums.
A prosthetic covering for a tooth.
A monocyclic ligand having three or more binding sites, capable of holding a guest in a central location.
(historical) A former predecimalization British coin worth five shillings.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: (historical) A coin or note worth five shillings in various countries that are or were in the British Commonwealth, such as Ireland or Jamaica.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: Of, related to, or pertaining to a crown.
senses.example: crown prince

senses.definition: Of, related to, pertaining to the top of a tree or trees.
senses.example: a crown fire

senses.definition: To place a crown on the head of.
To formally declare (someone) a king, queen, emperor, etc.
To bestow something upon as a mark of honor, dignity, or recompense; to adorn; to dignify.
To form the topmost or finishing part of; to complete; to consummate; to perfect.
To declare (someone) a winner.
To cause to round upward; to make anything higher at the middle than at the edges, such as the face of a machine pulley.
To hit on the head.
To shoot an opponent in the back of the head with a shotgun in a first-person shooter video game.
In checkers, to stack two checkers to indicate that the piece has become a king.
senses.example: “Crown me!” I said, as I moved my checker to the back row.

senses.definition: To spread to the crowns of the trees and thence move from tree to tree independent of the surface fire.
To widen the opening of the barrel.
To struggle to hold back an imminent, crowning bowel movement.
To shoot (someone) in the head.
To have its head's surface appear in the vaginal opening during the birthing process.
senses.example: The mother was in the second stage of labor and the fetus had just crowned, prompting a round of encouragement from the midwives.

senses.definition: To effect a lodgment upon, as upon the crest of the glacis, or the summit of the breach.
To lay the ends of the strands of (a knot) over and under each other.

core.definition: A jeweled headdress worn by a monarch as a symbol of royal authority.

pronunciation.tip: Pronounce the r clearly by curling your tongue back, and do not let it fade into a vowel. The vowel is a glide from a low starting point toward the back, so say 'krown' and not 'krawn' or 'kroon'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in the royal sense and positive in the sense of a reward or honor; the meaning depends on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'crown' most often for royal headwear, but also for sports trophies, pageant prizes and dental caps, so the context usually tells you the sense. In everyday talk you might say 'she won the crown' about a beauty pageant or 'a crown on a tooth' at the dentist. Outside of a royal or pageant context, the word sounds a little theatrical.

distinctions.note: A tiara is a jeweled ornament worn on the front of the head, usually by women, and it is smaller and less formal than a full crown.
A diadem is a band or circlet worn on the head, often used in literary or historical writing, and it is less common in everyday American speech than crown.
A coronet is a small crown worn by nobles below royal rank, so it is a lesser version of a crown.

examples.everyday: My daughter wore a paper crown to her birthday party all afternoon.
examples.professional: Our team claimed the crown for the highest sales growth in the company this quarter.
examples.analytical: In medieval political theory, the crown symbolized the sovereign's authority over the body politic rather than the person of the king alone.

nuance.analogy: A crown is like a badge of office that makes a person's status visible to everyone in the room.
nuance.etymology: From Old French corone, from Latin corona, wreath, from Greek korōnē, something curved.
common_mistakes: Saying 'crown' as if it rhymes with 'crowd' (/kɹaʊd/); the final sound is /n/.
Using 'crown to' with a person ('they crowned to king') instead of 'crown someone king' or 'crown someone queen'.
nuance.biblical_note:
In Scripture, the crown appears in two senses: the royal diadem, Hebrew keter, and the victor's wreath, Greek stephanos, which was given to athletes and as a symbol of reward. Paul uses the image of a victor's crown for eternal reward, and James and Peter speak of a crown of life and of glory. Note that the crown of thorns in the Passion narratives is a mocking royal image rather than an honor.
2 Timothy 4:8 speaks of a 'crown of righteousness' laid up for the faithful. James 1:12 promises the 'crown of life' to those who endure trial. 1 Peter 5:4 speaks of an unfading 'crown of glory' for faithful shepherds.

crown.etymology: Middle English *coroune*, from Anglo-Norman *corone*, from Latin *corōna* (“crown, wreath”), from Ancient Greek *κορώνη*.

senses.definition: Essential or decisive for determining the outcome or future of something; extremely important; vital.
senses.example: The battle of Tali-Ihantala in 1944 is one of the crucial moments in the history of Finland.

core.definition: Extremely important, because the outcome or future of something depends on it; decisive or essential.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, and the 'cia' is pronounced 'shuh' with the sh sound, not 'see-uhl'. Many learners add an extra syllable, so say it as two syllables, KROO-shuhl.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral, and it conveys urgency and importance.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'crucial' in everyday speech, at work and in writing, for things that really matter, like 'It's crucial that you call back today.' It is stronger than 'important' and is often used with 'to' or 'that'. Avoid using it for minor preferences, since it can sound dramatic.

distinctions.note: 'Important' is a general, neutral word, while 'crucial' means decisive or essential for an outcome.
'Essential' means absolutely necessary or basic to something, while 'crucial' emphasizes that a decision or moment determines what happens next.
'Critical' can mean serious or dangerous, as in critical condition, and in technical contexts it means a threshold, so 'crucial' is the better choice for a decisive moment.

examples.everyday: Bring your ID to the appointment, because it is crucial for check-in.
examples.professional: Clean labels are crucial to model performance, so let's audit them before we retrain.
examples.analytical: Justification by faith was crucial to the Reformers' critique of medieval penitential practice.

nuance.analogy: Like the keystone of an arch: if you remove it, the whole structure falls.
nuance.etymology: From Latin crux, cross; the figurative sense 'decisive' developed from the phrase 'crucial experiment', a test at a crossroads.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the stress on the second syllable as 'cru-SHAL'; the stress is on the first syllable.
Pronouncing the 'cia' as 'see-uhl' instead of the sh sound.

crucial.etymology: 1706, from French *crucial*, a medical term for ligaments of the knee, from Latin *crux* (“cross”) (English *crux*), from the Proto-Indo-European **ker-* (“to turn, to bend”).

senses.definition: A customary unit of measure.
senses.example: Add one cup of flour to the bowl and stir until the dough feels smooth.

senses.definition: A US unit of liquid measure equal to 8 fluid ounces (⁄16 of a US gallon; 236.5882365 mL) or 240 mL.
senses.example: The pancake recipe calls for two cups of milk, so I'll measure it carefully this time.

senses.definition: A Canadian unit of measure equal to 8 imperial ounces (⁄20 imperial gallon; 227.3 mL) or 250 mL.
senses.example: My Canadian cousin's cookbook calls for one cup of sugar, which is slightly larger than mine.

senses.definition: A metric unit of measure equal to 250 mL.
senses.example: The European cookbook lists every ingredient in grams, with metric cups for the liquids.

senses.definition: Prefixed with a letter, used as a measurement of bra or breast size.
senses.example: She went shopping because she had grown from a B to a D cup.

senses.definition: A concave vessel for drinking, usually made of opaque material (as opposed to a glass) and with a handle.
senses.example: Pour the tea into the cup.

senses.definition: A container in which dice are held and shaken before being thrown.
senses.example: He rattled the dice in the leather cup before rolling them across the table.

senses.definition: Any of various sweetened alcoholic drinks.
senses.example: cider cup; gin cup; claret cup

senses.definition: The contents of said vessel.
senses.example: I drank two cups of water but still felt thirsty.

senses.definition: A trophy in the shape of an oversized cup.
senses.example: The World Cup is awarded to the winner of a quadrennial football tournament.

senses.definition: A contest for which a cup is awarded.
senses.example: The World Cup is the world's most widely watched sporting event.

senses.definition: The main knockout tournament in a country, organized alongside the league.
senses.example: The club reached the national cup final after knocking out two league rivals this season.

senses.definition: A cup-shaped object placed in the target hole.
senses.example: The ball just misses the cup.

senses.definition: A rigid concave protective covering for the male genitalia.
senses.example: Players of contact sports are advised to wear a cup.

senses.definition: One of the two parts of a brassiere which each covers a breast.
senses.example: The cups are made of a particularly uncomfortable material.

senses.definition: The symbol ∪ denoting union and similar operations.
senses.example: On the exam, the cup symbol means the union of the two sets, not their intersection.

senses.definition: A suit of the minor arcana in tarot, or one of the cards from the suit.
senses.example: She turned over the ace of cups, which her reader said promised new emotional beginnings.

senses.definition: A defensive style characterized by a three player near defense cupping the thrower; or those three players.
senses.example: In ultimate, our coach switched to a cup, with three defenders crowding the thrower.

senses.definition: A flexible concave membrane used to temporarily attach a handle or hook to a flat surface by means of suction.
senses.example: I stuck the suction cup hook to the bathroom tile to hold my shower caddy.

senses.definition: Anything shaped like a cup.
senses.example: the cup of an acorn

senses.definition: That which is to be received or indured; that which is allotted to one; a portion of blessings and afflictions.
senses.example: He accepted his cup of suffering with patience, trusting that God's plan was good.

senses.definition: (historical) A cupping glass or other vessel or instrument used to produce the vacuum in cupping.
senses.example: The nineteenth-century doctor applied a heated cup to the patient's back to draw out blood.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: To pour (a liquid, drink, etc.) into a cup.
senses.example: We are cupping some new brands of coffee today.

senses.definition: To form into the shape of a cup, particularly of the hands.
senses.example: Cup your hands and I'll pour some rice into them.

senses.definition: To hold something in cupped hands.
senses.example: He cupped the ball carefully in his hands.

senses.definition: To make concave or in the form of a cup.
senses.example: to cup the end of a screw

core.definition: A small open container, usually with a handle, used for drinking hot or cold beverages.

pronunciation.tip: Use a short, relaxed vowel like the u in cut, and end with a crisp p without releasing a puff of air. Non-native speakers often lengthen the vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use cup for drinking containers of coffee, tea or water and for measuring ingredients in cooking. Americans say cup of coffee rather than cup of coffee in a British sense; a coffee cup is common, while a mug is usually bigger and handled. A cup of coffee at a coffee shop is a typical everyday order.

distinctions.note: A mug is usually larger, thicker and often used at home; a cup is smaller and may be more delicate.
A glass is made of glass or plastic and usually used for cold drinks; a cup is for hot drinks or any beverage in a cup-shaped container.

examples.everyday: Could I get a cup of coffee with a little milk, please?
examples.professional: Add one cup of flour to the recipe and whisk it before the meeting ends.
examples.analytical: In the measurement system, a cup is defined as a standard volume used for recipes rather than a drinking vessel.

nuance.analogy: Like a small bowl that you hold in your hands to drink from.
nuance.etymology: From Old English cuppe, from Late Latin cuppa, a drinking vessel.
common_mistakes: Using cup for a large drinking vessel, where mug is more natural
Confusing the measuring cup (8 fluid ounces in the US) with Canadian or metric cup sizes

cup.etymology: Middle English *cuppe*, *coppe*, from the merger of Old English *cuppe* (“cup”) and Old English *copp* (“cup, vessel”).

conversation.text: Add two cups of flour to the bowl.
The recipe calls for half a cup of milk.
Can I get a cup of coffee, please?

senses.definition: One who dabbles.
senses.example: Marissa was just a dabbler when it came to writing: she blogged a little, but had never submitted any work to a serious publication.

senses.definition: A dabbling duck.

core.definition: A person who does something only casually or superficially, without serious commitment; also a dabbling duck.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on DAB. The second syllable is a syllabic l followed by an American r-colored ending, so it sounds like DAB-ler with no separate uh vowel.

nuance.connotation: Mildly negative, suggesting shallow or non-serious involvement; less harsh than calling someone a fraud.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use dabbler for someone who tries many activities without mastering any, such as a dabbler in photography or investing. It can sound slightly dismissive when said about a colleague or friend. The duck sense is used mainly by birdwatchers and hunters. In friendly talk, you can say I just dabble in woodworking instead.

distinctions.note: An amateur is simply unpaid and can be very skilled, while a dabbler is defined by shallow, occasional involvement with a slightly negative tone.
Dilettante is more formal and literary, suggesting someone who pursues an art for pleasure without discipline; dabbler is more everyday.
A hobbyist has a steady, committed pastime, whereas a dabbler tries things briefly and moves on.

examples.everyday: Oh, I'm just a dabbler with the guitar, nothing serious.
examples.professional: We need a specialist for this migration, not another dabbler who read one blog post about it.
examples.analytical: A dabbler in theology may collect interesting ideas, but he rarely wrestles with the sources long enough to change his mind.

nuance.analogy: Like a person who tastes many dishes at a buffet but never sits down for a full meal.
nuance.etymology: From dabble, plus the agent suffix -er.
common_mistakes: Adding an extra vowel, saying DAB-uh-ler, which creates an extra syllable
Using dabbler to mean a skilled unpaid expert, when it implies shallowness

core.definition: The chief god of the Philistines, depicted as a fish-like or grain god, whose temple stood in Ashdod.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final vowel is a broad 'ah' in General American, because of the cot-caught merger. Avoid pronouncing the 'g' as a 'j.'

nuance.connotation: Negative in biblical contexts, where Dagon represents an idol that falls before the true God.
nuance.usage_note: Americans encounter Dagon in Bible study, religious history and ancient Near Eastern studies. It is not used in everyday conversation. In a sermon or class you might hear it as a symbol of false worship.

distinctions.note: Baal was a storm and fertility god often worshiped in Canaan, while Dagon was a Philistine god linked with grain and fertility.

examples.everyday: In my Bible study group we talked about how Dagon was the Philistine god whose statue fell before the ark.
examples.professional: Our historical analysis cited Dagon as an example of how ancient cities built temples to deities tied to agriculture.
examples.analytical: The narrative of the ark before Dagon shows the Lord's power over the idols of the nations, a theme repeated across the prophets.

nuance.analogy: Dagon is like a false idol on a pedestal that cannot stand up when the true God shows up.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew dagon, probably from dag, fish, though the meaning is debated.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it 'DAG-un' with a short 'a' in the first syllable.
Confusing Dagon with Baal, which is a different Canaanite god.
nuance.biblical_note: In Hebrew the name is Dagon. The Philistines worshiped Dagon, and their temple at Ashdod housed his image (1 Samuel 5:1-7). When the ark of God was placed before his statue, the image fell down and was broken, a sign of the Lord's power over false gods. Judges 16:23 records the Philistines gathering in Dagon's temple to celebrate their capture of Samson.

senses.definition: Having hair of a dark color, usually dark brown.

core.definition: Having hair of a dark color, usually dark brown or black.

pronunciation.tip: In this compound adjective, the stress falls on the second part, HAIRD, with dark slightly weaker. Pronounce the r in both dark and hair, and make the final -ed a /d/ sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a plain physical description, used in everyday talk, descriptions of people, and writing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use dark-haired to describe a person's hair color in ordinary conversation, police descriptions, casting calls, and fiction. It is neutral and polite, though in very casual speech people often just say 'She has dark hair.' Hyphenate it when it comes before a noun, as in 'a dark-haired woman,' but not after a verb, as in 'She is dark haired' is not standard. A natural reply might be 'Oh, like your sister?'

distinctions.note: Brunette is a noun, often used for a woman with brown hair, while dark-haired is an adjective that covers any dark hair color.
Fair-haired is a formal or somewhat old-fashioned term for light blond hair, while dark-haired describes the opposite end of the color range.
Dark-complected describes skin tone, not hair, and sounds more regional or formal in American English.

examples.everyday: My sister is dark-haired like our mom, but I got my dad's light brown hair.
examples.professional: The casting director is looking for a dark-haired actor who can play the lead role in the new drama series.
examples.analytical: The painting contrasts the dark-haired figure in the foreground with the pale background, which draws the viewer's eye directly to her face.

nuance.analogy: Dark-haired is like a color swatch label: it names the shade so others can picture it quickly.
nuance.etymology: Dark comes from Old English deorc, and hair comes from Old English hær.
common_mistakes: Dropping the -ed, saying 'dark-hair woman' instead of 'dark-haired woman'.
Placing the stress on dark instead of on the second part, HAIRD.

senses.definition: All the disciplines related to managing data as a valuable resource, such as data modeling or metadata management.
senses.example: Our data management team set standards for metadata and data modeling across all departments.

core.definition: The practice of planning, storing, organizing, securing and governing data as a valuable organizational asset.

pronunciation.tip: Stress MAN in 'management', and say it as three syllables in careful speech: MAN-ij-ment, with the j like the 'j' in 'judge'. Avoid adding an extra vowel between the n and the j.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a professional function and carries no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'data management' in business, government and IT, often in job titles or project plans. It is a broad umbrella term that includes modeling, storage and quality, so people often specify which part they mean. A natural reply in a meeting is 'Who owns data management on this project?'

distinctions.note: Governance sets the policies, rules and accountability for data, while management carries them out day to day.
Management concerns storing, organizing and protecting data; analysis concerns interpreting it to answer questions.

examples.everyday: My company is finally getting serious about data management, so I have to label every spreadsheet I keep.
