nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise scientific term, used with no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'fluorescence' mainly in science, medicine and engineering, for example 'fluorescence microscopy' or 'fluorescence imaging.' In everyday life, people say 'the glow of fluorescent lights' rather than using the noun. The word is used both for the process and for the light that is given off.

distinctions.note: Phosphorescence continues to glow after the light source is removed; fluorescence stops almost at once.
Bioluminescence is light produced by a living organism's own chemistry, while fluorescence needs light from outside to be absorbed first.

examples.everyday: The old poster glows because of fluorescence from the black light.
examples.professional: We measure the fluorescence signal to estimate how much of the protein is present in each sample.
examples.analytical: Fluorescence reveals the energy a molecule releases as light after it absorbs photons, so it offers a window into molecular structure.

nuance.analogy: Fluorescence is like a sponge that soaks up water and releases it quickly: the molecule absorbs light and gives it back almost at once.
nuance.etymology: From 'fluorescent,' from 'fluorspar' (fluorite), from Latin 'fluor' (flow) and 'fluere' (to flow).
common_mistakes: Confusing 'fluorescence' with 'florescence,' which refers to flowering, and is pronounced differently.
Stressing the wrong syllable; say 'floo-RESS-uns,' not 'FLOO-res-ence.'

senses.definition: In the fourth place; fourth in a row.

core.definition: In the fourth place, used to introduce the fourth point in a numbered list of arguments or reasons.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the first syllable, FOHRTH, and the th and l are close together. Keep the r clear and end with a light ee sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly stiff. It signals a formal, numbered structure in speech or writing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use fourthly mainly in formal speeches, sermons, essays or academic arguments to introduce a fourth point. In conversation, people say also, another thing, or finally instead. Using fourthly in casual talk can sound old-fashioned or humorous, so save it for organized argument.

distinctions.note: Fourthly marks a specific numbered point in a list; finally signals the last point, which might be the fourth or the fifth.
Fourth is an adjective or noun; fourthly is an adverb that introduces a point in an argument.

examples.everyday: Fourthly, you should really try the mango lassi, because it's amazing.
examples.professional: Fourthly, we need a rollback plan in case the migration fails in production.
examples.analytical: Fourthly, the author assumes that moral agency survives without any account of embodiment.

nuance.analogy: Fourthly works like a numbered sign on a trail: it marks one stop along a longer route.
nuance.etymology: From fourth (from Old English feortha) plus the adverbial suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Using fourthly in everyday conversation, where it sounds stiff.
Adding an extra syllable and saying FOHRTH-lee-ee.

senses.definition: To be upset or nervous; to be scared or unnerved.
To scare or unnerve someone.
senses.example: Don't take off your shirt when working behind the counter. You'll freak the customers out.

senses.definition: To react with extreme anger or fear, to the extent that one loses one's composure or behaves irrationally.
senses.example: When Peter saw the nail poking up through his foot, he freaked out and started hyperventilating.

senses.definition: To adopt an unconventional (especially countercultural) persona or appearance.
senses.example: After college, my cousin decided to freak out and dye his hair neon green and pierce his nose.

senses.definition: (dated) A negative or unpleasant experience with LSD or another psychedelic drug.
senses.example: Nobody wanted to talk about the freak-out he had after taking acid at the festival.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: To become very upset, nervous, or scared, or to make someone else feel that way.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on OUT, and freak has a long ee sound, not a short i. Link the k of freak smoothly into out so it sounds like freek-OWT with the t often softened.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. It is casual and often humorous, but it can describe real distress.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say freak out very casually with friends, family, or coworkers, for example, when someone panics about a deadline or a surprise. It is informal, so avoid it in formal emails or meetings. A common reply is to reassure the person, such as Don't freak out, it's fine. The past form is freaked out, and the noun form is rarely used outside drug contexts.

distinctions.note: Panic is stronger and more serious, suggesting a sudden loss of control, while freak out is casual and can be used for milder reactions.
Overreact means responding more strongly than the situation deserves, while freak out focuses on the emotional state of being upset or scared.

examples.everyday: Don't freak out if the flight is delayed, because they'll probably give us vouchers.
examples.professional: The client started to freak out when the deadline moved, so I scheduled a short call to explain the plan.
examples.analytical: People often freak out when they face an unfamiliar risk, which shows how emotion can distort judgment about probabilities.

nuance.analogy: Freaking out is like a pot that boils over suddenly: the pressure builds, and then everything spills out at once.
nuance.etymology: Freak, meaning a sudden fit or whim, combined with out; the phrasal sense developed in twentieth-century American slang.
common_mistakes: Using freak out as a noun in ordinary speech, when the usual noun is freak or a freakout.
Placing the object between freak and out only sometimes; freak someone out is correct, but freak out someone is awkward.
Saying the vowel of freak as a short i instead of a long ee.

conversation.text: I freaked out when I couldn't find my passport.
Don't freak out, but I scratched your car.
That horror movie really freaked me out.
My mom freaked out when I came home with a tattoo.

senses.definition: Without friends (without a friend).
senses.example: friendless homebody

core.definition: Having no friends, so that a person feels alone or lacks anyone close to them.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. Say the d clearly before the -less, which is a reduced 'luhs', not 'less' with a strong vowel.

nuance.connotation: Negative and sad. It describes a painful social state, so it should be used with care about other people.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'friendless' to describe someone who has no close companions, often a new arrival in a city, a lonely child or an older person. Everyday speech often prefers 'I don't have many friends here' or 'I feel alone', which is softer. The word is more common in stories, songs and serious conversation than in casual talk.

distinctions.note: Lonely describes a feeling of sadness about being alone; friendless describes the fact of having no friends.
Alone describes being physically without others; friendless refers to the lack of friends, even in a crowd.

examples.everyday: After we moved across the country, I felt pretty friendless for the first few months.
examples.professional: The mentoring program pairs new hires with a buddy so that no one starts out friendless on their first day.
examples.analytical: Dickens often portrays the friendless child as morally exposed, since a lack of social bonds leaves him vulnerable to exploitation.

nuance.analogy: Like a house with no one to knock at the door, a friendless person has a home but few visitors.
nuance.etymology: From friend, plus the suffix -less meaning 'without'.
common_mistakes: Dropping the d, saying 'fren-less' or 'freen-luss'.
Using friendless for a temporary situation where 'I don't know anyone yet' is more natural.
Confusing friendless with unfriendly, which describes someone's behavior, not their social circle.

friendless.etymology: From Middle English *frendles*, from Old English *frēondlēas*.

senses.definition: To disappoint or defeat; to vex by depriving of something expected or desired.
senses.example: It frustrates me to do all this work and then lose it all.

senses.definition: To hinder or thwart.
senses.example: My clumsy fingers frustrate my typing efforts.

senses.definition: To cause stress or annoyance.
senses.example: This test frustrates me because if I fail, it'll destroy my grade.

senses.definition: Ineffectual; useless; fruitless.
senses.example: Her frustrate efforts to revive the dying garden came to nothing.

core.definition: To block someone's plans or efforts, or to leave them annoyed and helpless because something they want cannot happen.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The str cluster is quick, and the final -ate is 'ayt,' not 'at.' Don't add an extra syllable between the s and the t.

nuance.connotation: Negative: suggests being blocked or annoyed by an obstacle.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use frustrate for plans, efforts, and people's feelings, like 'The traffic frustrates me.' It is a fairly strong word. In casual talk, people often say 'annoy' or 'drive me crazy' instead. For plans, 'thwart' sounds more deliberate and intentional.

distinctions.note: Annoy is mild and everyday; frustrate implies being blocked from a goal, so it is stronger.
Thwart means deliberately stopping something; frustrate can happen without anyone intending it.

examples.everyday: The slow Wi-Fi really frustrates me when I'm trying to finish a call.
examples.professional: Unclear requirements kept frustrating the engineers, so we set a firm scope before the next sprint.
examples.analytical: Hard questions about divine action frustrate those who seek a single, neat explanation.

nuance.analogy: Like a dam across a river: the water keeps pushing but cannot flow where it wants to go.
nuance.etymology: From Latin frustrari, to disappoint or deceive, from frustra, in vain.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable or giving the first vowel too long a sound; keep it FRUHS-trayt.
Writing 'I am frustrate' for the feeling; use 'I am frustrated.'

frustrate.etymology: From Middle English *frustraten* (“to prevent, disappoint, render useless”), from Latin *frūstrātus*, perfect passive participle of *frūstrō* (“to deceive”), see *-ate*.

core.definition: Gaal son of Ebed, a man who led a revolt against Abimelech in the city of Shechem in the Book of Judges.

pronunciation.tip: Pronounce it as one syllable, like 'gale', with a long a and a clear final l. Do not add a second syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a name used in Bible study and religious discussion.
nuance.usage_note: Americans hear Gaal mainly in Bible study or sermons about the book of Judges. It is a proper name, so it is used without an article. In conversation you would say 'Gaal son of Ebed' to identify him.

distinctions.note: Gaal is a character in Judges; Gabael is a man in the apocryphal book of Tobit, so they are not related.

examples.everyday: Our Bible study group read about Gaal son of Ebed, who tried to take over Shechem and ended up losing.
examples.professional: In my lesson on Judges, I explain that Gaal's revolt shows how quickly loyalty can shift in a divided city.
examples.analytical: The narrative presents Gaal as a foil to Abimelech, illustrating the theme of divine retribution for violence against kinsmen.

nuance.analogy: Like a minor character in a long political drama who appears briefly, causes trouble, and exits.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew Gaʾal, a personal name whose meaning is uncertain, possibly connected to a word for loathing.
common_mistakes: Adding an article, saying 'the Gaal', since it is a personal name.
Confusing Gaal with Gabriel or Gabael because the names look similar.
nuance.biblical_note: Gaal son of Ebed appears in Judges 9, where he is a leader who moves into Shechem with his kinsmen and gains the trust of the citizens. Judges 9:26-29 describes his entry and his speech against Abimelech. Judges 9:39-41 describes how Abimelech defeats him and drives him out of the city.

senses.definition: In a gallant or gentlemanly manner; with social graces.
senses.example: He gallantly offered his seat to the elderly woman and bowed before she sat down.

senses.definition: In a brave or valiant manner.

core.definition: In a courteous, chivalrous way, or in a brave, heroic way.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and keep the middle syllable weak, so it is GAL-uhnt-lee rather than three full syllables. The t between n and l is often unreleased, so the word sounds smooth.

nuance.connotation: Positive: it praises polite, brave or chivalrous conduct and is complimentary when used about a person.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use gallantly mostly in writing or formal speech to describe chivalrous behavior, such as holding a door for a woman, or courageous conduct in battle or a crisis. In casual talk people usually say nicely, politely or bravely instead. The word sounds old-fashioned but warm, so it works well in a toast, a letter or a story.

distinctions.note: Bravely stresses courage in the face of danger, while gallantly adds a sense of noble, polite conduct.
Courteously is about ordinary good manners, while gallantly implies a chivalrous, sometimes old-fashioned, gesture toward someone.

examples.everyday: He gallantly offered to carry my grocery bags up the stairs.
examples.professional: The team fought gallantly through the outage, even though the launch date was already lost.
examples.analytical: The medieval knight acted gallantly toward the weak, though his courtesy often served his own reputation.

nuance.analogy: Like a knight opening a door for someone: the act is small, but it shows a code of honor.
nuance.etymology: From French galant, meaning splendid or courteous, from galer, to make merry.
common_mistakes: Using gallantly where you need the noun gallantry, as in 'he showed great gallantry', not 'great gallantly'.
Pronouncing the middle syllable with a full vowel, as GAL-ant-lee, instead of a weak GAL-uhnt-lee.

senses.definition: (archaic) A person who deserves, or is likely, to be hanged.
senses.label: archaic

core.definition: (archaic) A person who deserves, or is likely, to be hanged; a hardened criminal or troublemaker.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first word and give bird a weaker secondary stress, so it is GAL-ohz burd. The final s of gallows is a z sound, even though the word refers to one structure.

nuance.connotation: Negative: it calls someone a criminal or troublemaker in a dramatic way.
nuance.usage_note: Americans almost never use gallows bird now, except in old novels, westerns or jokes about an unruly relative. Calling someone a gallows bird today sounds old-fashioned and dramatic. The modern equivalent is jailbird.

distinctions.note: Jailbird is the everyday modern word for a convicted person, while gallows bird is archaic and suggests someone who deserves hanging.

examples.everyday: Grandpa tells stories about his cousin, an old gallows bird who was always in trouble with the sheriff.
examples.professional: The old manager was a gallows bird who courted trouble, so we kept a close eye on his expense reports.
examples.analytical: The novelist draws the gallows bird as a figure of fate, a man whose character already seems to condemn him.

nuance.analogy: Like a wanted poster from an old Western film.
nuance.etymology: Gallows from Old English galga, a cross or gibbet; bird is an old informal word for a person.
common_mistakes: Using gallows bird as a playful insult today; it sounds strange and dated.
Saying gallow as the singular; use gallows even when referring to one structure.

senses.definition: Synonym of fuel economy.

core.definition: How far a vehicle can travel on one gallon of gasoline, usually measured in miles per gallon; another name for fuel economy.

pronunciation.tip: Stress GAS, the first word of this compound. In mileage the first syllable is strong, but the second is a short 'ij' sound, not 'ledge'. Americans clearly say the 'j' sound at the end.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a practical, everyday measure, and people often compare it positively or negatively when talking about cars.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say gas mileage constantly when talking about cars, for example about buying a new car or commuting costs. Gas here means gasoline, a usage that does not work the same way in British English, where the word is petrol. Fuel economy is the more formal or official term, often used by the EPA and in car advertising.

distinctions.note: Fuel economy is the formal or official term used in government reports and advertising, while gas mileage is the everyday American phrase.
MPG is the number itself, for example 30 mpg, while gas mileage refers to the general measure.
Range is the total distance a car can travel on one full tank, which depends on both mileage and tank size.

examples.everyday: This hybrid gets great gas mileage, so my weekly commute costs me about twenty dollars.
examples.professional: Fleet managers compare gas mileage across the vehicles before deciding which models to renew next year.
examples.analytical: Official gas mileage ratings come from standardized test cycles, so real drivers often see noticeably different numbers.

nuance.analogy: Gas mileage is like a calorie count for your car: it shows how efficiently fuel turns into distance.
nuance.etymology: Gas is short for gasoline, a 1900s American usage; mileage is formed from mile with the suffix -age.
common_mistakes: Using petrol mileage, which sounds British to American ears.
Stressing mileage as much as gas, when the main stress falls on GAS.

senses.definition: The action of gasifying.
senses.example: Gasification of the coal produced a synthesis gas used to generate electricity.

senses.definition: The process of transforming carbon-based materials into a mix of carbon monoxide and hydrogen that can serve as fuel.

core.definition: The process of turning coal, wood or other carbon-based material into a gas, mainly carbon monoxide and hydrogen, that can be burned as fuel.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on KAY, and the final -tion is pronounced 'shun.' Non-native speakers often over-pronounce the reduced middle syllables as 'fi-KAY' with full vowels; keep them short and weak.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. In energy and environmental discussions it is usually presented positively as a cleaner way to make fuel from waste, but the word itself carries no value judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mainly in engineering, energy, waste management and environmental policy, for example when a utility or university describes a plant. You will rarely hear it in casual talk, where people say 'turning trash into fuel' instead. Do not use it for the carbonation of soda; that process is called carbonation.

distinctions.note: Pyrolysis heats material with little or no oxygen to make char, liquids and gas, whereas gasification uses a controlled amount of oxygen or steam to produce mainly synthesis gas.
Combustion burns material fully with excess oxygen to release heat, while gasification stops short of burning and creates a fuel gas that can be stored or burned later.
Carbonation dissolves carbon dioxide into a liquid, as in soda; gasification changes a solid or liquid feedstock into a gas through chemical reactions.

examples.everyday: My neighbor works at a plant that uses gasification to turn wood scraps into fuel, which he says is cleaner than burning them outdoors.
examples.professional: The engineering team compared gasification and anaerobic digestion to see which would convert our city's green waste into usable energy at the lowest cost.
examples.analytical: Gasification shifts the question from simply releasing energy to controlling how carbon is rearranged into a fuel gas, which makes the chemistry of the process central to its value.

nuance.analogy: Gasification is like cooking food slowly over a low fire until it breaks down into smaller pieces, rather than setting it on fire and letting it burn away.
nuance.etymology: From gasify, plus the suffix -ation meaning the act or process of; the root gas was coined by the chemist Jan Baptist van Helmont in the 1600s.
common_mistakes: Confusing gasification with carbonation, the process of adding carbon dioxide to a drink
Stressing the wrong syllable as gas-i-FI-ca-tion instead of gas-uh-fuh-KAY-shun

senses.definition: A socially tactless or awkward act.
Lack of tact; tactlessness; awkwardness.

core.definition: A socially tactless or awkward act, or a general lack of social polish.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the last syllable, REE, with a lighter secondary stress on goh. The sh is followed by a reduced vowel, and the final ee is long.

nuance.connotation: Negative, criticizing a lack of tact or polish.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use gaucherie in conversation; it appears mainly in literary criticism, memoir, or sophisticated writing. In everyday speech, people say awkward moment or social blunder. Using it in casual talk would sound pretentious unless the speaker is deliberately witty.

distinctions.note: A faux pas is a specific social mistake, while gaucherie can be a general quality or a broader pattern of awkwardness.
Blunder is a broader word for any serious mistake, while gaucherie is specifically about social tact.

examples.professional: Her email had a moment of gaucherie that I'll help her fix before she sends the next one.
examples.analytical: The narrator's gaucherie reveals his longing to belong to a class he does not yet understand.

nuance.analogy: Gaucherie is like a wrong note in a piano recital: a small error that exposes a lack of practice in social rhythm.
nuance.etymology: From French gauche, meaning awkward, with the French noun suffix -erie.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as goh-SHEER-ee, with stress in the wrong place.
Using it as an adjective, which is gauche.

senses.definition: Related to a topic of discussion or consideration.
Germanium tetrahydride, GeH4.
senses.example: Germane is a toxic gas, so the lab keeps it in sealed cylinders.

senses.definition: Any organic derivative of this compound.
senses.example: Chemists synthesized a germane derivative with an added methyl group for the semiconductor study.

core.definition: Relevant and closely connected to the subject being discussed or the question being considered.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, MAYN, and keep the first syllable as a quick jer. It is not pronounced like the word German, and the final n is clear.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use germane mainly in formal writing, academic discussion, legal and policy settings, and polite but firm meetings. Saying something is not germane is a polite way to say it is off topic. In casual talk, Americans usually say relevant or that is not really the point.

distinctions.note: Relevant is common in everyday and professional speech, while germane is more formal and implies a close, logical connection to the subject.
Pertinent is also formal and often applies to a specific question or fact, while germane emphasizes the broader topic under discussion.

examples.everyday: That story about your cousin isn't really germane to what we were talking about, so let's get back to the trip.
examples.professional: Please keep the comments germane to the proposal so we can finish the review by three.
examples.analytical: Only evidence germane to the question of causation should enter the argument, since the rest only distracts from the claim.

nuance.analogy: A germane point is like a key that fits the lock you are actually trying to open.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English germain, from Old French germain, from Latin germanus, meaning full-blooded or closely related.
common_mistakes: Confusing germane with German or with germ, since the spellings look similar.
Omitting the preposition to, as in germane the topic, when it should be germane to the topic.
patterns: germane to sth (not before a noun)

germane.etymology: A variant form of *german* (“having the same parents; related”), adapted in this sense in allusions to its use in Shakespeare's Hamlet (see quotations at *germaine*).

senses.definition: To cause to grow; to produce.
Of a seed, to begin to grow, to sprout roots and leaves.

core.definition: To begin to grow, as a seed or spore does when it sprouts roots and leaves; or to cause something to start developing.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the g is hard, as in 'go', not 'jam'. The vowel in the first syllable is the r-colored 'er' sound, so don't say 'JOOM'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a natural process and is used in both everyday and scientific contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use germinate mostly for seeds, bulbs and spores, especially in gardening, farming and biology. In casual talk, people more often say 'sprout' or 'start to grow'. The figurative sense, 'to begin to develop an idea', is less common but natural in professional or academic writing.

distinctions.note: Sprout is the everyday word for a seed putting up its first shoot. Germinate is more technical and can also describe ideas or processes.
Grow is general and covers any increase in size. Germinate names only the specific beginning stage of growth from a seed or spore.

examples.everyday: The beans I planted in the garden finally germinated after a week of rain.
examples.professional: Our agronomist said the test batch failed to germinate because the soil was too cold.
examples.analytical: The author argues that the seed of the reform idea germinated long before the political movement that made it visible.

nuance.analogy: A seed is like a sealed envelope holding a full set of instructions; germinating is the moment someone opens it and starts following them.
nuance.etymology: From Latin germinare, 'to sprout', from germen, 'bud or sprout'.
common_mistakes: Using germinate for plants that have already grown tall; it applies only to the start of growth.
Pronouncing the first syllable as 'jeem' instead of the r-colored 'JUR'.

germinate.etymology: From oblique stem of Latin *germen* (“shoot, sprout, bud”) *-ate*, from *germinātus* (“sprouted, budded, grown”), past participle of *germinō* (“to sprout, bud, grow”), from *germen* (“shoot, sprout, bud”).

senses.definition: Prone to; in the habit of (doing); inclined towards.
senses.example: She is given to taking a nap in the afternoon.

core.definition: Having a habit or tendency to do something, often something unwelcome; prone to doing it regularly.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on GIV, and to is weak, often sounding like tuh before a consonant. The n in given is light, so the phrase flows as one unit.

nuance.connotation: Mostly negative, describing a bad or annoying habit, though it can be neutral with words like reflection.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use given to in writing and formal speech to describe a person's habits, as in he's given to exaggeration. In casual talk people say prone to, tend to, or always does. It sounds slightly old-fashioned in speech, so it works best in reviews, character descriptions, and writing.

distinctions.note: Prone to suggests a vulnerability or likelihood, often to something harmful like injury, while given to suggests a settled personal habit.
Inclined to is a softer and more neutral phrase for a tendency or willingness, while given to often describes a regular habit.
Addicted to is much stronger and refers to dependence, while given to describes a habit and does not imply addiction.

examples.everyday: My uncle is a sweet guy, but he's always been given to long stories at dinner.
examples.professional: Our project lead is given to making big promises in meetings, so we should check her timelines.
examples.analytical: Some Enlightenment writers were given to viewing religious enthusiasm as a sign of psychological weakness.

nuance.analogy: Like a dog that runs to the door at every knock, a person given to a habit reacts to the same triggers again and again.
nuance.etymology: From given, the past participle of give, plus to; the sense of being devoted to something comes from giving oneself over to it.
common_mistakes: Following given to directly with a bare verb; use a gerund or noun, as in given to exaggerating.
Confusing given to with give to, which is a verb phrase for handing something to someone.
Using given to in the sense of given a gift; that is a different use of given.

senses.definition: In a glad manner; happily.
senses.example: I would gladly help you move the couch on Saturday if you bring the pizza.

senses.definition: Willingly; certainly.
senses.example: Would you like a beer? ― Gladly, thank you.

core.definition: Willingly and with pleasure, without hesitation.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on the first syllable. The final -ly is a clear "lee" sound, and the a is short as in cat.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it signals eagerness and kindness.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use gladly to show they are happy to do something, as in "I'd gladly help" or "I'll gladly take that." It is polite and common in service and business settings, such as "We'll gladly refund you." It can sound slightly formal, but it is natural in customer service and emails.

distinctions.note: Willingly stresses choice without reluctance; gladly adds a feeling of pleasure.
Happily often describes a mood; gladly usually refers to accepting or doing something.

examples.everyday: If you need a ride to the airport, I'd gladly drive you.
examples.professional: We will gladly review your proposal and send feedback by Friday.
examples.analytical: The author argues that a true believer gladly accepts suffering for a higher purpose.

nuance.analogy: Like someone holding the door open with a smile: help offered without any hesitation.
nuance.etymology: From glad plus the adverbial suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Using gladly to mean happily in a mood sense, as in "I feel gladly"; use happily or glad instead.
Placing gladly awkwardly before the verb; say "I'd gladly help" rather than "I gladly would help" in casual speech.
nuance.biblical_note: Gladly appears in the RSV to translate Greek words meaning with pleasure or most readily. In 2 Corinthians 12:9 Paul says he will boast all the more gladly of his weaknesses, so that Christ's power may rest upon him. In 2 Corinthians 12:15 he says he will most gladly spend and be spent for the Corinthians, showing a willingness to sacrifice for others.

senses.definition: Roughly spherical in shape; globe-shaped.
Comprising globules.
senses.example: The sample was a globular mass of tiny droplets suspended in oil.

senses.definition: A globular cluster.
senses.example: The telescope revealed that the globular contained hundreds of ancient stars packed tightly together.

core.definition: Round or roughly spherical in shape, like a ball or globe, and sometimes made up of small round parts.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, GLAB. Pronounce the 'o' as a short ah sound, as in 'cot,' and make the final -er sound rhotic, as in 'ler.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise descriptive term, usually used in science.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'globular' mainly in biology, chemistry, and astronomy, for shapes such as globular proteins or globular star clusters. In everyday speech, people say 'round' or 'ball-shaped.' 'Globular' suggests roughly round rather than perfectly spherical.

distinctions.note: Spherical is precise and geometric; globular means roughly round, often with irregularities, especially in natural objects.
Round is a general everyday word; globular is more technical and specific to ball-like forms in science.

examples.everyday: The sprinkles on the cake were little globular blobs of color that stuck to the frosting.
examples.professional: The enzyme is a compact globular protein, so our lab uses a standard column to purify it.
examples.analytical: In protein biophysics, the central question is how a long chain of amino acids folds into a globular shape that still works as a machine.

nuance.analogy: A globular shape is like a bunch of grapes: roughly round, but not perfectly smooth or exact.
nuance.etymology: From Latin globulus, meaning small sphere, plus the adjective suffix '-ar.'
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, as in 'glob-YOO-lar'; the stress is on the first syllable.
Using 'globular' for 'global' in everyday sentences, which changes the meaning from shape to scope.

senses.definition: The state or condition of being gloomy.

core.definition: The state or quality of being gloomy; a dark, dim or sad condition.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, GLOO. The final syllable is a reduced vowel followed by s. Do not add an extra syllable after m.

nuance.connotation: Negative, suggesting sadness, dimness or pessimism.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use gloominess to describe weather, rooms, moods or outlooks, such as the gloominess of the sky. It is correct but usually less common than gloom, which is shorter and more natural in conversation. It is used both for physical dimness and emotional sadness.

distinctions.note: Gloom is the more common noun; gloominess emphasizes the quality or state of being gloomy.
Darkness refers to a lack of light; gloominess can also describe mood, atmosphere or outlook.

examples.everyday: I cannot stand the gloominess of this rainy weather.
examples.professional: The team noticed a gloominess in the reports, so we scheduled a more hopeful discussion.
examples.analytical: The critic argues that the novel's gloominess is not simply mood but a considered philosophical position.

nuance.analogy: Gloominess is like a window painted over with gray: little light gets through.
nuance.etymology: From gloomy, from gloom, plus the noun ending -ness.
common_mistakes: Using gloominess when gloom is more natural in everyday American speech.
Pronouncing the middle syllable too strongly.

senses.definition: To make an extra effort; to do a particularly good job.
senses.example: Our contractor really went the extra mile, staying late to finish the kitchen before the party.

core.definition: To make a special effort to do something better or more helpful than what is expected.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on GO, and the phrase's stresses are on EX in extra and on MILE. Say extra with the stress on the first syllable, and do not pronounce it as eks-tra with a long a; the -tra is reduced to struh.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises someone who puts in extra care or effort, often at work or in service.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase at work, in customer service, and in praise of friends or family. It is often said as a compliment, such as 'She always goes the extra mile for her clients.' It can also be used as a request: 'We need someone to go the extra mile on this.' A natural reply is 'Thanks, I try to do good work for people.'

distinctions.note: Do your best is a general phrase for trying hard, while go the extra mile emphasizes doing more than expected.
Step up means to take responsibility or improve when needed, and it is often used in a crisis, while go the extra mile is about voluntary extra effort.

collocations: go the extra mile for customers
go the extra mile for your family
willing to go the extra mile

examples.everyday: My neighbor went the extra mile and drove me to the airport at five in the morning.
examples.professional: Thanks to Maria, who went the extra mile to clean the training data before the model launch.
examples.analytical: Jesus's teaching about walking a second mile shows a demand that exceeds what the law requires.

nuance.analogy: Like running past the finish line you were told to reach, just to be sure you cleared it.
nuance.etymology: Mile comes from Latin mille passuum, 'a thousand paces'; the Roman mile was the origin of the idiom's image.
common_mistakes: Saying 'go an extra mile' with a, which is possible but less common than 'the extra mile'; Americans almost always say 'the extra mile'.
Pronouncing extra with a long a, as in 'EKS-tra'; say EK-struh.
nuance.biblical_note: The phrase comes from Matthew 5:41, where Jesus teaches his followers to go a second mile with someone who forces them to walk one mile, a reference to Roman soldiers who could compel civilians to carry their gear. The Greek word is angareuo, meaning to compel or press into service. Key passages are Matthew 5:41, Matthew 5:38-42 on not resisting evil, and Matthew 5:43-48 on loving enemies.

go-the-extra-mile.etymology: * Possibly from the gospel of Matthew ch.5: v.41

conversation.text: Our nurse really went the extra mile to make my mom comfortable.
If you want that promotion, you'll need to go the extra mile.
The team went the extra mile and added a demo for the client.

senses.definition: May God bless you; said as a short prayer, benediction, or valediction for the recipient; usually religiously; sometimes nonliterally but rhetorically or culturally.
senses.example: I heard you helped them with clearing away the downed tree. God bless you! The Lord provides!

senses.definition: Said to somebody who has sneezed, as a rhetorical response; alternative form of bless you.
senses.example: When Dad sneezed at dinner, my mother quickly said, 'God bless you.'

core.definition: A blessing said to someone who has sneezed, or as a warm wish for another person's well-being.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on BLESS, while God and you are lighter. The you is often reduced to yuh in fast speech.

nuance.connotation: Positive and warm; religious in origin but used even by nonbelievers as politeness.
nuance.usage_note: After a sneeze, Americans usually say bless you, which is shorter and more casual. God bless you is warmer and often used with friends, family or children. A natural reply is thanks or thank you. As a farewell it is common in churches and among older Americans, and it sounds sincere rather than rude.

distinctions.note: Bless you is the usual short response to a sneeze; God bless you is warmer and more explicitly religious.
Goodbye is neutral, while God bless you as a farewell adds a wish for the other person's well-being.

examples.everyday: Oh, you sneezed? God bless you.
examples.professional: Thanks for covering my shift today, and God bless you and your family.
examples.analytical: In the Pauline greetings, a blessing is more than a wish; it is a prayer that God's grace will rest on the hearers.

nuance.analogy: Like a warm hand on the shoulder, it offers good will in the form of a prayer.
nuance.etymology: Bless from Old English blētsian, to consecrate, probably from blōd, blood.
common_mistakes: Replying with God bless you to a sneeze instead of simply saying thank you.
Stressing God rather than bless; the main stress falls on bless.
nuance.biblical_note: In Scripture, to bless translates Hebrew barak and Greek eulogein, meaning to invoke God's favor or to speak words that convey it. Genesis 12:2 records God's promise I will bless you, making blessing the core of Abraham's calling. Numbers 6:24 begins the priestly blessing, which asks the LORD to bless and keep his people. The blessing is an act of God's favor, not just a wish.

god-bless-you.etymology: From Middle English *God blesse you*, *God blisse you*.

core.definition: In the Bible, a prince or leader of the land of Magog who leads nations against Israel in an end-time attack.

pronunciation.tip: One short syllable with the open 'ah' vowel and a hard g at both ends. Do not add a vowel at the end.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in the Bible; it names an enemy of God's people. In casual talk the name is rare.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mostly meet Gog in Bible study, sermons or discussions of Ezekiel and Revelation. It is rarely used outside religious contexts, except in the phrase Gog and Magog, meaning a hostile foreign power or a fearsome enemy.

distinctions.note: Gog is the person or leader; Magog is the land or people he rules, and the two are almost always named together.

collocations: Gog of the land of Magog

examples.everyday: Our pastor mentioned Gog and Magog during the sermon, and I had to look up who they were.
examples.professional: In the seminar we compared how different commentators identify Gog in the prophecy of Ezekiel.
examples.analytical: The identity of Gog in Ezekiel 38 has been debated, with some reading him as a historical enemy and others as a symbol of hostile powers.

nuance.analogy: Gog is like a fictional villain named in an ancient prophecy whose name becomes shorthand for a dangerous enemy that rises up against the good.
nuance.etymology: The name's origin and meaning are uncertain; scholars have proposed several explanations and none is fully established.
common_mistakes: Confusing Gog with Magog; Gog is the leader and Magog is the land.
Pronouncing it with a long o as GOHG.
nuance.biblical_note: Gog appears in Ezekiel 38:2 and 39:1 as the prince of Rosh, Meshech and Tubal, from the land of Magog, who is commanded by God to attack the restored people of Israel. In Ezekiel 38-39 Gog is defeated by God in a dramatic judgment. In Revelation 20:8 Gog and Magog are named as nations that Satan deceives after the thousand years, when they gather for battle against God's people before being destroyed. Genesis 10:2 names Magog as a son of Japheth, which helps explain the connection of the land.

senses.definition: A mild expression of surprise or enthusiasm.
senses.example: Gosh, I didn’t realize I’d cause so much trouble!

core.definition: A mild exclamation used to show surprise, enthusiasm, or mild frustration.

pronunciation.tip: Use the short 'ah' vowel of 'cot' and end with the 'sh' sound. American speakers often keep the vowel open and short, so avoid making it sound like 'goes'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to mildly positive. It is a soft, harmless expression, and it sounds clean, so it is used around children and in polite company.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use gosh with friends, family, and coworkers when they are surprised or impressed, or when something is a little annoying. It is a mild alternative to stronger exclamations like 'oh my God', which can offend some people. Often it is said with 'oh' at the start, as in 'Oh, gosh!' A natural reply is simply to laugh or continue the conversation, since no answer is expected.

distinctions.note: Wow expresses strong amazement or admiration; gosh can express surprise, mild worry, or embarrassment.
Oh my God is much stronger and can be offensive in some settings; gosh is a mild, family-friendly substitute.

examples.everyday: Gosh, I didn't realize it was already ten o'clock, so I have to run.
examples.professional: Gosh, the model's accuracy jumped from 71 to 94 percent after we fixed the labels.
examples.analytical: Gosh, the argument collapses the moment we ask what would count as evidence against it.

nuance.analogy: Gosh is like a soft nudge of surprise: it tells people you noticed something, without making a big scene.
nuance.etymology: A euphemism for God, formed as a softened exclamation in the 1800s.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the vowel like 'goes' or 'gosh' with a long 'o' sound; the vowel is short and open, like 'cot'.
Using gosh in very formal writing, where it sounds too casual.

senses.definition: In a governmental way; by or through a government.

core.definition: In a way that involves or is done by a government, or through official government action.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on MEN, and the final -ally is usually pronounced 'uh-lee' in American speech. Many learners put the stress on GUV or drop the middle syllables. Keep the first two syllables light and the stress strong on MEN.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise, somewhat technical term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use governmentally in everyday talk; they usually say by the government or through government channels instead. You will mainly see the word in academic writing, policy analysis, or legal writing. In speech, it can sound overly formal.

distinctions.note: Politically refers to parties, elections, or power struggles, while governmentally refers to official government action or structure.
Publicly means in view of the public or open to people generally, while governmentally means through official government channels.

examples.everyday: The park was built governmentally, so the city pays for its upkeep.
examples.professional: Our research grant is governmentally funded, so the reporting requirements are strict.
examples.analytical: A policy is legitimate only if its aims are governmentally justified and publicly accountable.

nuance.analogy: Governmentally is like a stamp on a document: it shows the action carries official authority from the government.
nuance.etymology: From governmental plus the adverb suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Confusing governmentally with politically, which covers a wider range of meanings.
Stressing the first syllable, as in 'GUV-ern-MEN-tal-ly'; the main stress belongs on MEN.

senses.definition: Given to using language in a showy way by using an excessive number of difficult words to impress others; bombastic; turgid.

core.definition: Using big, showy words in speech or writing to impress others; bombastic or overblown.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on -DIL-, and the -quent ending is pronounced with a short uh, like 'kwunt.' Many learners stress the final syllable or pronounce the middle -lo- as a long vowel.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It implies that the speaker cares more about sounding impressive than being clear.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it mainly in literary criticism, academic writing, or sharp commentary on public speakers. In conversation it sounds stiff, so people would more often say 'pompous' or 'full of hot air.' It is rarely used as praise.

distinctions.note: Eloquent praises speech that is clear and persuasive, while grandiloquent criticizes speech that is inflated and showy.
Pompous describes a person's self-importance in general, while grandiloquent describes a specific style of language.

examples.everyday: Dad gave one of his grandiloquent toasts, and everyone was rolling their eyes by the second minute.
examples.professional: The manager's grandiloquent status update made it hard to tell what the team had actually finished.
examples.analytical: Gibbon's grandiloquent sentences are magnificent, yet they sometimes obscure the precise evidence he is weighing.

nuance.analogy: A grandiloquent speaker is like a stage actor playing to the back row, with gestures so large that the story is lost.
nuance.etymology: From Latin grandiloquus, from grandis (grand) and loqui (to speak).
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'eloquent' and using it as praise.
Misplacing the stress as gran-di-LOH-kwent.

grandiloquent.etymology: From Middle French *grandiloquent*, from Latin *grandiloquus*, from *grandis* (“great, full”) + *loquēns*, present participle of *loquor* (“to speak”).

senses.definition: In a granular way.

core.definition: In a granular way; in fine, detailed units rather than in broad totals.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on GRAN. The -ularly ending is quick and reduced, with the r clearly pronounced before the final -lee.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical adverb with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use granularly mostly in data, software, or analysis discussions, for example 'the metrics are tracked granularly by user.' It is less common in casual speech. Many people would say 'in detail' or 'at a fine level' instead.

distinctions.note: In detail is the everyday phrase; granularly is a more technical way to say the same thing about units of data or analysis.
Precisely stresses accuracy; granularly stresses the fineness of the units being measured or described.

examples.everyday: The fitness app tracks my steps granularly, so I can see exactly how many I walked each hour.
examples.professional: We should report the conversion funnel granularly by device and region, not just as one overall number.
examples.analytical: The argument proceeds granularly, examining each premise before drawing any conclusion about the whole system.

nuance.analogy: Measuring granularly is like counting coins one by one instead of estimating a total from the weight of the jar.
nuance.etymology: From granular plus the adverb suffix -ly, from Late Latin granularis (of grain).
common_mistakes: Using it in everyday conversation where 'in detail' sounds more natural.
Confusing it with 'grainy,' which describes texture or image quality.

senses.definition: The level of the ground, the surface of the earth.
The ground floor (of a building).
Ground state, the stationary state of lowest energy of a particle.
senses.example: The electron dropped back to its ground level, releasing a photon of light.

core.definition: The level of the surface of the earth; in a building, the floor at street level, which Americans usually call the first floor.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the word level, with a lighter stress on ground. The second syllable is a weak schwa, so it sounds like LEH-vul, not LEH-vell.

nuance.connotation: Neutral.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use ground level for the surface of the earth and for the street-level position of something, as in an apartment at ground level. In a building, Americans say the first floor, while British speakers say the ground floor, so avoid ground floor in US settings. As an adjective, ground-level appears with a hyphen, as in a ground-level view or ground-level ozone.

distinctions.note: Ground floor is mainly British for the level at street level; Americans would say first floor.
Street level is used mostly for city settings, while ground level can describe any surface of the earth.
Ground state is a physics term for the lowest energy state of a system, not a place or height.

examples.everyday: Our apartment is at ground level, so we can walk right out to the backyard.
examples.professional: The new office puts the reception desk at ground level, but the conference rooms are on the third floor.
examples.analytical: Ozone measured at ground level differs from stratospheric readings, so the study compares both layers separately.

nuance.analogy: Ground level is the stage floor a building stands on, the baseline from which every height is measured.
nuance.etymology: From ground, meaning the earth's surface, and level, from Old French livel, from Latin libella, a small balance.
common_mistakes: Saying ground floor for the American first floor, which is at street level.
Confusing ground level with ground state, a physics term for the lowest energy state.

senses.definition: Any meat that has been finely chopped, often with a meatgrinder.

core.definition: Meat, usually beef, that has been finely chopped in a grinder, used for burgers, tacos, and meatballs.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the word meat, with a lighter stress on ground. Make meat a long ee sound, and do not add an extra syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral.
nuance.usage_note: In American grocery stores, ground meat is the general term, but most people mean ground beef, and you will see ground turkey, ground chicken, and ground pork labeled separately. Americans do not say mince, which is the British term; in the US mincemeat means a sweet fruit filling for pie. Ground chuck is a specific beef cut used for burgers. Use ground meat when you are shopping or cooking and you need a general term.

distinctions.note: Ground beef is a specific kind of ground meat, while ground meat covers beef, pork, turkey, chicken, or other meats.
Hamburger can mean the ground beef patty or the sandwich itself, and it is not a general term for ground meat.
Mince is the British word for ground meat; Americans would say ground meat or ground beef.

examples.everyday: Can you grab a pound of ground meat for tacos on your way home?
examples.professional: Our kitchen audit flagged the ground meat storage temperature, so we need to recheck the walk-in cooler.
examples.analytical: Food ethicists note that ground meat hides its origin, turning individual animals into a homogeneous commodity.

nuance.analogy: Ground meat is like flour milled from many grains: once it is ground, the individual pieces are no longer visible.
nuance.etymology: From the past participle of grind, and meat from Old English mete, meaning food in general.
common_mistakes: Saying mince or minced meat, which Americans rarely use for ground meat.
Saying grounded meat instead of ground meat.

senses.definition: Covered by growth; overgrown.
senses.example: What once was a farm was grown with trees.

senses.definition: Of a person: adult.
senses.example: grown woman/man/adult

core.definition: Fully developed; an adult, as in a grown man or a grown woman.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable with a clear long o, the same vowel as grow, followed by a final n. Do not add a vowel between the r and the o.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. Calling someone grown can be a compliment about maturity or a mild rebuke.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say grown man or grown woman for adults, often when they want to suggest someone should act responsibly. Grown-up is more common for children or for describing mature behavior. Grown also describes plants covered in growth, as in an overgrown lawn, and it is informal compared with adult.

distinctions.note: Adult is the neutral, formal term for someone who has reached full age, while grown is informal.
Grown-up is more common as a noun or as an adjective meaning mature in behavior, while grown is usually used with man or woman.

examples.everyday: You're a grown man, so you can cook your own dinner.
examples.professional: Most of our users are grown adults, so the default settings assume they can manage their own accounts.
examples.analytical: Ethicists ask when a child becomes a grown person with full moral responsibility, a question law and religion answer differently.

nuance.analogy: Like a seed that has become a full plant: the growing is finished, and it stands on its own.
nuance.etymology: Past participle of grow, from Old English growan.
common_mistakes: Using grown as a past tense, as in 'I grown up in Ohio'; the past tense is I grew up in Ohio.
Using grown for an adult in formal writing, where adult is clearer.

senses.definition: A ravine-like or deep V-shaped valley, often eroded by flash floods; shallower than a canyon and deeper than a gully.

core.definition: A narrow, steep-sided valley or ravine cut by water, deeper and steeper than a gully but shallower than a canyon.

pronunciation.tip: It is a single syllable with a short u like the vowel in 'cup'. The ch is like the ch in 'church', so avoid 'gulsh' or 'gulk'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes a landform without judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use gulch mainly in the West and Southwest for dry washes and mountain valleys, and hikers, ranchers, and geologists use it often. In the East, people more often say ravine or hollow. A natural small-talk reply to 'We hiked up a gulch' is 'Was there water in it?'

distinctions.note: A gully is smaller and shallower, often cut by rain runoff, while a gulch is deeper and larger.
A canyon is larger, wider and usually has steep walls carved by a river, while a gulch is smaller and narrower.
Ravine is a general word used across the US, while gulch is especially common in Western American English.

examples.everyday: We hiked up the gulch to see the waterfall after the storm.
examples.professional: The survey crew mapped the gulch to plan drainage for the new road.
examples.analytical: Geomorphologists distinguish a gulch from a canyon mainly by its smaller scale and the flash-flood processes that carve it.

nuance.analogy: A gulch is like a crease in the land made by water rushing down after rain.
common_mistakes: Using gulch for any valley; in the East, ravine or hollow is more natural.
Mispronouncing the vowel as in 'gulsh' or stretching it into two syllables.

gulch.etymology: From earlier *gulsh* (“sink in, gush out”), from Middle English *gulchen* (“to gulp, spew”), probably from the source of *gulp*.

senses.definition: Grime, dirt, slime; any vague, messy, or unknown substance.
senses.example: I washed all the gunk off the light fixture, and found that it was white, not brown.

senses.definition: A subculture of 21st century American males, combining elements of modern gothic culture with punk rock.
senses.example: The gunk scene in our city blends gothic fashion with punk rock, drawing loyal teenagers and twenty-somethings.

senses.definition: An entity with no atomic parts; infinitely divisible.
senses.example: Some philosophers argue that space itself is gunk, with no smallest parts.

senses.definition: A member of the gunk subculture.
senses.example: At the concert, a few gunks stood near the back in black leather and silver chains.

senses.definition: To soil or make dirty.
senses.example: Don't gunk up the kitchen sink with bacon grease; pour it into a can instead.

core.definition: A thick, sticky, dirty substance that builds up on surfaces, such as grease, grime or residue.

pronunciation.tip: It is a single syllable with a short u vowel, as in 'luck' and 'duck'. Be sure to pronounce the -nk ending clearly, as a nasal n followed by a k sound, not a vowel before it.

nuance.connotation: Negative, describing something dirty or unpleasant. It is casual and often used with a shrug or a bit of humor.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say gunk in casual talk about grime, buildup, or any sticky mess, such as a clogged drain, grease on the stove, or ear gunk. It is mostly uncountable, so say 'some gunk' rather than 'a gunk'. The phrasal verb 'gunk up' means to clog or make dirty, as in 'The filter is all gunked up.'

distinctions.note: Grime is dirt that has built up on a surface over time; gunk is usually sticky or greasy and more casual.
Sludge is a thick, wet mass of mud or waste, often in industrial or environmental contexts; gunk is a more everyday word.

examples.everyday: Can you help me clean the gunk out of the bathroom drain? It smells terrible.
examples.professional: The old cooling system is full of gunk, so the maintenance team will flush it before we reinstall the new pumps.
examples.analytical: The author treats the political debate as gunk, a vague residue that obscures the actual arguments underneath.

nuance.analogy: Gunk is like the sticky film that builds up in a kitchen drawer over the years, hard to see until you try to clean it.
common_mistakes: Using 'a gunk' or 'gunks' as a countable noun; it is normally uncountable.
Pronouncing the vowel as a long oo sound, as in 'goonk'.
Confusing gunk with junk, which means discarded objects rather than a sticky substance.

gunk.etymology: Apparently from Gunk, trademark name for a liquid soap; perhaps taken as a *grime* + *funk*.

senses.definition: Sickening.
senses.example: The footage of the flood victims was gut-wrenching to watch on the evening news.

senses.definition: Difficult to tolerate.
senses.example: The rent increase was gut-wrenching for our family, so we decided to move.

core.definition: Extremely upsetting or emotionally painful to watch, hear or experience, often making you feel sick or tense.

pronunciation.tip: Gut gets the main stress and wrenching a secondary stress, with the vowel in the second syllable pronounced 'en.' The w in wrenching is silent, so say 'REN-ching,' not 'WREN-ching' with a hard w.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes painful or distressing experiences, though it is often used with admiration for a powerful film or performance.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use gut-wrenching for movies, news stories, goodbyes, sports losses and hard decisions. It is informal and often a little dramatic. Use it before a noun with a hyphen, as in 'a gut-wrenching decision,' and without a hyphen after a verb, as in 'The decision was gut wrenching.'

distinctions.note: Heartbreaking focuses on sadness and loss. Gut-wrenching adds a physical sense of tension or nausea.
Harrowing is more formal and suggests terrifying or severe suffering, often in writing or reportage.

examples.everyday: Watching her say goodbye to her dog was gut-wrenching, and I still think about it.
examples.professional: Telling the team that the launch was canceled was a gut-wrenching conversation, but it was the right call.
examples.analytical: Job's lament is gut-wrenching in its honesty, because it refuses the easy comfort of pretending that suffering makes sense.

nuance.analogy: A gut-wrenching moment feels like a rope twisted tight in your stomach.
nuance.etymology: Gut comes from Old English guttas; wrench comes from Old English wrencan, 'to twist.'
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the w in wrenching, which should be silent.
Using a hyphen after the verb, as in 'was gut-wrenching'; the hyphen belongs before the noun.

core.definition: The Egyptian servant of Sarah and mother of Ishmael by Abraham, whose story appears in Genesis.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, HAY. The 'ar' is a rhotic r, so pronounce the r clearly, not as a long 'a' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral as a biblical name; it can carry sympathy because of her hardship.
nuance.usage_note: Americans know Hagar mainly from the Bible, and the name appears in Bible studies, sermons and church conversations. It is also used as a given name, though less often today. When discussing her story, people usually say 'Hagar and Ishmael' together.

examples.everyday: At Bible study last night we talked about how Hagar was treated, and it really stuck with me.
examples.professional: Our sermon series on women in Genesis includes a session on Hagar and what her story shows about God's care for outsiders.
examples.analytical: Hagar's flight into the wilderness in Genesis 16 is often read as a figure of the vulnerable outsider whom God nonetheless sees and hears.

nuance.analogy: A woman whose story is told in the margins of a larger family drama, yet who turns out to be central to God's promises.
nuance.etymology: Hebrew name whose meaning is uncertain; it is sometimes linked to a word for flight or stranger, but this is disputed.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as HAH-ger, with a short 'a'.
Stressing the second syllable.
nuance.biblical_note: Hagar is an Egyptian servant of Sarah whom Abraham took as a secondary wife, and she bore Ishmael. Genesis 16:1-16 describes her flight into the wilderness, where the angel of the Lord finds her by a spring and promises descendants to her son. Genesis 21:9-21 tells how Sarah had her sent away with Ishmael, and God hears the boy crying and provides water. Galatians 4:21-31 uses Hagar allegorically to contrast the child of the slave woman with the child of the free woman.

core.definition: The name of several Old Testament men, including a Levite who helped explain the law to the people after the exile.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, HAY. The second syllable has an ah-like vowel, so say HAY-nan, not huh-NAN.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a personal name used in Bible study.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mostly meet this name in Bible study, especially when reading Nehemiah or Jeremiah. The name is uncommon as a personal name in the US, so context is needed to tell which Hanan is meant.

distinctions.note: Hanani is a different name, of a seer in Chronicles and Nehemiah's brother. Hanan is a separate name with a different spelling and person.

examples.everyday: In the Bible study, we talked about Hanan, a man mentioned in Nehemiah, and nobody in the group had heard of him before.
examples.professional: The commentary notes that Hanan appears among the Levites who helped the people understand the reading of the law.
examples.analytical: The lists of Levites in Nehemiah reflect a community organized around shared responsibility, and figures such as Hanan show how teaching roles were distributed.

nuance.analogy: Hanan is like a name on a roster of helpers: each person in the list has a small role that keeps the whole community working.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew hanan, meaning to be gracious, to show favor.
common_mistakes: Confusing Hanan with Hanani or Hananiah, which are different names.
Stressing the second syllable.
Using a long a in the second syllable, when the vowel is closer to ah.
nuance.biblical_note: Several men in the Old Testament are named Hanan. The name comes from the Hebrew hanan, meaning to be gracious. Nehemiah 8:7 lists Hanan among the Levites who helped the people understand the law as Ezra read it. Jeremiah 35:4 mentions Hanan the son of Igdaliah, a man of God in Jerusalem whose sons were associated with a room used by the prophets.

senses.definition: Not requiring one's hands to use.
A hands-free phone.
senses.example: He bought a hands-free for his car so he could take calls safely.

core.definition: Working or used without needing to hold the device, such as a phone or microphone, in your hands.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first word, 'hands,' and say the final 'z' clearly. Pronounce 'free' with an American r, not as 'fri'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It suggests convenience and safety, especially while driving.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'hands-free' most often for phones in cars, as in 'Do you have a hands-free set?' Many states require drivers to use hands-free devices instead of holding a phone. It is common in everyday speech and in product descriptions. The noun 'hands-free' usually refers to the earpiece or device itself.

distinctions.note: Wireless means there is no cable; hands-free means you can use the device without holding it, which may or may not involve wireless connection.
A speakerphone lets others hear through the device's speaker; a hands-free device usually refers to an earpiece or car system that frees your hands.

examples.everyday: I use a hands-free headset when I drive, since my state requires it.
examples.professional: During the meeting I used a hands-free headset so I could take notes while presenting.
examples.analytical: Hands-free technology changes the moral structure of driving, since it reduces physical distraction but not necessarily cognitive distraction.

nuance.analogy: A hands-free device is like a waiter's tray stand: it keeps your hands free to do other things.
nuance.etymology: Compound of hands and free, formed in the 20th century with the spread of telephones that do not require holding.
common_mistakes: Saying 'hands free' without the hyphen in writing; Americans normally hyphenate the compound adjective.
Stressing 'free' as strongly as 'hands', which makes the phrase sound unnatural.

senses.definition: A restraint or support, especially one consisting of a loop or network of rope or straps, and especially one worn by a working animal such as a horse pulling a carriage or farm implement.
senses.example: The farmer checked the leather harness on his tired mare before the long ride home.

senses.definition: A collection of wires or cables bundled and routed according to their function: a wiring harness.
senses.example: The technician traced the wiring harness behind the dashboard to find the faulty sensor.

senses.definition: The part of a loom comprising the heddles, with their means of support and motion, by which the threads of the warp are alternately raised and depressed for the passage of the shuttle.
senses.example: The weaver replaced a broken harness on the loom before starting the new wool pattern.

senses.definition: Equipment for any kind of labor.
senses.example: The miners strapped on their harness and lamps before descending into the shaft.

senses.definition: A software framework.
senses.example: test harness

senses.definition: A system designed to manage the use of AI agents, specifically in software development.
senses.example: harness engineering

senses.definition: (dated) The complete dress, especially in a military sense, of a man or a horse; armour in general.
senses.example: The knight rode out in full harness, his shield and armor gleaming in the morning sun.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: To place a harness on something; to tie up or restrain.
senses.example: They harnessed the horse to the post.

senses.definition: To capture, control or put to use.
senses.example: Imagine what might happen if it were possible to harness solar energy fully.

senses.definition: To equip with armour.
senses.example: The king ordered the smiths to harness every soldier before the siege began.

core.definition: A set of straps or rope fitted to an animal or person so it can pull, be controlled, or be held safely.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on HAR. The second syllable is a reduced vowel, so it sounds like "nus," not "ness."

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a practical word about equipment, though in climbing or safety contexts it is important.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use harness for horses, dogs, and safety gear such as a climbing or seat harness. In a car, people say "seat belt" rather than harness. A harness is also a wiring bundle in technical settings, so context matters.

distinctions.note: A strap is a single band of material; a harness is a system of straps fitted together to hold or control a body or animal.
A bridle goes on a horse's head to control it; a harness goes over the body to pull a load.

examples.everyday: Before we go climbing, make sure your harness is tied in tight.
examples.professional: The technician replaced the damaged wiring harness on the test rig.
examples.analytical: The author uses the image of a harness to suggest how tradition can restrain and also support human freedom.

nuance.analogy: A harness is like a seat belt for a body or animal: it spreads the pull or the load over the strong parts.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English harneis, from Old French harneis, equipment, of Germanic origin.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the second syllable as "ness"; it is reduced.
Using harness for a car seat belt in everyday American talk.

harness.etymology: From Middle English *harneys*, *harnes*, *harneis*, *harnais*, *herneis*, from Anglo-Norman *harneis* and Old French *hernois* (“equipment used in battle”), believed to be from Old Norse **hernest*, from *herr* (“army”) + *nest* (“provisions”) (from…

senses.definition: The characteristic of being heady.
senses.example: Winning the first round gave the team a dizzying headiness that carried them through the weekend.

core.definition: The quality of being intoxicating or exciting, or of making someone feel giddy or overconfident.

pronunciation.tip: Stress HED. The middle syllable is a clear long 'ee,' and the final -ness is weak, like 'nus,' not a strong 'NESS.'

nuance.connotation: Can be positive when it means exhilaration and negative when it suggests recklessness or overconfidence.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use heady much more often than headiness. The noun appears mainly in writing about a feeling or atmosphere, as in 'the headiness of success.' It usually sounds exciting but slightly risky, as if the excitement might cloud judgment. In casual speech, people more often say 'exciting' or 'intoxicating.'

distinctions.note: Excitement is general; headiness suggests a rush that can make you lose your balance.
Intoxication often refers to drunkenness or a drug effect; headiness can be figurative and needs no alcohol.

examples.everyday: There's a real headiness to being on vacation after a long winter.
examples.professional: The headiness of rapid growth can make a startup underestimate its risks.
examples.analytical: Philosophers have long warned that the headiness of abstract reasoning can draw thinkers away from ordinary experience.

nuance.analogy: Like the first sip of strong wine, headiness rushes to your head before you notice it.
nuance.etymology: From heady (head plus -y, originally meaning rash or headstrong) plus the suffix -ness.
common_mistakes: Using headiness for a physical headache or a head feeling; it describes exciting or intoxicating effects.
Stressing the final syllable as HED-ee-NESS.

senses.definition: In a heedless manner: with unawareness; without noticing; carelessly, inattentively.
senses.example: proceed heedlessly

core.definition: In a way that shows no attention to danger, warnings, or the effects of one's actions; carelessly.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on HEED. Keep the middle syllable short and reduced, and end with a clear -lee sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it describes careless action that causes harm or disregard for others.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'heedlessly' in writing and formal speech to describe reckless or inconsiderate actions, often in news or commentary. In everyday talk, people more often say 'carelessly' or 'without thinking'. It usually modifies a verb such as 'drove', 'spent', or 'threw'.

distinctions.note: Carelessly is the common everyday adverb, while heedlessly is more formal and suggests ignoring warnings or other people's welfare.
Recklessly implies a deliberate taking of risks, while heedlessly suggests a failure to notice or care about consequences.

examples.everyday: He heedlessly threw his cigarette out the car window, and it started a small fire in the dry grass.
examples.professional: The team heedlessly pushed the release forward without running the final safety tests.
examples.analytical: The author argues that modern institutions heedlessly accelerate change while ignoring its moral cost.

nuance.analogy: Acting heedlessly is like walking across thin ice while looking at your phone, moving forward without any thought for the crack beneath you.
nuance.etymology: Formed from heedless plus the adverb suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'heedlessly' with 'heedfully', which means the opposite, carefully.
Placing the adverb in an awkward position, such as 'heedlessly he drove', which sounds stiff; in conversation, 'he drove heedlessly' is more natural.

senses.definition: In a hegemonic fashion.
senses.example: The media industry hegemonically shaped public debate so that only corporate priorities seemed reasonable.

core.definition: In a way that dominates others by controlling ideas, culture, or institutions, so that the domination seems natural or accepted.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the third syllable, MAH, with a weaker stress on the first. Say the final -ally as -lee, and do not add an extra syllable between the j sound and the m.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to critical. It is used in social and political analysis, often to describe power that dominates quietly, so it usually carries a suggestion of unfairness.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mainly in academic writing, political theory, sociology, and cultural criticism, usually following the ideas of Antonio Gramsci. In casual talk, people would say 'they control things' or 'they dominate the conversation.' It can sound pretentious in everyday speech, so use it when you want to name a specific kind of cultural power.

distinctions.note: Dominantly describes simple numerical or physical superiority; hegemonically implies control through ideas, norms, and consent.
Authoritatively suggests legitimate expertise or formal command; hegemonically suggests power that shapes what people accept as normal.

examples.everyday: My uncle talks so hegemonically at dinner that nobody else gets a word in.
examples.professional: The product team behaved hegemonically in the roadmap meeting, so the data engineers never had a real say.
examples.analytical: Gramsci argued that a ruling class maintains power hegemonically, through consent as much as through coercion.

nuance.analogy: Like a city that sets the rules everyone follows without ever posting a sign.
nuance.etymology: From hegemonic, from Greek hēgemonikos, 'of leadership', from hēgemōn, 'leader'.
common_mistakes: Using it as a synonym for 'powerfully' in ordinary speech, where it sounds stiff.
Pronouncing the middle syllables as separate words, such as 'heg-uh-MOH-nick-ally'.

core.definition: An Israelite warrior from Pelon, one of King David's thirty mighty men, listed in the books of Samuel and Chronicles.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, HEE. The h is clearly pronounced, and the final syllable is a short 'ez' rather than a long 'eez'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a biblical name mainly discussed in Bible study and scholarship.
nuance.usage_note: Americans would encounter Helez in Bible reading, church Bible study, or scholarly commentary, not in everyday talk. When mentioning him, people often say 'one of David's mighty men' and then give the name.

distinctions.note: Heled is an alternative name in some lists of David's mighty men (2 Samuel 23:29). Helez and Heled may be variant spellings or different men, and scholars debate this.
Helon is a different biblical name, not the same person. Helez is from Pelon, while Helon is a separate name in other contexts.

examples.everyday: In our Bible study we read about David's warriors, and the leader asked us who Helez was.
examples.professional: When teaching the list of David's mighty men, I include Helez to show the variety of their origins.
examples.analytical: The list of David's mighty men in 2 Samuel 23 and 1 Chronicles 11 names Helez the Pelonite, and comparison of the two lists reveals several variant readings.

nuance.analogy: Helez is like a name on a roster of a championship team: his role is small in the story, but he is part of the group that made the team strong.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew Ḥeleẓ (חֶלֶץ), a personal name, possibly meaning 'loin' or 'strength', though the exact meaning is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as 'HEH-lez' with a short e, instead of the long EE sound.
Confusing Helez with Helon or Heled, which are different names in the biblical text.
nuance.biblical_note: Helez the Pelonite appears as one of King David's thirty mighty men in 2 Samuel 23:26 and in the parallel list at 1 Chronicles 11:27. In 1 Chronicles 27:10 he is listed as the officer in charge of the course for the seventh month, drawn from the sons of Ephraim. The name is Hebrew Ḥeleẓ, possibly meaning 'strength' or 'loin', and the text presents him as a loyal warrior, not as a major narrative figure.

senses.definition: Search that uses a rule of thumb (a heuristic) to explore the most promising options first.
senses.example: The chess engine uses heuristic search to examine the most promising moves first.

core.definition: A search method that uses a rule of thumb to explore the most promising options first, rather than checking every possibility.

pronunciation.tip: Keep the main stress on RIS in heuristic and put the strongest phrase stress on SEARCH. Make the r clearly American and the ch in search a single sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a precise technical term.
nuance.usage_note: Computer scientists and AI engineers use heuristic search as a standard term, especially for algorithms such as A*. Non-specialists may only hear it in discussions of AI or games. It is not used in ordinary conversation.

distinctions.note: Brute-force search checks every possibility, while heuristic search uses a rule of thumb to skip unlikely options and find a good answer faster.

examples.everyday: My son says his game AI uses heuristic search to find the best move without checking every option.
