pronunciation.tip: Stress the first word on OB, and the second on TEK. In American speech, 'object' as a noun is stressed on the first syllable, unlike the verb 'obJECT' stressed on the second.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical; it is a standard term in machine learning and computer vision.
nuance.usage_note: In American data science and AI teams, 'object detection' is used in project plans, model reviews, and research papers. Engineers often shorten it to 'detection' in conversation. It is distinct from image classification, which labels an image without locating objects.

distinctions.note: Classification assigns one label to an entire image; object detection finds multiple objects and gives their locations.
Segmentation labels every pixel of an object's region; object detection usually marks objects with rectangular bounding boxes.

examples.everyday: My phone camera can use object detection to recognize when I point it at a dog or a bicycle.
examples.professional: Our object detection model has to run in real time on the warehouse cameras, so we need to optimize for latency.
examples.analytical: Evaluation of object detection systems depends on metrics such as mean average precision, which combine localization accuracy with classification correctness.

nuance.analogy: Object detection is like a lifeguard scanning a crowded pool: the goal is not just to see people, but to spot each one and mark exactly where they are.
nuance.etymology: 'Object' from Latin objectum, 'thing placed before', and 'detection' from Latin detegere, 'to uncover'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the verb form on the second syllable when using the noun phrase; in this phrase, put primary stress on OB-ject.
Using 'object detection' for classifying a whole image; it specifically means locating each object with a box.

conversation.text: Object detection finds each object in an image and draws a labeled bounding box around it.
We evaluate object detection with mean average precision across several IoU thresholds.
The warehouse robot relies on object detection to locate packages on the shelves.

senses.definition: To destroy (someone or something) completely, leaving no trace; to annihilate, to wipe out.
senses.example: The rainclouds obliterated the sun as they swept across the sky.

senses.definition: To hide (something) by covering it; to conceal, to obscure.
senses.example: The rainclouds obliterated the sun as they swept across the sky.

senses.definition: To make (a drawing, text which is printed or written, etc.) indecipherable, either by erasing or obscuring it; to blot out, to efface, to delete.
senses.example: Years of rain had obliterated the faded inscription on the tombstone.

senses.definition: To cancel (a postage stamp) with a postmark so it cannot be reused.
senses.example: The clerk obliterated the stamp with a heavy postmark so it could not be reused.

senses.definition: To be destroyed completely, leaving no trace.
To impair the function and/or structure of (a body cavity, vessel, etc.) by ablating or occluding it (in the latter case, chiefly by filling it with tissue).
senses.example: The surgeon obliterated the abnormal vessel by filling it with tissue during the procedure.

senses.definition: Of a body cavity, vessel, etc.: to close up or fill with tissue; of perfusion or a pulse: to cease owing to obstruction.
senses.example: distal pulses obliterate until perfusion is restored

senses.definition: (poetic) Completely destroyed or erased; effaced, obliterated.
senses.example: The storm had left the village obliterated, its homes reduced to ash and rubble.
senses.label: poetic

senses.definition: (rare) Of markings on an insect: difficult to distinguish from the background; faint, indistinct.
senses.example: The moth's wings bear obliterated bands that blend almost perfectly into the bark.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: To destroy something completely so that nothing is left, or to wipe out marks so they can no longer be seen.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on BLIT, and the unstressed syllables are reduced to a schwa and an r-colored vowel. Americans flap nothing here, but the second-to-last syllable is very weak, so say it quickly.

nuance.connotation: Negative, because it describes total destruction or erasure of something.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use obliterate for complete destruction in news, history and war talk, such as cities obliterated by a storm. In casual speech they more often say wipe out, destroy or erase. It is also used for hiding or deleting text, like obliterating a name on a document.

distinctions.note: Destroy is the everyday general word; obliterate stresses total erasure with no trace left.
Erase is used for marks, files or memories and is more casual; obliterate suggests more complete and forceful removal.
Efface is literary and means to rub out or make invisible; obliterate is more common and can describe large-scale destruction.

examples.everyday: The storm last summer obliterated our backyard fence, and we still haven't rebuilt it.
examples.professional: Our new deduplication step will obliterate the duplicate records before the model is trained.
examples.analytical: The regime sought to obliterate the cultural memory of the minority, so that nothing of its past would survive.

nuance.analogy: Obliterate is like a wave that washes a sandcastle until no shape remains.
nuance.etymology: From Latin obliterare, to erase, from ob- (over) and littera (letter).
common_mistakes: Using obliterate for minor damage; it implies total destruction.
Stressing the wrong syllable, saying uh-blih-TER-ate.

obliterate.etymology: (start of 17th century) From earlier *obliterat*, Latin *obliterātus*, *oblitterātus* (“having been blotted out, effaced, erased; having been forgotten”) (see *-ate*).

senses.definition: Offensive to standards of decency or morality.
Lewd or lustful.
senses.example: The judge ruled that the magazine's images were obscene and banned them from the shelves.

senses.definition: Disgusting or repulsive.
senses.example: The corporate bonuses paid during the layoffs were obscene to the workers who lost their jobs.

senses.definition: Beyond all reason; excessive.
senses.example: A salary of that size for a part-time role seems obscene to most people.

senses.definition: (rare) To act or speak in an obscene manner; to offend.
senses.example: Crude jokes at the funeral obscened the solemn service and offended the grieving family.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: Offensive to standards of decency or morality, especially sexually explicit material, or outrageously excessive.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SEEN, the second syllable, and the first syllable is a weak uh rather than OB. Learners often say OB-seen, so keep the first syllable light and say the final n clearly.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes something that is shocking, offensive or morally outrageous, and it is a strong word.
nuance.usage_note: Americans most often use obscene for vulgar or sexual material, such as obscene language, and for things that seem morally outrageous, such as obscene profits. In ordinary talk, calling something obscene is dramatic, so it can sound too strong for minor problems. Common reactions include 'That's crazy' or 'Yeah, it's ridiculous.'

distinctions.note: Indecent is often a legal or formal term for sexually improper material, while obscene is stronger and more repulsive.
Obscure means hard to see, understand or know; the words look similar but do not mean the same thing.
Lewd describes sexual suggestiveness, while obscene can also describe outrageous excess, such as obscene profits.

examples.everyday: Forty dollars to park downtown for two hours? That's obscene.
examples.professional: Our cloud costs are obscene for a team this size, so let's review the idle instances this week.
examples.analytical: Critics argue that when executive pay rises while wages stagnate, the gap becomes obscene in a way that productivity alone cannot justify.

nuance.analogy: Like a shout in a library: it is so out of place that it violates the whole setting.
nuance.etymology: From Latin obscenus, 'ill-omened or indecent'; the exact origin is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Confusing obscene with obscure, which means unclear or little known.
Using obscene for mild rudeness; in American speech it is a strong word.

senses.definition: Of, relating to, or having the shape of an octahedron.

core.definition: Of or relating to an octahedron, a solid shape with eight triangular faces, or having that shape.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the third syllable, HEE, which is the 'hed' part of octahedron. The 'ed' sounds like 'ee' in this word, so do not say 'hed' as in 'head.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a precise term used in mathematics, chemistry, and mineralogy.
nuance.usage_note: Octahedral is used in geometry, crystallography, and chemistry, especially for molecular shapes and coordination complexes. Americans rarely use it outside technical settings. In everyday speech, people would say 'eight-sided die' or 'diamond shape' for the physical object.

distinctions.note: Octahedral describes a three-dimensional solid with eight faces, while octagonal describes a flat eight-sided shape.
Tetrahedral refers to a solid with four triangular faces, so the two are different shapes.

examples.everyday: Those eight-sided dice are octahedral, so they show a number on each of their eight faces.
examples.professional: The chemistry group confirmed that the iron ion sits in an octahedral coordination environment.
examples.analytical: The octahedral arrangement of ligands around the central metal shapes the complex's magnetic and spectral behavior.

nuance.analogy: Like two square pyramids joined base to base.
nuance.etymology: From octahedron (Greek oktaedron, eight-faced), from okto (eight) and hedra (seat, base, face).
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as OCK-tuh-hee-dral.
Confusing octahedral with octagonal, which describes a flat shape rather than a solid.

senses.definition: A member of an oligopoly; one of a small number of sellers with undue influence over a market.

core.definition: One of a small number of companies that together dominate a market and can influence prices and competition.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on LIG, the second syllable. The -poly part reduces to 'puh' in this word, so don't say the full 'poh-lee' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in economics, but often negative in public debate, where it suggests that a few firms are gaming the market.
nuance.usage_note: Economists, business journalists, and antitrust lawyers use this word, and it appears in news coverage about airlines, telecom companies, and meatpackers. It is not a word for casual conversation. In everyday speech, Americans would more likely say that a few big companies 'control the market'.

distinctions.note: A monopolist is the only seller in a market, while an oligopolist is one of only a few sellers.
An oligopsonist is one of a few buyers, while an oligopolist is one of a few sellers.

examples.professional: Our pricing model assumes that each of the three main oligopolists will match any price cut within a week.
examples.analytical: A rational oligopolist must anticipate its rivals' reactions, which is why game theory is central to the study of industrial organization.

nuance.analogy: Like a lunch room with only three food trucks: each truck watches the others closely before changing its prices.
nuance.etymology: From oligopoly, from Greek oligos meaning few and polein meaning to sell, with the suffix -ist for a person.
common_mistakes: Confusing oligopolist (seller) with oligopsonist (buyer).
Placing the stress on the final syllable or saying oh-lee-GOP-uh-list.

senses.definition: Going out of fashion.
In the process of becoming redundant or obsolete.
senses.example: The incandescent light bulb is on its way out.

senses.definition: Likely to break in the near future.
senses.example: This phone is on its way out, it can barely hold a charge.

core.definition: Going out of use, fashion or existence; declining and likely to disappear or be replaced soon.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on OUT, with a lighter stress on 'way'. In fast speech 'its' becomes a short 'its' and the words link together, so say 'its-way-OWT' smoothly.

nuance.connotation: Negative or neutral, depending on the thing described. It can sound like a sad or inevitable decline, or a welcome change.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase in casual conversation, business talk and journalism, for technologies, habits or institutions. It is often used with 'is' or 'are' and a specific subject, such as 'landlines are on their way out.' A natural reply is 'Yeah, I know, I still have one though.' The phrase is informal, so avoid it in very formal writing where 'obsolete' or 'being phased out' fits better.

distinctions.note: Obsolete is more formal and technical and means no longer used at all; on its way out describes a process that is still underway.
Outdated means no longer current or modern, but it does not imply that something is actively disappearing.
Being phased out describes a planned, gradual removal; on its way out is more general and less formal.

collocations: the old system is on its way out
landlines are on their way out
print newspapers are on their way out
a model on its way out

examples.everyday: Honestly, flip phones are on their way out, aren't they?
examples.professional: The on-premises server is on its way out, so we are moving everything to the cloud this quarter.
examples.analytical: Many argue that the old sacramental model is on its way out, but its persistence suggests the decline may be slower than critics expect.

nuance.analogy: Like a tide going out, slowly pulling the old thing away from the shore.
nuance.etymology: An idiom from way, meaning a path, and out, meaning away from a place; the phrase is common in modern American English.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'on its way', which means arriving or moving toward a place.
Using it for something that is growing or becoming popular; it always means declining or ending.

senses.definition: On the topic that was just previously mentioned.
senses.example: I heard there's a lemon shortage. On that note, do we have any lemonade stocked up?

senses.definition: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see on,‎ that,‎ note.

core.definition: Relating to the subject just mentioned, often used to move to a related point or to close a talk or meeting.

pronunciation.tip: 'That' is weak and sounds like 'thut' in fast speech, and 'on that' links into 'ahn-THAT'. Stress falls on NOTE, and the vowel is a diphthong ending in oo, not 'not'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it signals a transition, friendly closing or light shift in topic.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it in meetings, speeches, toasts and casual conversation to close a point or connect to a related one: 'On that note, let's wrap up.' It is not used for unrelated topics; for a new subject, Americans say 'on another note' or 'by the way'. A natural reply is 'Good point' or 'Let's do it.'

distinctions.note: 'On another note' introduces an unrelated topic, while 'on that note' stays connected to what was just said.
'On that point' refers to a specific detail, while 'on that note' refers more broadly to the mood or topic.
'By the way' introduces an aside that may be unrelated, while 'on that note' ties the new comment to the previous topic.

examples.everyday: The soup was amazing, and on that note, do you want dessert?
examples.professional: Revenue came in above forecast, and on that note, I'd like to discuss the hiring plan.
examples.analytical: Kant locates the limits of knowledge in the structure of experience; on that note, Hume's skepticism provides the sharpest contrast.

nuance.analogy: Like a train changing tracks at the same station, staying close to the last stop.
nuance.etymology: 'Note' comes from Latin nota 'mark, sign'; 'on' comes from Old English.
common_mistakes: Saying 'in that note' instead of 'on that note'.
Using it for an unrelated topic, which can confuse listeners.

on-that-note.etymology: The idiom is likely from the musical sense of *note*.

senses.definition: Seemingly; to all appearances; as far as can be seen or determined without deeper investigation or analysis.
senses.example: On the face of it, his case seemed hopeless. But appearances can be deceptive.

core.definition: Judging by appearances alone, before any deeper examination; seemingly, but possibly not true once you look closer.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on FACE, and 'of' is reduced to 'uv', while 'it' is weak. Keep the 'th' in 'the' voiced, so it sounds like 'thuh', not 'thee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, but it often introduces a challenge: the first impression may be misleading.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it in analysis, debate, planning and careful conversation: 'On the face of it, the plan looks fine, but the costs are hidden.' It sounds thoughtful, though slightly formal, and it often precedes a 'but'. A natural reply is 'Right, let's dig deeper.'

distinctions.note: 'Apparently' reports what seems true, while 'on the face of it' signals that a deeper look may change the answer.
'At first glance' refers to an initial impression, while 'on the face of it' emphasizes the limits of appearances in an argument.
'Superficially' implies shallowness and is negative, while 'on the face of it' is a neutral way to qualify a claim.

collocations: on the face of it seems
on the face of it looks
on the face of it a good idea
on the face of it reasonable

examples.everyday: On the face of it, the restaurant looks cheap, but the food was excellent.
examples.professional: On the face of it, the dashboard numbers look healthy, but we haven't checked for duplicate records.
examples.analytical: On the face of it, the argument from design seems persuasive, yet it depends on assumptions about purpose that need separate defense.

nuance.analogy: Like a painting that looks finished from across the room until you see the bare corner up close.
nuance.etymology: 'Face' comes from Latin facies 'form, appearance'; 'of' comes from Old English.
common_mistakes: Saying 'on the face of' without 'it', which is incomplete.
Using it for the literal face of a person, which is not the idiomatic meaning.

senses.definition: Resembling opal in having a milky white iridescence.
A clear to white liquid secreted by sea hares (genus Aplysia) that becomes viscous upon contact with water.
senses.example: The attack on a sea hare by a spiny lobster causes release of the whitish opaline, followed the co-release of both opaline and ink.

senses.definition: Any of several minerals resembling opal, including a variety of yellow chalcedony.
senses.example: The jeweler showed me a pale yellow opaline stone that looked like opal but was far cheaper.

senses.definition: Synonym of opal glass.
senses.example: The vintage vase was made of milky opaline glass that glowed when light passed through it.

core.definition: Milky white with a soft, shifting iridescence, like the stone opal.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The final syllable can be said with a long 'ee' or with a short 'ih'; both are heard, but 'leen' is the clearest American choice.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests delicacy and soft luminosity, and it is mostly used in descriptive or art writing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use 'opaline' in daily speech. You will mostly meet it in art criticism, fashion, glassmaking, or literary description. For everyday conversation, 'milky,' 'pearly,' or 'opal-like' is more natural.

distinctions.note: Opaline and opalescent are close in meaning, but opaline usually names a milky white quality, while opalescent stresses shifting iridescence.
Milky is the everyday word for white and cloudy, while opaline is precise and literary.

examples.everyday: The old lamp had an opaline shade that made the room glow softly at night.
examples.professional: The designer chose an opaline finish for the vase because it reflects light without looking glossy.
examples.analytical: The painter's opaline surfaces blur the boundary between solid form and shimmering light.

nuance.analogy: Opaline is like a milky pearl that changes color slightly as you turn it in the light.
nuance.etymology: From 'opal,' the gemstone, with the suffix '-ine,' meaning resembling or of the nature of.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'opal,' which is the noun for the stone.
Using it in casual speech where 'milky' or 'pearly' would sound more natural.

senses.definition: Actively conducting or prepared to conduct business.
senses.example: Banks are not open on bank holidays.

senses.definition: Physically unobstructed, uncovered, etc.
senses.example: Come in – the door's open.

senses.definition: Able to have something pass through or along it.
senses.example: Come in – the door's open.

senses.definition: Not covered, sealed, etc. having an opening or aperture showing what is inside.
senses.example: The jewelry box was lying open.

senses.definition: Not physically drawn together, folded or contracted.
senses.example: She greeted them with open arms.

senses.definition: Of a space, free of objects and obstructions.
senses.example: It was a large, open room.

senses.definition: Unlocked or unlatched but not physically open.
senses.example: The latch is open, so the gate swings inward even though it looks shut.

senses.definition: In a position allowing fluid to flow.
senses.example: Make sure the drain valve stays open so the water can flow freely.

senses.definition: Of a sandwich, etc.: composed of a single slice of bread with a topping.
senses.example: open sandwich

senses.definition: Able to be used or interacted with in some way.
senses.example: Your bank account is now open.

senses.definition: Available for use or operation.
senses.example: Your bank account is now open.

senses.definition: Allowing entrance to visitors or the public.
senses.example: I hereby declare this fete open.

senses.definition: Receptive.
senses.example: I am open to new ideas.

senses.definition: Susceptible or vulnerable (to the stated means).
senses.example: open to question; open to attack; open to criticism

senses.definition: In current use; connected to as a resource.
senses.example: I couldn't save my changes because another user had the same file open.

senses.definition: Running.
senses.example: You're getting short of memory because you have too many apps open.

senses.definition: Not hidden or restricted.
senses.example: It is a blatant example of open criminality.

senses.definition: Not concealed; overt.
senses.example: It is a blatant example of open criminality.

senses.definition: Of a person, not concealing their feelings, opinions, etc. candid, ingenuous.
senses.example: Nowadays people are more open about their sexuality.

senses.definition: Public.
senses.example: He published an open letter to the governor on a full page of The New York Times.

senses.definition: With open access, of open science, or both.
senses.example: We hope that all aspects of the project will be open rather than paywalled.

senses.definition: Made public, usable with a free license and without proprietary components.
senses.example: Our analytics team released the model as open source under an Apache license.

senses.definition: Characterized by free-flowing play.
senses.example: Compared to their last match, which was a dour and defensive affair, this was a very open game.

senses.definition: Not completed or finalized.
senses.example: an open question

senses.definition: Not settled; not decided or determined; not withdrawn from consideration.
senses.example: an open question

senses.definition: Not fulfilled or resolved; incomplete.
senses.example: I've got open orders for as many containers of red durum as you can get me.

senses.definition: Not having one end joined to the other; not forming a closed loop.
senses.example: an open curve, an open circuit

senses.definition: In a position such that a circuit is not completed, preventing electricity from flowing.
senses.example: When the relay trips, the circuit becomes open and the motor stops immediately.

senses.definition: Having different first and last vertices.
senses.example: In graph theory, an open walk starts and ends at different vertices.

senses.definition: Ending in a vowel; not having a coda.
senses.example: In Spanish, many words end in an open syllable, such as casa.

senses.definition: Having a free variable.
senses.example: The formula is open because the variable x is not bound by any quantifier.

senses.definition: Which is part of a predefined collection of subsets of X, that defines a topological space on X.
senses.example: A set is open in this topology if it belongs to the chosen collection.

senses.definition: Of a note, played without closing any finger-hole, key or valve.
senses.example: The low E string is played open, so you hear its natural pitch.

senses.definition: Uttered with a relatively wide opening of the articulating organs; said of vowels.
senses.example: The vowel in father is open, so the jaw drops noticeably during articulation.

senses.definition: Uttered, as a consonant, with the oral passage simply narrowed without closure.
senses.example: Linguists classify the sound in you as an open consonant, a type of approximant.

senses.definition: Source code of a computer program that is not within the text of a macro being generated.(Can we add an example for this sense?)
senses.example: Any open code outside the macro body is copied verbatim into the expanded output.

senses.definition: Having component words separated by spaces, as opposed to being joined together or hyphenated; for example, time slot as opposed to timeslot or time-slot.
senses.example: Many style guides prefer the open compound time slot over timeslot or time-slot.

senses.definition: Resulting from an incision, puncture or any other process by which the skin no longer protects an internal part of the body.
senses.example: an open fracture

senses.definition: Written or sent with the intention that it may made public or referred to at any trial, rather than by way of confidential private negotiation for a settlement.
senses.example: You will observe that this is an open letter and we reserve the right to mention it to the judge should the matter come to trial.

senses.definition: Of a tournament or competition, allowing anyone to enter, especially or originally irrespective of professional or amateur status.
senses.example: The open tournament welcomed amateurs and professionals alike, so the field was large.

senses.definition: Of a note, played without pressing the string against the fingerboard.
senses.example: Play the open G string on the cello to get a rich, resonant tone.

senses.definition: Of a club, bat or other hitting implement, angled upwards and/or (for a right-hander) clockwise of straight.
senses.example: Her driver had an open face, so the ball launched high and drifted right.

senses.definition: Not of a quality to prevent communication, as by closing waterways, blocking roads, etc. hence, not frosty or inclement; mild; used of the weather or the climate.
senses.example: an open winter

senses.definition: To make or become physically unobstructed, uncovered, etc.
senses.example: Turn the doorknob to open the door.

senses.definition: To make or become accessible or clear for passage by moving from a shut position.
senses.example: Turn the doorknob to open the door.

senses.definition: To make or become clear by removal of objects and obstructions, so as to allow passage, access, or visibility.
senses.example: The icebreaker opened the channel.

senses.definition: To unseal or uncover, or become unsealed or uncovered.
senses.example: You can open your eyes now!

senses.definition: To spread; to expand into a wider or looser position.
senses.example: to open a closed fist

senses.definition: To make (a bed) ready for a patient by folding back the bedcovers.
To reveal one's hand.
senses.example: Jeff opens his hand revealing a straight flush.

senses.definition: To move to a position allowing fluid to flow.
To cause or allow a gap to form or widen.
senses.example: Mudchester Rovers opened a sizeable lead on their rivals.

senses.definition: To move to a position preventing electricity from flowing.
To make or become available for use or interaction.
senses.example: He opened a secret bank account in Switzerland.

senses.definition: To make or become operative or available.
senses.example: He opened a secret bank account in Switzerland.

senses.definition: To make or become accessible to customers, clients or visitors.
senses.example: I will open the shop an hour early tomorrow.

senses.definition: To make or become receptive or susceptible (to something).
senses.example: Reading this book will open you to new ideas.

senses.definition: To connect to a resource (a file, document, etc.) for viewing or editing.
senses.example: I can't open the file because someone else is editing it.

senses.definition: To turn on; to switch on.
senses.example: Please open the lights, the (electric) fan, the TV.

senses.definition: To start or begin.
senses.example: The show was opened by a terrible Elvis impersonator.

senses.definition: To start (an event or activity) as the first performer or actor.
senses.example: The show was opened by a terrible Elvis impersonator.

senses.definition: To precede another as a performer at a concert or show.
senses.example: Our band opened for Nirvana.

senses.definition: Of an event, activity etc. to start or get underway.
senses.example: The meeting opened with a statement from the chairman.

senses.definition: To bring up, broach.
senses.example: I don't want to open that subject.

senses.definition: To enter upon, begin.
senses.example: to open a discussion

senses.definition: To start running (a program or application, especially one with a screen-based interface).
senses.example: Click this icon to open Microsoft Word.

senses.definition: To bet before any other player has in a particular betting round in a game of poker.
senses.example: After the first two players fold, Julie opens for $5.

senses.definition: To make an open relationship or marriage, i.e. with possible additional relationships.
To angle (a club, bat or other hitting implement) upwards and/or (for a right-hander) clockwise of straight.
To begin a side's innings as one of the first two batsmen.
Open or unobstructed space; an exposed location.
senses.example: I can't believe you left the lawnmower out in the open when you knew it was going to rain this afternoon!

senses.definition: Public knowledge or scrutiny; full view.
senses.example: We have got to bring this company's corrupt business practices into the open.

senses.definition: A defect in an electrical circuit preventing current from flowing.
senses.example: The electrician found the open in the circuit after a few minutes of testing.

senses.definition: A sports event in which anybody can compete, especially or originally irrespective of amateur or professional status.
senses.example: the Australian Open

senses.definition: The act of something being opened, such as an e-mail message.

core.definition: Currently doing business and available for customers to come in or buy things.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the first syllable, and the second syllable is a reduced schwa, so it sounds like 'OH-pun,' not 'oh-PEN.' The word is only two syllables in ordinary speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and practical. It is a basic word used in everyday life, especially for stores and services.
nuance.usage_note: In American life, 'open' is the most common way to ask or say whether a store or restaurant is serving customers, as in 'Are you open?' or 'We're open until nine.' Use 'open' with the time or day for clarity. The opposite is 'closed,' and signs often say 'Open' or 'Closed' on the door.

distinctions.note: Available is used for people or items that can be obtained, while open is used for a place or business that is operating.
Ready means prepared, but open means the business is actually receiving customers at that time.

examples.everyday: Is the hardware store still open, or should we go to the one on Main Street?
examples.professional: The client asked whether the support office is open on holidays, so we need to confirm the schedule.
examples.analytical: A store that is open at all hours changes the expectations of a neighborhood, not just its customers.

nuance.analogy: Open is like a welcome mat laid out at the door: it tells people they can come in right now.
nuance.etymology: From Old English 'open,' meaning not closed or not covered.
common_mistakes: Using 'open' as a verb with the wrong preposition, as in 'open at nine' when you mean 'opens at nine.'
Saying 'The store is opening' when you mean it is currently operating; 'open' describes the state.

open.etymology: Adjective from Middle English *open*, from Old English *open* (“open”), from **opan*, from Proto-Germanic **upanaz* (“open”), from Proto-Indo-European **upo* (“up from under, over”).

conversation.text: Is the pharmacy open on Sunday?
We're open until ten tonight, so take your time.
Don't open the box until you're sure you want to keep it.

senses.definition: Not withholding information from the participants of a clinical trial, as opposed to double-blind.
senses.example: The open-label extension study let patients know which treatment they were receiving.

core.definition: Describing a clinical trial in which both researchers and participants know which treatment is being given.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on LAY, and the last syllable is a reduced 'buhl' with no strong vowel. Do not stress the first word OPEN heavily.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It describes a study design rather than judging a person or treatment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use open-label in medical research, pharmaceutical reports, and clinical trial protocols, usually in the phrase open-label study or open-label trial. It is the opposite of a blinded design, where participants or researchers do not know the treatment. Outside medicine, most Americans would not use it, so keep it for formal technical contexts.

distinctions.note: In a double-blind trial neither participants nor researchers know who gets which treatment; an open-label trial has no such masking.
In a single-blind trial only participants are kept unaware of the treatment, while an open-label trial reveals it to everyone.

examples.everyday: My uncle joined an open-label study for a new drug, so he knows exactly what he is taking.
examples.professional: The team will run an open-label phase two trial first, then move to a blinded design if the results look promising.
examples.analytical: An open-label design raises the risk of expectation bias, so the authors should explain how they measured their outcomes.

nuance.analogy: An open-label trial is like a cooking test where everyone can see the recipe card, so the judgment may be shaped by what people already know.
nuance.etymology: Open from Old English opan; label from Anglo-French or Middle English labelle, a strip or tag.
common_mistakes: Using open-label for ordinary open-ended tasks; it has a specific meaning in research.
Confusing open-label with open-source or open-access, which are unrelated terms.

senses.definition: Of or relating to software where the source code is freely available and licensed in a manner that permits modification and redistribution.
senses.example: Linux is an open-source operating system.

senses.definition: Of or relating to digital resources made publicly available alongside their source files to enable their modification and redistribution.
senses.example: open-source hardware (with editable CAD files)

senses.definition: Describing any product whose composition or method of manufacturing is public knowledge and not proprietary.
senses.example: open-source hardware (schematics provided for free)

senses.definition: Relying on publicly available information (open sources).
senses.example: open-source intelligence

senses.definition: To release the source code of, so as to permit modification and redistribution.
senses.example: The company decided to open-source its database engine so volunteers could improve it.

core.definition: Describing software whose source code is publicly available for anyone to view, modify, and redistribute under a license.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, with a lighter secondary stress on 'source.' The 'r' in 'source' is strong in American speech, and the 'ou' in 'open' is a diphthong that moves toward 'oo.'

nuance.connotation: Positive in software and technology circles, suggesting transparency and community. In policy debates it can be neutral or contested.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'open-source' as a compound adjective before nouns, as in 'open-source software' or 'open-source model.' In casual talk, developers may shorten it to 'open source' as a noun phrase. It often appears in technology news, job postings, and policy debates about AI, so it is important for professional conversation.

distinctions.note: Free software emphasizes freedom of use and modification in philosophy, while open-source emphasizes practical access to the source code and collaborative development.
Proprietary means owned and restricted by a company, while open-source means the source code is publicly available.

examples.everyday: My brother is a developer, and he only uses open-source tools for his home projects.
examples.professional: We plan to release the model as open-source once the security review is finished.
examples.analytical: Whether an open-source model is truly open depends on whether its training data and weights are also available for inspection.

nuance.analogy: Open-source software is like a recipe that is published with the full list of ingredients, so anyone can cook it, change it, and share the new version.
nuance.etymology: From 'open,' meaning available or unrestricted, plus 'source,' meaning the original code or material; the term was coined in the late 1990s.
common_mistakes: Writing 'open source software' without a hyphen when it is used before a noun.
Saying 'open-source' for a product that only shows its interface, when the source code is actually closed.

conversation.text: Most of our ML tooling is open source, so we can inspect and modify the code.
Whether a model counts as open source depends on its license and on how much code and data detail is shared.
Advocates say open source AI enables scrutiny; critics worry it makes misuse harder to control.

senses.definition: A yellow-brown, addictive narcotic drug obtained from the dried juice of unripe pods of the opium poppy, Papaver somniferum, and containing alkaloids such as morphine, codeine, and papaverine.
senses.example: Opium was once sold legally in pharmacies, and many families became dependent on it.

senses.definition: Anything that numbs or stupefies.
senses.example: For many workers, television became the opium that dulled the boredom of factory life.

core.definition: An addictive narcotic drug made from the dried sap of unripe opium poppy seed pods, used to relieve severe pain.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, OH. The final syllable is a reduced schwa, so it sounds like 'um', not 'ahm'.

nuance.connotation: Negative, linked to addiction and social harm; in figurative use it suggests something that dulls people or distracts them from reality.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use opium mainly for the drug itself, which is tightly controlled, and for historical topics like the Opium Wars. In everyday talk, people usually say heroin, opioids or painkillers for modern drug problems. The figurative phrase 'the opium of the people' comes from Karl Marx's critique of religion and is still used in political and academic discussions.

distinctions.note: Opiate refers to drugs derived from opium, such as morphine; opium is the raw sap itself.
Narcotic is a broad legal term for many drugs that dull pain; opium is one specific natural source.

examples.everyday: Those old movies sometimes show people smoking opium in dark rooms, but that's not something you see much today.
examples.professional: Our compliance team tracks every shipment of opium-derived medicines, since the DEA regulates them very tightly.
examples.analytical: Marx called religion the opium of the people, suggesting that it dulls the pain of social injustice rather than curing its causes.

nuance.analogy: Like a fog that hides the hard edges of life, opium numbs the pain but leaves the causes untouched.
nuance.etymology: From Latin opium, from Greek opion 'poppy juice', a diminutive of opos 'juice, sap'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the last syllable as 'ahm' instead of the reduced 'um'.
Treating opium as countable, as in 'an opium', when it is normally uncountable.

opium.etymology: Latin *opium* and Ancient Greek *ὄπιον*, from *ὀπός* (“juice of a plant”), from Proto-Indo-European **sokʷós* (“juice, resin”).

senses.definition: Opposing, antagonistic, contrary.

core.definition: Opposing or hostile to something; antagonistic or contrary, especially in argument or in principle.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, PYOON. The g is silent, as in the verb oppugn, so the word ends in a simple -nunt sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative or strongly critical. It describes active opposition, usually in argument or principle.
nuance.usage_note: This is a rare and bookish word. Americans would normally say opposing, opposed, or antagonistic in everyday talk, and reserve oppugnant for formal writing or sharp philosophical argument. It is not a casual word, and using it in conversation may sound pretentious.

distinctions.note: Opposing is ordinary and neutral; oppugnant implies a more hostile, combative stance.
Antagonistic is common and describes hostile attitudes; oppugnant is rarer and more literary, often used for ideas or positions.

collocations: oppugnant to the spirit of the law

examples.professional: The two teams took oppugnant positions on the budget, and the meeting ended without a decision.
examples.analytical: Kant's ethics seems oppugnant to utilitarian calculation, since it refuses to treat persons as quantities to be traded.

nuance.analogy: Like two magnets turned to repel each other: the forces push against one another rather than attract.
nuance.etymology: From Latin oppugnare, 'to attack, fight against', from ob- 'against' and pugnare 'to fight'.
common_mistakes: Confusing oppugnant (adjective) with opponent (noun), which is far more common.
Pronouncing the g, as in 'uh-PUG-nunt'; the g is silent in this word.

senses.definition: To act optimistically or as an optimist.
senses.example: Even after the layoffs, she continued to optimize about the company's future.

senses.definition: To make (something) optimal.
senses.example: We need to optimize the supply chain to reduce costs.

senses.definition: To make (something) more efficient, such as a computer program.
senses.example: The website was redesigned to optimize user experience.

senses.definition: To become optimal.
senses.example: The engine's fuel mix should optimize once the sensors finish recalibrating.

core.definition: To make something as good, effective, or efficient as possible.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The final '-ize' is pronounced 'eyez,' and the middle vowel is a reduced 'ih.'

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests a deliberate, effective improvement, though some people find it jargon when used for everyday tasks.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'optimize' all the time at work, especially in tech, marketing, and project management, as in 'optimize the workflow.' Outside work, it sounds slightly corporate, so people might say 'make it better' or 'streamline it' instead. In the 'optimistic' sense, it is archaic and rare.

distinctions.note: 'Improve' means make better in general; 'optimize' means make as good as possible, often with measurable goals.
'Streamline' means simplify and remove steps; 'optimize' can mean changing any part to increase performance.

examples.everyday: I'm trying to optimize my morning routine so I don't rush out the door.
examples.professional: Let's optimize the meeting agenda so we finish the project review in thirty minutes.
examples.analytical: Any attempt to optimize human flourishing must first decide what flourishing means, and that decision cannot be purely technical.

nuance.analogy: Like adjusting the sails on a boat until it moves as fast as the wind allows.
nuance.etymology: From Latin optimus, 'best,' with the verb suffix -ize.
common_mistakes: Saying 'optimize to' instead of 'optimize for' when naming the goal, as in 'optimize for speed.'
Stressing the second syllable, as in 'op-TIM-ize.'
patterns: optimize sth with respect to sth

conversation.text: We need to optimize the website for mobile users.
I spent the morning optimizing the query, and it's ten times faster now.
How can we optimize our ad spending?

senses.definition: To speak formally; to give a speech.
To speak passionately; to preach for or against something.
senses.example: The senator began to orate about the dangers of the proposed tax, pacing across the stage.

senses.definition: Competent in oracy; having good speaking skills.
senses.example: Students who are orate can explain complex ideas clearly without relying on written notes.

core.definition: To make a formal speech to an audience, often in a grand, lengthy or pompous way.

pronunciation.tip: There is one stressed syllable, OR, and the second rhymes with 'rate'. Do not add a syllable; it is not 'or-AY-tuh' or 'or-ATE' with stress on the end.

nuance.connotation: Often negative or mocking. It suggests a speaker who is pompous, long-winded or theatrical, though it can be neutral in formal writing about public address.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use orate in everyday talk, since it sounds literary or ironic. You might see it in news or political commentary, as in 'He orated for two hours.' For ordinary speaking, say 'give a speech', 'talk' or 'lecture'. If someone starts to orate at a dinner table, a natural response is to ask them to get to the point.

distinctions.note: A lecture is an organized talk meant to teach; orate suggests a grand or emotional speech that is more about performance than instruction.
Declaim means to speak with dramatic emphasis, often reciting; orate is broader and can describe any formal public speech.

examples.everyday: Whenever my uncle gets a glass of wine, he starts to orate about the economy.
examples.professional: Our CEO liked to orate at all-hands meetings, so we kept the updates short and visual.
examples.analytical: The preacher did not reason with his audience; he orated, appealing to fear and pride rather than argument.

nuance.analogy: To orate is to perform a speech the way an actor plays a monologue, with the audience as the stage.
nuance.etymology: From Latin orare, 'to speak, plead, pray', the same root as orator.
common_mistakes: Using orate for ordinary talking; in American English it suggests a grand or pompous speech.
Confusing orate, the verb, with orator, the person who gives the speech.

orate.etymology: Partly Latin *ōrātus*, of *ōrō* (“to speak; to pray”) and/or partly, from Latin *ōrātiō* (“speech, discourse, oration”); either way, see *-ate* and *-ate*.

senses.definition: Orthopraxy.

core.definition: Correct practice or right action in religious life, in contrast with orthodoxy, which means correct belief.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on OR, the first syllable. Keep the American r in both syllables and end with a short sis sound, not sees.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It describes a valued emphasis on living out faith through action.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mainly in theology, religious studies, and seminary discussions. In church or everyday conversation, people more often say right living or put faith into practice. Using orthopraxis in casual talk may sound academic, but it is natural in a seminary class.

distinctions.note: Orthodoxy means correct belief, while orthopraxis means correct practice or action.
Praxis means practice informed by theory or reflection, while orthopraxis focuses on whether religious practice is correct.

examples.everyday: At our church, we talk less about being right and more about doing right, which is a kind of orthopraxis.
examples.professional: Our seminary course compares orthodoxy and orthopraxis in early Christian communities.
examples.analytical: In many traditions, orthopraxis carries as much weight as orthodoxy because the faith is meant to be lived in practice.

nuance.analogy: If orthodoxy is the map, orthopraxis is the walking on the path.
nuance.etymology: From Greek orthos, meaning right or correct, and praxis, meaning action or practice.
common_mistakes: Confusing orthopraxis with orthodoxy, which means correct belief.
Pronouncing the final syllable as sees, when it should be a short sis.

traditions.view: Orthodoxy and orthopraxis are both essential, and worship, especially the liturgy, is the main place where right practice is learned and expressed.
Right practice includes the sacraments and the moral life, and Catholic teaching holds that faith must be formed by charity, so belief and practice are not separated.
Protestants generally teach that good works flow from faith and do not earn justification, though Lutheran and Reformed traditions differ on the role of the law in the Christian life.

senses.definition: The most widespread species of that order, known as the common ostrich (Struthio camelus).
senses.example: The common ostrich is the largest living bird, native to Africa's savannas.

senses.definition: One who buries their head in the sand instead of acknowledging problems.
senses.example: Refusing to discuss the budget deficit, the mayor acted like an ostrich.

senses.definition: The hypothetical completion of a hole five strokes under par (a quintuple birdie, quadruple eagle, triple albatross, or double condor).
senses.example: He nearly recorded an ostrich on the par-five, a score almost nobody ever achieves.

senses.definition: A large flightless bird of the order Struthioniformes.

core.definition: A very large flightless bird of Africa with long legs and a long neck, known for running fast.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable. Many Americans pronounce the first vowel like 'aw' (cot-caught merger means it may also sound like 'ah'). The r is clear, and the ending -ich sounds like 'itch' without the t being strong.

nuance.connotation: Neutral when describing the bird. Negative when used figuratively for someone who avoids facts or problems.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use ostrich literally for the bird, and also in the idiom 'bury your head in the sand' or 'stick your head in the sand' to describe someone who refuses to face a problem. The figurative use is common in news and everyday talk. The bird is often mentioned in zoo visits and nature shows.

distinctions.note: An emu is a large flightless bird native to Australia with a smaller head and feathers that are brown and shaggy. An ostrich is African with black and white feathers in males.
Head in the sand is an idiom for denial. Ostrich is the noun for the bird and used in the same figurative sense, but 'ostrich' alone is less common in casual speech.

collocations: bury your head like an ostrich

examples.everyday: We saw a huge ostrich at the zoo, and the kids couldn't stop laughing.
examples.professional: Leadership's ostrich approach to the budget shortfall only made the eventual cuts more painful.
examples.analytical: The ostrich metaphor describes denial, but it misrepresents the bird, which does not actually bury its head in the sand.

nuance.analogy: Like a person who pulls the covers over their head when the alarm goes off, hoping the problem goes away.
nuance.etymology: From Latin struthio, from Greek strouthion, 'ostrich' or 'sparrow', with a French form influencing the English.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the word with a long o sound as 'OH-strich'.
Saying 'ostritch' with a t after the s, which is not standard English.
nuance.biblical_note: In Hebrew the bird is called ya'anah, often rendered ostrich. Leviticus 11:16 lists it among the unclean birds that are not to be eaten. Job 39:13-18 describes the ostrich as careless with its eggs and swift in running, an image of God's sovereign and unexplained ways. Lamentations 4:3 compares the cruelty of the people to the ostriches of the wilderness, which leave their young.

ostrich.etymology: From Middle English *ostrich*, *ostriche*, *ostryche*, *ostrige*, borrowed from Anglo-Norman *ostrige* and Old French *ostruce*, from Vulgar Latin **austruthio*, from Latin *avis* (“bird”) + *strūthiō* (“ostrich”), from Ancient Greek *στρουθίων*, or…

senses.definition: Having an age that is greater than a stipulated minimum.
senses.example: The club allows members who are overage for the youth league to join the adult team.

senses.definition: Too old to be of use in a particular situation.
senses.example: The old computer was overage for the software project, so we replaced it with a new server.

senses.definition: To have too long an aging process.
senses.example: Wine left in the cellar too long will overage and lose its bright fruit flavors.

senses.definition: A surplus of inventory or capacity or of cash that is greater than the amount in the record of an account.
senses.example: The warehouse audit revealed a large overage of printer paper that nobody had recorded.

senses.definition: Excess; a state of being more than it ought to be.
senses.example: You're entitled to bring a bag weighing fifty pounds onto the airplane, and will be charged extra for any overage.

senses.definition: Any additional sums payable following the purchase of land, calculated on a prearranged basis, on the occurrence of certain specified events that are deemed to increase the value of that land; usually in the context of the development and further sale of that land.
senses.example: The developer agreed to pay the landowner an overage whenever the rezoned parcel sold.

core.definition: An amount or charge beyond a set limit, such as extra data use on a phone plan or extra cash in a register.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, OH, and the -age ending is reduced to a short ij sound, not age as in page. As an adjective or verb, the stress shifts to the last syllable, so it is oh-ver-AYJ.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative, since it often refers to an extra charge or an accounting difference.
nuance.usage_note: Americans see overage most often in phone and cable bills, such as data overage charges, and in retail or banking, such as an overage in the cash drawer. In casual conversation people may say extra charges or going over. The noun is a little technical, so it fits billing, accounting and business talk best.

distinctions.note: Surplus is usually a planned or neutral extra amount, while overage often suggests a limit that was exceeded and may trigger a charge.
Excess is a general word for too much, but overage is specific to limits, quotas or accounting.
Overrun describes a project that goes over its budget or schedule, while overage is about exceeding a set amount or limit.

examples.everyday: I got hit with a twenty-dollar overage on my phone bill because I streamed too much last month.
examples.professional: The register came up with a ten-dollar cash overage at close, so we logged it for the manager.
examples.analytical: The contract's overage clause sets the price for usage beyond the committed amount, shifting most of the risk onto the customer.

nuance.analogy: Like a parking meter that keeps charging after your time is up.
nuance.etymology: From over plus the suffix -age.
common_mistakes: Stressing the final syllable like age in page; the noun is OH-ver-ij.
Using overage to mean general excess weight or size, when it refers to going beyond a set limit.

senses.definition: To surmount (a physical or abstract obstacle); to prevail over, to get the better of.
To prevail.
To recover from (a difficulty), to get over.
To win against or prevail over in some sort of battle, contest, etc.
senses.example: to overcome enemies in battle

senses.definition: To come or pass over; to spread over.
senses.example: I was overcome with anger.

senses.definition: That has been overcome, prevailed over.

core.definition: To successfully deal with or defeat a difficulty, problem, or obstacle and get past it.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the last syllable, COME, not on OH. The middle syllable is a reduced, rhotic 'er', and the final vowel is short, like 'sum'.

nuance.connotation: Positive: it describes a struggle that was won, so it sounds encouraging. It is neutral enough for everyday talk and speeches alike.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use overcome constantly for personal and practical struggles, such as 'I finally overcame my fear of flying' or 'We can overcome this.' It sounds a bit more deliberate than 'get over' or 'beat', which are more casual. A natural reply to 'How did you get through that?' is 'I just took it one day at a time.'

distinctions.note: Defeat means to win against an opponent in a contest or war; overcome is broader and can apply to fear, illness or a habit with no opponent.
Get over is informal and used mostly for emotional hurts or illnesses; overcome sounds more deliberate and is common in writing and speeches.
Conquer suggests total control or taking territory and sounds grander or more military; overcome is more personal and everyday.

examples.everyday: Honestly, I finally overcame my fear of heights and went zip-lining last weekend.
examples.professional: The team overcame the integration problems by writing a shared schema before the next sprint.
examples.analytical: The author argues that the early church overcame persecution through patient witness rather than through political power.

nuance.analogy: Like a swimmer crossing a strong current: the water does not disappear, but you get across it.
nuance.etymology: From Old English ofercuman, from ofer 'over' and cuman 'come'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as OH-ver-kum; the stress belongs on the last syllable, kum.
Mixing up the forms: the past tense is overcame, and the past participle is overcome, as in 'I have overcome it'.
Saying 'overcome from' instead of 'overcome by' when describing a feeling, as in 'overcome by grief'.
nuance.biblical_note: In the New Testament, overcome usually translates the Greek nikao, to conquer or prevail. John 16:33 says that Jesus has overcome the world, even though his disciples will face trouble. Romans 12:21 tells believers not to be overcome by evil but to overcome evil with good. Revelation 2:7 uses the same word for the one who conquers, who is promised the tree of life.

senses.definition: To spend too much money; especially, to spend more than one earns.
senses.example: To get out of debt, first keep a budget and be careful not to overspend.

senses.definition: The amount by which someone or something is overspent.
senses.example: The overspend on the kitchen renovation came to nearly four thousand dollars above the budget.

core.definition: To spend more money than you have or can afford, especially spending more than you earn.

pronunciation.tip: As a verb the main stress falls on SPEND; the noun 'overspend' stresses OH instead. Keep the 'er' in the middle reduced to a light 'ur' sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative or cautionary, because it implies a financial mistake or lack of control, though it is said without much drama.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this in everyday money talk, such as budgets, credit cards, and holiday shopping. It can sound a little judgmental if said directly to someone, so people often soften it: 'We may be overspending a bit this month.' A common reply is 'Yeah, let's cut back.'

distinctions.note: Spend too much is the plain everyday phrase; overspend is a single verb that sounds slightly more precise or financial.
Overspent is the past tense or adjective meaning already past the budget, as in 'I am overspent this month.'

collocations: overspend by a few hundred dollars

examples.everyday: We really overspent at the grocery store this week, so let's eat at home for a while.
examples.professional: The project team overspent its budget in the second quarter, so finance has asked for a revised forecast.
examples.analytical: A household that consistently overspends relative to income is not necessarily irrational; its behavior may reflect expectations of future earnings or limited access to savings.

nuance.analogy: Like filling a glass past the rim, you spend more than the container can hold and the extra spills onto the table.
nuance.etymology: From over- (beyond, too much) plus spend, from Latin expendere, 'to weigh out'.
common_mistakes: Putting the stress on OH as in the noun; say oh-ver-SPEND for the verb.
Using 'overspend' with a direct object that is wrong; say 'overspend on' something rather than 'overspend something' unless you mean exceed a budget.

senses.definition: A step.
senses.example: Even at the duel, standing 10 paces apart, he could have satisfied Aaron’s honor.

senses.definition: A step taken with the foot.
senses.example: She took a careful pace forward and examined the broken railing.

senses.definition: The distance covered in a step (or sometimes two), either vaguely or according to various specific set measurements.
senses.example: Even at the duel, standing 10 paces apart, he could have satisfied Aaron’s honor.

senses.definition: A way of stepping.
senses.example: We set off at a round pace.

senses.definition: A manner of walking, running or dancing; the rate or style of how someone moves with their feet.
senses.example: We set off at a round pace.

senses.definition: Any of various gaits of a horse, specifically a 2-beat, lateral gait.
senses.example: The mare's smooth pace made the long ride across the ranch far easier.

senses.definition: Speed or velocity in general.
senses.example: The project kept a steady pace, and we finished two weeks ahead of schedule.

senses.definition: A group of donkeys (asses).
senses.example: A pace of donkeys carried the supplies up the narrow mountain trail.

senses.definition: Synonym of Easter.
senses.example: Children in our town still go pace egging on the Saturday before Easter.

senses.definition: A measure of the hardness of a pitch and of the tendency of a cricket ball to maintain its speed after bouncing.
senses.example: He didn't bowl a lot of pace in the first T20I.

senses.definition: To walk back and forth in a small distance.
senses.example: The expectant father began to pace the hallway outside the delivery room.

senses.definition: To walk along or through sth with regular strides.
senses.example: The sentry paced the perimeter fence every hour through the night.

senses.definition: To set the speed.
senses.example: I helped her train for the marathon by pacing her on a bike.

senses.definition: To measure by walking.
senses.example: Before building the shed, he paced off the backyard to check the dimensions.

senses.definition: With all due respect to.
senses.example: Pace Professor Smith, the evidence does not support that conclusion.

senses.definition: Describing a bowler who bowls fast balls.
senses.example: She is a pace bowler who has been picked for the national squad.

core.definition: The speed at which something happens or someone moves, or the rate of progress in a task or activity.

pronunciation.tip: The word has one syllable with the diphthong 'ay' and ends in a clear s sound, not a z. Keep the vowel smooth and avoid adding a second syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes speed or rhythm without judgment, though a fast or slow pace can be praised or criticized depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use pace constantly for work, travel and sports, as in 'a steady pace' or 'keep up the pace.' As a preposition, pace means 'with all due respect to' and is formal, so use it only when you disagree politely in a serious discussion. In everyday talk, people usually say 'with respect' or 'no offense' instead.

distinctions.note: Speed is the general word for how fast something moves, while pace suggests a steady rate or the rhythm of progress over time.
Rate is more technical and numerical, while pace is more natural for people walking, running or working.

examples.everyday: We walked at a comfortable pace, so my dad could keep up without getting tired.
examples.professional: Our team needs to keep pace with the release schedule, so let's review the sprint tasks on Friday.
examples.analytical: The historian argues that the pace of social change accelerated sharply after the industrial revolution.

nuance.analogy: Pace is like the beat of a song: it sets the rhythm that everyone else follows.
nuance.etymology: From Latin passus, meaning a step, through Old French pas.
common_mistakes: Saying 'in pace with' instead of the correct phrase 'keep pace with'
Confusing pace with pass or path, which sound similar but have different meanings
Using the preposition sense casually, where it sounds stiff or confrontational

pace.etymology: From Middle English *pase*, from Anglo-Norman *pas*, Old French *pas*, and their source, Latin *passus*. compare also *pass*.

senses.definition: To bring peace to (a place or situation), by ending (or suppressing) war, fighting, violence, anger or agitation.
senses.example: Their orders were to pacify the province by destroying resistance.

senses.definition: To mollify, placate or soothe (someone or something).
senses.example: She bought him an ice cream cone to pacify him during the long wait.

senses.definition: To appease (someone).
senses.example: The government offered concessions to pacify the protesters before the vote.

core.definition: To calm someone who is angry or upset, or to bring peace to a place by ending fighting or unrest.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The final '-ify' is pronounced 'eye', not 'ee', and the middle syllable is a short reduced vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, sometimes condescending. It can imply that someone is being managed or handled rather than sincerely reassured.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'calm down' or 'settle down' in casual speech, and they use 'pacify' in more formal or political writing. The word can sound manipulative when used about people, as if their feelings were being managed. In American English, a baby's pacifier is common, while British English often uses 'dummy'.

distinctions.note: Appease means giving in to someone's demands to avoid conflict, while pacify means calming them, which may not involve giving anything.
Soothe suggests gentle comfort for pain or distress, while pacify suggests calming an agitated person or group.

examples.everyday: I gave the kids some crackers to pacify them until dinner was ready.
examples.professional: The manager offered a discount to pacify the frustrated client before the call ended.
examples.analytical: Leaders sometimes pacify public anger with symbolic gestures rather than substantive reform.

nuance.analogy: To pacify someone is like lowering the volume on a loud radio: the noise drops, but the station is still playing.
nuance.etymology: From Latin pacificare, 'to make peace', through French pacifier.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'pacify' with 'pacific', which means peaceful or refers to the Pacific Ocean.
Stressing the second syllable, as in 'pa-SIF-eye'.

pacify.etymology: From Middle French *pacifier*, from Latin *pāx* (“peace”) + *faciō* (“to do, make”).

senses.definition: In a palatable manner.

core.definition: In a way that is pleasant to taste or acceptable to people.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, and the -ably ending is a reduced schwa followed by blee. Do not say it as pa-LAY-ta-bly, since the stress is on the first syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a fairly formal word used to describe food or ideas.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use palatably in casual speech. It appears mainly in cookbooks, food writing, or formal descriptions. In conversation, say 'It tastes good' or 'It goes down easy.' It is more natural in writing than speech.

distinctions.note: Deliciously expresses strong pleasure in taste, while palatably simply means acceptable or pleasant enough.

examples.everyday: The soup was thick, but the chef had prepared it palatably, so I finished the bowl.
examples.professional: The team presented the bad quarterly numbers palatably to the board by adding context and a clear recovery plan.
examples.analytical: The author argues that the hard truth is presented palatably only when its moral cost is not hidden.

nuance.analogy: Something served palatably is like a hard truth delivered with a spoonful of sugar.
nuance.etymology: From palatable plus the adverb suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Using palatably in casual talk where 'tastily' or 'good' would sound more natural.
Stressing the second syllable, as in pa-LAY-tab-ly.

senses.definition: A long, strong stake, one end of which is set firmly in the ground, and the other sharpened.
A line of cliffs, especially one showing basaltic columns.
senses.example: Hikers stopped at the palisade to admire the basalt columns rising above the river.

senses.definition: A wall of wooden stakes, used as a defensive barrier.
An even row of cells, e.g. palisade mesophyll cells.
senses.example: Under the microscope, the palisade cells in the leaf appeared tightly packed and rectangular.

senses.definition: To equip with a palisade.
senses.example: The settlers palisaded the village with sharpened logs before winter arrived.

core.definition: A fence or wall of strong, sharpened wooden stakes set upright in the ground, used as a defensive barrier.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the last syllable, SAYD, with a lighter stress on PAL. The middle syllable is a reduced 'uh.' Do not stress the first syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; in history and military writing it implies defense and frontier forts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use palisade mostly for historical forts, frontier stockades, and wooden defensive walls. In modern US usage it often means a cliff face, as in the Palisades along the Hudson River. Ordinary backyard fences are called fences, not palisades.

distinctions.note: A fence is any barrier; a palisade is a specific defensive wall of upright stakes.
A stockade is a similar enclosure, often a fort wall or prison yard made of logs; palisade is the more general term for rows of stakes.

examples.everyday: The kids built a little palisade of sticks around their sandbox fort.
examples.professional: The historic reconstruction includes a replica palisade built from pressure-treated timber.
examples.analytical: The palisade marks the boundary between the settlement's protected space and the wilderness beyond it.

nuance.analogy: Like a row of sharpened pencils standing guard around a castle.
nuance.etymology: From French palissade, from palis 'stake,' from Latin palus 'stake'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as in PAL-ih-sade.
Using palisade for an ordinary garden fence.

palisade.etymology: Middle French *palissade*, from Old French, from Old Occitan *palissada*, from *palissa* (“stake”), probably from *pal* (“stake”), or possibly from Gallo-Romance **pālīcea*, from Latin *pālus* (“stake”) *ade*.

senses.definition: Of, similar to, or related to paper.
senses.example: The old letters had a papery texture that crumbled slightly when I unfolded them.

core.definition: Thin, dry, and light like paper, often in texture or appearance.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on PAY. The middle syllable is a reduced, r-colored vowel, and the final -y is a clear ee sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to descriptive. It can suggest fragility, age, or dryness.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use papery mostly in descriptions of texture, such as leaves, skin, or old documents. It is less common in everyday speech and sounds more descriptive or literary. Use it when you want to convey dry thinness rather than thickness alone.

distinctions.note: Paper-thin refers to extreme thinness, while papery describes a texture or quality that resembles paper.
Thin is a general word for small thickness, while papery adds the sense of dry, crisp, or fragile material.

examples.everyday: The old letters had a papery feel, thin and crackly at the edges.
examples.professional: The sample has a papery texture, so it tears easily under the scanner's rollers.
examples.analytical: The manuscript's papery surface records centuries of handling, a material memory of its many readers.

nuance.analogy: Like a dried onion skin: thin, dry, and crackling at the edges.
nuance.etymology: From paper with the suffix -y, meaning like or resembling paper.
common_mistakes: Using papery for a person's thinness; it usually describes surface texture.
Confusing it with paper-thin, which emphasizes extreme thinness.

senses.definition: The number of learned weights in a model, often used as a rough measure of its size.
senses.example: The new model's parameter count is roughly seventy billion, so it needs several GPUs.

core.definition: The total number of learned weights in a model, often used as a rough measure of its size.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on KOUNT, the second word, while the first word has a secondary stress on AM. Learners often stress both words equally or stress the -er ending of parameter.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use parameter count in AI discussions and tech news to compare how large models are, such as 'a model with seven billion parameters'. In casual conversation, people may just say 'the model has billions of parameters'. It is a neutral measure, not a judgment of quality.

distinctions.note: Model size is a broader term that can include memory footprint and file size, while parameter count specifically counts learned weights.
Dataset size refers to the amount of training data, while parameter count refers to the model itself.

examples.everyday: My brother-in-law is impressed that the new model's parameter count is in the hundreds of billions.
examples.professional: Before we commit to the budget, let's compare the parameter count of each candidate model against our inference latency targets.
examples.analytical: A larger parameter count does not guarantee better generalization, so the scaling argument must account for the quantity and quality of training data.

nuance.analogy: Like counting the number of knobs on a huge control panel, where more knobs usually allow finer control but make the machine harder to run.
common_mistakes: Confusing parameter count with dataset size or number of training examples.
Assuming parameter count alone decides a model's quality.

conversation.text: The parameter count alone doesn't tell you how good a model is; data and training matter too.
Vendors love to quote parameter count, but we should ask about evaluation results.

senses.definition: A company that owns or controls one or more other companies.

core.definition: A company that owns or controls one or more other companies, which are called its subsidiaries.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on KUM in company, with parent lighter. The second syllable of company is a weak schwa, so say KUM-puh-nee, not KOM-pahn-ee with the stress at the end.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes corporate structure and carries no positive or negative judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this term in business news, finance, and job talk, for example saying the store is owned by a larger parent company. In casual talk people often say the big company or the owner. The term has a precise legal and financial meaning in contracts and filings.

distinctions.note: A holding company mainly owns shares in other firms and may run no business itself, while a parent company may also run its own operations.
A subsidiary is the company that is owned or controlled, so the parent company and subsidiary describe the two sides of one ownership relationship.

collocations: a wholly owned subsidiary of a parent company
the parent company of a well-known brand

examples.everyday: My tax preparer said the store where I work is actually owned by a bigger parent company in Ohio.
examples.professional: The parent company approved the budget for both subsidiaries, so our team can start hiring next quarter.
examples.analytical: The legal question is whether a parent company can be held responsible for environmental harm caused by its subsidiary.

nuance.analogy: A parent company is like a family business owner who holds the controlling shares of several smaller shops.
nuance.etymology: Parent from Latin parens, one who begets; company from Latin com, together, and panis, bread, meaning people who share bread, then a group of partners.
common_mistakes: Dropping the article, as in parent company is the owner; say the parent company or a parent company.
Adding a final vowel sound, as in KUM-puh-nee-ah; the word ends with a soft ee.

senses.definition: A collection of non-empty, disjoint subsets of a set whose union is the set itself (i.e. all elements of the set are contained in exactly one of the subsets).
senses.example: Every element of the set belongs to exactly one block of this partition.

senses.definition: An action which divides a thing into parts, or separates one thing from another.
senses.example: the partitions of Poland

senses.definition: A part of something that has been divided.
senses.example: the Russian Partition

senses.definition: An approach to division in which one asks what the size of each part is, rather than (as in quotition) how many parts there are.
senses.example: In the partition approach, we ask how large each group is rather than how many groups.

senses.definition: The division of a territory into two or more autonomous ones.
senses.example: Monarchies where partition isn't prohibited risk weakening through parcellation and civil wars between the heirs.

senses.definition: A vertical structure that divides a room.
senses.example: a brick partition; lath and plaster partitions

senses.definition: That which divides or separates; that by which different things, or distinct parts of the same thing, are separated; boundary; dividing line or space.
senses.example: The Berlin Wall was a stark partition that divided families for decades.

senses.definition: A part divided off by walls; an apartment; a compartment.
senses.example: Our tiny apartment had a flimsy partition that separated the bedroom from the kitchen.

senses.definition: The severance of common or undivided interests, particularly in real estate. It may be effected by consent of parties, or by compulsion of law.
senses.example: The court ordered a partition of the inherited farm so each sibling received a share.

senses.definition: A section of a hard disk separately formatted.
senses.example: I created a separate partition on the laptop's drive for Linux.

senses.definition: A division of a database or one of its constituting elements such as tables into separate independent parts.
