senses.example: We split the orders table into a partition for each year to speed up queries.

senses.definition: A division of a data stream, such as a messaging queue or topic (often representing a unit of parallelism, and of fault tolerance).
senses.example: Increasing the partition count on our Kafka topic let more consumers process messages in parallel.

senses.definition: A musical score.
senses.example: The partition of the Bach cantata lay open on the organ bench.

senses.definition: To divide something into parts, sections or shares.
senses.example: to partition a hard drive

senses.definition: To divide a region or country into two or more territories with separate political status.
senses.example: Poland was progressively partitioned by Russia, Austria, and Prussia in the late 18th century.

senses.definition: To separate or divide a room by a partition (ex. a wall), often use with off.
senses.example: We partitioned off the back corner of the garage to make a workshop.

core.definition: A wall or screen that divides a room, or the division of something into parts (the partition of a country); in mathematics, a collection of nonempty, non-overlapping subsets whose union is the whole set.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on TISH, the second syllable. The -tion ending is 'shun', and the first syllable is a reduced 'par' with a clear American r.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It's a precise technical term in math and logic, and also a general word for dividing something.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American English, partition usually means a wall or divider in a room or office, or dividing a place into sections. In math and logic, it has a precise meaning about splitting a set into non-overlapping subsets. Americans also say 'divide' or 'split' in casual talk, while 'partition' sounds more formal or technical.

distinctions.note: Division is broader and common in everyday use; partition implies separating something into defined parts, often with a boundary.
A subset is one part of a set; a partition is a collection of subsets that cover the whole set without overlapping.

examples.everyday: We put up a partition in the basement to make a separate space for my home office.
examples.professional: Before training the model, we'll partition the dataset into training, validation, and test sets.
examples.analytical: A partition of a finite set into disjoint blocks corresponds exactly to an equivalence relation on that set.

nuance.analogy: A partition is like cutting a pizza into slices where each slice is separate, no slice overlaps another, and together they make the whole pizza.
nuance.etymology: From Latin partitio, from partiri, 'to divide into parts,' from pars, 'part.'
common_mistakes: Confusing the noun with the verb, which is stressed the same way but used differently.
Using partition to mean a single part; a partition is the whole collection of parts.
Mispronouncing it as 'par-tish-EE-on'.
patterns: [C, U] partition of sth into sth
a partition between A and B

partition.etymology: Recorded c.1430, "division into shares, distinction," from Middle English *particioun*, from Old French *particion* (modern *partition*), from Latin *partitio* (“division, portion”), from *partitus*, the past participle of *partio* (“to split, part”).

senses.definition: To cause to move or go; to send; to transfer from one person, place, or condition to another.
senses.example: The waiter passed biscuits and cheese.

senses.definition: To be conveyed or transferred by will, deed, or other instrument of conveyance.
senses.example: The estate passes by the third clause in Mr Smith's deed to his son.

senses.definition: To transcend; to surpass; to excel; to exceed.
senses.example: Her piano playing simply passes anything I have ever heard from a student.

senses.definition: To decline something that is offered or available.
senses.example: He asked me to go to the cinema with him, but I think I'll pass.

senses.definition: To decline or not attempt to answer a question.
senses.example: I haven't any idea of the answer, so I'll have to pass.

senses.definition: In turn-based games, to decline to play in one's turn.
senses.example: It's your turn in the board game, but you can pass if you want to sit out.

senses.definition: In euchre, to decline to make the trump.
senses.example: With only one face card in her hand, Maria decided to pass on the trump call.

senses.definition: To change place.
senses.example: They passed from room to room.

senses.definition: To move or be moved from one place to another.
senses.example: They passed from room to room.

senses.definition: To go past, by, over, or through; to proceed from one side to the other of; to move past.
senses.example: You will pass a house on your right.

senses.definition: To make various kinds of movement.
senses.example: The Patriots passed on third and long.

senses.definition: To kick (the ball) with precision rather than at full force.
senses.example: Instead of blasting the ball, he passed it softly with the inside of his foot.

senses.definition: To move (the ball or puck) to a teammate.
senses.example: She saw her open teammate on the wing and passed him the ball.

senses.definition: To make a lunge or swipe.
senses.example: The angry cat tried to pass at the dangling string, missing by an inch.

senses.definition: To throw the ball, generally downfield, towards a teammate.
senses.example: The Patriots passed on third and long.

senses.definition: To go from one person to another.
senses.example: The bottle passed from hand to hand around the campfire until it was empty.

senses.definition: To put in circulation; to give currency to.
senses.example: pass counterfeit money

senses.definition: To cause to obtain entrance, admission, or conveyance.
senses.example: pass a person into a theater or over a railroad

senses.definition: To put through a sieve.
senses.example: When it's finished cooking, you should pass the sauce to get rid of any lumps.

senses.definition: To change in state or status.
senses.example: He passed from youth into old age.

senses.definition: To progress from one state to another; to advance.
senses.example: He passed from youth into old age.

senses.definition: To depart, to cease, to come to an end.
senses.example: At first, she was worried, but that feeling soon passed.

senses.definition: To die.
senses.example: His grandmother passed yesterday.

senses.definition: To achieve a successful outcome from.
senses.example: He attempted the examination, but did not expect to pass.

senses.definition: To advance through all the steps or stages necessary to become valid or effective; to obtain the formal sanction of (a legislative body).
senses.example: Despite the efforts of the opposition, the bill passed.

senses.definition: To cause to advance by stages of progress; to carry on with success through an ordeal, examination, or action; specifically, to give legal or official sanction to; to ratify; to enact; to approve as valid and just.
senses.example: He passed the bill through the committee.

senses.definition: To make a judgment on or upon a person or case.
senses.example: The jury will pass judgment on the defendant after hearing all the evidence.

senses.definition: To utter; to pronounce; to pledge.
senses.example: The judge passed sentence on the man, handing down ten years in prison.

senses.definition: To change from one state to another (without the implication of progression).
senses.example: After the storm, the sky passed from gray to a brilliant blue.

senses.definition: To move through time.
senses.example: Their vacation passed pleasantly.

senses.definition: To elapse, to be spent.
senses.example: Their vacation passed pleasantly.

senses.definition: To spend.
senses.example: What will we do to pass the time?

senses.definition: To allow to go by without noticing; to omit attention to; to take no note of; to disregard.
senses.example: She decided to pass over the mistake in his report rather than mention it.

senses.definition: To continue.
senses.example: Hours passed while we waited for the test results at the clinic.

senses.definition: To proceed without hindrance or opposition.
senses.example: You're late, but I'll let it pass.

senses.definition: To live through; to have experience of; to undergo; to suffer.
senses.example: Her grandmother passed through the Depression and never forgot the hunger.

senses.definition: To happen.
senses.example: It will soon come to pass.

senses.definition: To be accepted.
senses.example: It isn't ideal, but it will pass.

senses.definition: To be tolerated as a substitute for something else, to "do".
senses.example: It isn't ideal, but it will pass.

senses.definition: To be accepted by others as a member of a race, sex, or other group to which one does not belong or would not have originally appeared to belong; especially to be considered white although one has black ancestry, or a woman although one was assigned male at birth or vice versa.
senses.example: The novel follows a light-skinned woman who passes as white in 1920s Chicago.

senses.definition: To refrain from doing something.
senses.example: He asked me to go to the cinema with him, but I think I'll pass.

senses.definition: To reject; to pass up.
senses.example: The committee decided to pass on the proposal and fund a different project.

senses.definition: To do or be better.
senses.example: Our new software passes the old system in speed and reliability by a wide margin.

senses.definition: To eliminate (something) from the body by natural processes.
senses.example: He was passing blood in both his urine and his stool.

senses.definition: To take a turn with (a line, gasket, etc.), as around a sail in furling, and make secure.
A document granting permission to pass or to go and come; a passport; a ticket permitting free transit or admission.
senses.example: a railroad pass; a theater pass; a military pass

senses.definition: A run through a document as part of a translation, compilation or reformatting process.
senses.example: Most Pascal compilers process source code in a single pass.

senses.definition: A passing of two trains in the same direction on a single track, when one is put into a siding to let the other overtake it.
The act of overtaking; an overtaking maneuver.
An act of declining to play one's turn in a game, often by saying the word "pass".
senses.example: A pass would have seen her win the game, but instead she gave a wrong answer and lost a point, putting her in second place.

senses.definition: An opening, road, or track, available for passing; especially, one through or over some dangerous or otherwise impracticable barrier such as a mountain range; a passageway; a defile; a ford.
senses.example: mountain pass

senses.definition: A channel connecting a river or body of water to the sea, for example at the mouth (delta) of a river.
senses.example: the passes of the Mississippi

senses.definition: A single movement, especially of a hand, at, over, or along anything.
A single passage of a tool over something, or of something over a tool.
An attempt.
senses.example: My first pass at a career of writing proved unsuccessful.

senses.definition: A sexual advance (often in the phrase make a pass).
senses.example: The man kicked his friend out of the house after he made a pass at his wife.

senses.definition: Success in an examination or similar test.
senses.example: I gained three passes at A-level, in mathematics, French, and English literature.

senses.definition: A thrust or push; an attempt to stab or strike an adversary.
A thrust; a sally of wit.
Permission or license to pass, or to go and come.
The state of things; condition; predicament; impasse.
The area in a restaurant kitchen where the finished dishes are passed from the chefs to the waiting staff.
A password (especially one for a restricted-access website).
senses.example: Anyone want to trade passes?

senses.definition: The act of moving the ball or puck from one player to another.
senses.example: Everyone in the football stadium expected a pass play on third down.

senses.definition: An intentional walk.
senses.example: Smith was given a pass after Jones' double.

core.definition: To move past someone or something while going in the same direction, or to go by a place or point.

pronunciation.tip: Use the short a of 'cat' and make the final s clear. Do not add an aspirated puff or a long ah sound; the word is a single short syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes ordinary movement, and it can also mean to decline or to finish a test or class.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use pass constantly while driving, walking, or getting through places, and it is informal but completely standard. For driving, people say 'Pass on the left' or 'Pass that truck.' When refusing an offer, Americans say 'I'll pass' or 'I'm going to pass,' which is casual and polite.

distinctions.note: Overtake is more formal and focuses on going ahead of a moving vehicle; pass is the everyday word.
Go by is more casual and means to travel past a place or pass time; pass often describes a clear movement past something.

examples.everyday: Could you pass the salt, please?
examples.professional: Let's pass the project to the data team after the review, so they can start the next phase.
examples.analytical: In Hebrews 4:14 the author describes Jesus as having passed through the heavens, which is used to show his exalted position.

nuance.analogy: Passing someone is like two boats moving in the same direction on a river, where one moves ahead and the other is left behind.
nuance.etymology: From Old French passer, from Latin passare, meaning to step or to pass along.
common_mistakes: Using pass for 'pass away' in casual talk, which can confuse listeners.
Forgetting the preposition in phrases such as 'pass by' or 'pass through', where the meaning changes.

pass.etymology: From Middle English *passen*, from Old French *passer* (“to step, walk, pass”), from Vulgar Latin **passo* (“step, walk, pass”), derived from Latin *passus* (“a step”), from Proto-Italic **pattus*, from Proto-Indo-European **peth₂-* (“to spread, stretch out”).

conversation.text: My monthly bus pass covers unlimited rides.
Don't pass on the right; it's dangerous.
We passed the exit a mile ago.
"Want to drive?" "I'll pass. I'm exhausted."

senses.definition: Lacking in passion.
senses.example: The lecturer had a cold, passionless approach towards his subject.

core.definition: Lacking strong feeling, energy or emotional commitment; flat, cold or uninterested.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the first syllable. The 'ion' is 'shun,' and the final '-less' is a weak, quick 'lus' with no long vowel, so it sounds like 'PASH-uhn-lus.'

nuance.connotation: Negative. It criticizes a person, performance or relationship for lacking warmth or energy.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this to criticize a speech, a performance, a marriage or a piece of writing that feels routine or emotionally empty. It is common in reviews and conversation but can sound harsh if used about a person directly. A softer alternative is 'a little flat' or 'kind of blah.'

distinctions.note: Dispassionate means calm and impartial, free of emotional bias, and is often positive in analysis, while passionless means emotionally empty and is usually negative.
Apathetic describes a lack of interest or concern in what is happening, while passionless describes a lack of emotional intensity in the thing itself or the person doing it.

examples.everyday: The movie had great sets, but the lead actor's performance felt kind of passionless.
examples.professional: The status update was accurate but passionless, so nobody in the meeting asked any questions.
examples.analytical: Critics of purely academic theology worry that it can become passionless, a body of accurate claims without love for its subject.

nuance.analogy: A passionless speech is like a lamp with a bulb that gives light but no warmth.
nuance.etymology: From passion, from Late Latin passio 'suffering,' with the English suffix -less 'without.'
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'dispassionate,' which describes calm fairness rather than emotional emptiness
Stressing the last syllable, as in 'pash-un-LESS'

senses.definition: Able to cause (harmful) disease.
senses.example: While the environment is teeming with bacteria and fungi, most are not pathogenic.

senses.definition: Consisting of harsh, percussive, nonverbal sounds.

core.definition: Able to cause disease, especially a microbe, virus or other agent that makes a living thing sick.

pronunciation.tip: Stress JEN, the third syllable, and keep the first syllable light. Many learners stress the first syllable, which sounds wrong to Americans.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes something harmful that causes disease.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use pathogenic in medicine, food safety, public health and science news, for example 'pathogenic bacteria' in food. In everyday talk people usually say 'germs' or 'harmful bacteria.' The word is accurate and common in U.S. health contexts, but it can sound too technical for casual conversation.

distinctions.note: Infectious means able to spread from one person to another; pathogenic means able to cause disease, whether or not it spreads.
Harmful is a general word for anything damaging; pathogenic is specific to microbes or agents that cause disease.

examples.everyday: Most bacteria in the sink are harmless, but a few are pathogenic.
examples.professional: The lab confirmed that the sample contained a pathogenic strain, so we pulled the batch.
examples.analytical: Whether a microbe is pathogenic depends on the host and the context, not only on the organism itself.

nuance.analogy: Like a spark that is harmless in a damp forest but dangerous in dry grass, a pathogenic agent causes harm depending on conditions.
nuance.etymology: From pathogen plus -ic, from Greek pathos, 'suffering,' and -gen, 'producing.'
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, as in 'PATH-uh-JEN-ik.'
Using pathogenic for any harmful thing, when it applies only to disease-causing agents.

senses.definition: Of or relating to the theories of the Russian physiologist, psychologist, and physician Ivan Petrovich Pavlov, especially those related to behavioral conditioning.
senses.example: The app's endless notifications created a Pavlovian habit of checking my phone.

senses.definition: A proponent of Pavlov's theories.
senses.example: As a Pavlovian, my psychology professor insisted every behavior was a learned response.

core.definition: Relating to Ivan Pavlov's theory of conditioned reflexes, or describing an automatic, learned response triggered by a cue.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on LOH, not on PAV, which is the stress pattern of the surname Pavlov. The ending is pronounced 'vee-un', not 'vee-ahn'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in psychology; often mildly dismissive when used about people, suggesting they respond without thinking.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mainly in psychology, education and science writing, and in casual talk about habits, such as checking your phone out of habit. Calling someone's reaction Pavlovian can sound like a mild criticism that they are not thinking. The word always refers to Pavlov's conditioning theory, so it does not describe dog training in general.

distinctions.note: Skinnerian refers to B. F. Skinner's operant conditioning, where behavior is shaped by rewards and punishments, whereas Pavlovian refers to responses paired with a stimulus.
Reflexive is a general word for any automatic action; Pavlovian is narrower and implies that the response was learned through repeated pairing.

examples.everyday: Every time my phone buzzes I grab it right away, which is pretty Pavlovian, honestly.
examples.professional: Our users have a Pavlovian response to every pop-up, so we are testing a quieter notification design.
examples.analytical: Much of early behaviorism reduced learning to Pavlovian association, ignoring the role of expectation and meaning.

nuance.analogy: Like a dog salivating at the sound of a bell, a habit that fires automatically whenever a familiar cue appears.
nuance.etymology: Named for Ivan Pavlov (1849-1936), the Russian physiologist, with the suffix -ian.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable (PAV-lo-vee-un) instead of the second (pav-LOH-vee-un).
Using Pavlovian to mean any kind of animal training; it refers specifically to classical conditioning.

senses.definition: A teacher or instructor of children; one whose occupation is to teach the young.
senses.example: The kindly pedagogue spent every afternoon coaxing reluctant readers through their first chapter books.

senses.definition: A pedant; one who by teaching has become overly formal or pedantic in his or her ways; one who has the manner of a teacher.
senses.example: Nobody at the dinner party could stand his pedagogue tone, lecturing everyone about the proper fork.

senses.definition: (historical) A slave who led the master's children to school, and had the charge of them generally.
senses.example: In the novel, the pedagogue walked the young master to school each morning, carrying his books.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: To teach.
senses.example: She pedagogued her younger brothers on multiplication tables every evening after dinner.

core.definition: A teacher, especially one who is overly formal, strict, or preachy about teaching; sometimes used to mean a schoolteacher.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, PED. The second syllable is a reduced schwa, and the final syllable rhymes with dog, not with gogue. Americans say PED-uh-gog, not ped-uh-GOOG.

nuance.connotation: Often mildly negative. It can describe a teacher who is stiff, pedantic, or lecturing, though it can also be neutral in formal writing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use pedagogue in ordinary conversation. You will see it in literature, essays, or commentary, where it often describes someone who lectures too much. In everyday speech say teacher or instructor. Using it for a friendly teacher can sound odd or sarcastic.

distinctions.note: Teacher is the normal everyday word and is neutral or positive; pedagogue is formal or literary and often suggests stiffness or pedantry.
A pedant is a person who fusses over minor details; a pedagogue is a teacher who may act like one, so the two overlap but are not identical.

examples.professional: The trainer was too much of a pedagogue, lecturing for an hour when the team needed hands-on practice.
examples.analytical: Socrates in Plato's dialogues is less a pedagogue delivering doctrine than a questioner who draws out understanding.

nuance.analogy: A pedagogue is like a tour guide who insists on explaining every statue in the museum, even when you only wanted to look.
nuance.etymology: From Greek paidagogos, a slave who escorted boys to school, from pais, child, and agogos, leader.
common_mistakes: Using pedagogue as a neutral everyday word for teacher, which can sound odd or sarcastic.
Mispronouncing the final syllable as goo-gay or goo-gue; it rhymes with log.

pedagogue.etymology: From Middle English *pedagoge*, from Middle French *pedagogue*, from Latin *paedagōgus*, from Ancient Greek *παιδαγωγός*, from *παῖς* (“child”) + *ἀγωγός* (“guide”) (from *ἄγω* (“lead”)).

senses.definition: Something that penetrates.
senses.example: The steel tip acts as a penetrator, designed to pierce armor plating on impact.

senses.definition: A long-range fighter aircraft designed to penetrate enemy air defences.
senses.example: The squadron's penetrator jets slipped past radar before the enemy could scramble their interceptors.

core.definition: Something or someone that gets through a barrier, defense, or surface, such as a tool, projectile, or intruder.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and let the final -or become the American r-colored schwa, which sounds like ter. Do not add an extra syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in technical use. It can sound cold or military, and in some sexual contexts it is crude, so avoid those uses.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use penetrator mostly in military, security, and engineering writing, such as describing earth penetrators or armor-piercing projectiles. In everyday speech they would say intruder, hacker, or something that gets through. The word can sound overly technical outside those fields.

distinctions.note: An intruder is a person who enters a place without permission, while a penetrator can be a person, an object, or a technical threat that gets past defenses.
A projectile is any object thrown or fired, while a penetrator is specifically designed or able to break through a protected target.

examples.everyday: That tiny drill bit is a real penetrator; it goes through brick in a few seconds.
examples.professional: The security audit identified the phishing email as the main penetrator of our perimeter.
examples.analytical: In Kierkegaard's writing, the reader is less a penetrator of the text than a person penetrated by it.

nuance.analogy: A bullet is a penetrator, while a sieve is not, because it is designed to get through things rather than hold them back.
nuance.etymology: From penetrate with the agent suffix -or, from Latin penetrare 'to enter into'.
common_mistakes: Using penetrator for a casual intruder, which sounds too technical in everyday speech.
Mispronouncing the final syllable with a full o sound instead of the reduced American ter.

senses.definition: The capacity of language and expressive actions to perform a type of being.
senses.example: Our seminar on ritual speech spent weeks debating performativity and whether words can create identity.

senses.definition: The quality of being performative.

core.definition: The quality of language or acts that actually do what they say, like a vow that creates a marriage.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on TIV, the third syllable, and the -ity ending is a short ih-tee. The first syllable stays light but keeps its r sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a technical term with no emotional charge, though in gender theory it is often debated.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mainly in philosophy of language, gender studies and data science, where performative prediction is discussed. In J.L. Austin's sense, a performative is a sentence that does something, like 'I promise' or 'I now pronounce you married'. Do not use it to mean performance or showing off.

distinctions.note: Performance is the act or event of performing; performativity is the philosophical idea that some utterances bring about what they name.
A constative statement describes or reports something that can be true or false, while a performative changes the situation by being said.

examples.everyday: My sociology professor says a wedding vow is a perfect example of performativity, since the words themselves make the marriage happen.
examples.professional: In our ethics review, we discussed how an algorithm's labels can have performativity, shaping the behavior they were meant to describe.
examples.analytical: Austin's notion of performativity distinguishes utterances that describe the world from those that change it, such as promises and verdicts.

nuance.analogy: Like a referee's whistle: the act of blowing it stops the play.
nuance.etymology: From performative, from perform (from Anglo-Norman parfournir 'to complete') plus -ity.
common_mistakes: Using performativity as a synonym for performance or showing off, which is a different word.
Putting the stress on FOR instead of TIV, the syllable that carries the main stress.

senses.definition: With circumlocution or periphrasis.
senses.example: She asked periphrastically whether he might possibly consider leaving the meeting early.

core.definition: In a roundabout way, using several words where a direct, simple expression would do.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on FRAS, the third syllable, and the -ically ending becomes -ik-lee. Say the r clearly after the first vowel, and do not stress the first syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative. It describes wordy indirectness, which can sound evasive or pretentious.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this in writing about language and grammar, in literary criticism, and occasionally to describe someone who avoids a plain word. Speakers would more often say in a roundabout way or without saying it directly. In casual conversation it sounds bookish, and a friend might tease you for using it.

distinctions.note: Euphemistically replaces an unpleasant word with a milder one; periphrastically uses many words in place of one.
Verbosely means using too many words in general; periphrastically means specifically going around a direct expression.

examples.everyday: Instead of just saying he got fired, Dave said he's no longer with the company, which is his way of saying it periphrastically.
examples.professional: The memo describes the layoffs periphrastically as workforce realignment, so employees may not recognize what is actually happening.
examples.analytical: Many medieval theologians describe God periphrastically, through a series of negations rather than a direct predicate, which shows the limits of human language.

nuance.analogy: It is like taking the long way around the block: you arrive at the same place, but you pass many turns you did not need.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin periphrasticus, from Greek periphrastikos, from periphrazein 'to speak around, express in a roundabout way'.
common_mistakes: Using periphrastically for ordinary wordiness; it specifically means expressing something through a roundabout phrase in place of a direct one.
Stressing the wrong syllable, as PAIR-uh-fras-tik-lee; the stress belongs on FRAS.

senses.definition: Able to be permuted.

core.definition: Able to be rearranged into a different order without changing the basic result or meaning.

pronunciation.tip: The final -able is a reduced 'uh-bul'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise mathematical and technical term with no emotional content.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use permutable mainly in mathematics, statistics, computer science and data science, for example about variables or elements whose order can be changed. In everyday speech, people say that steps or items can be 'switched around' or 'done in any order'. The word is rare outside technical contexts.

distinctions.note: Interchangeable means that items can replace one another, while permutable means their order can be rearranged.
A variable is something whose value can change, while permutable refers only to changing the order of elements without changing their values.

examples.everyday: Honestly, the steps in that recipe are pretty much permutable, so you can do them in any order.
examples.professional: The loss function is symmetric, so the features are permutable and we can reorder them without changing the model's output.
examples.analytical: Such an operation is permutable only when its arguments commute, so the order of composition becomes a substantive question rather than a formality.

nuance.analogy: Permutable items are like cards in a deck you can shuffle into any order, as long as you keep every card in the deck.
nuance.etymology: From permute, from Latin permutare 'to change thoroughly', from per 'thoroughly' plus mutare 'to change', with the suffix -able.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable (PUR-myoo-tuh-bul) instead of MYOO.
Confusing permutable with variable, which is about changing values rather than order.

senses.definition: Enduring; persistent, resistant.
senses.example: The perseverant students kept practicing their proofs until every problem was solved.

core.definition: Continuing firmly and steadily in a course of action despite difficulty, opposition, or discouragement; persistent and unwilling to give up.

pronunciation.tip: Primary stress falls on VIHR, the middle syllable. The first syllable reduces to a quick 'pur' and the final -ant is weak, so it sounds like 'unt'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises steady endurance, and it is nearly always used approvingly.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use perseverant in speech. In conversation they say persistent, determined, or 'hang in there,' and perseverant appears mostly in formal writing, sermons, and essays. You may hear it in religious contexts to describe someone who keeps faith through hardship.

distinctions.note: Persistent is the everyday word and can be neutral or negative, as in a persistent cough. Perseverant always praises steady endurance through hardship.
Stubborn means refusing to change one's mind, often with a negative tone. Perseverant suggests steady effort toward a worthy goal.
Determined focuses on the intention to succeed. Perseverant focuses on continuing over a long period despite obstacles.

examples.everyday: My grandmother was so perseverant about learning English that she started taking classes at sixty-five.
examples.professional: The platform team stayed perseverant through three failed launches, and the final release was much stronger for it.
examples.analytical: The essayist argues that a perseverant commitment to truth matters more than any single brilliant insight.

nuance.analogy: Like a stone that keeps its place in a fast river while the water wears down everything around it.
nuance.etymology: From Latin perseverare, 'to persist thoroughly.'
common_mistakes: Using perseverant in casual speech where Americans would naturally say persistent or determined.
Stressing the second syllable as per-SEV-er-ant; the stress falls on VIHR.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek word hypomonē (ὑπομονή, 'steadfast endurance under pressure') stands behind perseverance in Scripture. Romans 5:3-4 describes how suffering produces endurance, which in turn produces character and hope. James 1:3-4 teaches that the testing of faith produces steadfastness, which should be allowed to finish its work. Hebrews 12:1 urges believers to run with perseverance the race set before them.

perseverant.etymology: From Middle English *perseveraunt*, from Middle French *perseverant*, from Latin *persevērāns*, present participle of *persevērō*.

senses.definition: In a petty manner.

core.definition: In a petty way; in a small-minded manner that focuses on trivial matters or resentments.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on PET. The tt is a flap that sounds like a soft d in fast speech, so it may sound like PED-ih-lee, and the word has three syllables, not four.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it criticizes behavior that is small-minded or vindictive over trivial matters.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use pettily in writing, reviews, commentary and formal criticism, and sometimes in everyday speech to describe a small revenge. It is stronger than mean, which can be used more lightly. In casual talk, Americans might say being petty or doing something to get back at someone.

distinctions.note: Meanly suggests unkindness toward people, while pettily suggests a focus on trivial matters or resentments.
Petulantly describes childish sulking or irritability, while pettily describes small-minded or spiteful behavior about trivial things.

examples.everyday: He pettily refused to share the Wi-Fi password after we argued about the thermostat.
examples.professional: She pettily removed my name from the team slide after our disagreement in the meeting.
examples.analytical: The critic pettily dismissed the novel over a few typos, ignoring its argument entirely.

nuance.analogy: Like someone who keeps score of tiny slights, pettily acting means letting small things grow into big grievances.
nuance.etymology: From petty, from Old French petit 'small', with the adverbial suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Using pettily as an adjective; the adjective is petty.
Confusing pettily with meanly; pettily focuses on trivial matters, while meanly focuses on unkindness.

senses.definition: Something seen but having no physical reality; a phantom or apparition.
An impression as received by the senses, especially an image, often prior to any interpretation by the intellect.
senses.example: The philosopher argued that a phantasm, or sensory image, forms before the mind judges what it means.

core.definition: Something that seems to be seen but has no physical reality; a ghostly image, illusion or apparition.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the first syllable. The last syllable is weak, like 'um', not 'azm'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly eerie; it suggests something unreal that a person sees or fears.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'phantasm' mainly in literature, philosophy and formal writing, where it sounds elevated. In everyday speech, people say 'ghost', 'phantom' or 'illusion'. Using it in casual talk may sound overly dramatic.

distinctions.note: 'Phantom' is the common word for a ghost or a fake sense of presence, while 'phantasm' is more literary.
An illusion is a false perception of something real, while a phantasm is an image that has no real existence.

examples.everyday: I thought I saw someone at the window, but it was just a phantasm of the streetlight.
examples.professional: The report warned that the forecast was a phantasm, since the model had been trained on bad data.
examples.analytical: For Hume, the idea of a physical substance may be a phantasm created by the mind's habit of connecting perceptions.

nuance.analogy: A phantasm is like a mirage in the desert: it looks real from a distance but vanishes when you approach.
nuance.etymology: From Greek 'phantasma' (appearance), from 'phantazein' (to make visible).
common_mistakes: Mispronouncing it as 'fan-TAZ-um'.
Confusing it with 'fantasy', which means an imaginative idea or daydream, not a ghostly image.

phantasm.etymology: A learned variant of *phantom*; from Middle English *fantosme*, from Old French *fantosme*, *fantasme*, from Latin *phantasma*, from Ancient Greek *φάντασμα*.

senses.definition: A person who engages in philology (historical linguistics), especially as a profession; a collector of words and their etymologies.
senses.example: The philologist traced the word's roots back to Proto-Indo-European in her new book.

senses.definition: A person devoted to general learning and literature.
senses.example: Her grandfather was a philologist who read Homer and Dante for pleasure every evening.

senses.definition: A person devoted to classical scholarship.
senses.example: As a philologist of Latin, he spent decades comparing manuscripts of Cicero's letters.

core.definition: A scholar who studies the history of languages and the texts written in them, usually as an academic profession.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on LAH, and the first o is a short sound, not oh. Non-native speakers often add a long ee sound to the final -ist; it is a short ih.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it suggests deep scholarly expertise. Americans may find it slightly old-fashioned or grand when used for ordinary language teachers.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mainly for academics in classics, Germanic or Romance studies, or historical linguistics. In everyday conversation people more often say linguist or language scholar. If someone asks what you do and you study old texts, you might answer, 'I'm a philologist, so I study how words and texts changed over time.'

distinctions.note: A linguist studies how language works in general, including speech today; a philologist focuses on written texts and the historical development of languages.
An etymologist traces the origin of individual words, while a philologist studies whole texts, languages and their history more broadly.

examples.everyday: My uncle is a philologist, so he can tell you where almost any English word came from.
examples.professional: As the philologist on our digital archive project, I'm comparing the manuscript versions line by line to date the scribal changes.
examples.analytical: The philologist must establish the reliable text before interpreting its meaning, because every reading depends on the surviving manuscript evidence.

nuance.analogy: A philologist is like an archaeologist of language, digging through old texts to uncover how words were used and how they changed.
nuance.etymology: From Greek philologos, 'fond of words or learning', from philo- 'loving' and logos 'word, reason'.
common_mistakes: Confusing philologist with philosopher because the words look alike.
Using it for any language teacher; a philologist studies historical texts and language change, not classroom instruction.

senses.definition: To collect or purchase an object, especially in passing.
senses.example: Can you pick up a pint of milk on your way home?

senses.definition: To collect a passenger.
senses.example: I'll pick you up outside the library.

senses.definition: To collect and detain (a suspect).
senses.example: The cops have picked up the man they were looking for.

senses.definition: To improve, increase, or speed up.
senses.example: Prices seem to be picking up again.

senses.definition: To answer a telephone.
senses.example: I'm calling him, but he just isn't picking up!

senses.definition: To learn, to grasp; to begin to understand; to realize.
senses.example: It looks complicated, but you'll soon pick it up.

senses.definition: To lift; to grasp and raise.
senses.example: When you pick up the bag, make sure to support the bottom.

senses.definition: To restart or resume.
senses.example: Let's pick up where we left off yesterday.

senses.definition: To acquire (something) accidentally; to catch or contract (a disease).
senses.example: I picked up a cold on my trip last week.

senses.definition: To be caught or accused of wrongdoing, usually criminal charges.
senses.example: He picked up a parole violation last month.

senses.definition: To clean up; to return to an organized state.
senses.example: You made a mess, aren't you going to pick up after yourself?

senses.definition: To obtain and publish a story, news item, etc.
senses.example: The story does not seem to have been widely picked up.

senses.definition: To reach and continue along (a road).
senses.example: Walter decided the best route home was to pick up the A5.

senses.definition: To receive (a radio signal or the like).
senses.example: With the new antenna, I can pick up stations all the way from Omaha.

senses.definition: To notice, detect or discern; to pick up on.
senses.example: Did you pick up his nervousness?

senses.definition: To point out the behavior, habits, or actions of (a person) in a critical manner; used with on.
senses.example: She's always picking me up on my grammar.

senses.definition: To meet and seduce somebody for romantic purposes, especially in a social situation.
senses.example: He was in the fabric store not to buy fabric but to pick up women.

senses.definition: To receive calls; to function correctly.
senses.example: I've tried his home number a couple times, but it isn't picking up.

senses.definition: To pay for.
senses.example: The company will pick up lunch with customers for sales calls.

senses.definition: To reduce the despondency of.
To take control (physically) of something.
To mark, to defend against an opposition player by following them closely.
To record; to notch up.
To behave in a manner that results in a foul. (Can we add an example for this sense?)
To promote somebody who was previously passed over.
Rare form of pickup.

core.definition: To collect someone or something, especially on the way somewhere, or to buy something you planned to get.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on UP, the particle, not on PICK. In fast speech, the final k of pick links to the u of up, so it sounds close to 'pi-ki-DUP'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is an everyday, practical phrase used for ordinary errands and pickups.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use pick up constantly: 'I'll pick you up at seven' means they'll drive to get you, and 'Can you pick up milk?' means buy it on the way. A natural reply is 'Sounds good' or 'Thanks, see you then.' Note that 'pick up the phone' means to answer a call, which is also very common.

distinctions.note: Drop off means to leave someone or something somewhere, which is the opposite of picking them up.
Get is more general and can mean obtain or receive, while pick up specifically implies collecting something from a place or person.

collocations: pick up on the way home

examples.everyday: Can you pick up some eggs on your way home? We're almost out.
examples.professional: I'll pick up the thread on the churn model after lunch and send you the results.
examples.analytical: Aquinas picks up Aristotle's distinction between potency and act and develops it in his account of creation.

nuance.analogy: It is like a hand reaching out to grab something from a shelf and lifting it up.
nuance.etymology: Combines the verb pick, from Middle English pikken of uncertain origin, with the adverb up.
common_mistakes: Placing an object pronoun incorrectly, as in 'pick up it' instead of 'pick it up'.
Using 'pick up' for a noun, when the noun form is 'pickup' as in pickup truck.
Pronouncing 'pick' as 'peek' with a long vowel.

conversation.text: I'll pick you up at seven, so be ready.
Can you pick up some milk on your way home?
I called twice, but she didn't pick up.
I picked up a little Spanish when I lived in Texas.
Business usually picks up around the holidays.
Pick up your toys before dinner.
Let's pick up where we left off yesterday.

senses.definition: Resembling or worthy of a picture or painting; having the qualities of a picture or painting; pleasingly beautiful.
senses.example: We looked down onto a beautiful, picturesque sunset over the ocean.

senses.definition: Strikingly graphic or vivid; having striking and vivid imagery.
senses.example: picturesque language

core.definition: Visually charming and pretty, like a picture, especially in a scenic landscape or old-fashioned village.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the last syllable, -RESK, with lighter stress on PIK-. Many learners put stress on the first syllable or pronounce the -esque as -ayesk; say RESK with a short e.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises scenery or places as beautiful and charming, sometimes with a hint of being quaint.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use picturesque mainly for landscapes, villages, towns and views, as in a picturesque town in New England. In casual speech, people often say pretty or scenic instead. Describing a person as picturesque is less common and sounds literary.

distinctions.note: Scenic describes a place with attractive views, while picturesque adds the idea that the scene looks like a painting.
Pretty is a general word for attractive, while picturesque suggests a composed, painterly beauty.

examples.everyday: That little town by the lake is so picturesque; we should stop there on the way home.
examples.professional: The client wants a picturesque setting for the photo shoot, so we are scouting locations in Vermont.
examples.analytical: Nineteenth-century landscape painters valued the picturesque as a balance of roughness, variety and charm.

nuance.analogy: A picturesque place is like a postcard that has come to life: every view seems arranged for a painter.
nuance.etymology: From Italian pittoresco, from pittore, painter, through the English term picture.
common_mistakes: Using it for ordinary, everyday pretty things, which sounds exaggerated.
Stressing the first syllable, PIK-tur-esk, instead of the final -RESK.

picturesque.etymology: From *picture* + *-esque*, a French *pittoresque*, from *picture* (“a picture, painting”).

senses.definition: The degree to which something is piquant, stimulating or exciting.
senses.example: The chef's sauce had a bright piquancy from fresh lime and crushed red pepper.

core.definition: The quality of being pleasantly sharp, spicy or stimulating, in taste or in interest.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the qu is pronounced like k. The final -ancy is unstressed and reduces to a weak schwa, so avoid the French-style 'pee-KAHNT'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises something that adds bite, wit or excitement, such as food, writing or a conversation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use piquancy mostly in writing, reviews, or when describing food or conversation with some flair. In casual speech, people more often say something has a kick, a bite or a little zing. Saying 'that dish has piquancy' is fine, but it sounds slightly literary at a restaurant table.

distinctions.note: Spiciness refers to heat from chili or pepper, while piquancy covers any pleasant sharpness, including tang, wit or intellectual edge.
Zest suggests enthusiasm or energy, while piquancy describes a sharp, contrasting flavor or quality that makes something more interesting.

examples.everyday: The lime and chili gave the mango salad a nice bit of piquancy.
examples.professional: Her presentation had a piquancy that kept the room awake through the whole Q3 forecast.
examples.analytical: The essay's piquancy comes from setting Kierkegaard's irony against Aquinas's sober metaphysics.

nuance.analogy: Like a squeeze of lemon on grilled fish, piquancy brightens something that would otherwise taste flat.
nuance.etymology: From French piquant, from piquer 'to prick'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, as in 'pee-KAN-see'.
Pronouncing the final syllable as 'see-ah' or 'shee'; the ending is the unstressed 'un-see'.

senses.definition: Of, relating to, or being a pivot.
senses.example: Her decision to adopt open-source tools was pivotal for the team's long-term success.

senses.definition: Being of crucial importance; central, key.

core.definition: Of crucial importance; central to the success, outcome, or development of something else.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The middle 'i' is a short, reduced vowel, and the final syllable is a light 'ul', not 'tall'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It emphasizes importance and can suggest that something is a turning point, for better or worse.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use pivotal in meetings, news, and reports to say that a decision, person, or event is the key factor. It is more formal than 'key' or 'important' and sounds natural in writing and business talk. In casual speech people often say 'a big deal' or 'really important' instead.

distinctions.note: Crucial stresses that something is absolutely necessary; pivotal stresses that it is a turning point or central hinge on which other things depend.
Key is more casual and common in everyday speech, while pivotal is more formal and implies a decisive moment.
Essential means something cannot be done without; pivotal means something changes the direction of events.

examples.everyday: Honestly, getting that job was pivotal for me because it changed how I think about my career.
examples.professional: The vendor's API change was pivotal, so we need to test our pipeline against it before Friday.
examples.analytical: Scholars argue that the 1517 controversy was pivotal in shaping the modern split between Catholic and Protestant theology.

nuance.analogy: A pivotal event is like the hinge of a door: small in itself, but everything else swings on it.
nuance.etymology: From pivot, a word of uncertain origin, probably from French.
common_mistakes: Saying 'pivotal' for any important thing; it is best for moments or people that change outcomes.
Pronouncing the middle vowel as a full 'ee' sound; it is reduced to a short 'ih'.

senses.definition: Characterized by clichés or platitudes.
senses.example: His platitudinous commencement speech offered nothing but tired advice about hard work and dreams.

core.definition: Full of platitudes; obvious, trite, and unoriginal, often in a way that makes speech or writing feel empty.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on 'tood,' and the final -ous is a weak syllable that sounds like 'us.' The middle vowels are reduced, so do not give each syllable an equal sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes speech or writing as empty, predictable, and unhelpful.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word in literary criticism, political commentary, and reviews of speeches. It is a judgment, so use it carefully and mainly in writing. In everyday speech, people more often say 'that was so generic' or 'he just repeated clichés.'

distinctions.note: Trite is the general word for overused and unoriginal, while platitudinous focuses on remarks that are commonplace and vague.
Banal means dull and ordinary, while platitudinous specifically refers to empty, overused statements.
Hackneyed describes a phrase or idea worn out by overuse, while platitudinous describes a whole speech or piece of writing as empty.

examples.everyday: His advice was so platitudinous that I couldn't tell whether he had actually listened to my problem.
examples.professional: The vendor's slides about empowering teams were platitudinous and gave us no real information about pricing.
examples.analytical: The essay's conclusion is platitudinous, since it restates the thesis in words anyone could have written, so it adds nothing to the argument.

nuance.analogy: Like a fortune cookie message, it is pleasant to read but could fit almost any day of the year.
nuance.etymology: From platitude (from French platitude, from plat, flat) plus the adjective suffix -ous.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, as in PLAT-ih-tud-nus, instead of the TOOD syllable.
Using platitudinous to mean simple or plain in a neutral sense, when it always carries criticism.

platitudinous.etymology: From *platitude* + *-ous* on analogy of other adjectives ending in -tudinous, from Latin *-tūdō* + *-ous*, the oblique stem of *-tūdō*.

senses.definition: To take a cautious, risk-free approach.
senses.example: Deciding to play it safe, he joined his father's accounting firm rather than pursue an acting career.

core.definition: To choose the cautious option that avoids risk, even if it means a smaller reward or result.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on SAFE, the last word. In fast speech 'it' is a reduced short vowel, and the words link so that 'play it' sounds like 'play-it'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to mildly negative; it can sound wise and prudent, or timid when used as criticism.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this in everyday decisions and workplace talk, such as 'Let's play it safe and book the refundable flight.' Tone decides whether it is praise or criticism. A natural reply is 'Yeah, that's probably smart' or 'Good call, let's take the safer route'.

distinctions.note: Be cautious describes an attitude; play it safe describes a specific choice to avoid any real risk.
Take a risk is the opposite; it means accepting uncertainty for a possible gain.

collocations: play it safe on the highway
when in doubt, play it safe

examples.everyday: I'm going to play it safe and bring a jacket in case it rains.
examples.professional: With the audit next week, let's play it safe and keep the current configuration until the review is done.
examples.analytical: Risk-averse agents often play it safe, accepting a lower expected payoff to avoid the chance of a catastrophic loss.

nuance.analogy: Like walking on a well-lit path instead of a shortcut through the dark woods.
nuance.etymology: 'Safe' comes from Latin salvus, meaning whole or unharmed; 'play' comes from Old English plegan.
common_mistakes: Placing the object wrongly; say 'play it safe', not 'play safe it'.
Using the wrong preposition with an object: say 'play it safe with your money', not 'play safe in your money'.

senses.definition: The quality of being poignant.

core.definition: The quality of being deeply moving or sad, so that it causes a strong feeling of sympathy or sorrow.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on POYN, which rhymes with coin. The t in the full form is usually silent in the noun, so the ending is -see.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral as a quality. It usually describes a sad moment that makes people feel something deeply.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use poignancy in writing, reviews, speeches and careful conversation about emotional events, such as a farewell or an old photograph. In casual talk they more often say it was so sad or it really got to me. The word is related to the adjective poignant, and the noun is more often used with the, as in the poignancy of the moment.

distinctions.note: Sadness is the feeling itself, while poignancy is the quality that makes something sad in a moving, memorable way.
Pathos is the quality in art or speech that evokes pity, and it is more technical in literary criticism.

examples.everyday: There was a real poignancy in seeing my grandfather's old fishing hat hanging by the door.
examples.professional: The video montage at the retirement party had a poignancy that made the whole team tear up.
examples.analytical: The poignancy of the novel lies in the gap between the narrator's hope and the reader's knowledge of what is already lost.

nuance.analogy: Poignancy is like the sweet and sour taste of a memory, pleasant and painful at the same time.
nuance.etymology: From poignant, from Old French poignant, pricking, from poindre, to prick.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle syllable as a separate word, like POYN-ee-yuhnt-see.
Using poignancy as a verb or adjective; the adjective is poignant.

senses.definition: A small dot or mark.
senses.example: The stars showed as tiny points of yellow light.

senses.definition: Something tiny, as a pinprick; a very small mark.
senses.example: The stars showed as tiny points of yellow light.

senses.definition: A full stop or other terminal punctuation mark.
senses.example: Place a point at the end of every declarative sentence in your essay.

senses.definition: A decimal point (now especially when reading decimal fractions aloud).
senses.example: 10.5 is "ten point five", or ten and a half.

senses.definition: Each of the marks or strokes written above letters, especially in Semitic languages, to indicate vowels, stress etc.
senses.example: Hebrew scribes added a point above each consonant to mark its vowel.

senses.definition: A note; a tune.
senses.example: He played a lovely point on the fiddle before the dancers started.

senses.definition: A zero-dimensional mathematical object representing a location in one or more dimensions; something considered to have position but no magnitude or direction.
senses.example: Every line in the plane is determined by any two distinct points.

senses.definition: A small discrete division or individual feature of something.
senses.example: The Congress debated the finer points of the bill.

senses.definition: An individual element in a larger whole; a particular detail, thought, or quality.
senses.example: The Congress debated the finer points of the bill.

senses.definition: A particular moment in an event or occurrence; a juncture.
senses.example: There comes a point in a marathon when some people give up.

senses.definition: A topic of discussion or debate; a proposition; a count.
senses.example: I made the point that we all had an interest to protect.

senses.definition: A focus of conversation or consideration; the main idea.
senses.example: The point is that we should stay together, whatever happens.

senses.definition: A purpose or objective, which makes something meaningful.
senses.example: Since the decision has already been made, I see little point in further discussion.

senses.definition: A specific location or place, seen as a spatial position.
senses.example: We should meet at a pre-arranged point.

senses.definition: A distinguishing quality or characteristic.
senses.example: Logic isn't my strong point.

senses.definition: An area of contrasting color on an animal, especially a dog; a marking.
senses.example: The point color of that cat was a deep, rich sable.

senses.definition: A tenth; formerly also a twelfth.
senses.example: Possession is nine points of the law.

senses.definition: Ellipsis of percentage point.
A unit of various numerical parameters used in a game, e.g. health, experience, stamina, mana.
senses.example: This attack deals 320 points of damage.

senses.definition: A unit used to express differences in prices of stocks and shares.
senses.example: The stock closed up three points after the earnings report.

senses.definition: A unit of measure equal to 1/12 of a pica, or approximately 1/72 of an inch (exactly 1/72 of an inch in the digital era).
senses.example: The headline was set in twelve-point type for the newspaper.

senses.definition: Either of the two metal surfaces in a distributor which close or open to allow or prevent the flow of current through the ignition coil. There is usually a moving point, pushed by the distributor cam, and a fixed point, and they are built together as a unit.
senses.example: The mechanic replaced the worn points in the distributor to fix the misfire.

senses.definition: A sharp extremity.
senses.example: Cut the skin with the point of the knife.

senses.definition: The sharp tip of an object.
senses.example: Cut the skin with the point of the knife.

senses.definition: Any projecting extremity of an object.
senses.example: The sharp point of the iceberg sank the small fishing boat.

senses.definition: An object which has a sharp or tapering tip.
senses.example: His cowboy belt was studded with points.

senses.definition: A spearhead or similar object hafted to a handle.
senses.example: The hunter fixed a stone point to the end of his spear.

senses.definition: Each of the twelve triangular positions in either table of a backgammon board, on which the stones are played.
senses.example: She moved her last checker onto the empty point near the edge.

senses.definition: A peninsula or promontory.
senses.example: The lighthouse stands on a rocky point overlooking the harbor.

senses.definition: The position at the front or vanguard of an advancing force.
senses.example: The sergeant led the patrol from the point, scouting ahead of the column.

senses.definition: An operational or public leadership position in a risky endeavor.
senses.example: He took point on the risky expansion into overseas markets.

senses.definition: Ellipsis of point man.
Each of the main directions on a compass, usually considered to be 32 in number; a direction.
senses.example: The ship sailed due north, following the north point on the compass rose.

senses.definition: Pointedness of speech or writing; a penetrating or decisive quality of expression.
senses.example: Her critique lacked point, so the committee forgot it by lunch.

senses.definition: A tine or snag of an antler.
senses.example: The buck's antler had a sharp point on each side.

senses.definition: The act of pointing.
senses.example: The dog came to a point.

senses.definition: The act of pointing, as of the foot downward in certain dance positions.
The gesture of extending the index finger in a direction in order to indicate something.
The attitude assumed by a pointer dog when he finds game.
senses.example: The dog came to a point.

senses.definition: The perpendicular rising of a hawk over the place where its prey has gone into cover.
A movement executed with the sabre or foil.
senses.example: tierce point

senses.definition: Lace worked by the needle.
senses.example: point de Venise; Brussels point

senses.definition: In various sports, a position of a certain player, or, by extension, the player occupying that position.
The position of the player of each side who stands a short distance in front of the goalkeeper.
A spot to which a straight run is made; hence, a straight run from point to point; a cross-country run.

A dot or mark used to designate certain tones or time. In ancient music, it distinguished or characterized certain tones or styles (points of perfection, of augmentation, etc.). In modern music, it is placed on the right of a note to raise its value, or prolong its time, by one half.
A unit of scoring in a game or competition.
senses.example: The one with the most points will win the game.

senses.definition: The difference between two points of the compass; a unit of bearing equal to one thirty-second of a circle, i.e. 11.25°.
senses.example: to fall off a point

senses.definition: One of the "corners" of the escutcheon: the base (bottom center) unless a qualifier is added (point dexter, point dexter base, point sinister, point sinister base), generally when separately tinctured. This is sometimes blazoned argent, four points gules; otherwise, it is vêtu.
An ordinary similar to a pile (but sometimes shorter), extending upward from the base.
A short piece of cordage used in reefing sails.
A fielding position square of the wicket on the off side, between gully and cover.
The position of the pitcher and catcher.
An item of private information; a hint; a tip; a pointer.
(dated) The chief or excellent features.
senses.example: the points of a horse
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: (historical) A string or lace used to tie together certain garments.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: Point taken; understood; got it.
To extend the index finger in the direction of something in order to show where it is or to draw attention to it.
senses.example: It's rude to point at other people.

senses.definition: To draw attention to something or indicate a direction.
senses.example: The arrow of a compass points north

senses.definition: To face in a particular direction.
To direct toward an object; to aim.
senses.example: to point a gun at a wolf, or a cannon at a fort

senses.definition: To give a point to; to sharpen; to cut, forge, grind, or file to an acute end.
senses.example: to point a dart, a pencil, or (figuratively) a moral

senses.definition: To indicate a probability of something.
To repair mortar.
To fill up and finish the joints of (a wall), by introducing additional cement or mortar, and bringing it to a smooth surface.
To cut, as a surface, with a pointed tool.
To direct or encourage (someone) in a particular direction.
senses.example: If he asks for food, point him toward the refrigerator.

senses.definition: To separate an integer from a decimal with a decimal point.
To mark with diacritics.
To direct the central processing unit to seek information at a certain location in memory.
To direct requests sent to a domain name to the IP address corresponding to that domain name.
To indicate the presence of game by a fixed and steady look, as certain hunting dogs do.
To mark (e.g. an Anglican psalm) with pointing.
To sail close to the wind.
senses.example: Bear off a little, we're pointing.

senses.definition: To approximate to the surface; to head.
(dated) To supply with punctuation marks; to punctuate.
senses.example: to point a composition
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: (dated) To give point to (something said or done); to give particular prominence or force to.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: The main idea or argument someone is trying to make, or the purpose behind what they say.

pronunciation.tip: Use the diphthong /ɔɪ/ as in 'boy,' not the vowel of 'pint' or 'paint.' The final t is often light or unreleased, so the word ends quickly.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a practical word used in everyday discussion, but phrases like 'What is your point?' can sound impatient or challenging depending on tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use point constantly in meetings, arguments, and casual talk, as in 'I see your point' or 'Let me get to the point.' Saying 'What's your point?' can sound sarcastic or rude if said sharply, so use a softer version like 'Where are you going with this?' A natural reply to a good argument is 'Point taken.'

distinctions.note: Point is the argument or meaning of what someone says, while purpose is the goal or intention behind an action.
Gist is a summary of the general sense of something, while point is the specific claim someone is making.

examples.everyday: I get your point, but I still think we should wait until Saturday to decide.
examples.professional: The key point of my email is that we need the revised budget by Friday.
examples.analytical: Her central point is that moral knowledge depends on lived practice rather than abstract theory alone.

nuance.analogy: A point is like the tip of an arrow: the argument can have many parts, but the point is where it lands.
nuance.etymology: From Old French point, from Latin punctum, 'a prick,' from pungere, 'to prick.'
common_mistakes: Pronouncing point like pint, with the vowel of 'pint' rather than the diphthong /ɔɪ/ as in 'boy.'
Saying 'What is the point of this?' sharply at work, which can sound dismissive; ask 'What's the goal here?' instead.

point.etymology: From Middle English *poynt*, from Old French *point* (“dot; minute amount”), from Latin *pūnctum* (“a hole punched in; a point, puncture”), substantive use of *pūnctus*, perfect passive participle of *pungō* (“to prick, punch”); alternatively, from Old…

senses.definition: The administration of a poison.
senses.example: Doctors suspected poisoning when the entire family fell ill after dinner.

senses.definition: The state of being poisoned.

core.definition: Illness or death caused by swallowing, breathing in or absorbing a harmful substance.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The second syllable is a weak zuh, and the final -ing is short, like 'ing' in 'sing', not 'eeng'.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it describes a harmful condition or act.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say I think I have food poisoning after feeling sick from a meal, even when a virus caused the illness. In medicine, carbon monoxide poisoning and lead poisoning are standard terms. If you suspect someone has been poisoned, call 911 or Poison Control right away.

distinctions.note: Intoxication means being drunk or affected by a drug, while poisoning is harm from a toxic substance, which may be accidental.
Contamination means something has become impure; poisoning means that a substance causes harm when taken in.
An infection is caused by germs such as bacteria or viruses, while poisoning is caused by a chemical or toxin.

examples.everyday: I think I got food poisoning from that gas station sandwich.
examples.professional: The health department traced the outbreak to poisoning caused by a mislabeled cleaning chemical.
examples.analytical: The philosophical debate about intent turns on whether accidental poisoning should be judged as harshly as deliberate murder.

nuance.analogy: Like a slow leak in a pipe, poisoning spreads harm through the system until the body can no longer clear it.
nuance.etymology: From the verb poison, from Old French poison, from Latin potio 'a drink'.
common_mistakes: Saying POH-zuh-ning with a long o; the vowel is the diphthong oy.
Using poisoning as an adjective; say a poisonous snake, not a poisoning snake.

senses.definition: In a political manner.
senses.example: tackle a matter politically

senses.definition: Regarding politics, in a way connected to politics.
senses.example: politically insensitive

core.definition: In a way connected with government, political parties, or the struggle for power and public support.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on LIT. The final -ally is pronounced as a reduced 'uh-lee', not as a full 'al-ly', and the first vowel is a schwa.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a connection to power or policy, and can be negative when it implies self-interest.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'politically' in news, workplace discussions, and everyday talk, as in 'politically difficult' or 'politically savvy.' When used to describe a choice, it often implies that appearance or support mattered as much as the merits. Speakers may also use it to say something is risky for a candidate or leader.

distinctions.note: Politely refers to good manners, while politically refers to government or power, so they are easily confused by learners.
Ideologically concerns belief systems, while politically also covers elections, parties, and bargaining for power.
Strategically emphasizes planning for advantage in any field, while politically specifically concerns public power and governance.

examples.everyday: Politically, the mayor is in a tough spot, so she's being careful about what she says.
examples.professional: Politically, the change is easier to sell if we frame it as a cost saving rather than a reorganization.
examples.analytical: A ruling can be legally sound and yet politically disastrous, because its legitimacy depends on public trust.

nuance.analogy: Like a chess move that is technically legal but places a piece where the opponent can easily attack it: the rules are met, but the position is weak.
nuance.etymology: From political plus the adverb suffix -ly, from Latin politicus, 'of citizens'.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'politically' with 'politely', which changes the meaning from power to manners.
Saying 'politically correct' as a neutral term; in American speech it is often used with a critical or sarcastic tone.

senses.definition: Having or relating to the ability to take multiple data types for a single parameter.
senses.example: In the function, the polymorphic parameter accepts either an integer or a string.

senses.definition: Relating to polymorphism (any sense), able to have several shapes or forms.
senses.example: The colony's polymorphic worker ants come in several distinct shapes and sizes.

senses.definition: Being or relating to polymorphic content; developed for multiple formats from the start, instead of being adapted later.
senses.example: Our publishing team built the site as polymorphic content, so every article renders for phones, print, and email.

senses.definition: Relating to a compound that can crystallize into two or more distinct forms (e.g. carbon, which can crystalize into coal, graphite, diamond, etc.)
senses.example: Carbon is polymorphic, so the same element forms both graphite and diamond.

core.definition: Able to take several forms or types; in software, a single interface that works with different data types.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the third syllable, 'mor'. Americans pronounce the 'or' with a clear r, and the final syllable is 'fik' with a short i.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term.
nuance.usage_note: Software engineers and computer scientists use polymorphic constantly, as in 'a polymorphic function' or 'polymorphic code.' Biologists also use it for organisms with several forms. Outside technical talk, Americans would rarely use this word and would say 'can take many forms' instead.

distinctions.note: Generic is a common term in programming for the same idea, while polymorphic is broader and can also describe biological forms.
Versatile is everyday praise for being useful in many ways, while polymorphic is technical and refers to literal forms or types.

examples.everyday: That app is polymorphic in a way, because the same button works with text, images, and video.
examples.professional: Our API uses a polymorphic handler, so new message types can be added without changing the core code.
examples.analytical: A polymorphic function must preserve its type guarantees across every instantiation, which is what makes its abstraction sound.

nuance.analogy: A polymorphic object is like a universal remote that can control many different devices with the same buttons.
nuance.etymology: From Greek polymorphos, having many forms, from polys, many, and morphē, form.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, such as pah-LIM-or-fik
Confusing polymorphic with polymer, which is a different concept

senses.definition: The quality of being ponderous.

core.definition: The quality of being ponderous: heavy, slow or dull in movement, speech or thought.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the 'der' and 'us' syllables are weak. The ending is two quick syllables, 'us' and 'nus', not 'ness' with a long vowel.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes a heavy, dull quality that listeners and readers usually find tiresome.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use ponderousness in book reviews, criticism and formal writing to describe a style, a speech or a process that feels heavy. In everyday talk people would say 'so heavy' or 'really slow'. Be careful not to confuse it with 'pondering', the act of thinking.

distinctions.note: Heaviness is the general physical or emotional weight; ponderousness adds slowness and dullness of movement or thought.
Pomposity focuses on self-importance in manner; ponderousness focuses on slow, heavy style or pace.

examples.everyday: I love the story, but the ponderousness of the middle chapters made me put the book down for a week.
examples.professional: The ponderousness of our review process means that small fixes can take months to ship.
examples.analytical: The ponderousness of the author's style is deliberate, as the long sentences force the reader to slow down and reflect.

nuance.analogy: Like a heavy wagon that takes forever to climb a hill.
nuance.etymology: From ponderous, from Latin ponderosus (heavy), from pondus (weight).
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'pondering', which is the act of thinking and has a different meaning.
Stressing the wrong syllable, saying 'pon-DER-us-ness' instead of 'PON-der-us-ness'.

senses.definition: Able to be carried or easily moved.
Able to be transferred from one organization to another.
senses.example: a portable pension plan

senses.definition: Of software: able to be run on multiple hardware or operating systems.
senses.example: The app is portable, so it runs on Windows, macOS, and Linux alike.

senses.definition: Of a program: able to be copied directly from one machine to another without the use of an installer.
senses.example: The utility is portable, so you can copy it to a USB drive and run it.

senses.definition: A portable building used for temporary purposes, particularly:
senses.example: The school put up a portable behind the gym for overflow classes.

senses.definition: Clipping of portable toilet.
senses.example: The construction crew rented a portable for the whole summer.

senses.definition: A trailer or other movable structure used for classes at a school.
senses.example: Her fourth-grade class moved into a portable near the parking lot.

senses.definition: Clipping of portable computer.
senses.example: I bought a portable for my classes, since the desktop is too heavy.

senses.definition: A hand-held video gaming device.
senses.example: On the long flight, he played his portable until the battery died.

core.definition: Able to be carried or moved easily from place to place, such as a laptop, a speaker or a small generator.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, and the last syllable is reduced to 'bul'. The t between vowels is a quick flap that sounds like a soft d, as in 'PAWR-duh-bul'.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral; it implies convenience and flexibility.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'portable' for devices and equipment that you can carry, such as a portable charger or portable air conditioner. For phones, Americans say 'cell phone' or 'cell', not 'portable phone' or 'mobile phone'. In software, portable means the code can run on several platforms.

distinctions.note: Mobile emphasizes movement or the ability to move, while portable emphasizes being light and easy to carry.
