common_mistakes: Using sketcher for a police artist; say sketch artist.
Stressing the second syllable, as in skech-UR.

senses.definition: To pass lightly; to glide along in an even, smooth course; to glide along near the surface.
senses.example: The seagull began to skim across the lake, its wings barely touching the water.

senses.definition: To pass near the surface of; to brush the surface of; to glide swiftly along the surface of.
senses.example: The speedboat skimmed the surface of the bay, throwing spray behind it as it raced.

senses.definition: To hasten along with superficial attention.
senses.example: I only had time to skim the report before the meeting, so I missed the details.

senses.definition: To put on a finishing coat of plaster.
senses.example: The plasterer will skim the walls with a thin final coat before we paint.

senses.definition: To throw an object so it bounces on water.
senses.example: skimming stones

senses.definition: To ricochet.
senses.example: The flat stone began to skim across the pond, bouncing four times before it sank.

senses.definition: To read quickly or describe summarily, skipping some detail.
senses.example: (through)

senses.definition: To scrape off; to remove (something) from a surface.
senses.example: Skim the foam off the top of the simmering broth with a slotted spoon.

senses.definition: To clear (a liquid) from scum or substance floating or lying on it, by means of a utensil that passes just beneath the surface.
senses.example: to skim milk

senses.definition: To clear a liquid from (scum or substance floating or lying on it), especially the cream that floats on top of fresh milk.
senses.example: to skim cream

senses.definition: To steal money from a business before the transaction has been recorded, thus avoiding detection.
senses.example: The bookkeeper began to skim cash from the register before sales were logged in the system.

senses.definition: To surreptitiously scan a payment card in order to obtain its information for fraudulent purposes.
senses.example: Someone placed a card skimmer inside the gas pump to skim customers' card numbers.

senses.definition: To become coated over.
senses.example: The pond had skimmed over with thin ice overnight, so the kids couldn't go skating.

senses.definition: Having lowered fat content.
senses.example: She bought skim yogurt because she was trying to lower her fat intake.

senses.definition: A cursory reading, skipping the details.
senses.example: I gave the article a quick skim before the lecture, mostly reading the headings.

senses.definition: Skim milk.
senses.example: Pour a cup of skim into the pan and whisk in the flour slowly.

senses.definition: The act of skimming.
senses.example: Her quick skim of the contract revealed three clauses that needed a closer look.

senses.definition: That which is skimmed off.
senses.example: Throw the skim from the top of the jam pot into the compost bin.

senses.definition: Theft of money from a business before the transaction has been recorded, thus avoiding detection.
senses.example: The auditor traced the skim to a cashier who pocketed receipts before they were recorded.

core.definition: To read something quickly, looking only for the main points and skipping most of the details.

pronunciation.tip: Use a short i, as in 'kit', not a long 'skeem'. The m is a closed final sound, so do not add a vowel after it.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. Skimming is a practical reading habit, but when a boss asks 'Did you just skim it?' the question can suggest carelessness.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'skim through' or 'skim over' an email, article or report when time is short. Saying 'I just skimmed it' is a common, honest answer in casual talk, but it can sound critical if you were expected to study the document closely. Americans also use skim for taking fat off milk or foam off soup, where 'skim milk' is a standard product name.

distinctions.note: Scan suggests looking quickly for a specific item, such as a name or number; skim means reading the main ideas of a whole text.
Skip means leaving out a part of a text entirely; skim means reading all of it quickly without stopping for details.
Browse means looking around casually with no set goal; skim is more purposeful, usually to get the gist of a text.

examples.everyday: I only skimmed the news this morning, so I'm not sure what happened overnight.
examples.professional: Before the meeting, skim the quarterly report so you know the main numbers, and we can go over the details together.
examples.analytical: Readers who skim a philosophical argument often miss the qualifications on which its conclusion depends.

nuance.analogy: Skimming is like a stone skipping across water: it touches the surface many times but never sinks in.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English skimmen, from Old French escumer 'to remove the scum from'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it with a long vowel as 'skeem'
Using skim to mean careful reading; if you need full understanding, say 'read carefully' or 'study'
Confusing skim with skip: skim covers all of the text quickly, while skip leaves parts out

skim.etymology: From Middle English *skemen*, *skymen*, variants of *scumen*, from Old French *escumer* (“to remove scum”), from *escume* (“froth, foam”), from **skūm* (“froth, foam”), from Proto-Germanic **skūmaz* (“foam”), from Proto-Indo-European **skew-* (“to cover,…

senses.definition: A short comic performance done by amateurs.
A jeer or sally; a brief satire.
senses.example: The comedian's skit mocked the senator's clumsy speech with sharp, well-timed jabs.

senses.definition: A short, sharp shower (of rain).
senses.example: A quick skit of rain drenched the picnic tables before we could pack up.

senses.definition: Diarrhea, in livestock; the scour.
senses.example: The veterinarian found that the calves had a bad skit, likely caused by spoiled feed.

senses.definition: To caper; to skip or run lightly and quickly.
senses.example: The puppies were skitting across the yard after the falling leaves, tails wagging madly.

core.definition: A short, light comic performance, usually by amateurs, such as a church, school, or company skit.

pronunciation.tip: One syllable with a short i like sit and a clear t at the end. Do not add an extra vowel: say skit, not skee-it.

nuance.connotation: Positive or lighthearted; it suggests fun and low stakes.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use skit for short, funny performances by amateurs, such as a youth group, a school talent night, or an office party. For professional TV comedy segments, sketch is the normal word, as in a sketch on Saturday Night Live. A natural reply to 'Did you see the skit?' is 'Yeah, it was hilarious.'

distinctions.note: Sketch is the usual American term for a short professional comedy bit on TV or stage; skit suggests amateur or community performance.
A play is longer and more structured, while a skit is brief and usually built around one joke or situation.

examples.everyday: The youth group did a skit about a lost sheep, and everyone was laughing.
examples.professional: For the team offsite, we'll do a quick skit showing how the onboarding process goes wrong.
examples.analytical: The skit inverts the sermon form, turning a moral lesson into a joke that exposes the audience's own assumptions.

nuance.analogy: A skit is a snack-sized comedy show: a quick bite, not a full meal.
nuance.etymology: Origin uncertain.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it with a long e like skeet; the vowel is a short i.
Using skit for a professional TV comedy segment; Americans usually say sketch.

senses.definition: Appropriate to or characteristic of a slattern.
senses.example: Her slatternly appearance at the office worried her manager, who asked her to dress more neatly.

senses.definition: In the manner of a slattern.
senses.example: She wore her apron slatternly over a stained blouse, her hair falling loose.

core.definition: Messy, untidy, and careless in appearance, habits, or housekeeping, especially in a way that seems unattractive or sloppy.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, SLAT. The middle syllable is reduced to a short ern sound, and the final ly is a simple lee. Keep the r rhotic in the middle syllable.

nuance.connotation: Negative, because it strongly criticizes untidiness and carelessness, often with a judgmental or old-fashioned tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use slatternly in everyday speech, and when they do, it sounds literary, old-fashioned, or harsh. It is more common in novels, reviews, or formal criticism. In conversation, Americans would more likely say messy, sloppy, or unkempt.

distinctions.note: Messy is everyday and neutral, while slatternly is literary and judgmental, usually suggesting a woman who is disheveled and careless.
Sloppy is common and can describe work or dress, while slatternly is more formal and focuses on a disordered, untidy person or house.
Unkempt describes an uncared-for appearance, while slatternly also implies careless habits and a dirty, disorderly state.

examples.everyday: I would not call the apartment slatternly, but it does need a good cleaning.
examples.professional: The manager's report was not slatternly, but it lacked the careful structure the client expected.
examples.analytical: The novelist portrays the boardinghouse as slatternly, using its disorder to reveal the moral decay of its tenants.

nuance.analogy: A slatternly room is like a closet where everything has been stuffed in without order, so nothing looks cared for.
nuance.etymology: From slattern, a slovenly woman, with the suffix -ly, from a root related to slatter, to spill or be untidy.
common_mistakes: Using slatternly as a casual synonym for messy in everyday conversation, which sounds harsh
Misplacing the stress on the second syllable

senses.definition: In the manner of a slave; abject.
senses.example: He followed his boss's every order with slavish devotion, never questioning a single instruction.

senses.definition: Utterly faithful; totally lacking originality, creativity, or reflection.
senses.example: a slavish reproduction

core.definition: Following or copying someone or something too closely, without thought, originality, or independent judgment.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, SLAY, and the second syllable is a short vish. Avoid turning the ish into a long ee sound, and keep the v clearly voiced.

nuance.connotation: Negative, because it suggests a lack of independence or dignity, though it can be neutral when describing faithful service.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use slavish in critical writing, reviews, and academic discussion to describe imitation or obedience that lacks thought. In casual speech, people more often say blindly or word for word. It can be insulting, so it is best used when describing work or behavior rather than a person's character directly.

distinctions.note: Servile emphasizes a humble, submissive attitude toward others, while slavish emphasizes uncritical copying or obedience.
Faithful is positive and implies loyalty, while slavish is negative and suggests a lack of independent thought.
Imitative simply describes copying, while slavish adds a judgment that the copying is excessive and unthinking.

examples.everyday: My friend follows every trend on social media, and I think that slavish copying gets boring.
examples.professional: Our team should not slavishly copy the competitor's dashboard, because our users have different needs.
examples.analytical: The scholar argues that a slavish adherence to the text's literal wording ignores its historical and rhetorical context.

nuance.analogy: Slavish imitation is like a tracing paper copy of a drawing, exact in every line but without the artist's own hand.
nuance.etymology: From slave, with the adjective suffix -ish, meaning like a slave.
common_mistakes: Confusing slavish with slave-like in neutral contexts, when the word is usually negative
Using slavish to describe a person's loyalty to a good cause without a negative sense

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to slime.
Resembling, of the nature of, covered or daubed with, or abounding in slime.
senses.example: The frog's body was all slimy.

senses.definition: Friendly in a false, calculating way; underhanded; two-faced; sneaky; slick; smarmy.
senses.example: The slimy salesman smiled too widely and promised us everything we wanted to hear.

senses.definition: Filthy; disgusting; unclean.
senses.example: The slimy sludge at the bottom of the trash can made me gag when I opened it.

senses.definition: A ponyfish.
senses.example: Fishermen hauled up a slimy from the harbor, which turned out to be a ponyfish.

core.definition: Covered in or resembling slime, the thick, wet, slippery substance; also, informally, too friendly in a false, sneaky way.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final -y is a clear 'ee' sound, not 'eye'. Don't stretch the first vowel into a long 'slah-eye' sound; keep it one quick diphthong.

nuance.connotation: Negative. Used literally for mud, pond water or gooey residue, and figuratively to describe someone whose flattery seems insincere, which is a sharp insult.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use slimy for both literal gunk and for people who seem untrustworthy. Calling a person slimy is a strong, informal criticism, so use it about someone you are talking about privately, not to their face. A slippery surface that is clean is not slimy; use slippery for that.

distinctions.note: Slippery describes a surface that is hard to hold or stand on; slimy implies a gooey, unpleasant film or, figuratively, a sleazy character.
Sleazy suggests seedy, low-class or morally dubious; slimy suggests a smarmy, oily personality that seems insincere.
Smarmy focuses on excessive, fawning charm; slimy adds the sense that the person is also manipulative or underhanded.

examples.everyday: Ugh, the bottom of this creek is so slimy I can't stand on it.
examples.professional: I don't trust that slimy vendor rep, so let's have legal review the contract before we sign anything.
examples.analytical: Modern readers often find Machiavelli's prince slimy, because his charm serves manipulation rather than honest persuasion.

nuance.analogy: A slimy character is like a wet bar of soap: it looks smooth and friendly, but you can never quite get a grip on what it really is.
nuance.etymology: From slime (Old English slīm, mud or sticky substance) plus the suffix -y; the figurative sense of sneaky is a later extension.
common_mistakes: Using slimy for any slippery surface; a wet, clean floor is slippery, not slimy.
Pronouncing the final -y as 'eye' (SLY-my) instead of 'ee' (SLY-mee).

slimy.etymology: From Middle English *slymy*, *slimi*, either derived from the Old English noun *slīm* or an unattested **slīmiġ*, replacing.

senses.definition: The skin shed by a snake or other reptile.
senses.example: That is the slough of a rattler; we must be careful.

senses.definition: Dead skin on a sore or ulcer.
senses.example: This is the slough that came off of his skin after the burn.

senses.definition: A marshy or muddy area.
senses.example: After the storm, our truck got stuck in the slough, and we spent hours pulling it free.

senses.definition: A type of swamp or shallow lake system, typically formed as or by the backwater of a larger waterway, similar to a bayou with trees.
senses.example: We paddled under a canopy of trees through the slough.

senses.definition: A secondary channel of a river delta, usually flushed by the tide.
senses.example: The Sacramento River Delta contains dozens of sloughs that are often used for water-skiing and fishing.

senses.definition: A state of depression.
senses.example: John is in a slough.

senses.definition: A small pond, often alkaline, many but not all formed by glacial potholes.
senses.example: Potholes or sloughs formed by a glacier’s retreat from the central plains of North America, are now known to be some of the world’s most productive ecosystems.

senses.definition: To shed skin or outer layers.
senses.example: This skin is being sloughed.

senses.definition: To slide off or flake off, as an outer layer, such as skin, might do.
senses.example: A week after he was burned, a layer of skin on his arm sloughed off.

senses.definition: To discard.
senses.example: East sloughed a heart.

senses.definition: To commit truancy, be absent from school without permission.
senses.example: Marcus sloughed school on Friday, so his mother got a call from the attendance office.

core.definition: To shed or cast off an outer layer, such as skin, or to get rid of something unwanted, like a habit or old identity.

pronunciation.tip: Rhymes with 'enough' and 'rough,' with a short u vowel like 'cut.' Do not confuse it with the swamp sense, which is pronounced like 'slow' in some regions and is rare.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a natural shedding process, but the figurative use can sound either positive or negative depending on what is discarded.
nuance.usage_note: Americans most often use slough in nature writing, biology, or figuratively, as in 'slough off' meaning to neglect work. The phrasal verb 'slough off' is common in casual American speech, as in 'He sloughed off his responsibilities.' The noun sense for a swamp is uncommon in the US.

distinctions.note: Shed is the everyday general word, while slough is more specific to skin or an outer layer.
Slough off means to neglect or avoid something, a more informal figurative use; slough alone is more literal.

examples.everyday: My cat keeps sloughing off little bits of fur all over the couch.
examples.professional: The team sloughed off the old reporting tool once the new dashboard was live.
examples.analytical: The author argues that the convert must slough off inherited assumptions before real understanding can begin.

nuance.analogy: Like a snake leaving its old skin behind on a rock, so the outer layer is shed and the new one shows.
nuance.etymology: From Old English slōh or related forms, originally meaning a snake's cast skin.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the noun swamp sense with the vowel of 'cow,' which may confuse listeners.
Confusing slough with slow, which has a different spelling and meaning.

slough.etymology: From Middle English *slogh*, *slugh*, *slouh*, from Proto-Germanic **sluk-*, perhaps related to **sleupaną* (“to slip, sneak”).

senses.definition: Appealing or stylish in appearance or manner; classy, flashy.
senses.example: a snazzy dresser

senses.definition: Of a person: elegant in dressing; of clothes: elegant, fashionable.
senses.example: a snazzy dresser

senses.definition: Adept or ingenious in behavior or operation; excellent, nifty.
senses.example: The new script is snazzy, cutting our weekly report time from hours to minutes.

core.definition: Stylish and flashy in appearance; sharp, classy and eye-catching.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on the first syllable, and the ending is a light 'ee' sound. The -zz is a voiced buzz like the z in 'zoo', not an s sound.

nuance.connotation: Positive but a little playful or flashy; can sound slightly over-the-top when describing clothes or cars.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use snazzy casually to praise a bold, stylish outfit, a car or a slick presentation, often with a smile. It sounds upbeat and a little old-fashioned, so it suits conversation with friends or family better than formal writing. In a professional setting, sharp or polished is usually the safer choice.

distinctions.note: Stylish is the neutral, everyday word for fashionable, while snazzy adds a note of flash and excitement.
Flashy often suggests showy or excessive, while snazzy is usually more positive and playful.

examples.everyday: You look snazzy in that blue jacket, is it new?
examples.professional: The new onboarding deck looks snazzy, but make sure the slides still explain the data clearly.
examples.analytical: Some critics complained that the film's snazzy visuals distracted from a thin plot.

nuance.analogy: A snazzy outfit is like a neon sign: it gets noticed before the store itself.
common_mistakes: Using snazzy for quiet, careful work, since it describes style; for a neutral sense, say well-designed or elegant.
Spelling it snazy with one z or snazzie; it has two z's and ends in -y.

senses.definition: Asking what someone's job is; very common when meeting someone new.

core.definition: A common question meaning "What is your job?" or "What kind of work do you do?" often asked when meeting someone new.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on WHAT and the final DO. The words "do you" link together, sounding like "doo-yoo", and the final do is stressed to mean "work".

nuance.connotation: Neutral and friendly. It is a standard opening question in American small talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans ask "So, what do you do?" at parties, networking events, or when meeting neighbors and friends of friends. It does not mean "What are you doing right now?" A natural reply is to give your job title or field, such as "I'm a data scientist, mostly working on forecasting models." Some people feel it pushes them to define themselves by work, so be ready for a short, friendly answer.

distinctions.note: What are you doing asks about current activity; What do you do asks about your occupation.
What's your job is more direct and slightly blunter; What do you do is the softer, standard small-talk version.

collocations: What do you do for work?
What do you do for a living?
So what do you do these days?

examples.everyday: At the barbecue, my neighbor asked, "So, what do you do?" and we ended up talking about coffee for an hour.
examples.professional: At the conference reception, a product manager asked me, "So, what do you do?" and I explained our model monitoring work.
examples.analytical: The question "So, what do you do?" quietly equates a person's identity with their paid work, which is a revealing habit of American social life.

nuance.analogy: The question is like a friendly door-knock: it opens a conversation without asking anything too personal.
common_mistakes: Answering with a verb phrase like "I work" alone; add your job title or field to continue the conversation.
Confusing it with "What are you doing?" and answering with your current activity instead of your job.

conversation.text: So, what do you do? Are you from around here?
"So, what do you do?" "I'm a nurse at the children's hospital."
"So, what do you do?" "I work in data science, mostly for retail companies."

senses.definition: A room, rooftop, balcony, or terrace, used for its abundant sunlight, especially when used as a medical treatment.
senses.example: In winter, the family gathered in the solarium to soak up sunlight beside the plants.

senses.definition: Synonym of tanning salon, a room or business used for its sunlamps or tanning beds.
senses.example: After her dermatologist warned her, she stopped going to the solarium before her wedding.

senses.definition: An earthen structure constructed by certain ants for the purpose of brood incubation.
senses.example: Biologists studied the solarium that the ants built on the forest floor each spring.

senses.definition: Synonym of sundial.
senses.example: Visitors photographed the garden's solarium, whose shadow marked the hours across the stone.

core.definition: A glass-walled room or rooftop space built to collect sunlight, often for relaxing, plants, or light therapy.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, LAIR, and the final -um is a weak, reduced vowel, not 'ahm'. Learners often stress the first syllable, as in 'SOH-lair-ee-um'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it sounds somewhat upscale or traditional for a house, and clinical in a medical setting.
nuance.usage_note: In American homes a solarium is a glassed-in sunroom, often in larger or older houses, and it sounds more formal than 'sunroom'. In the US, 'tanning salon' or 'tanning bed' is the usual term for artificial UV tanning, while 'solarium' in that sense sounds more British. In casual talk, say 'sunroom'.

distinctions.note: A sunroom is the everyday American term for a bright room with many windows; a solarium is the more formal or architectural word for the same kind of space.
A greenhouse is built to grow plants with controlled temperature; a solarium is built for people to sit in sunlight.
A tanning salon is a business offering artificial UV tanning; the solarium sense of that business is more common in Britain.

examples.everyday: Let's have coffee in the solarium, it's the sunniest room in the house.
examples.professional: The architect's proposal adds a solarium on the south side to reduce heating costs.
examples.analytical: The villa's solarium reflects a nineteenth-century belief that sunlight promoted health, a belief visible in the building's design.

nuance.analogy: A solarium is a sun-catching greenhouse built for people instead of plants.
nuance.etymology: From Latin solarium, a sundial or sunny terrace, from sol, sun.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as 'SOH-lair-ee-um'; the main stress is on LAIR.
Using 'solarium' for a tanning bed in casual American conversation, where 'tanning salon' is more natural.
Confusing the pronunciation with 'solar', which has its stress on the first syllable.

solarium.etymology: Latin *sōlārium* (“sundial, place for enjoying sunlight”), from *sōl* (“sun”) + *-ārium* (“-arium: indicating related places or devices”).

core.definition: A short book of Hebrew love poetry in the Old Testament, traditionally attributed to King Solomon.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable of Solomon, SOL, and reduce of to uhv. The word Solomon has three syllables, not 'so-lo-mon' with equal stress.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in religious and academic contexts, though the book's romantic imagery can surprise readers who expect a sober text.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use the Song of Solomon for the book in English Bibles, including the RSV, while Catholic and Jewish contexts often say Song of Songs. Many Americans also know the title from Toni Morrison's novel Song of Solomon, published in 1977. In church or Bible study, the book is usually discussed as a poem about love, and people do not expect a plot.

distinctions.note: Song of Songs is the title used in Catholic and Jewish Bibles, from the Hebrew Shir ha-Shirim, and it refers to the same book.
Proverbs is a collection of wise sayings also attributed to Solomon, while the Song of Solomon is a sequence of love poems.

distinctions.vs: Toni Morrison's novel Song of Solomon
distinctions.note: The novel shares the title but is an unrelated American work of fiction about a family in Michigan.

collocations: a sermon on the Song of Solomon
imagery in the Song of Solomon

examples.everyday: Our pastor chose a passage from the Song of Solomon for the wedding this summer.
examples.professional: In the Bible study we treated the Song of Solomon as a collection of love poems rather than as an allegory.
examples.analytical: Interpreters have long debated whether the Song of Solomon is a literal love poem, an allegory of God and Israel, or a figure of Christ and the church.

nuance.analogy: Like a love letter kept in a family Bible, the Song of Solomon places intimate poetry among ancient wisdom.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew Shir ha-Shirim, song of songs, with the attribution to Solomon taken from the superscription in 1:1.
common_mistakes: Stressing SO-lo-mon instead of SOL-uh-mun.
Expecting a story or sermon; the book is a set of poems in dialogue between lovers.
nuance.biblical_note: The Song of Solomon is in the Hebrew Bible among the Writings, and Jewish communities read it at Passover. Its Hebrew title is Shir ha-Shirim, and the Septuagint Greek title is Asma asmaton, both meaning song of songs, the highest or greatest song. In 1:1 the superscription attributes the song to Solomon, and in 8:6 and 8:7 the poem declares that love is as strong as death and that many waters cannot quench it.

traditions.view: Orthodox writers have often read the Song allegorically as the love between Christ and the Church or between God and the soul, with mystical commentaries such as those by Gregory of Nyssa.

Catholic interpreters have traditionally read the Song as an allegory of Christ and the Church, and some medieval readings applied it to the Virgin Mary, while modern scholarship also recognizes its literal love-poetry sense.
Many modern Protestant readers take the Song as a literal celebration of marriage and love, while older Protestant commentators often read it as an allegory of Christ and the church.

senses.definition: The dormant state of a deceased person's soul as it awaits the resurrection, according to psychopannychism.
senses.example: Some early Anabaptist writers argued that soul sleep kept the dead unconscious until resurrection.

core.definition: The belief that a person's soul remains dormant, unconscious, between death and the resurrection, rather than being conscious in God's presence or in judgment.

pronunciation.tip: Both words are one syllable, so the stress contrast is subtle: soul gets secondary stress and sleep gets primary. Keep the vowel in soul as a clear long 'oh' sound, not 'ah'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a theological position that some Christians find comforting and others reject as unscriptural. Tone depends on the speaker's confession.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this term mainly in theological discussion, Bible study, or debates about the afterlife, not in ordinary conversation. Within churches it can be a sensitive topic, so ask whether someone holds the view before assuming. Mainstream Catholic and Orthodox teaching rejects it, and many Protestant churches do too.

distinctions.note: Purgatory is a state of conscious purification in Catholic teaching; soul sleep is a state of unconscious rest, so the two are opposed in their understanding of the intermediate state.
Intermediate state is the general term for existence between death and resurrection; soul sleep is one specific, minority view of what that state is like.

examples.everyday: My Bible study group got into a long discussion about whether people are conscious after they die, and someone brought up soul sleep.
examples.professional: In the seminar paper, she summarized the historical arguments for soul sleep before explaining why most churches reject it.
examples.analytical: The author argues that soul sleep depends on a reading of Ecclesiastes and 1 Thessalonians that the broader canon of Scripture does not support.

nuance.analogy: Like a computer on sleep mode: it is still there and will wake up fully when the resurrection comes, but nothing is running in the meantime.
nuance.etymology: Soul comes from Old English sāwol; sleep comes from Old English slǣpan.
common_mistakes: Saying 'soul' with a short vowel like 'sull'; keep the long 'oh' sound.
Confusing soul sleep with simply being dead or with a peaceful rest in ordinary speech; it is a specific theological claim.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew word sheol and the Greek hades refer to the realm of the dead. Scripture often calls death sleep, in Greek koimaō, 'to fall asleep,' as a euphemism for dying. Ecclesiastes 9:5 says the dead know nothing, which supports the sleep view; 1 Thessalonians 4:13-17 speaks of those who have fallen asleep and of their resurrection; Philippians 1:23 has Paul expecting to be with Christ at death, which many read against soul sleep. Luke 16:19-31 describes the rich man and Lazarus in conscious states after death.

traditions.view: The Orthodox Church rejects soul sleep. Departed souls are conscious and await the General Judgment, with a foretaste of joy or sorrow, and the Church prays for the departed.
The Catholic Church rejects soul sleep. At death each person undergoes a particular judgment and is conscious in heaven, purgatory, or hell.

Most Protestant churches, including Lutheran, Reformed, Anglican, and Baptist, reject soul sleep and teach conscious existence after death. Some groups, such as Seventh-day Adventists and some Restorationist churches, hold a conditionalist or soul sleep view.

senses.definition: The state of being soulful.

core.definition: The quality of expressing deep, sincere feeling, especially in music, art, or a person's voice or manner.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable. Both -ful and -ness are reduced, and the final -ss is unvoiced, so it sounds like 'nuhss,' not 'ness' with a stressed vowel.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises emotional depth and authenticity, usually in art or performance.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'soulfulness' most often in music criticism, art reviews and discussions of a singer's voice. In casual talk, people more often say 'she has real soul' or 'it has a lot of soul.' The noun sounds somewhat formal and literary in everyday speech.

distinctions.note: Soul is the general quality or spirit of a person or work, while soulfulness is the expressed depth of feeling in a particular performance.
Sincerity means being honest in intention, while soulfulness is emotional depth in expression, which can exist even in performance.

examples.everyday: I love this old record, there's a soulfulness in his voice that modern pop just doesn't have.
examples.professional: The brand's soulfulness came through in the storytelling, but the conversion data showed the campaign was not working.
examples.analytical: Critics praise the album's soulfulness, but the term risks flattening a complex Black musical tradition into a vague mood.

nuance.analogy: Soulfulness is like the warmth of a candle's light compared with the flat brightness of an LED.
nuance.etymology: From soul plus -ful (full of) plus -ness (state or quality of).
common_mistakes: Using it for religious devotion in general, when it refers to emotional depth in expression.
Stressing the suffix, as in 'soul-FULL-ness,' which makes the word sound clumsy.

senses.definition: Seemingly well-reasoned, plausible or true, but actually fallacious.
senses.example: This idea that we must see through what we have started is specious, however good it may sound.

senses.definition: Employing fallacious but deceptively plausible arguments; deceitful.
senses.example: The senator's specious argument sounded logical but collapsed under basic scrutiny.

senses.definition: Having an attractive appearance intended to generate a favorable response; deceptively attractive.
senses.example: The brochure's specious promises of luxury hid a cramped, overpriced apartment.

core.definition: Seeming reasonable or true at first glance, but actually flawed or misleading.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and pronounce the 'ci' as 'sh', so the word has two syllables after the stress. Do not confuse it with 'spacious' (SPAY-shus), which has a different vowel.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It warns that something looks convincing but is deceptive or wrong.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'specious' mainly in academic, legal, political, and critical writing, or in careful argument. It is stronger than 'doubtful' and suggests intentional or at least careless deception. In casual talk, people more often say 'that sounds good but it's bogus' or 'that's a load of nonsense.'

distinctions.note: Plausible means believable and possibly true, while specious means it seems believable but is actually false or unsound.
Spurious means false, fake, or not genuine, often in origin, while specious describes an argument or appearance that seems reasonable but is flawed.

examples.everyday: Don't fall for his specious excuse that the store was closed for the whole week.
examples.professional: The vendor's specious claim that the model is unbiased falls apart once we check the training data.
examples.analytical: Hume's critique exposes the specious inference that a regular pattern in the past guarantees a regular future.

nuance.analogy: A specious argument is like a shiny coin that looks real until you bite it and find it is painted lead.
nuance.etymology: From Latin speciosus, 'showy, beautiful,' from species, 'appearance.'
common_mistakes: Confusing 'specious' with 'spacious' or 'suspicious' in pronunciation.
Using it to mean simply 'untrue' when the key idea is that the false argument seems convincing.

specious.etymology: From Middle English *speciose,specious*, from Anglo-Norman *specious*, Middle French *specieux*, and their etymon Latin *speciōsus* (“good-looking”).

senses.definition: A small spot or speck on the skin, plumage or foliage.
A cluster of interchromatin granules in a nucleus.
senses.example: Under the microscope, each nucleus showed a distinct speckle of interchromatin granules beside the chromatin.

senses.definition: The random distribution of light when it is scattered by a rough surface.
senses.example: Laser speckle appears on the wall because the rough surface scatters coherent light in random patterns.

senses.definition: To mark with speckles.
senses.example: She speckled the eggshell paint with brown dots using a stiff brush.

core.definition: A small spot or dot, often one of many, on skin, feathers, leaves, or a surface.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The final '-le' is a syllabic l with no extra vowel, so say it as 'SPEK-l' with a weak schwa before the l.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and descriptive. It usually suggests something attractive or natural, like a bird's feathers or a trout's skin.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'speckle' for patterns of small spots, especially in nature, cooking, or art, such as 'speckles on a robin's egg.' It is often used in the plural. As a verb, 'speckled' is more common in everyday speech than 'speckle.'

distinctions.note: A spot is a single mark that stands out, while speckles are many small marks scattered across a surface.
A dot is a small round mark that is usually deliberate, while speckles are irregular and natural in appearance.

examples.everyday: My grandmother has a speckled hen that lays the prettiest brown eggs.
examples.professional: The camera flagged a speckle pattern on the sensor, so we recalibrated it before the next run.
examples.analytical: Light scattering from a rough surface produces a speckle pattern that carries information about the surface's micro-geometry.

nuance.analogy: A speckle is like sprinkles on a sugar cookie, many small dots spread across one surface.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English speckle, a diminutive form related to 'speck.'
common_mistakes: Using 'speckle' as a single spot; it usually refers to many small marks.
Adding an extra vowel after the final l, saying 'SPEK-uh-ul.'
nuance.biblical_note: Genesis 30:32-39 and 31:10 describe Jacob's flocks, where spotted and speckled animals are the agreed wages. The Hebrew word is naqod, meaning spotted or speckled, and the RSV uses 'speckled' for these animals. The passage shows how Jacob used pattern and breeding in his flocks.

speckle.etymology: The noun is from Middle Dutch *spekkel*; the verb was later coined from the noun, in the late 16th century.

senses.definition: In a spectacular manner, extraordinarily, amazingly.
senses.example: The startup spectacularly failed after spending millions on a product nobody wanted.

core.definition: In a way that is extremely impressive or dramatic, or to an extraordinary degree.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, 'tak'. The 'cu' in the middle is pronounced 'yuh', and the final '-ly' is a weak 'lee'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises something as remarkably impressive, though it can also be used ironically.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use spectacularly often in everyday speech, especially to praise food, views, or performances: 'The sunset was spectacularly beautiful.' It can also mean spectacularly bad, as in 'The launch failed spectacularly,' where it is used ironically for something going dramatically wrong. A natural reply is 'It really was!' or 'Right? I couldn't believe it.'

distinctions.note: Extremely is a neutral intensifier, while spectacularly adds a sense of dramatic, eye-catching impressiveness or failure.
Remarkably suggests something surprising or noteworthy, while spectacularly implies a visually or dramatically striking result.

examples.everyday: The sunset over the lake was spectacularly beautiful, so we stayed out there until it got dark.
examples.professional: Our new onboarding flow performed spectacularly in the pilot, with completion rates almost doubling.
examples.analytical: The theory fails spectacularly when applied to edge cases, which exposes its dependence on unexamined assumptions.

nuance.analogy: Spectacularly is like fireworks: it draws every eye and leaves a strong impression.
nuance.etymology: From spectacular, from Latin spectaculum, a sight, plus the adverb suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Mispronouncing the middle syllables, saying 'spek-tak-yoo-lar-ly' instead of 'spek-TAK-yuh-ler-lee'.
Using it as a plain synonym for 'very' in contexts where no visual or dramatic quality is involved.

senses.definition: The function of a front-end software system which processes input in the form of spoken language into a sequence of phonemes or characters, or into electronic commands for a computing system.
senses.example: Our team's speech recognition model transcribes customer calls with surprising accuracy.

core.definition: Technology that converts spoken language into written text or computer commands.

pronunciation.tip: The strongest stress is on -NISH, in recognition. Say 'speech' with a long ee sound, and do not add an extra vowel to recognition, which has a weak middle syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a technology, and people usually mention it in terms of accuracy or convenience.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use speech recognition for voice assistants, dictation, and phone menus. In casual speech, people often say voice recognition or just voice typing for dictation apps. In a meeting, you might say 'Our speech recognition error rate is too high for accents.'

distinctions.note: Speech recognition turns speech into text, while speech synthesis turns text into speech.
Voice recognition often means identifying who is speaking, while speech recognition means identifying what is said.

examples.everyday: My phone's speech recognition still gets confused when I give my address.
examples.professional: We need to improve the speech recognition accuracy for customers with regional accents.
examples.analytical: The debate about speech recognition raises questions about how machines interpret meaning, not merely sound.

nuance.analogy: Speech recognition is like a skilled transcriptionist who listens and writes down what was said, even when the speaker mumbles.
nuance.etymology: Recognition from Latin recognoscere, 'to know again'.
common_mistakes: Saying speech recognize as a verb phrase; the noun form is recognition.
Confusing speech recognition with speaker recognition, which identifies who is talking.

conversation.text: Speech recognition turns spoken audio into text.
Speech recognition still struggles with heavy accents, crosstalk, and noisy rooms.
We measure speech recognition quality with word error rate.

senses.definition: The electrical and mechanical connection between two pieces of wire or cable.
senses.example: The technician made a splice between the two cables and wrapped it in tape.

senses.definition: Bonding or joining of overlapping materials.
senses.example: The splice between the two sheets of laminate was reinforced with epoxy.

senses.definition: The process of removing intron sequences from the pre-messenger RNA, and then joining together exons.
senses.example: The splice of the pre-messenger RNA removed the introns before translation.

senses.definition: A junction or joining of ropes made by splicing them together.
senses.example: The sailor checked the splice where the two ropes were joined.

senses.definition: That part of a bat where the handle joins the blade.
senses.example: If the ball hits the splice, it is likely to dolly up for an easy catch.

senses.definition: To unite, as two ropes, or parts of a rope, by a particular manner of interweaving the strands, the union being between two ends, or between an end and the body of a rope.
senses.example: Dad showed me how to splice two ropes so the knot would not slip.

senses.definition: To unite, as spars, timbers, rails, etc. by lapping the two ends together, or by applying a piece which laps upon the two ends, and then binding, or in any way making fast.
senses.example: The carpenter had to splice the broken rail with a long oak plate.

senses.definition: To unite in marriage.
senses.example: The priest agreed to splice the couple at the small chapel by the lake.

senses.definition: To unite as if splicing.
senses.example: He argues against attempts to splice different genres or species of literature into a single composition.

senses.definition: To remove intron sequences from the pre-messenger RNA, and then join together exons.
senses.example: The cell machinery will splice the transcript before it leaves the nucleus.

senses.definition: To add, remove and/or replace several array/data elements in one operation.
senses.example: The script can splice several records out of the array in one operation.

core.definition: To join two ends of rope, wire or film by overlapping or interweaving them into one continuous piece.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable with a long i sound, like 'eye', and an unvoiced s at the end, as in 'nice'. Do not say it with a z or as 'splees'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a careful, technical joining, so it carries a sense of skill and precision.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use splice in film and video editing, electrical work, sailing and biology. In everyday talk people might say 'join' or 'connect' for less specialized cases. The informal phrase 'get spliced' means to get married, and people use it humorously.

distinctions.note: Join is the general word for connecting things, while splice implies an overlapping or interwoven technical join.
Connect is broad and can be electrical or social, while splice refers to a physical joining of the ends of material.

examples.everyday: Can you splice these two wires? The charger cord broke right in the middle.
examples.professional: We'll splice the logs from both servers so the incident timeline has no gaps.
examples.analytical: The historian splices scattered letters into a single narrative, though each join involves a guess.

nuance.analogy: Like braiding two ropes together so the join is as strong as the rest.
nuance.etymology: Probably from Middle Dutch splitsen, 'to split'; the exact source is not fully certain.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final s as z, as in SPLYZ.
Using splice for any ordinary joining of two things, when it specifically means an overlapping or interwoven join.

splice.etymology: Circa 1525, borrowed from Middle Dutch *splissen*; akin to Middle Dutch *splitten* (“to split”), *Spliss* (“split ends, hair breakage”), also from Dutch.

senses.definition: In a spontaneous manner; naturally; voluntarily.
senses.example: The crowd began singing spontaneously once the choir reached the final hymn.

core.definition: In a natural, unplanned way, without prior thought, a plan, or outside prompting.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the third syllable, TAY. The ending '-ly' is a short 'lee' sound, and the 'ous' in the middle is weak, pronounced 'ee-us'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests an enjoyable, natural or lively action, though it can sound careless in formal contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use spontaneously to describe a choice made in the moment, such as 'we went to the beach spontaneously.' It is also used for something that starts without obvious cause, such as a fire that ignites spontaneously. In casual talk people often say 'on a whim' or 'on the spur of the moment' instead.

distinctions.note: Impulsively suggests acting without thinking, sometimes with bad results; spontaneously is more neutral and often positive.
Naturally means in the normal way or as expected; spontaneously emphasizes that nothing was planned or prompted.

examples.everyday: We drove to the coast spontaneously last Saturday, and it turned out to be the best day of the summer.
examples.professional: The team agreed spontaneously to move the demo to Thursday, so please update your calendars.
examples.analytical: Children often respond spontaneously to music, before any conscious judgment has formed.

nuance.analogy: Like a sneeze, it happens without a plan or a decision.
nuance.etymology: From spontaneous plus the adverb ending -ly, from Latin spontaneus.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, as in 'SPON-tay-nee-us-lee'.
Pronouncing the ending as 'lie'; it is 'lee'.

senses.definition: The act by which something is squandered; wastage.
senses.example: The squandering of public funds on the stadium project angered many voters.

core.definition: The act of wasting something valuable, such as money, time, or resources, by using it carelessly.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, SKWAHN, and the vowel is the American open 'ah' sound, not the British 'o' of 'squond'. The middle syllable -der- is weak and becomes a schwa-r, so do not say 'skwan-dur-ring' with two strong beats.

nuance.connotation: Negative. The word always suggests waste and poor judgment, so it is used to criticize how something was spent or handled.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American speech, people more often use the verb squander, as in 'they squandered the money.' The noun squandering appears mainly in news, financial reporting, politics, and formal writing, for example in phrases like 'the squandering of public funds.' In casual talk, waste is a more common and natural choice.

distinctions.note: Waste is a general, neutral word for any use that produces no good result, while squandering suggests losing something valuable through carelessness or poor judgment.
Dissipation is a formal word for wasting energy or resources on pleasure or indulgence, and it often implies moral decline, while squandering focuses on careless loss.
Misuse means using something for the wrong purpose, which may not involve wasting it at all, while squandering always involves waste.

examples.everyday: After all that squandering on lottery tickets, he's broke again and nobody's surprised.
examples.professional: The audit flagged the squandering of cloud credits on idle GPU instances that nobody had shut down.
examples.analytical: Augustine reads the squandering of one's life on passing pleasures as a misdirection of love, which gives the wrong object the attention that belongs to God.

nuance.analogy: Squandering is like pouring water through a sieve: the water is real and valuable, but it runs out before anyone uses it.
nuance.etymology: Verbal noun from the verb squander, formed by adding the suffix -ing.
common_mistakes: Using squandering as a neutral word for normal spending; it always implies waste that should have been avoided.
Saying 'squandering time on' and 'squandering time in' interchangeably with 'squandering of time'; the 'of' form is more natural when used as a noun.

senses.definition: Yielding easily to pressure; very soft.
senses.example: The toy was soft and squishy, making it fun to squeeze.

senses.definition: Soft and wet.
Subjective or vague.
Politically moderate.
senses.example: The senator's squishy stance on taxes frustrated both parties' activists.

senses.definition: Vulnerable to physical damage; having low hit points or defense.
senses.example: The paladin was too squishy to survive the dragon's first fiery breath.

senses.definition: Making a squish sound.
senses.example: The wet sneakers made a squishy sound with every step on the gym floor.

senses.definition: A squeezable stress reliever, especially one made of foam.
senses.example: I keep a foam squishy on my desk to relieve stress during long meetings.

senses.definition: A term of endearment. (Can we add an example for this sense?)
senses.example: Good morning, squishy, did you sleep well after our long drive?

core.definition: Soft and easy to squeeze or press, giving under pressure; in some contexts, vague or not precisely defined.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the first vowel is short, like 'sk-wih'. The final y is pronounced 'ee', not 'eye'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use squishy for soft fruit, a sponge-like couch, or a foam stress ball, and it is casual and friendly in everyday talk. In professional or academic settings, calling a rule or definition squishy suggests it is vague and can be criticized. As a noun, it can be a stress toy, or an affectionate name for a baby or partner.

distinctions.note: Soft is the general word for not hard, while squishy adds the sense of giving under pressure and sometimes a wet, squeezable quality.
Squashy is somewhat more common in British English, while Americans usually say squishy for the same soft, yielding quality.
Vague means not clearly defined; squishy in its figurative sense is more informal and suggests a flexible, unclear standard.

examples.everyday: These peaches are getting squishy, so let's eat them tonight before they go bad.
examples.professional: The requirements are too squishy for an engineer to build against, so we need a precise spec.
examples.analytical: Her distinction between belief and knowledge is squishy, and it lets almost any claim pass unexamined.

nuance.analogy: Like a ripe peach, a squishy standard gives under the slightest pressure and loses its shape.
common_mistakes: Mispronouncing the first vowel as a long 'ee' sound, like 'skweesh-ee'
Using squishy only for physical softness and missing its informal figurative meaning for vague ideas

senses.definition: In a staid manner.

core.definition: In a calm, sober, conventional way, without excitement or surprising behavior.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the single first syllable. The -ly ending is a short ee sound, not 'lie,' and the d before l is light, so say it smoothly.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative: respectable and steady, but suggesting dullness.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use staidly mainly in writing or formal comment, for example describing a company, a town or an older person's manner. In speech people more often say calmly or conservatively. Calling someone's behavior staid is polite but mildly dull, and it is rarely an insult.

distinctions.note: Sedate stresses calm, slow movement or pace; staidly stresses conventional, serious respectability.
Sober can mean serious or not drunk; staidly means steady and conventional in manner.
Conservatively often refers to political views or cautious money decisions; staidly describes general manner.

examples.everyday: My grandparents lived pretty staidly, going to bed early and never missing church.
examples.professional: The board met staidly and approved the budget without any real debate.
examples.analytical: The essay argues that the old university governed itself staidly, preferring tradition to rapid reform.

nuance.analogy: Staidly is like a gray suit at a party: appropriate and steady, but never the center of attention.
nuance.etymology: From staid (steady, sober), a shortened form of stayed, the past participle of stay.
common_mistakes: Using staidly for quiet physical movement; sedately is closer for slow, calm motion.
Misspelling it as stadly or staidley.

senses.definition: American and Oxford British standard spelling of standardize.

core.definition: To make things follow the same standard, format or method so that they can be compared or used consistently.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on the first syllable, STAN. The middle syllable is a quick, weak 'der', and the final '-ize' is pronounced 'dyze', not 'dize'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it suggests making things fair, reliable or consistent.
nuance.usage_note: American English uses 'standardize' with a z, and this is standard in the United States. British spelling 'standardise' is not used in American writing. In offices and schools you will hear phrases like 'We need to standardize the template,' and in statistics you may standardize a variable before modeling.

distinctions.note: Normalize often means adjusting to a normal or typical state, while standardize means applying the same rule or format.
Unify means bringing separate things together, while standardize focuses on making them conform to a shared specification.

examples.everyday: My brother and I finally standardized our family recipes so they came out the same every time.
examples.professional: Let's standardize the naming convention in our dashboards before we roll it out to the whole company.
examples.analytical: To compare the models fairly, we must standardize the features so that each one is measured on the same scale.

nuance.analogy: Like tuning every instrument in an orchestra to the same A: everyone plays from the same reference pitch.
nuance.etymology: From 'standard' plus the verb-forming suffix '-ize', from Greek -izein.
common_mistakes: Writing 'standardise', the British spelling, in American writing.
Using 'standardize' to mean simply 'to standardize' something that is already the same.

senses.definition: The branch of mechanics concerned with forces in static equilibrium.

core.definition: The branch of mechanics that studies forces acting on objects at rest or in equilibrium, so that the net force and torque are zero.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, STAT, and pronounce the ending as a clear ks sound. The word is singular in meaning, so it takes a singular verb: statics is required.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it names an academic subject and carries no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: American engineering students take statics as a required first course, often before dynamics. Because it names a field, it is uncountable and takes a singular verb, as in statics is a hard course. Do not use it for a single problem; say a statics problem or a statics exam.

distinctions.note: Statics studies forces when things are at rest or in balance, while dynamics studies forces that cause motion.
Static as an adjective describes a state of rest, while statics is the name of the whole branch of study.

examples.everyday: My son is taking statics in engineering school and says it is the hardest class he has had.
examples.professional: The bridge design passed the statics check, so we can move on to the dynamic loading analysis.
examples.analytical: Statics treats forces as balanced, which idealizes the physical world, yet the static case is the foundation from which dynamics is developed.

nuance.analogy: Statics is like a photograph of a bridge under load: every force is in balance, and nothing moves.
nuance.etymology: Statics comes from Greek statikos, causing to stand, through the Latin and French forms of the word for the science of weights.
common_mistakes: Using statics as a plural noun with a plural verb, as in statics are hard.
Confusing statics with static, which is an adjective or a noun in other senses.

senses.definition: In a stealthy manner, furtively.
senses.example: The cat crept stealthily across the kitchen floor toward the bowl of cream.

core.definition: In a quiet, secret way, so that no one notices or sees you.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on STEL, and the th is the voiceless sound of think, not a t. The ending -ily is weak, so it sounds like thih-lee and not stel-tee-lie.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. It can describe a quiet, careful movement or a secret action that is sneaky or dishonest.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it in news writing, fiction, and everyday talk to describe quiet movement or secret action, as in 'He stealthily opened the door.' More casual speakers often say 'sneakily' or 'on the sly.' It is seldom needed in simple conversation, but it sounds natural in storytelling.

distinctions.note: Secretly is the general, neutral word for doing something hidden, while stealthily emphasizes quiet, careful movement that avoids being noticed.
Sneakily is informal and often suggests trickery or mischief, while stealthily is more neutral or literary.
Covertly is formal and often used for official or military secret operations, while stealthily describes everyday or narrative action.

examples.everyday: The cat stealthily climbed onto the couch while we were watching TV.
examples.professional: The competitor stealthily acquired three small startups through shell companies, and we only learned about it from the filings.
examples.analytical: The novel's narrator stealthily undermines the authority of the church, so readers notice the critique only on a second reading.

nuance.analogy: Like a cat crossing a wooden floor without a single creak, stealthily means moving so that no one hears or sees you.
nuance.etymology: From stealthy plus the adverb suffix -ly; stealth comes from Middle English stelthe, related to steal.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the th as a t, saying 'stel-tee-lee' instead of 'STEL-thih-lee'.
Using 'stealthily' for ordinary secret actions like planning a party, which sounds overly dramatic.

senses.definition: To be nosy; to meddle or interfere in the affairs of another.
senses.example: I was doing just fine before he came and stuck his nose in.

core.definition: To interfere in someone else's private business or affairs when you were not asked to get involved.

pronunciation.tip: The word 'one's' reduces to a weak 'wuhnz', and the final 'in' is the stressed word. Link the phrase smoothly: 'stik-wuhnz-nohz-IN'.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it implies someone is being nosy or intrusive.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use stick your nose in to criticize someone who meddles in private matters, such as a family argument or a coworker's personal life. It is informal and can sound rude if said directly to someone's face. A natural reply, to someone who is interfering, is to say 'Mind your own business' or 'That is none of your business'.

distinctions.note: Butt in means to interrupt a conversation or activity; stick your nose in means to interfere in a private matter.
Meddle is a more formal and general word for interfering; stick your nose in is more casual and common in speech.
Pry means to try to learn private information; stick your nose in means to interfere, which may not involve asking questions.

collocations: stick your nose into other people's business

examples.everyday: My mom is always sticking her nose in my dating life, and it drives me crazy.
examples.professional: Please do not stick your nose in the other team's budget decisions unless you have been asked to review them.
examples.analytical: Mill's harm principle suggests that society should not stick its nose in private conduct unless others are harmed.

nuance.analogy: Like a neighbor who leans over the fence to listen to every conversation, the person who sticks a nose in is too close to other people's business.
common_mistakes: Using 'stick my nose' in the wrong person, such as 'stick your nose' when you mean 'my nose'.
Saying 'put nose in' instead of 'stick nose in', which Americans do not use.

senses.definition: To make (an animal or person) unconscious or cause (an animal or person) to die by preventing breathing; to smother, to suffocate.
To cause (someone) difficulty in breathing, or a choking or gagging feeling.
senses.example: The heat was stifling the children.

senses.definition: To prevent (a breath, cough, or cry, or the voice, etc.) from being released from the throat.
To make (something) unable to be heard by blocking it with some medium.
To keep in, hold back, or repress (something).
senses.example: The army stifled the rebellion.

senses.definition: To prevent (something) from being revealed; to conceal, to hide, to suppress.
To treat (a silkworm cocoon) with steam as part of the process of silk production.
To die of suffocation.
senses.example: Two firemen tragically stifled in yesterday’s fire when trying to rescue an old lady from her bedroom.

senses.definition: To smother; to make breathing difficult.
senses.example: This heat is stifling.

senses.definition: To cause (a dog, horse, or other four-legged mammal) to dislocate or sprain its stifle joint.
The joint between the femur and tibia in the hind leg of various four-legged mammals, especially horses, corresponding to the knee in humans.
A bone disease of this region.
(rare) An act or state of being stifled.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: To hold back or suppress a feeling, sound, or reaction; or to make someone have trouble breathing.

pronunciation.tip: Stress on the first syllable and the second syllable is a reduced 'l' with no separate vowel. Non-native speakers often say 'stye-fel' with a full vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative; it suggests holding something back or suffocating, depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'stifle' most often for holding back a yawn, a laugh, or a cough in polite company. The sense of suffocating is more literary or formal. In everyday talk, 'hold back' or 'suppress' is common, but 'stifle a yawn' sounds natural and polite.

distinctions.note: Suppress is broader and can apply to emotions, information, or movements; stifle often refers to a sound, breath, or reaction.
Suffocate means to die or nearly die from lack of air; stifle can mean to restrict or prevent a sound or feeling without a physical death.

examples.everyday: I tried to stifle a yawn during the long phone call, but my coworker noticed anyway.
examples.professional: Too many approval steps can stifle innovation on the team.
examples.analytical: Rigid curricula can stifle students' curiosity, and the effect is often invisible to the people who design them.

nuance.analogy: Like a lid on a pot, stifle keeps steam or sound from escaping.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English stiflen, from Old French or related words for choking; the root sense is suffocation.
common_mistakes: Using 'stifle' to mean to be stifled physically in ordinary speech; the common everyday use is holding back a reaction.
Pronouncing it like 'stile' with a long i and an extra syllable.

stifle.etymology: The verb is derived from Late Middle English *stuflen* (“to have difficulty breathing due to heat, stifle; to suffocate by drowning, drown”); further etymology.

senses.definition: Capable of being stretched.
senses.example: The stretchable fabric in these running tights makes them comfortable for long runs.

senses.definition: Of a pseudoline arrangement: combinatorially equivalent to a line arrangement, such that one can straighten each line while maintaining the order in which they cross.
senses.example: The researcher proved that every small pseudoline arrangement is stretchable, so straight lines suffice.

core.definition: Able to be pulled longer or wider without tearing or breaking, such as stretchable fabric or a stretchable band.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and keep the ending weak. The final -able is a schwa followed by a light l, not a strong 'ay-bul.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it describes a useful property of materials and clothing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use stretchable mainly for fabrics, bands, films and materials, as in 'stretchable waistband.' For everyday clothing they more often say 'stretchy.' In mathematics, stretchable is a technical term for certain line arrangements.

distinctions.note: Stretchy is more casual and describes how something feels or behaves; stretchable describes whether it can be stretched at all.
Elastic is more technical and implies returning to the original shape; stretchable does not promise that.

examples.everyday: These jeans have a stretchable waistband, so they're comfortable on long flights.
examples.professional: We are designing a stretchable sensor patch for remote patient monitoring.
examples.analytical: Kant's account is strong because it shows which concepts are stretchable enough to cover new experience without losing their meaning.

nuance.analogy: Like a rubber band that can be pulled considerably before it reaches its limit.
nuance.etymology: From stretch plus the suffix -able, meaning able to be done.
common_mistakes: Putting the stress on the ending, as in 'stretch-ABLE'.
Using stretchable to describe a tired person; say stretched thin instead.

senses.definition: The remains of something that has been cut off; especially the remains of a tree, the remains of a limb.
senses.example: A rotten stump blocked the trail, so we had to climb over it.

senses.definition: The place or occasion at which a campaign takes place; the husting.
senses.example: The senator spoke from the stump at the county fairgrounds on Saturday afternoon.

senses.definition: A place or occasion at which a person harangues or otherwise addresses a group in a manner suggesting political oration.
senses.example: The union leader took the stump outside the factory gates and denounced the new contract.

senses.definition: An artists’ drawing tool made of rolled paper used to smudge or blend marks made with charcoal, Conté crayon, pencil or other drawing media.
senses.example: She blended the charcoal shadows with a stump, leaving soft gray edges.

senses.definition: A wooden or concrete pole used to support a house.
senses.example: Engineers drove concrete stumps deep into the soil to support the raised house.

senses.definition: A leg.
senses.example: to stir one's stumps

senses.definition: A pin in a tumbler lock which forms an obstruction to throwing the bolt except when the gates of the tumblers are properly arranged, as by the key.
senses.example: The lock's stumps must align with the key's cuts before the bolt slides.

senses.definition: A pin or projection in a lock to form a guide for a movable piece.
senses.example: A small stump inside the drawer guided the sliding tray along its track.

senses.definition: One of three small wooden posts which together with the bails make the wicket and that the fielding team attempt to hit with the ball.
senses.example: The bowler struck the middle stump, and the batsman was out.

senses.definition: To stop, confuse, or puzzle.
senses.example: The tricky tax question completely stumped me, so I called my accountant.

senses.definition: To baffle; to make unable to find an answer to a question or problem.
senses.example: This last question has me stumped.

senses.definition: To campaign.
senses.example: He’s been stumping for that reform for months.

senses.definition: To travel over (a state, a district, etc.) giving speeches for electioneering purposes.
senses.example: The candidate stumped every county in the district during the final month.

senses.definition: To walk heavily or clumsily, plod, trudge.
senses.example: Exhausted, we stumped up the muddy trail toward the cabin.

senses.definition: To reduce to a stump; to truncate or cut off a part of.
senses.example: Crews stumped the diseased maples along the boulevard before replanting in spring.

senses.definition: To strike unexpectedly; to stub, as the toe against something fixed.
senses.example: I stumped my toe on the cellar step and swore loudly.

senses.definition: To get a batsman out stumped.
senses.example: The keeper stumped the batter who had wandered too far from his crease.

senses.definition: To bowl down the stumps of (a wicket).
senses.example: The bowler stumped the wicket twice in the opening over, leaving the batsmen dazed.

core.definition: To confuse or baffle someone so completely that they cannot answer a question or solve a problem.

pronunciation.tip: Pronounce it as one syllable ending in a clear 'mp' cluster; the 'p' is a soft stop, and the 'm' links directly into it. Do not insert a vowel between 'm' and 'p.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'That stumped me' when they cannot answer a question, which is common in everyday talk and in classrooms or meetings. The noun sense for a campaign appearance is political and used mainly in American politics, as in 'campaigning on the stump.' Context usually makes the meaning clear.

distinctions.note: Confuse means to make unclear, while stump specifically means to make someone unable to find an answer.
Baffle is more formal and suggests deep puzzlement, while stump is a casual everyday word for not knowing an answer.

examples.everyday: That crossword clue really stumped me, so I looked up the answer on my phone.
examples.professional: That question about our data pipeline stumped me, so I'll follow up with the engineering team by Friday.
examples.analytical: The objection stumps the proponent of the theory because it exposes a gap between the premises and the conclusion.

nuance.analogy: A stump is what remains of a tree after it is cut; stumping someone is like cutting off their path to an answer, leaving them stuck in place.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English 'stumpe,' a tree stump; the verb sense of baffling developed from the image of being stopped short.
common_mistakes: Using 'stump' as a noun for a question, as in 'That is a good stump,' which is not natural.
Confusing the verb 'stump' with 'stumble' in meaning.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew word behind 'stump' in Job 14:8 is 'geza' (a stump or stock of a tree). In Job 14:8, Job describes how a tree's root may grow old in the ground and its stump die, a picture of human mortality and the apparent permanence of death. In Daniel 4:15, King Nebuchadnezzar's dream describes a tree whose stump is left in the earth, a sign of humbling and eventual restoration. In Isaiah 6:13, a holy seed remains as a stump after the land is cut down, a promise of a remnant.

stump.etymology: From Middle English *stumpe*, *stompe* (“stump”), from or akin to *stump* (“stump”) or Middle Dutch *stomp*, from or **stump*, from **stump*, from Proto-Germanic **stumpaz* (“stump, blunt, part cut off”).

senses.definition: Having subdued colors.
senses.example: She wore a subfusc gray dress with a muted brown shawl to the funeral.

senses.definition: Dark clothing.
senses.example: All the mourners arrived in sober subfusc, dark coats and muted scarves.

senses.definition: Clothing acceptable, by regulation at certain universities, for an examination or official event.
senses.example: Students at Oxford must wear subfusc, a dark suit and white bow tie, for examinations.

senses.definition: Formal clothing worn on special academic occasions.
senses.example: Graduates attended the Encaenia ceremony in subfusc, gowns over dark suits.

core.definition: Dark, drab, or muted in color; in British academic use, the dark clothing worn for formal examinations.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, and both vowels are the same short uh sound. The final k is clearly pronounced, not silent.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes muted, dark dress or colors and carries a bookish, slightly old-fashioned tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use this word. It comes from the Oxford and Cambridge tradition, where subfusc is the dark clothing students wear for formal exams. In American English, say dark, drab, or muted clothing, or simply a dark suit. You are most likely to meet it in British novels or academic writing.

distinctions.note: Drab suggests dull and unattractive; subfusc suggests dark, muted, and often deliberately formal.

examples.everyday: Grandpa showed up to the party in his old subfusc suit, looking like he was headed to a funeral.
examples.professional: The ceremony dress code is subfusc, so bring a dark suit and a white shirt.
examples.analytical: The subfusc robes of the medieval scholar signaled humility and discipline rather than wealth.

nuance.analogy: Like a gray stone among painted flowers.
nuance.etymology: From Latin subfuscus, somewhat dark, from sub- meaning somewhat and fuscus meaning dark.
common_mistakes: Adding an extra syllable, as in 'sub-FUSS-kuh'; the word has only two syllables.
Using it in ordinary American speech for any dark clothing, which sounds stiff and odd.

senses.definition: The state of being subjective.
A subjective thought or idea.
senses.example: His reviews kept returning to his own subjectivities rather than the actual evidence.

core.definition: The quality of being shaped by personal feelings, perspective, or interpretation rather than by objective facts.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on TIV, and the first syllable has a secondary stress. The final ty is a quick ih-tee, with the last vowel reduced to a short ih sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It names a quality without judging it, though it can imply bias in everyday debates.
nuance.usage_note: In American speech, people more often say a subjective view or it is subjective. Subjectivity is typical in academic, philosophical, and professional writing about research and interpretation. Using it casually can sound a bit heavy, so simple subjective language is often more natural.

distinctions.note: Bias is a systematic tilt that distorts judgment, while subjectivity is a broader fact that all perception involves a personal perspective.
Objectivity is the goal of reporting facts independent of the observer; subjectivity is the observer's own point of view.

examples.everyday: Let's not argue about the ending; there is too much subjectivity in what makes a story satisfying.
examples.professional: Our reviewers need guidelines to reduce subjectivity in how they score candidate projects.
examples.analytical: Phenomenologists insist that the first-person perspective is an irreducible subjectivity that any account of experience must acknowledge.

nuance.analogy: Like a window with a slight tint: you still see the view, but the color comes partly from the glass.
nuance.etymology: From subjective, from Late Latin subjectivus, with the suffix -ity meaning state or quality.
common_mistakes: Using subjectivity as a countable noun for a single opinion; say a subjective opinion or a subjective idea instead.
Mispronouncing the word with the stress on the first syllable, as in SUB-jek-TIV-ih-tee.

senses.definition: In a subtextual way.

core.definition: In a way that relates to the hidden meaning beneath the surface of a text, speech, or performance.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on TEKST, with a weak secondary stress on the first syllable. The final -ly is a reduced 'lee' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a specialized critical term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans almost never use subtextually in everyday speech; it belongs to literary criticism, film analysis, and academic writing. In casual talk people would say underneath or between the lines. Use it only when discussing what a text implies beneath its words.

distinctions.note: Implicitly means in a way that is suggested without being stated; subtextually is specific to meaning hidden beneath a text or performance.
Subtly means in a delicate or clever way; subtextually refers to the layer of meaning under the words.

examples.professional: The script works subtextually, so the actors should show the conflict through silence rather than dialogue.
examples.analytical: The novel reads subtextually as a critique of the church, even though its surface plot is a simple love story.

nuance.analogy: Reading subtextually is like listening to a song and hearing the sadness under the cheerful melody.
nuance.etymology: From subtextual with the adverb suffix -ly.
