common_mistakes: Confusing subtextually with subtly, which means something different.
Stressing the wrong syllable, saying 'sub-tex-CHOO-uh-lee' instead of 'sub-TEKST-choo-uh-lee'.

senses.definition: The populated area surrounding a city.
senses.example: Many families move to the suburbs once their children are old enough for school.

core.definition: The residential areas on the outer edge of a city, usually with houses, yards, and a quieter lifestyle.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the first syllable, and the second syllable is the r-colored vowel 'ur', which is rhotic in American speech. Non-native speakers often pronounce the r weakly or use a long 'oo' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, though it can carry associations with family life, car dependence, or middle-class living.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use the suburbs in everyday talk about where people live, commute from, or shop. You would say I live in the suburbs or we moved to the suburbs. The word is almost always plural in this sense, and it is very common in ordinary conversation.

distinctions.note: City refers to the dense urban center, while suburbs are the residential areas around it.
Outskirts describes the edge of a town or city in general, while suburbs refers to organized residential communities with their own character.

examples.everyday: We moved out to the suburbs last year because the schools and yards are better for our kids.
examples.professional: Our retail analysis shows that most of our customers come from the suburbs, so the new store should be located there.
examples.analytical: Urban sociologists have long argued that the growth of the suburbs reshaped American family life and the relationship between work and home.

nuance.analogy: The suburbs are like a ring of smaller villages around a big town, each one connected to the center by a road.
nuance.etymology: From Latin suburbium, area near a city, from sub- (under, near) and urbs (city).
common_mistakes: Using the singular suburb when speaking generally about the outer residential areas, where the plural is more natural.
Saying 'in suburb' instead of 'in the suburbs' when talking about where someone lives.

conversation.text: They moved to the suburbs when their first kid was born.
Life in the suburbs means you drive everywhere.
He commutes from the suburbs and spends an hour on the train.

senses.definition: The process of adding a suffix to a word.

core.definition: The process of adding a suffix to a word to form a new word or an inflected form.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on SAY, in the -ation ending, and the -tion sounds like 'shun'. The middle syllable -fix- keeps a short i, and the x is 'ks'. The stress moves from the first syllable of 'suffix', so do not say 'SUF-ih-kay-shun'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise linguistic term used in academic and technical contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mainly in linguistics, language teaching and computational text analysis. It is rare in everyday speech, where people say 'adding a suffix' instead. It is a specialized term, so use it in academic or technical settings.

distinctions.note: Prefixation adds a morpheme to the beginning of a word, and suffixation adds one to the end.
Affixation is the broader term for adding any affix, including prefixes and infixes. Suffixation names only the end-of-word case.

examples.everyday: My daughter is studying suffixation in her English class, so at dinner we've been turning adjectives into nouns by adding -ness.
examples.professional: The tokenizer handles suffixation by splitting words like deployment into a stem and a suffix, so the model sees the root word.
examples.analytical: Suffixation in English is highly productive, since -ness and -ize can attach to many bases without changing their core form.

nuance.analogy: Suffixation is like sewing a patch onto the end of a hem: the garment stays the same, but its shape and use change.
nuance.etymology: From suffix plus -ation, the noun-forming suffix.
common_mistakes: Keeping the stress on the first syllable as in SUF-ix, instead of moving it to SAY.
Using 'suffixation' in casual conversation, where 'adding a suffix' sounds more natural.

senses.definition: First-rate; of the highest quality; exceptionally good.
senses.example: This champagne is superb.

senses.definition: Grand; magnificent; august; stately.
senses.example: a superb edifice; a superb colonnade

senses.definition: Haughty.
senses.example: The duchess gave the footman a superb glance and turned away without speaking.

core.definition: First-rate and of the highest quality; exceptionally good or impressive.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the single syllable 'purb,' with the r-colored vowel in the middle. Do not stress the first syllable, as in 'SOO-perb.'

nuance.connotation: Strongly positive; it signals high praise and can sound slightly polished or formal in casual talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'superb' for excellent food, service, performance, or work, especially in reviews, toasts, and professional praise. In casual conversation people more often say 'great' or 'awesome,' so 'superb' can sound a bit formal or bookish. It fits well in a formal thank-you or written feedback.

distinctions.note: 'Great' is the most common everyday word of approval; 'superb' is more formal and implies a higher standard of quality.
'Excellent' is measured and suitable for professional evaluation; 'superb' is warmer and more emphatic.
'Magnificent' suggests grandeur or impressive size; 'superb' emphasizes quality and skill.

examples.everyday: The tacos were superb, and the service was fast, so we'll definitely come back.
examples.professional: Your analysis was superb, and the client will appreciate how clearly you explained the risks.
examples.analytical: The argument is superb in its economy, although its central premise deserves more scrutiny than it receives.

nuance.analogy: Like a top-rated chef's signature dish: the quality is clear to everyone who tastes it.
nuance.etymology: From Latin superbus (proud, haughty, magnificent), which gave the English sense of splendid as well as the older sense of haughty.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, as in 'SOO-perb.'
Using 'superb' in very casual speech where 'great' would sound more natural.

senses.definition: In AI: In interpretability, a network representing more features than it has neurons by sharing neurons between features.
The placing of one thing on top of another.
senses.example: The superposition of one photo over another created a double-exposed image on the wall.

senses.definition: The situation in quantum mechanics where two or more quantum states are added together (superposed) to yield another valid quantum state.
senses.example: In quantum mechanics, the electron's superposition of spin states can be measured only once.

senses.definition: The deposition of one stratum over another; the principle that in a series of sedimentary strata, the lower strata are the older.
senses.example: Geologists used superposition to determine that the lowest rock layer was the oldest.

core.definition: In AI interpretability, a network representing more features than it has neurons by sharing neurons between features.

pronunciation.tip: Primary stress falls on ZI, the fourth syllable, and the -tion ending is pronounced 'shun.' The middle syllables are reduced, so do not add an extra syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It has no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: In AI, superposition is a specialized term from interpretability research, where models store more features than they have neurons. In everyday English and in physics, it means placing one thing on top of another or the combination of quantum states, so context matters. Americans in tech use it in this AI sense mainly in research or engineering talks.

distinctions.note: Overlay means placing one layer on top of another, often for display. Superposition in AI describes how many features share the same neurons, not a visible layering.
In physics, superposition refers to quantum states combining. In AI, it refers to sharing neurons. The same word has different technical meanings.

examples.everyday: When my friend explained superposition in neural networks, I had to ask her to slow down.
examples.professional: Our interpretability team argues that superposition explains why single neurons often respond to several unrelated concepts.
examples.analytical: If superposition holds, then the interpretability of a model cannot be read off one neuron at a time, since each neuron participates in many features at once.

nuance.analogy: Superposition is like sharing one apartment among several roommates by using different corners of the same rooms, so the space holds more people than its rooms would suggest.
nuance.etymology: From Latin superpositio, from superponere, 'to place upon,' from super, 'above,' and ponere, 'to place.'
common_mistakes: Using superposition in AI to mean simply 'layering,' which misses the technical meaning.
Stressing the wrong syllable, as in 'SU-per-po-ZI-shun' with an extra stress on the first part.

conversation.text: Superposition is when a network represents more features than it has neurons by using overlapping directions.
Because of superposition, a single neuron often responds to several unrelated concepts.
In quantum mechanics, superposition means a system can be in a combination of states at once.

senses.definition: A system of organizations, people, technology, activities, information and resources involved in moving a product or service from the supplier to the customer.
senses.example: A single fire at one supplier disrupted our entire supply chain for six weeks.

core.definition: The network of companies, people, and resources that moves a product from its supplier to its customer.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on PLY, and chain gets a weaker secondary stress, so do not stress both words equally. Say the ch in chain cleanly, and link the words smoothly as suh-PLY-chayn.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is business language and can carry a negative sense when a supply chain breaks down.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use supply chain in business, manufacturing, and news, often in phrases like supply chain disruption during shortages. Outside work, people say shipping delays or talk about where things come from. As an adjective, it is usually hyphenated, as in supply-chain problems.

distinctions.note: Logistics focuses on moving and storing goods, while supply chain covers the whole network, including sourcing, production, and sales.
Value chain focuses on how each step adds value, while supply chain focuses on the flow of goods and information.
A distribution network only gets products to customers, while a supply chain also includes sourcing and production.

examples.everyday: Did you hear the store is out of cereal again? Something went wrong somewhere in the supply chain.
examples.professional: The supply chain team is reworking the inventory plan to reduce delays from our overseas plant.
examples.analytical: A supply chain is best understood as a network of information flows, not just the physical movement of goods.

nuance.analogy: Like a relay race where each runner hands the baton to the next until it reaches the finish line.
nuance.etymology: Supply comes from Latin supplere, 'to fill up'; chain comes from Latin catena, 'chain'.
common_mistakes: Stressing both words equally; the main stress is on SUP-ply, and chain is weaker.
Confusing supply chain with supply line, which is a military term for moving troops and equipment.

senses.definition: A doctrine held by certain Calvinists that God predestined the fall of man.

core.definition: A Calvinist doctrine holding that God decreed the election and reprobation of people before decreeing that the fall of humanity would occur.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on SAIR, the fourth syllable, and the long 'ee' and 'uh' endings are light. Learners often stress the -lap- syllable or pronounce the -ian- ending as a separate, heavy syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise term from theology, used in debate and description.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mainly in seminaries, theology classes, and historical discussions of Reformed Calvinism. It is often paired with infralapsarianism, and speakers usually explain the difference in the same breath. In casual conversation, people say 'the view that God decided who would be saved before the fall.'

distinctions.note: Infralapsarians hold that God decreed the fall before decreeing election and reprobation, which is the reverse order of supralapsarianism.
Arminianism rejects unconditional predestination, while supralapsarianism is a strongly deterministic form of Calvinist predestination.

examples.everyday: My seminary roommate argued about supralapsarianism until midnight, and I still don't fully understand it.
examples.professional: In the seminar, the professor contrasted supralapsarianism with infralapsarianism when we discussed the Westminster Confession.
examples.analytical: Supralapsarianism places God's decree of election logically before the decree to permit the fall, which intensifies the question of whether God is the author of sin.

nuance.analogy: Like an architect who decides who will live in the house before drawing the floor plan.
nuance.etymology: From Latin supra ('above, before') plus lapsus ('fall'), with the adjective and noun suffixes -arian and -ism.
common_mistakes: Confusing supralapsarianism with infralapsarianism, which reverses the order of God's decrees.
Stressing the wrong syllable, such as 'su-pra-LAP-sar-ee-an-ism'.
nuance.biblical_note: The term is not in Scripture but is a later theological construction. Its basis is Ephesians 1:4-5 (the Greek word eklegomai, meaning 'to choose out,' describes God choosing believers before the foundation of the world), Romans 9:11-13 (God's choice of Jacob over Esau before their birth), and Romans 9:21 (the potter's authority over the clay). These passages are read differently by supralapsarians and infralapsarians.

traditions.view: Eastern Orthodox theology generally does not use the Western Augustinian-Calvinist framework of unconditional predestination, so the debate over the order of divine decrees is largely foreign to it. Orthodoxy emphasizes God's foreknowledge and human cooperation with grace.

Catholic teaching holds that God predestines the saved to glory by grace, but the official tradition rejects double predestination in which God wills damnation. The supralapsarian ordering of decrees is not a Catholic dogma and is generally seen as a Reformed speculative question.

Among Protestants, the debate is internal to Reformed Calvinism, where supralapsarians and infralapsarians both accept the sovereignty of God's grace but differ on the logical order of the decrees. Lutherans generally reject double predestination, and Arminians reject unconditional election.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to the surface of something, particularly the surface of the Earth.
senses.example: When the soil swells on wetting, the former surficial material is mixed with the subsoil.

core.definition: Relating to or located at the surface of the Earth or of a material, especially in geology and hydrology.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, fish. The first syllable is a weak r-colored vowel, and the final -al is a reduced syllable, so say it quickly.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and precise. It is a technical descriptor with no emotional weight.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use surficial mainly in geology, soil science, hydrology, and engineering reports, such as surficial deposits or surficial aquifer. In everyday speech, people say surface, top layer, or near the surface instead. Do not confuse it with superficial, which means shallow in character.

distinctions.note: Superficial means shallow or not thorough, as in a superficial analysis, while surficial refers to physical position at the surface.
Subsurface means below the surface, the opposite spatial sense of surficial.

examples.everyday: The rain washed away the loose surficial dirt, so you can see the gravel underneath now.
examples.professional: The geotechnical report found surficial soil that is too loose to support the new building's foundation.
examples.analytical: Surficial processes such as erosion and deposition shape the landscape more than deep tectonic forces in this region, the authors argue.

nuance.analogy: Surficial is like the frosting on a cake: it covers the top layer, not the whole cake.
nuance.etymology: From surface, from Old French sorface, from sur- over plus face face, with the suffix -ial.
common_mistakes: Confusing surficial with superficial, which has a different meaning.
Stressing the second syllable incorrectly as ser-FISH-uhl; some speakers wrongly place stress on the first syllable.

senses.definition: One who surrenders.

core.definition: A person who gives up or yields to an opponent, authority or demand.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on REN, the second syllable, so the first syllable is weak. The endings '-der' and '-er' are both reduced to quick r-colored vowels, which learners often overpronounce.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative depending on context; in military or conflict stories it suggests defeat, while in personal or moral contexts it can be neutral or even positive.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use 'surrenderer'. They more often say 'the one who surrendered' or 'the person giving up'. The word is found mainly in historical, military or legal writing, and in everyday speech it sounds unusual and can be playful.

distinctions.note: A defector switches sides or leaves a country or group, while a surrenderer gives up and stops resisting.
A captive is someone held by an enemy, while a surrenderer chooses to give up, although capture may follow.

examples.everyday: My brother was the first surrenderer in our card game, so he had to fold and watch the rest of us play.
examples.professional: In the negotiation, the vendor became the surrenderer and accepted every one of our terms.
examples.analytical: In the theology of conversion, the surrenderer is not defeated but finally admits his dependence on God.

nuance.analogy: A surrenderer is like a player who throws in the towel after the final round.
nuance.etymology: From surrender, from Anglo-French surrendre (to give up), with the agent suffix -er.
common_mistakes: Using 'surrenderer' where 'surrendered' is needed as a verb or adjective.
Stressing the last syllable, as in 'suh-ren-DER-er'; the main stress is on REN.

senses.definition: One who swaggers.

core.definition: A person who walks or acts in a boastful, overconfident way that seems designed to impress others.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and keep the g hard, as in 'bag'. The final -er is a weak, unstressed syllable, so do not stretch it into 'swag-AIR'.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it suggests arrogance and empty bravado, though it can be playful when describing a character.
nuance.usage_note: This is a rare word; Americans more often say braggart, show-off or cocky guy for the same kind of person. You will meet it in older fiction, reviews or wry commentary. It is not offensive, but calling someone a swaggerer is a pointed insult. A natural reply to describing one is 'Yeah, he never stops bragging.'

distinctions.note: A braggart talks boastfully; a swaggerer shows off through posture and manner as well as through talk.
Show-off is informal and everyday; swaggerer is more literary and stresses the physical swagger.

examples.professional: Please keep the swaggerer on the sales team from dominating our planning meeting.
examples.analytical: Shakespeare's swaggerers, such as Pistol, reveal how bravado often hides insecurity.

nuance.analogy: A rooster strutting around the yard with its chest out, showing the hens who is boss.
nuance.etymology: From swagger (verb, of uncertain origin) plus the agent suffix -er.
common_mistakes: Using swaggerer as a neutral word; it always implies arrogance.
Stressing the final -er syllable instead of keeping it weak.

senses.definition: A group whose elements are all the transformations under which a given object remains invariant and whose group operation is function composition.
senses.example: The symmetry group of a square has eight elements, including four rotations and four reflections.

core.definition: A set of transformations, such as rotations and reflections, that leave an object unchanged, together with composition as the operation.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress is on GROUP, while SIM has secondary stress and the rest of 'symmetry' is weak. Learners often stress 'SIM' too strongly or say 'sim-MET-ree' with a stressed middle syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term with no evaluative meaning.
nuance.usage_note: This is a term used in mathematics, physics, chemistry, and crystallography, and mostly in university courses or research papers. Americans use it in lectures and textbooks rather than in everyday speech. Specialists often name a specific group, such as the dihedral group of a square, rather than saying 'symmetry group' alone.

distinctions.note: 'Symmetry' is the property an object has, while the symmetry group is the set of all transformations that preserve that property.
A symmetric group is the group of all permutations of a finite set; a symmetry group is the group of symmetries of a particular object.

collocations: the symmetry group of a square
the symmetry group of the molecule

examples.everyday: My physics roommate kept talking about the symmetry group of a snowflake, and I still don't really get it.
examples.professional: The data team used the symmetry group of the image transformations to reduce the number of training examples needed for the model.
examples.analytical: A symmetry group captures what remains invariant under transformation, so it reveals structure that the object's shape alone might obscure.

nuance.analogy: Think of a square: the set of all rotations and flips that leave it looking the same forms its symmetry group.
nuance.etymology: 'Symmetry' is from Greek symmetria, meaning proportion; 'group' is from French groupe, from Italian gruppo.
common_mistakes: Using 'symmetry group' as a synonym for 'symmetry' in everyday sentences, when it refers to a specific mathematical structure.
Stressing the first syllable of 'symmetry' too heavily and reducing the stress on 'group'.

senses.definition: The quality of being systemic.

core.definition: The quality of being systemic; the degree to which a problem or property belongs to the whole interconnected system.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on 'SIS', the syllable from '-icity' that follows the stressed 'stem' of 'systemic'. Keep the 'e' in 'tem' clear and unstressed, and flap the 't' so it sounds like a quick 'd'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise analytical term, often used when discussing risk or injustice.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this in economics, risk analysis, systems research and social theory. It is uncommon in everyday talk, where people say 'the problem is built into the system.' It is a more abstract word than 'systemic,' so use it when you want to name the quality of being systemic.

distinctions.note: Systemicity concerns belonging to a system's interconnected whole; systematicity concerns orderly, planned method.
Systemic is the adjective describing a thing; systemicity is the noun naming the quality.

examples.everyday: We kept calling the outage a one-off, but the more the bus delays repeated, the clearer their systemicity became.
examples.professional: Before we call it a bug, we should check the systemicity of the failure across all three regional data centers.
examples.analytical: The argument turns on the systemicity of the injustice: it lies not in individual choices but in the rules that shape them.

nuance.analogy: Like a fever that signals infection throughout the body, instead of a single sore spot.
nuance.etymology: From 'systemic' (Greek systēma, 'organized whole') plus the suffix '-icity' (Latin -icitas).
common_mistakes: Using 'systemicity' when you mean 'systematicity,' which concerns planned order.
Stressing the 'tem' syllable of 'systemic' in the noun instead of the 'SIS' syllable.
Using it in casual talk, where 'systemic' or 'built into the system' is more natural.

senses.definition: A large spoon, used for eating food from a bowl.

A unit of volume, the value of which varies regionally; in the US: three teaspoons or one half fluid ounce or roughly 15 ml; in Britain and Canada: exactly 15 ml; in Russia 18 ml; in Australia: four teaspoons or 20 ml.
senses.example: The recipe calls for one tablespoon of olive oil, roughly fifteen milliliters.

core.definition: A large spoon for serving or eating food, and also a standard measuring unit in US recipes equal to three teaspoons, about 15 milliliters.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress is on TAY, and 'spoon' carries secondary stress. Do not add an extra syllable; 'tablespoon' has three syllables in the stressed form, 'TAY-bul-spoon'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and practical; it belongs to cooking and everyday life.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use tablespoon constantly in cooking and recipes, usually abbreviated as 'tbsp' or 'T'. A US tablespoon is about 14.8 milliliters, slightly smaller than the metric version used in many other countries. When someone asks for a tablespoon of something, they mean the measuring unit, not necessarily the spoon.

distinctions.note: A teaspoon is one third of a tablespoon and is used for smaller amounts of seasoning or medicine.
A ladle is a deep spoon with a long handle for serving soup or sauce, and it is larger than a tablespoon.

examples.everyday: Just add a tablespoon of honey to the tea and stir it well.
examples.professional: The nutrition label lists two tablespoons as one serving.
examples.analytical: The recipe's vague use of tablespoons affects the result, since a US tablespoon differs slightly from the metric one.

nuance.analogy: A measuring spoon big enough to hold three teaspoons.
nuance.etymology: From 'table', meaning the dining table, and 'spoon'; originally a larger spoon used for serving at the table.
common_mistakes: Confusing tablespoon (tbsp) with teaspoon (tsp) in recipes.
Assuming a tablespoon has the same exact volume in every country.
Stressing the second syllable as tay-BUL-spoon.

conversation.text: Add two tablespoons of olive oil.
One tablespoon of butter is enough.
How many tablespoons of sugar does it need?

senses.definition: A maneuver, or action calculated to achieve some end.
senses.example: Her tactic of asking open questions helped the team uncover the real problem before the deadline.

senses.definition: A maneuver used against an enemy.
senses.example: The general's tactic of drawing the enemy into the valley surprised their forces at dawn.

senses.definition: A sequence of moves that limits the opponent's options and results in an immediate and tangible advantage, typically in the form of material.
senses.example: By sacrificing his knight, Marco set up a tactic that won his opponent's queen two moves later.

senses.definition: Describing a polymer whose repeat units are identical.
senses.example: Chemists prefer a tactic polymer when they need uniform stereochemistry along the chain.

senses.definition: (dated) Tactical; of or relating to the art of military and naval tactics.
senses.example: The old textbook offered a tactic analysis of cavalry charges that students memorized for examinations.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: A planned action or method used to achieve a specific goal, especially in sports, business, politics or war.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The final -ic is a short 'ik', not 'eek', and the c is silent-free, pronounced as a hard k.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It can be neutral or slightly negative when a tactic seems manipulative, as in 'delay tactics' or 'scare tactics'.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often use 'tactic' in the plural, 'tactics', for general methods, and 'tactic' for a single move. In a negative context, such as 'a stalling tactic' in a negotiation, the word suggests the method is unfair or manipulative. In a positive context, such as 'a smart tactic', it means a clever approach.

distinctions.note: Strategy is the overall plan for reaching a major goal, while a tactic is one specific method used within that plan.
Method is a general word for any way of doing something; tactic implies a deliberate move aimed at an opponent or obstacle.

examples.everyday: My kid's bedtime tactic is asking for one more glass of water, and it works every time.
examples.professional: Our team used a tactic of releasing the beta to a small group first, to reduce risk before launch.
examples.analytical: Each tactic in a debate is a local move, but its value depends on the larger argument it serves.

nuance.analogy: A tactic is a single chess move, while strategy is the plan to win the whole game.
nuance.etymology: From Greek taktikos, 'of arranging', from tassein, 'to arrange'.
common_mistakes: Using 'tactic' to mean the overall plan; use 'strategy' for that.
Using 'tactic' as a synonym for 'tact', which is a different word.

tactic.etymology: Borrowed from New Latin *tactica*, from Ancient Greek *τακτικός* (“fit for ordering”), from *τάσσω* (“to order, to arrange”).

senses.definition: One who or that which tags.
The player who tries to catch others in the game of tag.
senses.example: As the tagger, Maya had to chase down everyone at the park before the whistle blew.

senses.definition: A person who writes graffiti using a specific mark.
senses.example: Police believed the tagger had painted the same crown symbol on bridges across the city.

senses.definition: A program or algorithm that adds tags for purposes of categorization, e.g. grammatical information to words in a document, or genres to songs in a music collection.
senses.example: The tagger assigns part-of-speech labels to every word in the corpus before training the model.

senses.definition: A device for removing taglocks from sheep.
senses.example: The farmer used a tagger to snip the matted taglocks from the sheep before shearing.

senses.definition: That which is pointed like a tag.
senses.example: The tagger on the lace end had worn down, so the string would not thread through the eyelets.

senses.definition: The penis.
senses.example: The boys in the locker room snickered when Eddie bragged about his tagger.

senses.definition: Sheets of tin or other plate which run below the gauge.
senses.example: The tagger below the gauge was bent, so the plate no longer sat flush against the frame.

core.definition: A program or person that assigns labels, or tags, to data or text, such as a part-of-speech tagger in natural language processing.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, TAG. The second syllable is reduced, and the r is clearly pronounced in General American, so it ends with a soft r sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. In technical settings it is simply descriptive.
nuance.usage_note: Data scientists and engineers use tagger for software that labels text, images or events. In everyday talk, Americans also use tagger for the player who is it in the game of tag. Graffiti writers are sometimes called taggers in slang, which is an informal sense.

distinctions.note: A classifier usually assigns each item to one category from a fixed list. A tagger often labels each part of a sequence, such as each word in a sentence.
Labeler is a general term for a person or tool that adds labels. Tagger is the more common term in software and text processing.

examples.everyday: Okay, I'm the tagger this round, so everybody run!
examples.professional: The new tagger labels each support ticket by product area before it reaches the queue.
examples.analytical: A part-of-speech tagger must resolve ambiguity, deciding whether book is a noun or a verb from its context.

nuance.analogy: Like a librarian who puts a call-number sticker on every book so it can be found later.
nuance.etymology: Formed from tag with the agent suffix -er, meaning one who tags.
common_mistakes: Using tagger for any kind of classifier, when the term refers to labeling sequences or items with tags.
Confusing the noun tagger with the verb tag, as in saying tagger the data when you mean tag the data.

senses.definition: Synonym of take a seat.
senses.example: Take your seat, Richard! It's time to start class.

core.definition: To sit down in one's assigned or reserved place, such as at a meeting, in a theater, at a dinner table, or in a legislative chamber.

pronunciation.tip: Seat carries the stress, and one's reduces to a quick, weak wunz. The final t in seat is often a soft stop rather than a strong release, so don't stretch the vowel into seed.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; polite when a host, chair or usher asks people to sit down.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this when a chairperson, host or usher asks guests to find their places, such as 'Please take your seats, the meeting is starting.' In casual talk, 'take a seat' or 'have a seat' is more common. A natural response is simply to thank the person and sit down.

distinctions.note: Take a seat is the friendlier, more common invitation; take one's seat suggests a specific, assigned or formal place, like a judge or a delegate.
Sit down is simpler and casual; it describes the action without implying a designated place.

collocations: take one's seat at the table
take one's seat in the chamber
take one's seat on the board
take one's seat in the front row

examples.everyday: Dinner's ready, so please take your seat at the table.
examples.professional: The board chair asked the directors to take their seats so we could begin the quarterly review.
examples.analytical: When the new senator finally took her seat, the debate shifted from campaign promises to the responsibilities of legislative office.

nuance.analogy: Like a player walking onto the court to claim a designated position before the game starts.
nuance.etymology: Seat comes from Old Norse sæti, and sit from Old English sittan.
common_mistakes: Saying 'sit your seat' instead of 'take your seat'.
Pronouncing one's as 'won's'; it sounds like 'wunz'.

senses.definition: To happen or to occur.
senses.example: Unfortunately, the meeting never took place.

core.definition: To happen or occur, especially at a planned time and location.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on place, with a clear long a. Take is light, and the final s in place is a true s, not a z.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes an event or change without judging it.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this for scheduled events, meetings, changes and news: 'The wedding took place in June.' In casual speech people often say 'happen' or 'go down', but take place is standard in announcements, emails and news. It does not describe people's bad luck; say 'happen to' for that.

distinctions.note: Happen is casual and general, and can describe chance events; take place often suggests a planned or scheduled event.
Occur is more formal and often used for errors, symptoms or ideas that appear; take place suggests a set time or location.

examples.everyday: The fireworks take place at nine, so we should leave by eight-thirty.
examples.professional: The migration will take place over the weekend, so plan for limited access on Monday.
examples.analytical: Any real change of belief must take place within a community that already shares its language and practices.

nuance.analogy: Like a stage play: the action takes place on a set at a specific time.
nuance.etymology: Take comes from Old Norse taka; place comes from Old French place, from Latin platea, 'broad street'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'He took place at the meeting' for a person; say 'He attended the meeting'.
Using take place for things that happen by chance; say 'happen' in those cases.

take-place.etymology: A verb phrase, with *place* functioning as the direct object of the transitive verb *take*.

senses.definition: Tending to talk a lot.
senses.example: a talkative girl

senses.definition: Speaking openly and honestly, neglecting privacy and consequences.
senses.example: My talkative neighbor told the whole street about our divorce before lunch.

core.definition: Tending to talk a lot, especially in social situations, and enjoying conversation.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, TAW. The middle 't' is a flap, sounding like a soft 'd,' and the final '-ive' is 'iv' rather than 'eve.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative. It can describe a friendly person, but it may also suggest someone who talks too much.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use talkative to describe people who enjoy chatting, such as a cab driver or a neighbor. It can be positive, but if someone is interrupting others, it sounds like a criticism. For a warmer compliment, people often say 'chatty' or 'friendly.'

distinctions.note: Chatty is more informal and usually friendly, while talkative can be neutral or mildly critical.
Verbose is formal and refers to using too many words, while talkative describes a general tendency to talk.
Outspoken means frank and open about opinions, not necessarily talking a lot.

examples.everyday: Our taxi driver was so talkative that I almost missed my stop.
examples.professional: The talkative team lead tends to dominate our meetings, so we now set a time limit for each speaker.
examples.analytical: The essay describes the talkative narrator as a figure whose speech reveals more than he intends.

nuance.analogy: A talkative person is like a radio that never switches off: pleasant when the station is good, exhausting when it isn't.
nuance.etymology: Formed from talk and the suffix -ative, which forms adjectives meaning inclined to.
common_mistakes: Using talkative to mean articulate or eloquent; talkative describes quantity of speech, not quality.
Shifting the stress to the second syllable, as in tuh-KAY-tiv.
Using it as an adverb, as in 'she spoke talkative' instead of 'she was talkative.'

senses.definition: Camaraderie; willingness to co-operate with others.
senses.example: The coach praised the players for their team spirit after the tough loss.

core.definition: The feeling of loyalty and cooperation among members of a group working toward a shared goal.

pronunciation.tip: Stress 'team' most strongly and 'spirit' a bit less. The last syllable is a short 'it', not 'uht', and the r in 'spir' is clearly American.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It describes admirable loyalty and cooperation, though it can sound like a pep talk when used in a workplace.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use team spirit mostly in sports, schools and workplaces, often when praising a group's attitude or a boss's motivational effort. People say 'We need more team spirit' or 'The whole office had great team spirit this year.' It is informal and friendly, and it sounds a little old-fashioned or cheerleader-like in serious business writing.

distinctions.note: Team spirit describes loyalty and willingness to cooperate; morale describes the group's general confidence and mood.
Esprit de corps is a more formal, often military phrase for pride in a shared group identity; team spirit is everyday.

examples.everyday: Wear your jersey tomorrow, that's the team spirit we need for the playoffs.
examples.professional: The offsite was designed to build team spirit between the engineering and product groups.
examples.analytical: Durkheim's idea of solidarity helps explain how team spirit binds members beyond their individual interests.

nuance.analogy: Team spirit is like the warmth in a crowded room on a cold night: it comes from everyone sharing the same space and purpose.
nuance.etymology: Team (from Old English tēam) plus spirit, from Latin spiritus, meaning breath or spirit.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the last syllable as 'spear-ut' instead of a short 'SPIR-it'.
Using 'team spirit' for one person's enthusiasm; the phrase describes a group's attitude.

senses.definition: Boredom or tediousness; ennui.
senses.example: The tedium of the three-hour meeting was broken only by the occasional joke from the manager.

core.definition: The state of being bored by something long, repetitive, or dull; boredom caused by routine.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and make the final syllable a reduced 'um', not 'ee-yum'. The flapped or quick middle vowel should be short.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It names the unpleasant boredom of routine, often in the phrase 'the tedium of'.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use tedium in writing, speeches, and thoughtful conversation, usually with 'the tedium of' followed by an activity, such as 'the tedium of daily commuting.' In casual talk, people say 'boring' or 'the grind.' Tedium is uncountable and does not take 'a' or a plural.

distinctions.note: Boredom is the general everyday feeling; tedium refers specifically to the wearying dullness of a routine task or situation.
Monotony stresses sameness and lack of variety; tedium stresses the tiring, time-consuming quality of the work.

examples.everyday: After three hours on the highway, the tedium of the drive was getting to me.
examples.professional: Automating the weekly reports will remove much of the tedium from our team's workflow.
examples.analytical: Pascal saw in the tedium of ordinary diversion a sign of humanity's restless avoidance of itself.

nuance.analogy: Tedium is like a clock ticking in an empty room: nothing happens, yet every second is felt.
nuance.etymology: From Latin taedium, 'weariness, disgust', via French ennui-like usage in English.
common_mistakes: Using 'a tedium' or pluralizing it, since it is an uncountable noun.
Confusing tedium with the adjective tedious when a noun is required, as in 'the tedious of the work'.

senses.definition: A legal action intended to set a precedent.
senses.example: The lawsuit was filed as a test case to challenge the city's new zoning law.

senses.definition: Any of a set of conditions and variables used to test an application.
senses.example: QA engineers wrote a test case for every login scenario before releasing the mobile app.

core.definition: In software engineering, a set of inputs, conditions and expected results used to check whether a program works correctly.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on test, the first word, as with most American compound nouns. Case gets a lighter secondary stress and ends in a clear s sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and precise. In legal contexts it has a different and more formal meaning.
nuance.usage_note: Software teams use test case constantly: a tester writes one, and a developer adds it to the test suite. In law, a test case is a lawsuit brought to set a precedent, so say in our code or in court to be clear. For an exam question, Americans say test question or simply question.

distinctions.note: A test suite is a collection of test cases run together. A test case is one individual check.
A test plan describes the overall strategy and scope of testing. A test case is one specific check within that plan.

examples.everyday: I'm still fixing one test case that keeps failing.
examples.professional: I added a test case for the empty-input bug, so it won't come back.
examples.analytical: A good test case specifies the input, the expected output and the conditions under which the test is valid.

nuance.analogy: Like a single lab measurement: one controlled check that tells you whether one specific part behaves correctly.
nuance.etymology: Combines test, from Latin testum, earthen pot, and case, from Latin casus, occurrence.
common_mistakes: Writing it as one word, testcase, which is less standard in most American technical writing.
Using test case for a school exam question. Americans say test question or question.

senses.definition: Generating images from a text description.
senses.example: The team tested a text-to-image model that turned our product descriptions into catalog photos.

core.definition: Generating an image from a written description, usually by an AI model.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on IM in image. The word to is weak and sounds like 'tuh' in speech, not 'too'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. In public debate it can sound loaded, because of arguments about artists' copyright.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it as a compound adjective ('a text-to-image model') and sometimes as a noun ('text-to-image is improving quickly'). It is common in AI news and product descriptions, with tools such as DALL·E and Midjourney. Keep the hyphens in writing.

distinctions.note: Reverses the direction: it describes a picture in words, as in automatic captioning.
Produces moving images rather than a single still picture.

examples.everyday: My daughter used a text-to-image app to draw a dragon for her school project.
examples.professional: We're evaluating two text-to-image models to produce concept art for the marketing team.
examples.analytical: Text-to-image systems learn associations between captions and pixels, so their outputs inherit the biases present in their training data.

nuance.analogy: It is like handing a sketch artist a written description and getting a finished picture back.
nuance.etymology: A modern compound coined in AI research from the English words text, image and to.
common_mistakes: Dropping the hyphens in writing, as in 'text to image model'.
Confusing it with image recognition, which goes from picture to label.

conversation.text: A text-to-image model turns a written prompt into a picture.
Text-to-image prompts often need details about lighting, style, and composition.
Text-to-image models raise questions about artists' styles and the images used in training.

senses.definition: The ruler of a theocracy, a priest-king.
A proponent of theocracy.

core.definition: A ruler of a theocracy, usually a religious leader who holds political power; also a supporter of rule by religious authority.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, THEE, and the vowels in theo are two distinct syllables. The final syllable rhymes with cat.

nuance.connotation: Often negative in political discussion, implying that religious authority overrides civil freedom; neutral in theology or history.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use theocrat mostly in political commentary, history and religious studies, especially to describe leaders who rule in God's name. It is rarely used in casual talk. The adjective theocratic is more common, as in 'a theocratic regime.' Calling someone a theocrat is a strong accusation.

distinctions.note: A priest serves a religious community, while a theocrat holds political power over a state in the name of religion.
An autocrat holds absolute power of any kind, while a theocrat specifically rules in God's name or by religious law.

examples.everyday: My neighbor says the new leader is basically a theocrat who wants religious law in every courtroom.
examples.professional: Our policy memo describes the regime as theocratic, since its supreme cleric overrides the elected government on key decisions.
examples.analytical: Hobbes's sovereign is not a theocrat, because sacred authority remains subordinate to the civil power.

nuance.analogy: Like a referee who is also the team captain, a theocrat holds both religious and political authority over the same game.
nuance.etymology: From Greek theos 'god' and kratos 'rule', with the suffix -crat.
common_mistakes: Confusing theocrat with theologian, which refers to a scholar of God, not a ruler.
Stressing the last syllable, saying theo-KRAT, instead of THEE-oh-krat.

senses.definition: Of or relating to theory; abstract; not empirical.
senses.example: The physicist spent weeks on theoretical models before the lab could test any of them.

core.definition: Based on theory or ideas rather than practice or observation, so not yet tested or applied in real situations.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on RET, the third syllable. Keep the r rhotic and the middle vowel short, and do not add an extra syllable at the end.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It can describe a sound idea, but in casual speech it may suggest the idea is impractical or has not been tested.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use theoretical in science, business, philosophy and everyday discussions about possibilities. In everyday talk, people might say that's theoretical, meaning it works on paper but may not in practice. It is common and not formal, though it can sound slightly academic when used for abstract arguments.

distinctions.note: Hypothetical describes something assumed for discussion, while theoretical describes a system of ideas or principles that may or may not be tested.
Empirical means based on observation or experiment, which is the opposite of theoretical in many scientific contexts.

examples.everyday: That plan sounds good in theory, but I'm not sure it would work in real life.
examples.professional: We have a theoretical model for churn, but we need to test it against last quarter's customer data before the launch.
examples.analytical: The author's theoretical framework separates explanation from justification, though the empirical evidence does not clearly support this distinction.

nuance.analogy: A theoretical idea is like a map drawn before the trip: it shows the route clearly, but the ground may not match it until you walk it.
nuance.etymology: From theory, from Greek theōria 'contemplation, speculation,' from theōros 'spectator.'
common_mistakes: Saying 'in theoretically' instead of 'in theory' or 'theoretically speaking.'
Stressing the wrong syllable as 'thee-uh-REH-tih-kul' rather than thee-uh-RET-ih-kul.

theoretical.etymology: From Middle English *theorothycall*, probably from Latin *theōrēticus* + *-al*,

senses.definition: Of, related to, or associated with heat; thermal.

core.definition: Relating to heat; having to do with heat or temperature. It means the same as thermal but is rare in American usage.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, 'THUR'. The final syllable has a short 'ik' sound, with no long vowel. Learners often pronounce the 'th' as a 't', which changes the word's sound entirely.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It sounds dated or specialized to most Americans.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use 'thermic' in everyday speech or in modern technical writing. They prefer 'thermal' in almost every context. You may see 'thermic' in older texts or in some specialized fields, but it is not the normal choice for most speakers.

distinctions.note: 'Thermal' is the standard American word with the same meaning and is far more common. 'Thermic' is rare and sounds specialized.
'Thermodynamic' refers to the principles of energy and heat in physical systems, while 'thermic' simply means related to heat.

examples.professional: The thermic output of the reactor is measured hourly, so the reading should be checked against the standard.
examples.analytical: The author's thermic theory of the early universe relies on assumptions that later physicists found untenable.

nuance.analogy: 'Thermic' is like an old-fashioned word for a common object, such as a 'horseless carriage' for a car; it means the same thing but sounds dated.
nuance.etymology: From Greek thermē, meaning heat, with the adjective suffix -ic.
common_mistakes: Using 'thermic' when 'thermal' is the normal American word.
Pronouncing the 'th' as a 't'.
Stressing the second syllable instead of the first.

senses.definition: A form of magic designed to allow for worship or conjuration of, or communication with spirits or deities.
senses.example: The medieval mage claimed theurgy could summon the gods' presence through carefully timed rituals.

senses.definition: A supernatural intervention in human affairs.
senses.example: Many worshippers in the village saw the sudden recovery as theurgy, not medicine.

core.definition: Ritual practice, in some ancient and Neoplatonic traditions, aimed at uniting the worshipper with divine powers or summoning spirits.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The "eu" is pronounced as "ee-er," and the final "gy" is a soft "j" sound, as in "jee." Do not pronounce the "g" as hard, as in "get."

nuance.connotation: Neutral in scholarly use, but it can sound occult or exotic to nonexperts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use "theurgy" almost only in academic study of religion, classics, philosophy, and history of magic. It is not a common word in ordinary conversation. Speakers often explain it when they use it, since it is closer to a specialist term than to everyday English.

distinctions.note: Theology is the systematic study of God and faith, while theurgy is a practice intended to act on or unite with the divine.
Magic is a broad term, while theurgy specifically refers to a religious ritual approach within certain philosophical traditions.

examples.everyday: I'm reading a book on ancient magic, and the author keeps talking about theurgy, which I think means something like religious ritual.
examples.professional: The seminar paper compares theurgy in Iamblichus with the sacramental language used in later Christian liturgy.
examples.analytical: Iamblichus defends theurgy against Porphyry by arguing that the gods themselves, not human intellect alone, must initiate the soul's ascent.

nuance.analogy: If theology is the map of the divine, theurgy is an attempt to walk the road itself by ritual.
nuance.etymology: From Greek theourgia, 'god-working,' from theos 'god' and ergon 'work.'
common_mistakes: Confusing theurgy with theology, which is the study of God.
Pronouncing the "g" as a hard sound, as in "thur-gee."
Using "theurgy" as a synonym for any kind of magic.

theurgy.etymology: From Late Latin *theūrgia*, from Ancient Greek *θεουργίᾱ* (“sorcery”), from *θεός* (“god”) + *ἔργον* (“work”).

senses.definition: When one is in the middle of a process, activity, or conversation, to adjust rapidly, effectively, and intelligently to new developments or changing circumstances.
senses.example: When the client changed the requirements mid-meeting, Maria had to think on her feet.

core.definition: To respond quickly and skillfully to unexpected questions or changing situations without advance preparation.

pronunciation.tip: The strongest stress falls on FEET, and on and one's are reduced. Say 'wunz' with a short u, and do not give on a full vowel.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises quick, capable thinking under pressure.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this idiom to praise someone who handles surprises well, such as in meetings, presentations, interviews, or customer calls. The usual forms are 'She's great at thinking on her feet' or 'He had to think on his feet'. Do not use it to describe careful planning, which is the opposite.

distinctions.note: Improvise can refer to creative invention in music or theater, while think on your feet focuses on solving practical problems quickly.
Wing it is informal and suggests doing something without preparation, sometimes carelessly, while think on your feet describes skillful adaptation.
Ad lib means speaking or performing without a script, so it is narrower than think on your feet.

collocations: good at thinking on your feet
had to think on her feet
think on his feet in a meeting

examples.everyday: My sister always knows what to say at parties, because she can think on her feet.
examples.professional: When the client changed the requirements mid-call, Maria thought on her feet and proposed a phased plan.
examples.analytical: Good scientists must think on their feet when experiments fail in unexpected ways, adjusting hypotheses without losing rigor.

nuance.analogy: Like a goalie who reacts to a shot before it is fully aimed.
nuance.etymology: An idiom combining think with on one's feet, meaning standing up and active; the exact origin is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Saying 'think in your feet' or 'think with your feet' instead of 'think on your feet'.
Using it for careful planning rather than quick adaptation.

senses.definition: The ordinal form of the cardinal number three; Coming after the second.
senses.example: The third tree from the left is my favorite.

senses.definition: The person or thing in the third position.
senses.example: Jones came in third.

senses.definition: One of three equal parts of a whole.
senses.example: He ate a third of the pie. Divided by two-thirds.

senses.definition: Ellipsis of third gear (of a gearbox).
senses.example: Now put it into third.

senses.definition: A handicap of one stroke every third hole.
senses.example: Ray plays with a third, so he gets one stroke every third hole all afternoon.

senses.definition: A third-class degree, awarded to the lowest achievers in an honors degree program.
senses.example: She graduated with a third from the honors program, which disappointed her badly.

senses.definition: An interval consisting of the first and third notes in a scale.
senses.example: They sing in thirds.

senses.definition: Third base.
senses.example: The play ended with Jones standing on third.

senses.definition: To agree with a proposition or statement after it has already been seconded.
senses.example: Once the motion was seconded, Maria thirded it, and the vote proceeded.

senses.definition: To divide into three equal parts.
senses.example: Let's third the inheritance so each of the three sisters gets an equal share.

core.definition: Coming after the second in position, order, or rank; the ordinal form of the number three.

pronunciation.tip: The vowel is the r-colored 'ur' sound, and the word ends in a clear d. Do not say 'tird' or add a vowel after the d.

nuance.connotation: Neutral.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'third' every day for floors, grades, and order, such as 'third floor' or 'third grade'. Note that in the US the first floor is the ground floor, so the third floor is two floors above ground. Be careful with 'third' as a verb in meetings: it means agreeing with a motion that has already been seconded, which is a parliamentary term.

distinctions.note: 'Tertiary' is a more technical word meaning third in a sequence of levels, such as tertiary education, while 'third' is the everyday ordinal.
'Three' is the cardinal number, used for counting, while 'third' is the ordinal, used for position.

examples.everyday: We live on the third floor, so the elevator is worth it after the groceries.
examples.professional: We will review the results in the third quarter, once the pilot data is complete.
examples.analytical: In the third chapter the author shifts from description to argument, which changes the whole reading.

nuance.analogy: Like a relay runner who takes the baton after the second leg, 'third' names the position that follows the first two.
nuance.etymology: From Old English thridda, related to 'three', with the ordinal suffix '-d' added.
common_mistakes: Saying 'the three floor' instead of 'the third floor' for ordinal position.
Pronouncing it with a vowel after the r, such as 'thur-id'; keep it as one syllable.
nuance.biblical_note: In Scripture, 'third' often marks a completed or decisive stage, most importantly the third day in the resurrection narrative. The Greek word behind it is 'tritos' (third, a third). In 1 Corinthians 15:4 the RSV says Christ was raised on the third day in accordance with the scriptures. Luke 24:46 and Matthew 16:21 describe the same timing as part of Jesus's teaching about his death and resurrection. In 2 Corinthians 12:2 Paul speaks of being caught up to the third heaven.

third.etymology: From Middle English *thirde*, *thridde*, from Old English *þridda*, from Proto-Germanic **þridjô*, from Pre-Germanic, a remodeling of Proto-Indo-European **tr̥tyós*.

senses.definition: How you say your name on the phone: "Hi, this is Maria."

core.definition: The phrase used on the phone to introduce yourself by name.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on THIS, and 'is' is weakly pronounced as 'iz' with a short vowel. Don't say 'this-iss'; the 's' of 'this' links into 'iz' smoothly.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and polite. It is the standard, friendly way to identify yourself on a call.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'Hi, this is Maria' or 'This is John speaking' when they call someone or answer a call from a colleague. In formal business calls people often add their company, as in 'This is Maria from Acme.' A natural reply from the other person is 'Hi Maria, how are you?'

distinctions.note: 'This is' is the normal phone introduction; saying 'I am Maria' on the phone sounds unnatural.
'Speaking' is used when asked for a person, as in 'Is this Maria? Speaking.'

collocations: Hi, this is John from accounts
Is this Maria? Yes, this is

examples.everyday: Hi, this is Maria, I'm calling about the apartment listing.
examples.professional: Hi, this is Maria from the data team, returning your call about the quarterly report.
examples.analytical: In a phone call, the phrase 'this is' establishes identity before any content is exchanged, which shapes how the conversation begins.

nuance.analogy: Like putting your name tag on before you walk into a room, so people know who you are right away.
nuance.etymology: Combines the demonstrative 'this' (Old English thes) with the verb 'is' (Old English is), used to identify a speaker.
common_mistakes: Saying 'I am Maria' or 'My name is Maria' on the phone, which sounds stiff; 'This is Maria' is the natural form.
Saying 'This is speaking' instead of 'This is Maria speaking' or 'Speaking' by itself when asked for the person.

conversation.text: Hi, this is Rachel from Dr. Kim's office.
"Is this Paul?" "Yes, this is Paul. Who's this?"
This is Mark returning your call from this morning.

senses.definition: Having or made of tiers.
senses.example: a tiered wedding cake

senses.definition: Having or made of a certain number of tiers.
senses.example: two-tiered justice system

core.definition: Arranged in layers or levels, one above another, often ranked by price or rank.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable: 'teer' with a voiced d at the end. Do not turn the vowel into a long 'ee' as in 'tear' or 'tier-ed.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral, describing structure or levels.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use tiered for pricing plans, seating, wedding cakes, school systems and software architecture. Tiered pricing means different price levels for different customers. The word describes separate levels rather than a smooth slope.

distinctions.note: Layered can describe any stacking, while tiered suggests distinct levels, often ranked by price or authority.
Stepped suggests a stair-like shape, while tiered suggests a set of separate levels.

examples.everyday: We ordered a tiered cake for her birthday party.
examples.professional: Our cloud plan uses tiered pricing, so heavy users pay more per gigabyte.
examples.analytical: A tiered model of authority describes power as distributed across several overlapping levels.

nuance.analogy: A tiered cake is like a stack of smaller cakes, each sitting neatly on the one below.
nuance.etymology: From tier, from Middle English tire, a row, plus -ed.
common_mistakes: Saying 'tear-ed' instead of 'teerd.'
Using tiered to mean many; it means arranged in distinct levels.

senses.definition: The acrobatic feat of walking on a tightrope.

core.definition: The acrobatic skill of walking along a thin rope or wire high above the ground.

pronunciation.tip: Primary stress falls on WAW in walking, with light stress on TYTE. The vowel in walk is the cot-caught sound, like 'saw', not 'wok'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it refers to a demanding and admired skill.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use tightrope walking for the circus skill and, figuratively, for the difficult act of balancing risks, as in 'Managing this merger is tightrope walking.' When used figuratively, it often sounds slightly negative because it implies danger of failure.

distinctions.note: Balancing act is a common figurative phrase for managing competing needs; tightrope walking often adds a stronger sense of danger.
Walking is general movement on foot; tightrope walking names the specialized, dangerous skill on a rope.

examples.everyday: My uncle took tightrope walking classes as a hobby, and now he can cross the backyard on a rope.
examples.professional: Negotiating with two departments at once feels like tightrope walking, but the budget depends on it.
examples.analytical: Tightrope walking is a useful metaphor for ethical judgment, because the balance must be kept without a fixed foothold.

nuance.analogy: Like a skater who must stay upright on a single blade of steel.
nuance.etymology: Tightrope from tight plus rope; walking from walk, from Old English wealcan, to roll, then to move on foot.
common_mistakes: Misplacing the stress, saying 'tight-ROPE-walking' with equal emphasis
Using the vowel of 'wok' in walk; American English uses the 'saw' vowel
Writing it as two words in American spelling

senses.definition: To call for a suspension of activity or conversation.
senses.example: Time out! Let's stop for a minute so I can check the map.

senses.definition: Used to announce the end of time in and the beginning of time out.
senses.example: Time out, everyone, we're leaving character for the lunch break now.

senses.definition: To call for a time-out.
senses.example: Let's time out for a minute so the coach can explain the new play.

senses.definition: The period of a live action roleplaying event when players are out of character.
senses.example: During time out, the players drop their characters and talk about the plot openly.

senses.definition: The point at which such a period begins.
senses.example: The marshal announced the start of time out, and the actors began laughing and stretching.

senses.definition: To end (an incomplete task) after a time limit.
senses.example: The software will time out the login session after ten minutes of inactivity.

senses.definition: Of a task, to be terminated because it was not completed before a time limit.
senses.example: The download timed out because your Internet connection was disrupted.

senses.definition: To record the end of one's day or shift at work.
senses.example: I always time out at five o'clock, even when the project is almost done.

senses.definition: To declare (the batsman) out for having taken longer than two minutes to appear on the field.
senses.example: The umpire timed the batsman out after he took three minutes to reach the crease.

core.definition: A short break from an activity, or a penalty that removes someone from play for a short period.

pronunciation.tip: As a noun, time out has main stress on time, unlike the verb, which stresses out. The final syllable has the 'ow' diphthong of 'house.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral. In parenting it can sound like a mild punishment, while in sports or everyday talk it is a neutral pause.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use time-out as a noun in sports, for children's discipline, and in ordinary speech for a short break. In sports the spelling is often one word, timeout, while parents usually write time-out. A natural reply is 'Sure, let's take a break.'

distinctions.note: Break is a neutral word for any pause; time-out often suggests stopping an activity on purpose, as in sports or discipline.
Intermission is a formal term for a pause in a show or performance, while time-out is more informal and everyday.

examples.everyday: Let's take a time-out so we can grab some coffee before the movie starts.
examples.professional: I'm calling a time-out on the rollout until the security review is finished.
examples.analytical: A time-out in a moral debate can help participants cool down, yet it can also let an urgent question slip away unanswered.

nuance.analogy: A time-out is like pressing pause on a video game: everything stops, and the game resumes exactly where it was left.
nuance.etymology: From time, from Old English tīma, and out, from Old English ūt, meaning away or outside.
common_mistakes: Stressing out in the noun form, as in 'time OUT'; the noun stresses time.
Using time out as a verb meaning to end a task, which is a different sense from the noun meaning a pause.

senses.definition: A policy of formally complying with efforts to achieve a goal by making small, token gestures; especially to hire a minimal number of ethnically diverse or disadvantaged people.
senses.example: Critics say the company's diversity hiring amounts to tokenism rather than real change.

core.definition: The practice of making small, symbolic gestures, such as hiring a few minority candidates, to appear to meet a goal without real change.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on TOH, and the second syllable is a weak schwa. The final -ism is pronounced 'iz-um', with the last syllable reduced to a weak 'um'.

nuance.connotation: Strongly negative. Calling something tokenism accuses a person or organization of insincerity.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use tokenism in discussions of diversity, hiring, corporate pledges and politics. Accusing a company or colleague of tokenism is a serious charge, so use it carefully and with evidence. In casual conversation people often say it's just for show or box-checking.

distinctions.note: Symbolism is any meaningful gesture, while tokenism is a gesture used to avoid real change.
Affirmative action is a formal policy aimed at equal opportunity; tokenism is a superficial imitation of such efforts.
Diversity is the presence of different people and views; tokenism is a shallow way of appearing to include them.

examples.everyday: My friend thinks the company's new diversity ad is pure tokenism.
examples.professional: Putting one junior designer on the hiring panel is tokenism unless we also change who gets promoted.
examples.analytical: Critics argue that symbolic representation without structural change is tokenism rather than genuine inclusion.

nuance.analogy: Like paying with a plastic token instead of real money: it looks like a payment, but it does not carry real value.
nuance.etymology: From token, from Old English tācen, sign or symbol, plus the suffix -ism.
common_mistakes: Using tokenism to describe any symbolic act; the word implies insincerity or a failure to change.
Stressing the wrong syllable, as in 'toh-KEN-ism'.
Confusing token, the noun for a symbol or coin, with the adjective tokenistic.

senses.definition: A set of tools kept together, especially comprising all the tools suitable for some particular type of work.
A set of personal abilities, skills, or resources to draw on.
senses.example: a financial planning toolkit for small businesses

senses.definition: A set of software tools or components.

core.definition: A set of tools kept together for a type of work. In technical settings, a collection of software tools or resources for a particular job.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first word, TOOL. Say it as one compound word, with the second syllable 'kit' short and clear.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive, suggesting readiness and capability.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'toolkit' for physical sets of tools (a mechanic's toolkit) and, in business and tech, for a set of skills, methods, or resources (the analyst's toolkit). A 'toolbox' is usually the physical box that holds the tools. A natural reply to 'Do you have a toolkit?' is 'Yes, it's in the trunk.'

distinctions.note: 'Toolbox' is usually the physical box for tools, while 'toolkit' can also mean a set of skills, methods, or software.
'Kit' is any set of items for a purpose, while 'toolkit' is specifically about tools or methods.

examples.everyday: My dad keeps a basic toolkit in the trunk in case we get a flat tire.
examples.professional: The team released an open-source toolkit for model evaluation, so other groups can reuse our metrics.
examples.analytical: Good judgment is part of the analyst's toolkit, not just the statistical methods she knows.

nuance.analogy: A toolkit is like a chef's knife roll: each tool is for a specific job, and together they cover the whole kitchen.
nuance.etymology: Compound of 'tool' and 'kit', the latter from Middle English meaning a container or set of equipment.
common_mistakes: Using 'toolkit' for a physical box; in ordinary American talk, 'toolbox' is more common for the box.
Pronouncing the stress on the second syllable; American speech stresses 'TOOL'.

senses.definition: A settlement; an area with residential districts, shops and amenities, and its own local government; especially one larger than a village and smaller than a city, historically enclosed by a fence or walls, with total populations ranging from several hundred to more than a hundred thousand (as of the early 21st century)
senses.example: This town is really dangerous because these youngsters have Beretta handguns.

senses.definition: Any more urbanized center than the place of reference.
senses.example: I'll be in Yonkers, then I'm driving into town to see the Knicks at the Garden tonight.

senses.definition: The residents (as opposed to gown: the students, faculty, etc.) of a community which is the site of a university.
senses.example: The town residents complained about students' noise near the campus.

senses.definition: Used to refer to a town or similar entity under discussion.
senses.example: Call me when you get to town.

senses.definition: A major city, especially one where the speaker is located.
senses.example: Everyone in town is headed to the stadium for tonight's game.

senses.definition: A townhouse.
senses.example: Their new town has three floors, a small garage, and a shared courtyard.

senses.definition: A municipal organization, such as a corporation, defined by the laws of the entity of which it is a part.
senses.example: The town council voted to approve the new budget for road repairs.

senses.definition: An interconnected maze of tunnels in which prairie dogs live.
senses.example: Prairie dogs dug an extensive town beneath the grassland near our ranch.

core.definition: A community larger than a village and smaller than a city, with its own residential areas, shops and local government.

pronunciation.tip: The vowel is the 'ow' of 'down', not the 'oh' of 'tone'. Keep the final n crisp and do not add a vowel after it.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; can sound warm and community-minded or small-scale, depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use town for a small-to-mid-sized community, often the place where you live, which may have its own mayor or town council. Saying 'I'm going into town' usually means heading to the nearby commercial center. In New England and some other states, towns are also the basic unit of local government, so a town can be a legal entity even without a dense center. Use 'city' when a place is clearly large.

distinctions.note: A city is generally larger and has a formal charter, and the line is set by state law, so a place of similar size may be a city in one state and a town in another.
A village is usually smaller than a town and, in many states, a less formal or lower-level municipality, sometimes within a town.
A county is a larger administrative division that contains many towns and cities.

examples.everyday: We moved to a quiet town about an hour north of Denver, and I love the small-town feel.
examples.professional: Our team is piloting the new scheduling tool in three towns before rolling it out statewide.
examples.analytical: The historian argues that the New England town, with its shared commons and elected selectmen, shaped American ideas of local self-government.

nuance.analogy: A town is like a neighborhood that has grown its own government and main street.
nuance.etymology: From Old English tūn, meaning an enclosure or farmstead.
common_mistakes: Using 'town' for a large metropolis; Americans say 'city' for places like Chicago or Houston.
Saying 'to the town' when you mean the central business area of a big city; say 'downtown' instead.

senses.definition: Capable of being easily led, taught, or managed.
senses.example: The toddler proved surprisingly tractable, happily following her parents' instructions at bedtime.

senses.definition: Easy to deal with or manage.
Capable of being shaped; malleable.
senses.example: The softened clay was tractable enough to shape into delicate bowls.

senses.definition: Sufficiently operationalizable or useful to allow a mathematical calculation to proceed toward a solution.
senses.example: We simplified the nonlinear model so that the differential equations became tractable.

senses.definition: Algorithmically solvable fast enough to be practically relevant, typically in polynomial time.
senses.example: The shortest path problem is tractable, since Dijkstra's algorithm solves it in polynomial time.

core.definition: Easy to manage, control, or work with, especially a problem that can be solved or a person who is willing to cooperate.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The 'able' ending is reduced to 'uh-bul', and the 'ct' cluster is pronounced clearly, not as 'tra-tuh-bull' with the T dropped.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It describes something manageable or cooperative, usually praised in technical or formal contexts.
nuance.usage_note: In American professional and academic writing, 'tractable' often describes problems in mathematics, computing, or policy that can be solved with available methods. In everyday speech, people prefer 'manageable' or 'easy to work with'. In a computing context, 'computationally tractable' means solvable within reasonable time.

distinctions.note: Manageable is everyday and general, while tractable is more formal and often implies that a problem can be solved with a method.
Docile describes a naturally submissive temperament, whereas tractable describes a willingness to be guided or a problem that yields to treatment.

examples.everyday: My landlord was surprisingly tractable about the repair, so we agreed on a date quickly.
examples.professional: We reframed the forecasting problem so that it becomes tractable with the data we already have.
examples.analytical: Whether moral disagreements are tractable depends on whether the parties share a common account of the good.

nuance.analogy: A tractable problem is like a knotted rope that loosens when you pull it in the right direction: difficult, but it responds to the right method.
nuance.etymology: From Latin tractabilis, from tractare 'to handle', from trahere 'to draw'.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'tractable' with 'traceable', which means able to be followed or found.
Saying 'tractable' to mean 'attractive' or 'pleasant'.

tractable.etymology: From Middle English *tractable*, *tractabel*, from Latin *tractābilis* (“that may be touched, handled, or managed”), from *tractō* (“take in hand, handle, manage”), frequentative of *trahō* (“draw”).

senses.definition: A dazed or unconscious condition.
senses.example: After the car crash, she stayed in a trance, staring blankly at the shattered windshield.

senses.definition: A state of awareness, concentration, or focus that filters experience and information (for example, a state of meditation or possession by some being).
senses.example: The monk fell into a deep trance during the long evening chant.
